TI Educator workload and psychosocial well-being in South African secondary
   schools: a qualitative study in Limpopo Province
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE learners; policy reform; psychosocial factors; psychosocial support;
   teacher responsibilities
ID INTERVENTION
AB Psychosocial challenges in schools are becoming a challenge that is experienced in different parts of the world. This might be due to pressure and expectations of schools. This article is based on a study that focused on psychosocial challenges faced by secondary school educators in Mankweng Circuit, South Africa. While recent studies emphasise overcrowding, violence and learners' poor performance as key stressors, administrative duties, lack of support, conflicted relationships and lack of recognition are equally significant, yet these remain absent from current policy responses. The study aimed to explore psychosocial challenges with the intention of developing a framework that is responsive to the rural context. A qualitative methodological approach was adopted using a case study design. 11 educators were interviewed, and document frameworks and policies were analysed to compare the findings. Common themes were found and developed using thematic analysis. The study reveals that a lack of institutional support, educators' workload and systemic barriers not only increase existing challenges but also actively transform perceived challenges into continuous psychosocial challenges, thereby making educators burnout highly likely under current school settings. Therefore, the study recommends that digital integration be explored as a potential supporting strategy, alongside adequate rural infrastructure, training and institutional support, for improving resource efficiency and easing workload, overcrowding and violence. Through the provision of rural infrastructure and digital literacy workshops, centralised data management, digital assessment systems, and automated reporting, the use of digital tools and online platforms can help to minimise, adequately resourced and supported, administrative tasks. The Department of Basic Education may directly address workload-induced burnout by giving educators the psychosocial support and tools they need to use technology for administrative effectiveness, innovative education, and learner engagement. In order to enable future advanced digital educational systems in schools, future research should concentrate on educators' support programmes using grounded theories.
C1 [Mpyana, Nkoata B.; Mabasa, Layane T.; Macaskill, Katlego; Buthelezi, Michael M.] Univ Limpopo, Dept Educ Studies, Sovenga, South Africa.

TI Exploring basic school leaders' AI readiness: The role of professional
   development
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; School leadership; Professional development; AI
   readiness; Educational technology; Technology adoption; Secondary
   education
ID TECHNOLOGY; TEACHERS
AB The UNESCO declaration that teachers should be AI-competent by 2030 poses a challenge for basic school leaders, who should be at the forefront of integration within the school system. This study explored the perceptions of basic school leaders regarding AI readiness in selected Nigerian schools and the role of professional development in preparing school leaders for the effective adoption of AI in their daily instructional and administrative roles. A generic qualitative design was employed to explore school leaders' perceptions and readiness for integrating AI into daily activities. Purposive and snowball sampling techniques were used to select participants. A thematic approach was implemented to analyse the data obtained using the Atlas. ti software. The results showed that although the participants were generally aware of AI and had positive attitudes toward it, their understanding was mostly shallow and focused primarily on functional digital tools. Most leaders learned on their own through the internet without formal training. Some of the biggest challenges to being ready included a lack of infrastructure, unreliable electricity, high data costs, and insufficient institutional support. Despite these limitations, participants were eager to learn about and utilise AI innovations. The study finds that professional development is the most crucial aspect that Nigerian school leaders need to prepare for in the context of AI. This research contributes to the field of educational leadership by demonstrating that structured, context-specific professional development, supportive infrastructure, and policy frameworks are necessary to ensure the fair and effective integration of AI in basic education.

TI Implementing emerging 3D printing technologies into pharmaceutical
   sciences education: Pedagogical strategies and learning outcomes
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE 3D printing; Semi-solid extrusion; Pharmaceutical education; Process
   optimization; Mathematical modeling
ID RHEOLOGY; LINKING
AB Introduction: Semi-solid extrusion 3D Printing (SSE-3DP) has emerged as a promising technology to support pharmaceutical compounding, but its implementation in pharmacy education demands specific pedagogical strategies. Beyond introducing a new tool, educators must help students navigate complex formulation-process-performance relationships, fostering technological literacy, problem-solving and critical thinking. Aim: This study aimed to design, implement and evaluate a structured pedagogical strategy to integrate SSE-3DP into the Integrated Master's in Pharmaceutical Sciences, using active-learning methodologies. A flipped classroom approach and laboratory activities supported this implementation, while mathematical equations were introduced to deconstruct the complexity of process optimization and simplify the learning experience. Methods: A flipped classroom engaged students with pre-class materials on SSE-3DP principles, followed by problem-based laboratory sessions combining guided discussion with hands-on activities in formulation preparation, process optimization and design of printed dosage forms. Multiple Linear Regression models for extrudability and filament deposition were introduced to teach core optimization strategies. Learning outcomes and self-reported gains were assessed postclass. Results: The activity showed positive outcomes. Evidence from classroom implementation demonstrated that the introduction of mathematical models allowed students to virtually explore formulation-process-performance relationships, supporting the learning experience. Students reported high engagement and strong appreciation for the activity, recommending it to future classes, and recognizing the professional relevance of SSE-3DP. Conclusion: A pedagogically driven integration of SSE-3DP - grounded in flipped classroom, problem-based laboratory work and model-guided reasoning - can successfully embed advanced manufacturing technologies into pharmacy curricula, promoting experience-based and technology-oriented learning.

TI Quality assurance in pharmacy education: Accreditation outcomes of
   Vietnamese Bpharm programs under the national accreditation framework
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacy education; Program accreditation; Quality assurance;
   Outcome-based education; National accreditation; Vietnam
AB Background: Program accreditation is central to quality assurance in higher education. However, evidence on accreditation outcomes under Vietnam's first national program accreditation framework remains limited, particularly regarding criterion-specific quality gaps in pharmacy education. Identifying these gaps is needed to prioritize quality improvement and inform implementation of the revised framework, which places greater emphasis on outcome-based education (OBE) and continuous quality improvement. Objective: To examine accreditation outcomes of Bachelor of Pharmacy (BPharm) programs in Vietnam and identify strengths and weaknesses in OBE implementation. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study analyzed official external evaluation reports of 32 nationally accredited BPharm programs. Performance was examined at program, standard, and criterion levels. Public (n = 10) and private (n = 22) institutions were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test with effect size r. Results: All 32 programs met accreditation requirements (>= 80% of criteria rated >= 4), yet 62.5% had mean scores below 4.0. The highest non-achievement rates were observed for assessment methods (Criterion 5.3, 84.4%), constructive alignment (Criterion 3.2, 78.1%), program learning outcomes (Criterion 1.2, 50.0%), and course syllabi (Criterion 2.2, 46.9%). Public institutions scored moderately higher than private institutions (r = 0.44-0.46) on three criteria concerning assessment methods and academic staff; differences for the remaining 47 criteria were not evident. Conclusion: Vietnam's framework established a quality assurance baseline, but substantial OBE-related gaps remain despite accreditation. These findings identify priorities for continuous quality improvement and highlight the importance of examining criterion-level performance when accreditation systems seek to move from minimum compliance toward outcome-based quality enhancement.

TI Rethinking academic literacies in the age of GenAI: International MA
   TESOL students' challenges and tool-mediated practices in UK higher
   education
SO JOURNAL OF ENGLISH FOR ACADEMIC PURPOSES
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic challenges; International students; Language proficiency;
   TESOL; GenAI
ID EXPERIENCE; ENGLISH; PERCEPTIONS; STRATEGIES; L2
AB The rapid uptake of Generative AI (GenAI) in higher education is reshaping how international students engage with academic work in L2 English, including how they navigate academic challenges. However, the implications of GenAI for academic literacies remains underexplored. This study investigates how international MA TESOL students in the UK engage with GenAI as a mediational tool in response to academic English challenges. Grounded in sociocultural theory and a practice-oriented conceptual framework which combines academic literacies and toolmediated activity, the study employs a mixed-methods design. Survey data were collected from 82 students, and semi-structured interviews were conducted with 8 students and 5 lecturers from MA TESOL programmes. Findings indicate that MA TESOL students' academic challenges extend beyond L2 English proficiency to encompass a range of academic discourse practices, including academic writing, critical thinking, and understanding and meeting assessment requirements. Furthermore, findings provide rich descriptions of how students use GenAI tools to mediate critical thinking and academic engagement. However, lecturers raised concerns that students' GenAI use was masking academic challenges, thus highlighting a potential tension in the effectiveness with which students are mobilising GenAI as a mediational tool. By situating students' challenges within an academic literacies framework, this study shows that GenAI use is not merely a coping strategy but a tool-mediated activity that has the potential to reshape how academic literacies are manifested in L2 English higher education.

TI Mock Paging in a Surgical Boot Camp: A Pre/Post Evaluation of
   Self-reported Confidence, Anxiety, and Communication With Nurses Among
   Senior Medical Students
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE boot camp; communication; senior medical students; surgical education;
   mock paging; transition to internship
ID EDUCATION; WORKING; PAGES
AB OBJECTIVE Senior medical students entering surgical internship often have limited experience managing nurse pages and common cross-cover problems. Mock paging may help fill this gap, but paired learner-centered outcomes data within surgical boot camps remain limited. We evaluated whether a mock paging exercise was associated with changes in self-reported confidence, anxiety, and communication with nurses. DESIGN Single-center pre/post evaluation using identical surveys administered before and after a mock paging intervention. Surveys assessed confidence and anxiety across 11 common on-call scenarios and communication with nurses across 8 Likert items. Scores were standardized to a 0-100 scale, and primary analyses were restricted to matched preintervention and postintervention surveys. SETTING A senior medical student surgical boot camp at the University of New Mexico. PARTICIPANTS Senior medical students who completed the preintervention survey; the paired analytic cohort comprised those who also completed the postintervention survey. Results Of 46 students who completed the preintervention survey, 42 (91.3%) completed the postintervention survey and comprised the paired analytic cohort. All 3 standardized self-reported composite outcomes changed significantly from preintervention to postintervention. Mean confidence increased from 41.0 (SD 13.6) to 73.1 (SD 11.7), for a mean paired change of 32.1 points on the 0 to 100 scale (95% CI, 27.5-36.7; p < 0.001). Mean anxiety decreased from 53.0 (SD 15.6) to 33.2 (SD 17.5), for a mean paired change of -19.8 points (95% CI, -26.5 to -13.2; p < 0.001). Mean communication increased from 60.6 (SD 13.8) to 81.7 (SD 9.8), for a mean paired change of 21.1 points (95% CI, 17.0-25.3; p < 0.001). Sensitivity analyses were concordant. Conclusions Following a surgical boot camp that included mock paging, senior medical students reported greater confidence in responding to common nurse-page scenarios, lower anxiety related to those scenarios, and better self-rated communication with nurses. Future studies should determine whether these immediate gains endure and translate into demonstrably better nurse-rated communication and on-call performance during internship.

TI Communicative-cognitive activation in primary EFL education:
   Psychometric evidence on a novel subject-specific student scale
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Cognitive activation; EFL education; Early language learning;
   Instructional quality; Primary level; Scale development; Structural
   equation modeling
ID TEACHING QUALITY; INSTRUCTIONAL QUALITY; TEACHERS; SCHOOL; RELIABILITY;
   FRAMEWORK; INDEXES
AB Most research into instructional quality has been conducted in the context of STEM education, with issues relating to subject-specificity being addressed explicitly only recently. Subject-specific approaches might increase validity by capturing aspects of instructional quality that generic frameworks fail to acknowledge. This is particularly true for cognitive activation, which is largely dependent on the lesson content. We present psychometric evidence on the validity of a scale designed to assess students' perceptions of cognitive activation in English as a foreign language education at primary level. Drawing on a sample of 513 German 4th graders (49% female, Mage = 10 years, SD = .59), we investigated the construct and criterion validity of a novel scale. We confirmed our theoretical model of communicative-cognitive activation, which included one general factor and six specific factors. Communicative-cognitive activation and its subdimensions are, to some extent, positively related to other generic dimensions of instructional quality, such as classroom management and student support. However, findings on the relation between communicative-cognitive activation and students' EFL reading proficiency are inconclusive.

TI Evaluation of the new Egyptian undergraduate medical program from the
   perspectives of faculty and institutional leadership: a nationwide,
   mixed-method study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Undergraduate medical education; Program evaluation; Faculty perception;
   Curriculum reform; Competency-based education; Egypt
ID HEALTH-PROFESSIONS EDUCATION; TEACHING EFFECTIVENESS; CURRICULUM;
   FUTURE; IMPROVE
AB Background In response to global calls for medical education reform, Egypt restructured its national undergraduate medical education program from a 6 + 1 model to a competency-based "5 + 2" model. This reformed program emphasizes early clinical exposure, integration of basic and clinical sciences, student-centered learning, and alignment with national academic reference standards. With the graduation of the first cohort in 2023, this study aimed to evaluate the program's effectiveness from the perspectives of faculty and institutional leadership. Methods A concurrent mixed-methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected through a validated, researcher-developed online survey distributed to faculty across 27 Egyptian medical colleges. A total of 10,728 responses were received. Exploratory factor analysis confirmed the construct validity of the survey, which comprised 42 items grouped into five domains: Program Goals, Content, Learning Resources, and Student Assessment; Program Impact on Students' Professional and Research Skills; Faculty Involvement and Support; Students' Academic Guidance and Support; and Physical and Learning Facilities. Qualitative data were obtained from nine focus group discussions (FGDs) involving 100 academic leaders. Thematic analysis of the FGDs offered complementary insights into program implementation. Results Faculty responses indicated borderline to moderate overall satisfaction (mean score 2.99). Higher scores were reported for accessibility and relevance of learning resources and fairness of student assessment. Satisfaction was lower regarding opportunities for faculty to participate in curriculum design and institutional support for research. No significant gender-based differences were found. Junior faculty reported higher satisfaction than senior faculty (p < 0.001). Thematic analysis revealed the academic leaders' appreciation for integrated teaching, early clinical exposure, and modern pedagogies, but also highlighted challenges such as inadequate infrastructure, faculty resistance to change, and variability in curriculum delivery. Leadership support, student feedback mechanisms, and faculty development were noted as essential enablers for successful implementation. Conclusions This evaluation documented faculty and leadership perceptions of strengths in curriculum integration, learning resources, and assessment strategies, while also identifying critical implementation challenges. Ongoing faculty development, equitable institutional support, and sustained stakeholder engagement are essential to ensure the long-term success of the reformed program. Findings may offer insights for policymakers and educators working within similarly centrally coordinated, competency-based curriculum reform initiatives, particularly in contexts with comparable national governance structures.

TI AI training and science student teachers' TPACK in campus-based and
   distance education: a comparative study
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence integration; Distance and campus-based learning;
   Science teacher education; Sustainable development goals (SDG 4 and SDG;
   TPACK framework
ID PEDAGOGICAL CONTENT KNOWLEDGE; IMPACT
AB Despite AI's growing educational potential, little is known about science student teachers' preparedness to integrate it into classroom practice. This study examined whether AI training level and institutional context were associated with student teachers' TPACK. Using a quantitative, comparative, descriptive survey design, data were collected from final-year Bachelor of Education science students at one campus-based and one distance education university in South Africa (n = 186). Final-year students were selected because they are nearing entry into the profession, which makes their self-reported readiness to integrate AI particularly informative. Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis, reliability testing, nonparametric comparisons, and regression analysis. The findings revealed that while 64% of participants at the campus-based university reported strong TPACK, only 47.4% at the distance university did so. Regression results indicated that AI training was associated with self-reported TPACK only among students at the distance university. Specifically, completing a short course was associated with significantly weaker self-reported TPACK than receiving no training (p = .039), whereas no significant association was observed at the campus-based university (p = .607). Given the modest variance explained, these associations are interpreted cautiously. Pedagogical knowledge was the weakest TPACK component across both institutions. The findings suggest that uniform AI training may not produce consistent outcomes across contexts. In South Africa, where teacher education includes both distance and campus-based provision amid uneven digital access, AI training should be context-responsive, infrastructuresensitive, and pedagogically grounded.

TI Assessing assessment: The role of institutional data in understanding
   awarding gaps
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF ECONOMICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Assessments; Awarding gaps; Higher education; Attainment; Inclusivity
AB This study provides a robust quantitative analysis of how different assessment modes relate to awarding gaps in undergraduate Economics programmes at a UK research-intensive university. Drawing on over 15,000 assessment-level observations across three academic years-Pre-COVID (2018-19), COVID (2020-21), and Post-COVID (2022-23)-it offers unique, fine-grained evidence on patterns of attainment inequality. While awarding gaps in Economics are well documented, evidence at the level of individual assessments remains limited; our data granularity enables better examination of how assessment design shapes these gaps. Using three multilevel mixed-effects models we identify disparities across ethnic groups while controlling for student, module, assessment, and institutional characteristics. Attainment trajectories provide contextual evidence on the conditions underpinning changes in awarding gaps. We find that ethnic awarding gaps vary across assessment designs, time periods, and institutional conditions. For most groups, ethnic disparities narrowed during the pandemic, particularly in structured timed online exams, but re-emerged for some (e.g., Black students). Post-COVID in written coursework reports and untimed digital final examinations. Moreover, in coursework, narrower gaps coincided with declining attainment across all groups, whereas in COVID-era digital timed examinations they coincided with improved attainment, suggesting that similar gap changes may arise from very different attainment trajectories. Beyond ethnicity, findings reveal intersectional inequalities. Free School Meals-eligible male students emerged as a new Post-COVID vulnerability, extending concerns about gender inequalities in Economics. Findings have implications for assessment practice. They suggest assessment design shapes attainment inequalities, and highlight the need to consider both attainment trajectories and awarding gaps when evaluating equity in higher education.

TI Teaching monetary policy through interactive simulation: An
   active-learning application for undergraduate macroeconomics
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF ECONOMICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE macroeconomics teaching; monetary policy; central banking; simulation;
   active learning; inflation expectations; Phillips curve
ID CLASSROOM; ECONOMICS; DISCRETION; INFLATION; RULES
AB This paper presents an interactive classroom simulation for teaching monetary policy in intermediate macroeconomics. The activity places students in the role of a central bank committee that chooses the policy interest rate over repeated rounds while observing inflation, unemployment, inflation expectations, credibility, and macroeconomic shocks. The simulation is intentionally stylized, but it incorporates the core mechanisms emphasized in modern macroeconomics: an expectations-augmented Phillips curve, gradual adjustment in real activity, partially anchored expectations, endogenous policy credibility, and stochastic disturbances. The paper describes the model, the classroom design, the scoring rule, suggested debriefing questions, and illustrative game paths. Illustrative runs show that a simple Taylor-style rule outperforms both "always hawkish" and "always dovish" strategies on a composite loss, a result students can discover experientially before it is presented as theory. The complete tool is provided in two interchangeable, economically identical implementations, a self-contained browser application that runs offline with no installation, and an open Python notebook. The tool is openly available for adoption, replication, and further development under a Creative Commons Attribution license.

TI A Novel Experimental Setup for the Visualization of Dosing Strategy in
   Drinking Water Engineering
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE High School/Introductory; Second-Year Undergraduate; Chemical
   Engineering; Demonstrations; Colloids; Conductivity; Laboratory
   Equipment; Water/WaterChemistry
AB Drinking water treatment is one of the most important processing techniques in the world, and access to clean water is recognized as a human right by the UN General Assembly. However, the sources and quality of raw water differ immensely in chemical and biological composition, which leads to different treatment strategies. Coagulation-flocculation is an important treatment step used in most water treatment facilities. In this method, the addition of multivalent cations induces flocculation of the negatively charged colloid particles (e.g., clay or humic substances). A novel experimental setup for the visualization of flocculation is introduced, and demonstrations related to two aspects of the dosing strategy of flocculants are presented. This setup complements the traditional jar test used in water management. These demonstrations aim to highlight the practical difficulties in the dosing strategies for coagulation and flocculation when water quality varies, which will benefit students of water engineering as well as students of physical or colloid chemistry.

TI Ethical challenges in the inclusion of pupils with special needs in
   mainstream schools: A social ecological model perspective
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE ethical dilemmas; inclusive education; social ecological model; special
   educational needs; teacher decision-making
ID FACE
AB The inclusion of pupils with special needs in mainstream schools presents complex ethical dilemmas for educational staff, school leaders and families. This research explores these dilemmas through Bronfenbrenner's social ecological model in the context of Israel's 2018 inclusion reform, highlighting the interaction between schoolchildren and their environment across five subsystems. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 83 educators holding diverse school roles across Israel. Using grounded theory analysis, findings demonstrated that although ethical dilemmas appeared across all ecological systems, they were concentrated within the exosystem where organisational structures, resource limitations and policy implementation conditions constrained educators' ability to enact inclusive practices. Two dominant categories of ethical dilemmas were identified: balancing inclusive participation with effective classroom functioning, and managing tensions between parental preferences and professional educational judgement. The research demonstrates that educators' experiences are shaped by organisational structures, resource availability, leadership support and policy implementation processes. Findings contribute to the international literature on inclusive education by illustrating how ethical dilemmas are distributed across interconnected ecological systems and by highlighting the importance of systemic support for sustainable inclusion practices. The findings highlight the importance of systemic conditions and organisational support for translating inclusive education policies into sustainable practice.

TI Enhancing creativity and digital skills in motion: TikTok in higher
   education
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE TikTok; Social media; Twenty-first century skills; Active learning;
   Technological integration; Educational innovation
ID 21ST-CENTURY SKILLS; TECHNOLOGY
AB In a rapidly evolving digital society, higher education must equip students with essential twentyfirst century skills such as creativity and digital literacy. This study explored the educational potential of TikTok through an active learning experience implemented in a "Foundations of Body Expression" course within a sport sciences degree program. A quantitative, quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design, complemented by a qualitative descriptive component based on students' responses to one open-ended question was used to investigate the perceptions of 156 university students regarding TikTok's impact on their creativity, digital skills, and overall learning engagement. Quantitative findings showed statistically significant improvements in all variables, with self-perceived creativity displaying the greatest perceived growth. The qualitative analysis identified five thematic areas: (1) learning and creativity, (2) psychological and social benefits, (3) teaching methods and tools, (4) promotion and digital skills, and (5) critical considerations and warnings. Students described TikTok as an engaging, accessible, and motivating tool that promoted creative expression, active participation, and digital skills development. They particularly valued its integration of music, rhythm, and visual effects, which enhanced their ability to communicate and express through movement. Some students also noted potential risks such as distraction or misalignment with academic objectives. Overall, the findings support TikTok's potential to enrich university teaching when framed within a student-centred, pedagogically sound approach.

TI Culturally relevant school support profiles are associated with academic
   achievement trajectories post-COVID dual pandemic onset
SO CHILD DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE academic achievement; academic resilience; adolescence; culturally
   relevant school support; COVID-19 pandemic; dual pandemic
ID TEACHER-STUDENT RELATIONSHIPS; ETHNIC-RACIAL IDENTITY; FALSE DISCOVERY
   RATE; CRITICAL CONSCIOUSNESS; RELIABILITY; ENGAGEMENT; CLIMATE; SCALE
AB The COVID-19 pandemic and the 2020 racial awakening posed challenges to adolescents' academic functioning. Culturally relevant school supports are one potential source of resilience in the dual pandemic. This study examined whether heterogeneous culturally relevant school support profiles buffered declining grade point average (GPA) trajectories from 2019 to 2021 among sixth- and ninth-grade students in the U.S. Southwest (N = 717; Mage = 13.7; 49.9% girls; 31.8% Hispanic/Latinx, 31.5% Multiethnic, 25.7% White, 11.1% Black/African American, Asian American, American Indian, or AMENA). Ninth-grade students experiencing high general, moderate cultural, & critical support or low general, devoid cultural, & critical support had significantly better GPA trajectories than those experiencing moderate general & cultural, devoid critical support. Among sixth-grade students, no differences emerged. Discussion of these complex patterns focuses on implications for academic resilience after the dual pandemic.
   We examined whether experiences of school support before the COVID-19 pandemic and 2020 racial justice movement informed the grade point averages (GPAs) of sixth- and ninth-graders in the U.S. Southwest across two academic years (2019-2021). For sixth-graders, pre-pandemic school support did not predict GPA declines. GPA did not decline for ninth-graders who entered the pandemic with strong teacher support and opportunities to discuss cultural/social issues, or ninth-graders who received little school support, perhaps due to out-of-school support. Students receiving teacher and cultural support without opportunities to discuss social issues experienced greater declines, suggesting these supports work best together. Meaningful school engagement with students' cultural identities and experiences potentially buffers against high school students' academic declines during uncertain times.

TI An interactive workshop for first year pharmacy students on caring for

SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Vision impairment; Person-Centred; Disability training; Pharmacy
   education; Pharmacy students
ID COMMUNICATION; EMPATHY
AB Background: Patients with disabilities, such as those are visually impaired (VI), require an individualised approach to care by pharmacists. However, disability awareness training is not widely implemented across modern pharmacy curricula. To address this gap, a workshop was developed for first year students focusing on caring for VI patients. Educational activity: A two-hour workshop was developed, using a mixture of didactic teaching, active learning activities and group work exercises. Workshop elements included; tasks involving braille, VI patient experience videos, use of low vision simulation glasses and a group exercise involving VI patient counselling. Most students (97.2%, n = 68) either strongly agreed or agreed that the workshop increased their confidence to communicate with VI patients. All students (100%, n = 70) strongly agreed/agreed that they will apply the knowledge and skills gained in their future practice. Almost all (98.6%, n = 69), would welcome wider implementation of disability training. Students provided various recommendations for minor workshop improvements in open text comments. Analysis of educational activity: Students who undertook the workshop strongly supported inclusion of disability training in their course. This work highlights how simulation activities and inclusion of a patient voice can effectively promote the human aspects of healthcare.

TI Graduates employability readiness among pharmacy students: Insights from
   Bachelor of Pharmacy and PharmD programs at the University of Jordan
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Employability readiness; Competencies; Workforce development; Students'
   satisfaction
ID EDUCATION
AB Background As pharmacist's roles evolve, ensuring that graduates possess strong employability skills becomes essential. Evaluating students' readiness helps inform curricular development and aligns training with workforce needs. Objective This study assessed employability readiness among senior Bachelor of Pharmacy and Doctor of Pharmacy students at the University of Jordan and examined differences across the two programs. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among senior students at the university in the Bachelor of Pharmacy and Doctor of Pharmacy programs during the 2024-2025 academic year. Data were collected using an online, self-administered questionnaire comprised of the 19-item Work Readiness Scale, covering four domains: Work Competence, Social Intelligence, Personal Work Characteristics, and Organizational Acumen. Descriptive and inferential statistics were used to analyze the data. Results A total of 258 students completed the survey. Comparable outcomes were observed across most sociodemographic variables. Overall, work readiness scale scores were moderate. The students within the two study groups showed comparable overall mean scores and domain-specific mean scores, while item-level analysis revealed some differences (p < 0.05). For instance, Doctor of Pharmacy students showed higher clinical confidence, while Bachelor of Pharmacy students expressed stronger multitasking abilities and greater capacity for continuous learning. Conclusion Senior students at the School of Pharmacy at the University of Jordan demonstrate moderate levels of employability readiness, with meaningful item-level differences across programs of study. These findings highlight the need for targeted interventions focusing on workplace competencies and organizational preparedness. Curricular and experiential changes are needed to improve employability readiness. Strengthening career readiness training can support a smoother transition from academic study to professional practice.

TI Enjoyment and Engagement in AI-Mediated Informal Digital Learning of
   English: A Latent Growth Curve Modelling Study
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-mediated IDLE; engagement; enjoyment; latent growth curve modelling;
   semi-structured interviews
ID FIT INDEXES
AB Enjoyment and engagement are critical for effective language learning, yet little is known about how these experiences evolve over time in AI-mediated informal digital English learning (IDLE). Previous studies have mainly relied on cross-sectional designs, limiting understanding of the dynamic development of emotional and behavioural engagement. This study aims to examine the longitudinal trajectories of students' enjoyment and engagement in AI-mediated IDLE and to identify factors influencing these changes. A total of 494 university students participated in a semester-long study, completing three waves of surveys to capture changes in enjoyment and engagement. Latent growth curve modelling was used to estimate initial levels, growth trajectories, and the dynamic relationship between the two constructs. In addition, 20 students participated in follow-up semi-structured interviews to provide qualitative insights into contextual factors affecting their experiences, analysed using a grounded approach. Both enjoyment and engagement increased steadily over the semester, developing in parallel, with qualitative findings revealing that learner characteristics, peer interaction, teacher support, and access to resources shaped these trajectories. These results extend existing research by providing a longitudinal perspective on emotional experiences and engagement in AI-mediated IDLE. The findings highlight the importance of designing AI-mediated learning environments that foster positive emotional experiences and sustained engagement for diverse learners.

TI Critical decision-making skills of entering surgery residents: eight
   years of formative assessment results from the American college of
   surgeons entering resident readiness assessment (ACS ERRA)
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Surgical education; Clinical decision-making; resident readiness;
   Formative assessment; Transition to residency; Precision surgical
   education
ID KEY FEATURES; PROFESSIONAL ACTIVITIES
AB Purpose Each year, thousands of entering surgery residents assume clinical responsibility within days of completing medical school, yet residency programs have limited objective data regarding decision-making readiness at the point of entry. The American College of Surgeons Entering Resident Readiness Assessment (ACS ERRA) is a national formative assessment designed to assess early clinical decision-making skills using a key-features approach focused on clinical scenarios and critical decision points during early surgery training to promote patient safety. Methods Data from eight consecutive annual ACS ERRA administrations (2018-2025) were analyzed. The assessment included 40 case-based clinical scenarios encompassing 140 decision points across 20 clinical topic areas. Resident performance, psychometric characteristics, and frequency of potentially harmful actions (PHAs) were examined using descriptive statistics and multi-year regression analyses. Results Data from 5869 PGY-1 surgery residents across 626 cohorts from 224 unique programs demonstrated consistent overall performance throughout the study period, with a mean score of 65% correct (SD = 8%). Performance varied substantially across clinical domains. Topics with consistently lower mean scores included change in respiratory rate (51%), abdominal pain (57%), and irregular heartbeat (58%), whereas higher scores were observed in somnolence (73%), hypotension (73%), and chest pain (73%). Mean scores in four domains-including change in respiratory rate, traumatic extremity ischemia, oliguria, and fever etiologies-declined significantly during the later years of the study period (3-8% decrease; all p < 0.05). Potentially harmful actions were most frequently identified in hypoxemia (46.3%), irregular heartbeat (33.8%), abdominal pain (32.0%), and fever-related scenarios (30.6%). Conclusion The ACS ERRA identified substantial variability in clinical decision-making readiness among entering surgery residents. Frequent potentially harmful actions and lower performance in specific clinical domains highlight that early assessment can help programs identify residents and domains that may benefit from closer supervision and early interventions at the beginning of surgical training.

TI Exploring Human-LLM Collaboration for Creativity Through the Lens of
   Concepts
SO JOURNAL OF CREATIVE BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE concept generation; concepts; creativity; Hegelian; human-AI
   collaboration; large language models
ID MODEL; LANGUAGE
AB We conducted a theoretical exploration into how human-LLM collaboration can facilitate the emergence of creativity through the lens of concepts-a notion that is central in the philosophical discussions regarding human knowledge creation. Kant considers concepts to be an epistemological tool that transforms people's perceptual, intuitive experiences into knowledge, while Hegel further postulates that concepts have a broader, ontological meaning: through concepts, individuals' experiences are socialized to a collective level, becoming part of the external world which, in turn, can be experienced and learned by others. Specifically, we first reviewed the philosophical discussions revolving around concepts and discussed how creativity is reflected in and can be facilitated through concept generation. We then reviewed the development of artificial intelligence and mapped it onto the development of human intelligence. We identified the commonalities and unique strengths of humans (providing drive to start and constraints to stop based on human embodiment) and artificial intelligence (carrying out extensive exploration of new concepts to supply potential options for reaching a creative goal). Based on these insights, we proposed a hybrid cycle of concept generation as a general framework or working approach to achieve human-AI creativity-a form of creativity that humans alone cannot reach.

ID RESTORATIVE JUSTICE; ORGANIZATIONAL JUSTICE; PROCEDURAL JUSTICE;
   CONSEQUENCES; ANTECEDENTS; GENDER; IMPACT; WORK; DETERMINANTS; CONTEXT
AB This pedagogical practice case examines the true story of "Sara" and her experience encountering sexual harassment in a nonprofit workplace. The article begins by defining sexual harassment and reviewing relevant literature on its prevalence and impact in nonprofit organizations. It then explores principles of organizational justice and their application to nonprofit responses to harassment. Through Sara's case of nonprofit workplace sexual harassment, we highlight the events leading up to the harassment, her pursuit of justice, and the challenges she faced. Designed for use in classes, workshops, and seminars, this case aims to raise awareness, foster critical discussions, and inspire further research.

TI What are we sharing? Faculty use of generative AI and the questions we
   have not yet asked in nursing education
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; Nursing education; Faculty practice;
   Data privacy; Informed consent; Pedagogical expertise; Professional
   ethics
AB Generative AI has entered nursing education rapidly and pervasively. While considerable scholarly attention has been directed toward student use of these tools, including concerns about academic integrity, citation fabrication, and the design of AI-resistant assessments. Far less attention has been paid to faculty practice. Yet many of us now routinely use generative AI in the work of teaching itself: generating grading rubrics, simplifying assignment instructions, aligning course materials to program outcomes, drafting feedback on student work, and refining policy language. This practice has spread without institutional guidance, without faculty disclosure norms, and with little professional conversation about what it means. This paper invites that conversation. It begins from the author's own practice and observations among colleagues, then examines three sets of questions raised by faculty AI use that have not yet been adequately engaged in the nursing literature. First, what is actually transferred when faculty paste assignments, rubrics, scenarios, and student work into commercial AI systems, and how do those transfers align, or fail to align, with the data practices of the platforms involved? Second, on whose behalf do faculty make these disclosure decisions, given that course materials embed the contributions of colleagues, clinical partners, prior developers, and students? Third, what does it mean for the development of nursing pedagogy when work once central to the formation of educators, including assessment design, feedback, and curricular alignment, is increasingly mediated through commercial generative tools? The paper does not argue that faculty should stop using generative AI. It argues that we should subject our own practice to the same reflection we have begun to ask of our students, and it offers a starting framework for that collective examination.

AB Roc Reading Partners (RRP) grew from the belief that when children feel joy and connection, they thrive as readers (Muhammad 2020). TI Rethinking data privacy for AI Adoption in African Higher Education: A
   meta-synthesis of stakeholder perceptions and policy implications
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE data privacy; artificial intelligence; AI adoption; higher education;
   stakeholder perceptions; Sub-Saharan Africa
AB The growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in African higher education offers opportunities for personalized learning, improved decision-making, and educational innovation. However, AI systems rely heavily on student and institutional data, raising significant privacy concerns within contexts characterized by evolving regulations, infrastructural challenges, and diverse socio-cultural norms. This study examines student and educator perceptions of data privacy in AI-enhanced learning and explores how these perceptions influence AI adoption in Sub-Saharan African higher education institutions. Guided by the ENTREQ framework and PRISMA procedures, a qualitative meta-synthesis was conducted on 18 studies published between 2020 and 2025. Data were analyzed using open, axial, and selective coding. The synthesis was informed by Privacy Calculus Theory and Contextual Integrity Theory. Findings indicate that students are primarily concerned about data security, transparency, consent, surveillance, and potential misuse of personal information. These concerns are intensified by limited digital literacy and infrastructural constraints. Educators acknowledge the pedagogical benefits of AI but emphasize governance, institutional accountability, ethical oversight, and capacity development. While both groups advocate stronger privacy protections and transparency, students focus on personal control and vulnerability, whereas educators prioritize compliance and governance. Privacy concerns reduce trust and constrain AI adoption, particularly in environments with weak regulatory and institutional safeguards. AI adoption in African higher education is shaped by privacy risk evaluation, contextual expectations regarding data use, and institutional trust. Strengthening governance frameworks, transparency, and institutional capacity is essential for responsible AI integration and sustainable adoption across the region.

TI Beyond the mechanism: moral agency and language policy implementation in
   the Global South
SO LANGUAGE POLICY
LA English
DT Article
DE Language policy; Agency; Morality; Mechanisms; English; Higher education
ID INDIVIDUAL AGENCY; EDUCATION POLICY; TEACHER AGENCY; POWER;
   MULTILINGUALISM; IDENTITY; ALGERIA
AB This paper examines teacher agency in the context of a state-initiated online English language programme in Global South higher education. Drawing on in-depth interviews conducted in Arabic alongside media documents, it argues that language policy implementation in this context was shaped by two distinct and partially competing registers of agency. The first is fractured agency as a political mechanism which is a governance arrangement that operates through the deliberate spatiotemporal organisation of teachers' professional autonomy. The second is moral agency which is a multi-layered force grounded in locally embedded virtues and religious epistemologies that sustained policy implementation independently of, and at times despite, the structural conditions imposed upon teachers. In reconceptualising moral agency through local epistemologies and Islamic ethical frameworks, the paper responds to calls for Southern theory in applied linguistics and contributes to understanding how language policy is lived, felt, and sustained in postcolonial contexts where institutional governance and moral selfhood operate according to fundamentally different logics.

TI When AI meets practiced language policy: multilingual students'
   negotiation of monolingual norms in a Canadian afterschool program
SO LANGUAGE POLICY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence in education; Practiced language policy;
   Multilingual learners; English-dominant schooling; Linguistic equity;
   After-school programs
ID REPERTOIRES; SCHOOLS
AB This study situates artificial intelligence (AI) use within broader structures of linguistic inequity in multilingual schools, where monolingual norms continue to shape learning despite increasing linguistic diversity. Challenging "AI hype" that frames educational technologies as neutral tools, the study draws on the concept of practiced language policy to advance an alignment-based account of AI efficacy across macro- (societal), meso- (programmatic), and micro-level (interactional) contexts, alongside students' and families' language practices. Using qualitative data from a design-based study conducted in an after-school literacy program serving elementary-aged (Grades 2-5) multilingual learners in British Columbia, Canada, the research examines students' engagement with AI-generated multilingual literacy supports, including text-to-home-language audio resources designed to support English reading development. Findings show that the pedagogical value of AI is not inherent but contingent on the degree of alignment across nested language policy contexts. When alignment was present, AI enabled students to mobilize their home languages as both linguistic and symbolic capital, supporting English comprehension while affirming multilingual identities. When alignment was weak or disrupted by English-dominant norms, AI became a site of tension and constraint, and in some cases reproduced existing inequities. By foregrounding alignment across practiced language policy scales, this study contributes a critical framework for understanding AI in education, demonstrating that technology-mediated equity for multilingual learners depends not only on access to AI tools, but also on the ideological and policy ecologies in which such tools are embedded.

SO CURRICULUM PERSPECTIVES

DT Article
DE Textbooks; Competency-based curriculum; Revised Bloom's Taxonomy;

ID BLOOMS TAXONOMY
AB This qualitative study investigates the cognitive processes within English as a Foreign Language (EFL) textbooks at the upper primary levels in Rwandan schools. Researchers used the Revised Bloom's Taxonomy (RBT) to analyze the levels of 1,531 cognitive activities within the textbooks. TI Toward Agent-Based Educational Science: Rethinking Educational Research
   in the Age of AI
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Agent-based education science; Artificial intelligence in education;
   Educational simulation
AB Educational science faces a structural mismatch between the pace of educational innovation and the methods used to evaluate its developmental impact. While new pedagogical approaches and AI-driven learning technologies are rapidly deployed, established classroom-based empirical research remains slow and fragmented, often generating evidence only after large-scale implementation has occurred. Here, we propose agent-based educational science (AES): a research agenda in which educational theories are formalized as interacting agents and environments, enabling in silico experimentation on developmental processes that are otherwise slow or infeasible to test empirically. By research agenda we mean not merely a list of open questions, but a coordinated invitation to the research community to reorient its priorities, workflows, data infrastructures, and validation practices around theory-constrained, dynamically updateable, and empirically examinable simulations of learner development. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence bring this agenda within practical reach. As a concrete instantiation, we introduce Student Development Agents, computational agents designed to generate developmental features under counterfactual educational environments. Rather than replacing empirical research, agent-based educational science reconfigures its role, enabling predictive, ethical, and cumulative theory building in the science of learning.

TI Academic resilience in mathematics and science: Gender and subject
   patterns across 47 education systems in TIMSS 2023
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cross-national comparison; Educational equity; Gender difference;
   Socioeconomical disadvantage; STEM education
ID TECHNOLOGY
AB Academic resilience refers to the ability of socioeconomically disadvantaged students to achieve high levels of academic performance despite adversity. This concept highlights students who succeed against the odds and provides insight into how education systems can better support equity and excellence. Drawing on data from TIMSS 2023 across 47 education systems, this study examines resilience in mathematics and science, with particular attention to subject- and gender-specific patterns. Socioeconomically disadvantaged students are identified as those in the bottom quartile of home educational resources distribution within each education system. Within this group, resilience students are identified using two commonly applied criteria: a fixed threshold using the TIMSS High International Benchmarks of 550 points, and a relative threshold identifying students who achieve in the top quartile of the national achievement distribution. The findings show that resilience patterns are partly definition-dependent, and underline the importance of examining resilience separately by subject and gender. Threshold-based indicators should be interpreted as descriptive measures of achievement among disadvantaged students rather than as comprehensive indicators of adaptive capacity or education-system effectiveness.

TI Instructor-Designed AI Tutors in University Foreign Language Education:
   A Mixed-Methods Study of Learner Motivation and Reflective Learning
   Experience Based on Self-Determination Theory
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE customized GPTs; self-determination theory; noticing hypothesis; foreign
   language education; instructor-designed AI; university Japanese
   education
ID 2ND-LANGUAGE
AB This study investigates the educational potential of instructor-designed Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) in a university-level Japanese course, drawing on self-determination theory (SDT) and the noticing hypothesis. Using a mixed-methods design, we examined how the continuous use of an instructor-developed Artificial Intelligence tutoring system (basic Japanese GPTs) relates to learners' psychological needs satisfaction, cognitive noticing, and perceptions of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted learning among 74 undergraduate students at a South Korean university. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation; qualitative data from open-ended items and reflective writing underwent systematic content analysis. The findings revealed three key patterns. First, learners reported relatively high levels of satisfaction across all three SDT needs-autonomy, competence, and relatedness-particularly in relation to self-directed reviews and affective safety. Second, qualitative analysis identified three distinct noticing experiences: AI-supported clarification of linguistic form, noticing through intentional error generation and AI feedback, and metacognitive regulation of learning strategies. Third, the learners perceived the instructor-designed GPTs not merely as a convenience tool but as a structured learning environment that supported output-oriented, interaction-based practice. These findings suggest that the educational effectiveness of generative AI in foreign language education is not determined by frequency of use alone but also by the quality of pedagogical design underlying its deployment. This study contributes a practice-based model for AI integration in general education language courses while acknowledging limitations related to its single-course scope and reliance on self-reported data.

TI Developing multilingual literacy for Mozambican immigrant learners in
   Nsanje, Malawi: A braided river in the borderland multilingualism
   framework
SO READING & WRITING-JOURNAL OF THE READING ASSOCIATION OF SOUTH AFRICA
LA English
DT Article
DE borderland literacies; immigrant learners; language-in-education policy;
   multilingual inclusion; Mozambique; Nsanje
ID EDUCATION; POLICY
AB Background: Border districts in southern Malawi experience recurrent cross-border displacement from Mozambique because of floods, cyclones and political instability. In Nsanje district, Mozambican immigrant learners enter schools with multilingual repertoires shaped by Sena and Portuguese, while Malawi's 2014 language-in-education policy mandates a monolingual (English) medium of instruction from Standard 1. Objectives: The study examined how literacy for immigrant learners in Nsanje could be re-conceptualised to address the linguistic exclusion created by the monolingual language policy. It focused on a specific borderland context to explore the broader implications for multilingual literacy education in African settings affected by mobility. Method: The study employed a qualitative conceptual design. It analysed literature on literacy, language policy, multilingualism, border studies, and inclusive education. A theoretical synthesis was undertaken to examine the relationship between linguistic realities, literacy practices, and language-in-education policy. Results: The analysis indicated that monolingual policy assumptions undermine learners' multilingual meaning-making practices, thereby limiting access to reading and writing. A braided river metaphor was developed to conceptualise literacy as fluid and mobile. Furthermore, a borderland multilingualism framework was proposed to explain how learners can draw on linguistic resources across languages. Conclusion: Literacy inclusion in borderland contexts requires pedagogical and policy approaches grounded in multilingualism, as literacy practices that embrace learners' full linguistic repertoires provide greater access to learning. Contribution: The study contributes a metaphor and a theoretical perspective for understanding borderland literacies. It also advances multilingualism as a policy-relevant strategy for inclusive literacy education in African contexts characterised by displacement and linguistic diversity.

TI Adaptive Digital Portfolio Assessment yields sustained equitable arts
   gains: a longitudinal randomized controlled trial with mixed-methods
   integration
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE assessment; digital portfolio; equitable arts learning; longitudinal
   study; low-resource schools; self-determination
ID PERCEPTIONS; COMPETENCE; MOTIVATION; EDUCATION; LEARNERS; AUTONOMY;
   DIVIDE
AB This study evaluates the Adaptive Digital Portfolio Assessment (ADPA) framework designed to address assessment inequities in arts education within the Global South. We conducted a 12-month longitudinal randomized controlled trial involving 1,200 senior secondary (SMA) students across 60 schools in West Java, Indonesia, as part of a broader national study across multiple Indonesian provinces. Utilizing Latent Growth Curve Modeling, Mediation Analysis, and Moderated Mediation, we tracked artistic competence trajectories and psychological pathways grounded in Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and Expectancy-Value Theory. Qualitative Reflexive Thematic Analysis (n = 135) provided mechanistic depth. The ADPA intervention group exhibited significantly steeper growth trajectories in artistic competence (slope = 2.34 points/month vs. control = 0.41 points/month; p < .001; d = 0.94), with 78% of these gains persisting at the 12-month follow-up (d = 0.61). Mediation analysis revealed that psychological internalization processes, specifically competence satisfaction, autonomy satisfaction, and task value realization, accounted for 37.8% of the total effect initially, declining to 28.4% by month 12, aligning with the theoretical framework. Crucially for equity, low-socioeconomic status (SES) students achieved effect sizes (d = 0.89) nearly identical to middle-SES peers (d = 0.99; interaction p = .674), demonstrating that ADPA substantially reduced differential effects associated with socioeconomic background as a predictor of artistic growth. Negative case analysis identified algorithmic opacity and device accessibility as critical boundary conditions. The ADPA framework demonstrates that equity-first educational technology design can effectively bridge achievement gaps, offering a scalable model to substantially reduce socioeconomic barriers to creative development in resource-limited environments.

   students and program managers

DT Article

AB Introduction Recent attention to graduate student mental health, changing career landscapes, the individual financial burden of graduate school and postdoctoral pathways, and continued challenges to diversify academic training signal that the time is ripe for reimagining the vision, design, and implementation of biomedical research education and training in the United States.Methods We sought to assess biomedical graduate student needs and how they arose within the context of a large midwestern institution's school of medicine. ID CONTEXT
AB Introduction The transition to University 4.0 requires higher education institutions to develop reliable and context-appropriate tools capable of evaluating digital, pedagogical, research, and governance transformations from the perspective of multiple stakeholders. In Morocco, the available evaluation tools remain limited, as they were developed in different institutional contexts or focus on isolated aspects of digital transformation. This study aimed to develop, test, and exploratorily refine a set of multi-stakeholder questionnaires designed to assess the transition to University 4.0 in Moroccan higher education institutions.Methods Six questionnaires were developed for students, faculty members and administrative staff, covering Education 4.0, Research 4.0 and Governance 4.0. TI Using activity theory to inform the design of academic resources for
   first-year engineering students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE contradictions; cultural historical activity theory; design; engineering
   education; help-seeking; student-centered
ID HELP-SEEKING; HIGHER-EDUCATION; CONTRADICTIONS; INTEGRATION
AB Introduction University academic resources such as tutoring, office hours, and peer-led study programs are key institutional tools for supporting student learning, but these resources are often underutilized by the students who need them most. A student's ability and willingness to seek academic help are strongly correlated with student retention. Academic resources play a role in both the academic and social spheres of a student's college experience and may impact a student's decision to persist in a challenging discipline or remain enrolled at their institution. This qualitative study examines how socio-institutional culture shapes first-year engineering students' navigation of academic resources.Methods Using cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) as an analytical lens, researchers conducted twenty semi-structured interviews to identify internal, social, and structural contradictions that shape help-seeking behaviors.Results Thematic analysis revealed three interrelated cultural norms: Hustle Culture, Collaborative Culture, and Academic Hierarchy. Each norm generated systemic contradictions, including belonging versus bandwidth, peer networks that gatekeep less popular resources, and the hidden curriculum surrounding expert support. When asked how to address these contradictions, study participants proposed consolidating resources, increasing transparency, and amplifying peer recommendations.Discussion The process of mapping activity system contradictions, naming cultural norms, and generating student-centered design opportunities is transferable across institutional contexts and useful to first-year experience practitioners, academic support directors, and advising offices seeking to co-create interventions that are responsive to their students' sociocultural realities.

AB Introduction The notion of historical thinking has become a central focus in the teaching of history, particularly in contexts affected by conflict where teaching certain topics is a priority. The aim of this study was to describe the presence of historical competencies in the subject syllabuses used during Initial Teacher Training (ITT) for specialists in "History, Geography and Social Sciences" at universities located in this macro-region, with a focus on the teaching of issues related to the conflict.Methods The study employed a mixed-methods approach and a descriptive-comparative design to analyse 56 course programmes from four higher education institutions, using an analysis matrix focused on four dimensions: learning outcomes, content, methodology and assessment.Results The results reveal that the "historical evidence" competence is the most frequently encountered in the programmes analysed, whilst "change and continuity" and "cause and effect" are rarely found and show little variation among institutions. TI Patterns of participation: describing student engagement across
   agricultural education components
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE agricultural education; career and technical education; SAE for all;
   student engagement; supervised agricultural experiences
AB Introduction Agricultural education aims to prepare students for careers in agriculture and related industries through three critical components: classroom and laboratory instruction, leadership through the National FFA Organization (FFA), and supervised agricultural experiences (SAEs). This combination of learning strategies is critical to agricultural education's student engagement, which can lead to increased career preparedness, the development of employability skills, and becoming an informed consumer of agricultural products.Methods This study analyzed data from the Agricultural Experience Tracker (AET), a web-based record-keeping platform used by agricultural educators for SAE and FFA records. The data were collected from 230,228 students in 1,245 agricultural education programs in nine purposively selected states. This data was utilized to describe patterns of student engagement in FFA and SAE activities. We used Welch's F-test to assess statistical differences in FFA and SAE engagement between states included in the study.Results We found that annual FFA and SAE engagement varied among students, with only 24.56% of members engaged in community service, 35.19% engaged in at least two FFA activities at the local level or higher, 33.37% of first-year students with an SAE project with over 10 h of engagement, and 29.29% of continuing students participating in an SAE project with over 50 h of engagement. Furthermore, the results indicated that some states included in the study engaged students in FFA and SAE at significantly higher rates than other states.Discussion Engagement in SAE was most common among first-year students participating in a foundational project, though this often did not translate into sustained involvement in an immersion project. It is recommended that educators further integrate FFA and SAE components into classroom instruction and that agricultural education continue to expand opportunities for participation and ensure equity for all students. Additionally, states with lower rates of FFA and SAE engagement should use states with higher rates as examples to identify effective strategies to increase participation.

TI Technology-supported methodological foundations for teaching innovative
   urban development in school geography
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE mobile learning; place-based learning; school geography; smart and
   sustainable cities; spatial thinking; urban geography education
AB Introduction Rapid urbanization, digitalization, and sustainability challenges require school geography to move beyond descriptive approaches toward analytical, technology-supported learning about urban systems. This study developed and evaluated a methodological framework for integrating smart and sustainable city concepts into secondary school geography through a place-based elective course focused on Almaty, Kazakhstan.Methods The framework was implemented in a 34-hour ninth-grade elective course, Geography of Cities: Almaty, combining a content-structural model, local case studies, authentic urban datasets, Google Earth materials, and mobile learning activities delivered through the Bilim All application. Because intact classes and non-random group assignment were used, the results indicate a significant association with improved learning outcomes rather than definitive causal effectiveness.

TI A comparative study of centralized upper secondary school-leaving
   mathematics examination tasks in Poland and North Rhine-Westphalia with
   respect to problem solving, modelling, and reasoning competencies
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE central examinations; cross-national comparative study; upper secondary
   education; mathematical competencies; task analysis
AB This study examines upper secondary school-leaving mathematics examination tasks from Poland (2005-2023) and the federal state of North Rhine-Westphalia (2007-2023) with regard to three central mathematical competencies: problem solving, modelling, and reasoning - and their competency levels. Drawing on the competency framework of Niss and H & oslash;jgaard, a comparative document analysis was conducted using three competency-specific coding schemes. The analysis covers complete corpora of centralized basic-level mathematics examinations, comprising 570 Polish and 2,731 North Rhine-Westphalian tasks. The study first identifies and describes the distribution of competencies and competency levels within each examination system reflected in the examination tasks over the course of time. It then compares both systems statistically, identifying similarities and differences in the distribution of competency demands. The results reveal distinct competency profiles in the mathematics examination tasks from Poland and North Rhine-Westphalia. In North Rhine-Westphalia, modelling constitutes the dominant competency demand, whereas problem solving and reasoning occur considerably less frequently. In contrast, Polish examination tasks show higher levels of problem solving, while modelling and reasoning play only a minor role. In both systems, higher competency levels occur only rarely across all three competencies. By providing the first comprehensive comparison of complete upper secondary school-leaving mathematics examination corpora from Poland and North Rhine-Westphalia, this study contributes to research on competence-oriented assessment. The findings contribute to discussions on examination design, the implementation of competency-oriented curricula, educational quality, and the comparability of upper secondary school-leaving qualifications within the European educational area.

TI Subjective AI decision-making significance (SAID) in high-school
   students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; decision-making; digital education; high school
   students; self-efficacy
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE
AB Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is now a widespread everyday tool and its impact has been researched in various domains of life. However, little is known about how AI affects decision-making in daily life, especially in young individuals, who experience the use of AI at an early age. This study explored how high school students perceive and use AI in everyday decision-making, thereby conducting an initial validation of a novel phenomenon termed subjective AI decision-making significance (SAID).Methods An online survey of 197 Austrian students assessed SAID with decision-making scenarios that were previously developed together with stakeholders. Moreover, attitudes toward AI, self-efficacy, and subjective physical and mental health were measured using questionnaires. Factor analyses were conducted to observe underlying constructs of SAID and regression analyses were administered to predict these factors from attitudes, self-efficacy, subjective health and demographic variables.Results Using factor analysis, two SAID factors emerged: ethical/social and practical decision-making. Both correlated with perceived AI helpfulness. Moreover, lower self-efficacy was linked to greater subjective significance of AI for decision-making in ethical/moral and social contexts.Conclusion These preliminary findings suggest that students perceive AI as a helpful tool for both ethical/moral and social decision-making as well as practical decision-making. However, they also underscore the need to enhance AI literacy, especially among students with lower self-efficacy, to support informed use, critical reflection and independent thinking. Future research should investigate additional variables, including AI experience and personality traits.

TI Pre-service teachers' general pedagogical knowledge and pedagogical
   learning opportunities at entry into induction: comparing traditional
   and alternative teacher education programs
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE alternative certification; educational sciences; general pedagogical
   knowledge; induction; opportunities to learn; professional knowledge;
   teacher competence; teacher education effectiveness
ID FUTURE TEACHERS
AB Globally, increasing numbers of individuals enter the teaching profession through alternative teacher education programs without prior university studies in teacher education or pedagogy. Compared to traditional programs, these alternative programs-for example, lateral entry programs in Germany, the country of the present study-are often considerably shorter and place a strong emphasis on in-school training. However, it remains unclear to what extent pre-service teachers (PST) in alternative programs (A-PST) possess general pedagogical knowledge (GPK) comparable to that of PST in traditional programs (T-PST), and whether potential gaps can be compensated for during in-school training as part of induction. This study conceptualizes GPK as a key outcome of university-based initial teacher education and additionally examines opportunities to learn (OTL) in pedagogical content and in-school learning activities that may underlie such knowledge development. Focusing on teacher education in North Rhine-Westphalia, the most populous federal state in Germany, the study compares A-PST and T-PST with respect to GPK, assessed using a standardized performance-based test, and self-reported OTL at the beginning of induction. Regression analyses reveal higher GPK among T-PST than A-PST in primary teacher education, whereas no significant differences emerge among secondary school PST. Across these teaching types, A-PST report fewer OTL related to pedagogical content but more extensive in-school OTL in lesson planning and teaching. After the preparatory semester of lateral entry, which precedes induction and requires teaching practice and pedagogical coursework, A-PST catch up with respect to content-related OTL but do not reach the same level of GPK as primary education T-PST at induction entry. Longitudinal analyses using latent change score models, however, reveal significant developments in both GPK and OTL among A-PST during the preparatory semester, although no significant associations between knowledge gains and OTL gains are found. Overall, the findings support that university-based teacher education effectively promotes GPK among primary school T-PST while also highlighting the potential of alternative programs to compensate for missing OTL through targeted training.
