TI Understanding student satisfaction in performing arts education: a
   grounded theory study of undergraduate musical theatre education in
   China
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE grounded theory; performing arts education; student satisfaction;
   training continuity; undergraduate musical theatre education
AB Student satisfaction is widely used as an important indicator of higher education quality and teaching effectiveness. However, existing research has largely been developed within general higher education contexts and offers limited explanation of how student satisfaction is formed in practice-intensive performing arts programmes. Undergraduate musical theatre education, which combines embodied training, cross-skill integration, rehearsal practice, and translation into stage performance, provides a valuable context for reexamining student satisfaction in performing arts education. Therefore, this study aims to explore how student satisfaction is formed in undergraduate musical theatre education and to develop a process-oriented model explaining its underlying mechanisms. Drawing on a procedural grounded theory approach, this study conducted semi-structured interviews with 15 students and recent graduates from five Chinese institutions with relatively well-established undergraduate musical theatre programmes. The interview data were analysed through open coding, axial coding, and selective coding. The analysis generated 36 open-coding categories, which were further organized into 12 main categories: teaching conditions, curriculum and time structure, performance support, training continuity, pedagogy and feedback, integrated training quality, creative and humanistic development, practice and external linkages, perceived capability development, perceived career readiness, commitment and alignment, and overall satisfaction. Based on these findings, the study developed a training-continuity model of student satisfaction. The results indicate that structural conditions shape students' learning experiences by enabling or disrupting training continuity, while pedagogical transformation mechanisms further influence perceived capability development and perceived career readiness. These perceptions contribute to overall satisfaction by strengthening professional identification, perceived assessment fairness, and willingness to remain engaged. This study shifts the understanding of student satisfaction from a service-quality perspective commonly used in general higher education to a training-system perspective suited to practice-intensive performing arts education. It identifies training continuity as a central mechanism linking structural conditions, pedagogical processes, and outcome perceptions, and provides practical implications for improving undergraduate musical theatre curricula.

TI Student Experiences of Immersive Block Learning in English-Medium
   Instruction Transnational Education: An Exploratory Case Study
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE immersive block learning; transnational education (TNE); English-medium
   instruction (EMI); student experience; student success; curriculum
   innovation; active learning; cross-cultural higher education; English as
   an additional language or dialect (EAL/D)
ID CHALLENGES; PERFORMANCE; PROGRAMS
AB The rapid expansion of English-medium instruction (EMI) in transnational education (TNE) has increased the need for evidence-based higher education (HE) curriculum models that support diverse student cohorts in cross-cultural contexts. This exploratory mixed-methods study examines the effectiveness of block models in EMI TNE partnerships by comparing English as an additional language/dialect (EAL/D) student outcomes across traditional semester-based models and immersive block-model delivery in China and Papua New Guinea, and by exploring students' block-model experiences. Implications emphasise the need for consistent operationalisation of the block model and pedagogical scaffolding to optimise effectiveness in cross-cultural higher education settings.

TI AI literacy and subject specialization in pre-service teacher education:
   a mixed-methods study of dimensional profiles and perceived pedagogical
   challenges
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence literacy; perceived pedagogical challenges;
   pre-service teachers; primary teacher education; subject specialization
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) literacy has become an important component of teacher preparation, yet limited evidence is available on pre-service teachers' self-reported AI literacy profiles and the challenges they perceive in connecting AI-related awareness with pedagogical practice. This study examined self-reported AI literacy and perceived pedagogical challenges among pre-service primary teachers using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. DT Article
DE critical literacy; transformative learning; digital literacy
AB In increasingly digital and AI-mediated educational environments, adult learners are required to navigate complex information landscapes shaped by artificial intelligence, digital platforms, and algorithmically generated content. In such contexts, digital literacy can no longer be understood solely as the acquisition of technical competencies. Rather, contemporary digital literacy requires the evaluative and reflective capacities traditionally associated with critical literacy, including the ability to question assumptions, critically evaluate information, engage dialogically with knowledge, and recognise the technological and ideological systems that shape contemporary communication and knowledge production. Consequently, critical literacy has become particularly important within adult and lifelong learning as learners seek to participate meaningfully and ethically within digitally mediated societies. Drawing on Freirean pedagogy and transformative learning theory, this paper revisits critical literacy as a reflective, emancipatory, and socially situated practice grounded in critical consciousness and perspective transformation. It explores how digital technologies can support the development of critical literacy when embedded within learner-centred pedagogies. It further examines the pedagogical potential of digital tools including digital badges, Turnitin Clarity, and Gather to foster reflection, dialogue, writing development, communicative learning, and evaluative judgement. Rather than positioning technology as inherently transformative, this paper argues that it is the pedagogical framing of digital tools that determines their capacity to support critical engagement and learner agency, preserving human criticality within AI-mediated educational systems. This paper highlights the continuing relevance of transformative learning theory in contemporary digital contexts and argues that critical reflection and dialogic learning remain central to adult education in an era shaped by artificial intelligence and digital communication. It concludes that critically informed digital pedagogies can create meaningful opportunities for learners to develop the reflective and evaluative capacities necessary for informed participation in contemporary digital society.

TI A Comparative Assessment of Homeschooling Experiences, Practices,
   Support, and Arithmetical Attainments in Greece and the UK
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE homeschooling; special educational needs; disabilities; arithmetical
   attainments; parental experiences; Greece; UK
ID CHILDREN; HOME
AB This preliminary study aims to compare homeschooling in Greece and the UK in terms of experiences, arithmetical attainments, parental motivations, implementation practices, and support structures. For this purpose, we employed a multiple case study design, enrolling a total of five Greek and fifteen British homeschooling families. Results suggested that the Greek parents primarily chose homeschooling in response to their child's severe and complex medical needs and reported limited access to support systems. British parents provided more varied motivations, higher engagement with educational resources, and stronger integration into informal support networks. The sample of UK children demonstrated higher arithmetical attainment than the Greek sample. Cultural, structural, and regulatory factors appear to shape homeschooling experiences differently across the Greek and UK educational systems. Differences also emerged in terms of daily routines, access to support, and parental confidence. Results are discussed in relation to educational provision and policy development.

TI From Experimentation to Integration: How Professional Learning Groups
   Supported Independent School Teachers' Use of Generative AI
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative AI; technology acceptance model; teacher professional
   learning; educational innovation
ID TECHNOLOGY ACCEPTANCE MODEL; ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE
AB This article investigates how secondary teachers in two Australian independent schools engaged with generative AI (GenAI) tools to support teaching and learning. Using a qualitative case study methodology and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a sensitising framework, the study examines teachers' perceptions of usefulness, ease of use, and the challenges they encountered. Over three months, teachers participated in professional learning groups supported by university-led workshops and peer collaboration. The findings show that teachers' adoption of GenAI was not simply determined by tool availability or perceived efficiency. Rather, teachers' perceptions of usefulness and ease of use developed through cycles of experimentation, prompt refinement, peer sharing, and ethical reflection. The study contributes a contextually grounded interpretation of TAM by showing how collaborative professional learning shaped teachers' movement from initial experimentation towards more purposeful pedagogical integration. The findings suggest the value of considering how perceptions of usefulness and ease of use may develop over time through sustained engagement with GenAI.

TI University Students' Perceptions of Gamified Learning: A Comparison of
   Students with and Without Prior Experience
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE gamification; student perceptions; higher education; comparative
   analysis
AB The growing integration of gamification and digital technologies in higher education has led to increasing interest in students' perceptions of gamified learning environments. While existing research predominantly focuses on the effectiveness of gamification in enhancing motivation, engagement, and learning outcomes, less attention has been paid to differences between students' expectations and actual experiences. This study addresses this gap by comparing the perceptions of students with and without prior experience with gamified learning. A quantitative survey was conducted among 189 engineering students from a technical university using a structured questionnaire based on a five-point Likert scale. Two groups were compared: students with prior experience in gamified learning and those without such experience. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, the Mann-Whitney U test and Cliff's Delta. The findings suggest that prior experience was associated primarily with differences in perceived learning interest. A statistically significant difference was identified only for this dimension, with students who had prior experience reporting significantly higher levels of agreement regarding the ability of gamification to make learning more interesting. For the remaining dimensions, including motivation, engagement, involvement, enjoyment of competitions, and distraction, differences between the groups were observed but were not statistically significant. Reliability analysis indicated higher internal consistency among students with prior experience. However, no formal statistical comparison of the Cronbach's alpha coefficients was performed, and this finding should therefore be interpreted with caution. The study compares the perceptions of students with and without prior experience of gamified learning and discusses the findings from a theoretical perspective. Rather than directly measuring expectations, the findings provide a conceptual interpretation of how prior experience may be associated with students' perceptions of gamified learning and offer implications for the design and implementation of gamification in higher education.

TI AI-Supported Interactive Flipped Learning in Language Education: A
   Multidimensional Perspective
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE flipped learning; AI-supported; language education; multidimensional
ID CLASSROOM
AB The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has not only challenged conventional learning environments but has also encouraged the adoption of innovative and active pedagogical approaches, such as flipped learning, particularly when these technologies are effectively integrated. In this context, the present study examined students' perceptions of the effectiveness of AI-supported flipped learning in fostering cognitive, affective, and 21st-century competencies among English Education students at Sultan Qaboos University (SQU). A convergent mixed-methods design was used. Quantitative data were obtained using a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire administered to 60 undergraduate English Education students, while qualitative data were collected from students' reflective journals. The findings revealed that students generally perceived AI-supported flipped learning as positively supporting cognitive outcomes, affective outcomes, and twenty-first-century competencies. Motivation and engagement emerged as the strongest affective outcomes, while students also reported positive perceptions of cognitive development, collaboration, digital competence, and self-regulated learning. Correlation analysis further demonstrated significant positive relationships among all six constructs, with the strongest associations observed between motivation and digital competence and between cognitive outcomes and both motivation and collaboration. Qualitative findings emphasized increased engagement, deeper learning experiences, and positive attitudes toward flipped learning. Despite minor challenges related to workload and time management, overall student perceptions were highly positive. The study concluded that students perceived AI-supported flipped learning as an effective pedagogical approach for fostering academic achievement and essential 21st-century skills in higher education.

TI Informed Undergraduate Teaching Reform in the Building Materials Course
   Under New Agricultural Science: Based on the "One Core, Two Channels,
   and Four-Dimensional Drivers" Model
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; new agricultural science; building materials;
   research-informed teaching; curriculum reform
ID STATISTICS
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new opportunities for evidence retrieval, data interpretation, experimentation, feedback, and evidence-based problem solving in engineering education. This study developed a theoretically grounded "One Core, Two Channels, and Four-Dimensional Drivers" model to align AI, research-informed teaching, and New Agricultural Science within an undergraduate Building Materials course, and examined preliminary between-cohort outcome differences. A 32-teaching-hour nonequivalent comparison-group study involving 123 students was conducted. The intervention integrated research-informed cases, rural and green-construction contexts, purpose-specific AI-supported tasks, laboratory work, staged projects, and multidimensional assessment. The intervention cohort scored higher on the final examination (mean difference 8.00 points; Hedges' g = 1.19), experimental grade (4.67; g = 1.28), continuous-assessment score (35.56; g = 3.34), and course evaluation (1.63 on a 70-point scale; g = 0.58). Project innovation data were highly sparse. The continuous-assessment difference should not be interpreted as a standalone AI literacy effect because structured AI-learning opportunities differed by condition, and equivalence of non-examination scoring was not independently established. Given nonrandomized allocation, the absence of participant-level baseline measures, and unequal measurement strength across outcomes, the findings represent preliminary between-cohort evidence rather than causal treatment effects.

TI Resident Selection in the Signaling Era: A Survey of General Surgery
   Program Directors
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE preference signaling; general surgery; graduate medical education;
   residency recruitment; program director
AB OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to characterize program director experiences with and attitudes toward preference signaling after transitioning from 5 to 15 signals per applicant. This study also aimed to determine how program director experiences and attitudes were influenced by program type and competitiveness. DESIGN: An anonymous, voluntary survey was distributed in 2025 to all general surgery program directors with publicly available email addresses (n = 348). Survey items explored program director experiences with signaling. Descriptive analysis was performed. SETTING: Electronic survey administered to general surgery program directors. PARTICIPANTS: Forty PDs (55% university-based programs, 77.5% became PDs pre-signaling) completed the survey. RESULTS: All PDs used signals when reviewing applicants for interview: 42.5% reviewed all signaled applicants, 22.5% only reviewed signaled applicants, and 25% used signals as part of a scoring system to decide who to fully review. The majority of PDs (61%) felt that signals overall decreased application review time. Compared to 5 signals, 15 signals further decreased application review time and the number of applications fully reviewed. There were no statistically discernible differences in signaling practices by program type or competitiveness. All PDs supported the continuation of signaling, rating the current system of 15 signals as highly beneficial both to applicants (mean = 7.1/10) and programs (mean = 8.2/ 10). Further, while only about half (58%) of PDs were historically transparent regarding use of signals in application screening, the majority (84%) endorsed full transparency moving forward. CONCLUSIONS: In the 15-signal era, general surgery PDs used signals in a variety of ways during residency recruitment. PDs are supportive of the current signaling system, with more than half finding that the increase to 15 signals improved application review efficiency. Moving forward, transparency from programs will be crucial to ensure applicants understand how their signals are interpreted in the recruitment process. ( J Surg Ed 83:104102. (c) 2026 The Author(s). AB As AI enters schools, the staff it affects are increasingly urged to consult conversational AI about whether to adopt it-yet that AI is built by organizations with a commercial stake in adoption, raising the possibility that systems consulted by skeptical users are predisposed to encourage it. We test this with a fixed prompt in which a rural Montana K-12 school administrative aide voices two concerns: that AI may threaten her job, and that AI companies do not have people like her in mind. Ten frontier models from ten laboratories are each sampled 500 times at temperature 0.7. The 5000 responses are scored by a blind three-model AI panel (three model families, two openness regimes) on a four-dimension rubric validated against researcher hand-scoring (quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa 0.704-0.932 at consensus, clearing a pre-specified kappa >= 0.70 threshold). Mean consensus composite scores range from 3.85 (Claude Sonnet 4.6) to 7.52 (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview) on an eight-point scale. The variation concentrates not in whether concerns are recognized (every model acknowledges them) but in what follows: eight of ten models redirect toward AI engagement, upskilling, or adaptation, often explicitly advocating adoption of the technology the persona named as a threat. This is neither the deference the sycophancy literature predicts nor the demographic divergence the political-bias literature documents; it is concern acknowledgment followed by systematic redirection, which the cross-model spread establishes as a model-dependent design outcome-not an inevitable property of large language models as a category. Because school staff increasingly consult such systems about adoption, the finding bears on trust calibration and AI literacy in education.

TI Integrating economic podcasts into online discussion forums:
   Instructional framework and evidence from community college courses
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF ECONOMICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Podcasts; Economics Education; Online Discussion Forums; Instructional
   Framework; Asynchronous Learning; Community Colleges
ID STUDENT ENGAGEMENT; MATH SKILLS; DETERMINANTS; PERFORMANCE; MOTIVATION;
   LECTURES; SUCCESS
AB This paper examines the integration of economic-themed podcasts into online discussion forums in asynchronous introductory economics courses at a community college. The study develops and implements a structured instructional framework across multiple course sections over five academic terms, in which weekly podcast episodes were paired with guided discussion prompts and peer interaction requirements. Drawing on survey responses and course performance data, we examine how students' perceived learning and engagement are associated with academic outcomes. TI Development of a relational reasoning skills test: psychometric evidence
   from validity and reliability analyses
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Reasoning skills; Relational reasoning; Test development; Test validity;
   Diagnostic branched-tree question
ID VALIDATION; STUDENTS
AB This study reports the development and initial validation of a relational reasoning test for middle school students in science/STEM education. The instrument consists of diagnostically branched tree items, scored 0-3, representing the first empirically evaluated implementation of this format in the assessment of relational reasoning in science contexts. The Relational Reasoning Skills Test (RRST) is grounded in Piaget's theory of formal operations. Evidence for its psychometric properties was examined using classical test theory analyses, including item difficulty and discrimination indices. The final version consists of 10 items, with a Cronbach's alpha coefficient of .70, which is generally considered acceptable for early-stage instrument development. Exploratory factor analysis indicated a two-factor solution explaining 44.60% of the variance, with factor loadings ranging above .40. Confirmatory factor analysis results indicated an acceptable model fit for the proposed structure. Overall, the findings suggest that the RRST may provide preliminary evidence for assessing relational reasoning in science contexts. However, further validation studies with larger and more diverse samples are required to strengthen the psychometric support and generalizability of the instrument. Future research may also explore the integration of diagnostically branched items into adaptive and technology-enhanced assessment systems.

TI Professional identity and occupational demands during wartime and their
   implications for burnout: The case of early childhood educators
SO EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE Professional identity; Occupational demands; Wartime; Burnout; Social
   support; Early childhood educators (ECEs); Childcare workers
ID STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELS; WAR
AB Armed conflict poses severe challenges to early childhood education systems and places exceptional psychological and emotional demands on early childhood educators (ECE). The present study examines the relationship between professional identity and burnout among ECEs during wartime, while integrating unique war-related job demands, children's behavior, occupational perception, social support, and psychological capital, within a comprehensive theoretical model. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources and Conservation of Resources frameworks, mix method research conducted among 181 ECEs in Israel during the ongoing war. Caregiving demands during wartime, perceived effects of the war on children's behavior, and the perceived impact of the war on occupational meaning were measured using validated and newly developed instruments. Structural equation modeling revealed that the overall model demonstrated acceptable fit. While the direct effect of professional identity on burnout was not significant, occupational perception during wartime significantly moderated this relationship, such that a stronger sense of meaning and mission enhanced the protective role of professional identity. In addition, social support buffered the relationship between caregiving demands and burnout. Psychological capital was positively associated with key resources but did not directly moderate burnout relationships. Qualitative findings further emphasized meaning at work as the dominant theme in educators' wartime experience. The results highlight the complex resource-demand dynamics shaping burnout during armed conflict and underscore the central role of occupational meaning and social support. Implications for theory, practice, and emergency preparedness training in early childhood education are discussed.

TI Explaining gender differences in mathematics achievement: Cross-country
   evidence from PISA
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Education development; Gender gap; Machine learning; Mathematics
   achievement; PISA
ID TEST-SCORES; COLLEGE; SCHOOL; MATH; DIVERSITY; STUDENT; CHOICES; GAP
AB This study examines factors associated with gender differences in mathematics achievement using data from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2018, covering secondary school students across 77 countries. The analysis focuses on disparities in both average performance and high achievement and considers a broad set of student, family, and school characteristics. To capture nonlinear relationships and interactions, the study employs machine-learning methods complemented by regression analyses that provide complementary parametric evidence on the main patterns. The results indicate that differences in students' career expectations are strongly associated with gender gaps in mathematics achievement across countries. Additional factors-including perceived task difficulty, learning autonomy, parental socioeconomic status, and exposure to bullying-are also systematically related to performance, with associations that vary across the achievement distribution. These findings suggest that gender disparities in mathematics are closely linked to differences in aspirations, learning environments, and social contexts rather than to inherent differences in ability. While the analysis does not establish causal relationships, it provides consistent cross-country evidence on the relative importance of key correlates of gender gaps. The results highlight the potential importance of policies that support students' aspirations and improve learning environments, particularly in efforts to broaden participation in mathematics-intensive fields.

TI Bridging learning and practice: Business simulations, soft skills, and
   the future of management education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Blended learning; Business simulation games; Learning transfer; Soft
   skills; Accounting education; Experiential learning
ID SPORT MANAGEMENT
AB Management education is increasingly expected to move beyond disciplinary knowledge and conventional skill acquisition toward learning environments that cultivate adaptability, collaboration, applied judgment, and the capacity to transfer knowledge across complex real-world settings. This study critically reflects on this transition by examining how learning-oriented teaching practices embedded within a blended learning environment and supported by a business simulation game shape students' perceptions of learning transfer and soft skill development. The study involved 55 senior undergraduate accounting students enrolled in a compulsory Enterprise Gaming course at a large nonprofit higher education institution in China. Data were collected through a structured survey using a 0-10 response scale and analyzed in Stata using descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha reliability analysis, Pearson correlations, and multivariate regression. Three composite measures were developed: the Tool Familiarity Index (TFI), Transfer Capacity Index (TCI), and Soft Skills Index (SSI). The findings suggest that students perceived simulation-based blended learning as supportive of both the application of academic knowledge to practical contexts and the development of transferable competencies, particularly adaptability and collaboration. Regression results showed that TCI and TFI jointly explained approximately 66.7% of the variance in SSI, with the overall model statistically significant at the 5% level, although the individual predictors were significant only at the 10% threshold. Rather than treating employability as a narrow collection of skills, the findings highlight the importance of designing management education around experiential learning, reflective practice, technological engagement, and contextual knowledge transfer. The study therefore contributes to wider debates about the future of management education by suggesting that curricula should move beyond syllabus completion toward integrated learning experiences that connect disciplinary knowledge, professional capabilities, and changing workplace expectations. Because the evidence is based on student perceptions rather than objective measures of performance, the conclusions should be interpreted cautiously and further tested through longitudinal and multi-institutional research.

TI Post-PandemicLearning Deficits: Declining BiochemistryPerformance among
   First-Year University Students
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic achievement; COVID-19; STEM education; remote education;
   learningdeficits
AB The COVID-19 pandemic led to an emergency transition from face-to-face to remote education, disrupting traditional learning and assessment methods. This study evaluates the impact of this transition by comparing student performance in in-person biochemistry courses for first-year undergraduate students before (2019) and after (2022) the pandemic at the University of Sao Paulo. A cross-sectional analysis was conducted using 21 identical exam questions from two biochemistry courses: Biochemistry and Biophysics (first semester) and Biochemistry of Exercise (second semester). Student scores were analyzed using descriptive statistics, categorical distributions, and Generalized Linear Models (GLM). In 2022, scores were significantly lower in 11 exam questions, compared with 2019. Histograms of mean scores described a significant decline in student performance, with the proportion of students achieving passing grades decreasing by approximately 50%. When analyzed separately, a significant performance decline was observed only in Biochemistry of Exercise, a second-semester course focused on functional and integrative concepts. The performance of first-year university students in biochemistry declined in 2022, after resuming in-person classes, compared with 2019. These findings highlight potential long-term learning deficits from the pandemic years and underscore the need for targeted educational interventions to address post-pandemic academic challenges.

TI An UndergraduateBiochemistry Lab Exploring Elastin-LikePolypeptide
   Behavior and Degradation: From Purification to Proteolysis
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Biochemistry; Hands-On
   Learning/Manipulatives; Proteins/Peptides; Electrophoresis; Laboratory
   Instruction
ID BIOCHEMISTRY; POLYPEPTIDES; STRATEGIES; SEQUENCE
AB The development of smart biomaterials that mimic the native extracellular matrix forms the basis for many innovations within the field of regenerative medicine. Elastin-like polypeptides (ELPs) are widely used in biomaterials due to their unique physicochemical properties. ELPs exhibit lower critical solution temperature behavior, meaning that, above their specific transition temperature, these polypeptides reversibly phase-separate and start to aggregate. Furthermore, their production via recombinant DNA techniques enables the incorporation of bioactive motifs such as enzyme-cleavable domains. Because of their attractive properties and broad applicability, the purification and characterization of ELPs are very relevant. Therefore, the goal of this laboratory experiment is to purify and characterize an ELP and to investigate its enzymatic degradation. Purification is done via inverse transition cycling, a technique that utilizes the thermoresponsive properties of ELPs. Students analyze the purity of the various fractions obtained during the purification process using sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE). Additionally, they incubate the purified ELP with a protease and evaluate the success of the degradation. This practical provides students with both a theoretical background and practical experience in the fields of recombinant protein production and physical chemistry, which can be valuable for their future career paths in biochemistry, biomedical sciences, bioengineering, and biology.

TI Administrative Evaluation Completion Is Weakly Associated With
   Trainee-Rated Teaching Effectiveness: A Retrospective Cross-Sectional
   Study
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE competency based medical education; faculty development; learner
   assessment; end of rotation assessment
AB OBJECTIVE: We sought to determine whether faculty End of Rotation evaluation (EOR-e) completion is associated with trainee-rated teaching performance. Our hypothesis was that timely assessment completion would correlate with stronger teaching performance. DESIGN: We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional study of faculty surgeons assigned >5 EOR-e over academic years 2023 to 2024 and 2024 to 2025. Outcomes included EOR-e completion rate, completion-lag time, and trainee-rated teaching effectiveness. Associations were examined using nonparametric analyses and linear and logistic regression models. SETTING: A General Surgery Residency Program within a tertiary care academic hospital. PARTICIPANTS: We reviewed data from faculty surgeons who were assigned at least 5 EOR-e. RESULTS: Our cohort of 120 surgeons was assigned a median of 9 (IQR 6-20) EOR-e, completing a median of 0 (IQR 0-15). Only 25% (30/120) completed all assigned evaluations. Surgeons received a median of 17 (IQR 7-30) resident evaluations and a median teaching score of 4.3 (IQR 4.0-4.6). Faculty completing all EOR-e had higher teaching scores than those who did not (median 4.5 vs 4.3, p < 0.001). Teaching score correlated modestly with EOR-e completion rate (Spearman's r = 0.27, p < 0.005) but not with completion-lag time. Controlling for the total number of EOR-e assigned, on multivariable linear regression, neither EOR-e completion number nor EOR-e completion percentage was significantly associated with average teaching score. Greater numbers of assigned EORe independently predicted a perfect completion rate. CONCLUSIONS: EOR-e completion reflects clustered participation in creating the artifacts of summative evaluation among a small subset of faculty. Teaching scores were modestly associated with completion, but this relationship was incomplete, indicating that evaluation engagement and teaching quality are related but distinct constructs. Using assessment behavior as a proxy for teaching effectiveness risks conflating structural engagement with pedagogical excellence and should be used with caution in faculty assessment. TI The longitudinal relationships between scientific motivation and
   critical thinking disposition: A cross-lagged panel network analysis
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical thinking disposition; Scientific motivation; Intrinsic
   motivation and personal relevance; Self-efficacy; Cross-lagged panel
   network analysis
ID SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY; INTRINSIC MOTIVATION; STUDENTS; EFFICACY;
   SCIENCE; SKILLS; ELEMENTARY; VALIDATION; ENGAGEMENT; CLASSROOM
AB Based on self-determination theory (SDT), meta-theory of personality (MTP), and social cognitive theory (SCT), scientific motivation (SM) and critical thinking disposition (CTD) may be reciprocally linked, yet longitudinal evidence remains limited. This study used cross-lagged panel network analysis to examine SM-CTD associations among 3898 students across upper elementary, junior high, and senior high schools. The overall network revealed bidirectional relationships between intrinsic motivation and personal relevance (IMPR) and inquisitiveness (INQ), IMPR and self-confidence (SC), and self-efficacy (SE) and SC. Upper elementary networks showed reciprocal links between IMPR and INQ, and between IMPR and SC. Junior high networks retained these and added bidirectional paths between IMPR and analyticity (ANA), and SC and SE. Senior high networks uniquely revealed a reciprocal link between SE and systematicity (SYS). These findings highlight IMPR and SE as potential intervention targets. Furthermore, stage-varying reciprocal relationships suggest that educational interventions should be tailored to specific developmental stages. Educational relevance statement: Understanding the co-development of scientific motivation and critical thinking disposition is vital, as modern educational frameworks increasingly demand the integration of motivational drivers and critical thinking dispositions. While traditional instructional models often assume a unidirectional influence between motivation and critical thinking dispositions, our findings suggest that they function as a mutually reinforcing, bidirectional system. Specifically, we identified intrinsic motivation and personal relevance (IMPR) and scientific self-efficacy (SE) as the core functional hubs driving this co-development. Consequently, rather than dispersing efforts across all cognitive traits, educators may achieve broader impact by focusing interventions on these specific targets. Connecting science curricula to students' real-world experiences (boosting IMPR) and designing achievable inquiry tasks (building SE) can naturally activate other critical thinking dispositions. Importantly, our cross-stage findings indicate that these dynamics are not uniform across age groups. Therefore, interventions should ideally evolve alongside students' development. Such efforts should begin by fostering foundational curiosity and self-confidence in elementary school, build upon this foundation to cultivate analytical thinking in junior high school, and ultimately shift toward systematic reasoning within autonomy-supportive environments in senior high school.

TI Perspectives on barriers and facilitators influencing twinned nurse
   leader partnerships during implementation of the Rwanda human resources
   for health program
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Global health; Nursing leadership; Workforce development; Capacity
   building; Twining partnernships
ID INTERNATIONAL ACADEMIC PARTNERSHIPS; 1ST 5 YEARS; CAPACITY;
   COLLABORATION; MEDICINE; MODEL
AB Background: The global nursing workforce shortage disproportionately affects low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), accounting for 89% of this deficit, with inadequately trained nurses due to limited resources. Addressing this shortage requires nurse leaders who are essential in education and training. One strategy to address this global health challenge is forming twining partnerships between high-income and LMIC institutions. The Rwanda Human Resources for Health (HRH) initiative (2012-2019) exemplified this partnership between Rwanda's Ministry of Health and U.S. academic institutions. However, little is known about the factors that affect the effectiveness of these global health nursing partnerships. Method: A qualitative descriptive approach was used to explore barriers and facilitators influencing twinned partnerships among global health nurse leaders in the HRH program. A purposeful sample of U.S. Faculty Nurse Leaders (USFNL) and Rwandan Nurse Leaders (RNL) who participated from 2013 to 2018 was recruited. The study was conducted at two teaching and referral hospitals and one University in Rwanda. Using Upvall and Leffers' revised conceptual model of partnership and sustainability in global health, data were collected through semi-structured interviews, document analysis, and observations. Results: The sample comprised 10 USFNL and 10 RNL (10 dyads). Participants were aged 30-80 years, with Associate to PhD education levels. Language barriers, particularly in clinical settings, presented limitations in knowledge transfer. In contrast, role modeling by USFNL emerged as a consistent, valuable facilitator in empowering RNL toward sustainable skill development. A clear framework and guidelines were absent, resulting in inadequate monitoring and evaluation. USFNL and RNL notably initiated the first master's nursing program at the University of Rwanda. Conclusion: This qualitative exploration revealed that twinning partnerships led to collaborative nursing workforce development, challenged by language barriers. Future global health nurse leadership initiatives should emphasize the proper use of frameworks that support effective monitoring and evaluation and align with cultural and historical considerations.

TI Predicting training outcomes for developmental dyslexia from EEG data
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Dyslexia; Learning disabilities; Reading; EEG; Machine learning;
   Training
ID ELECTRIC-STIMULATION SAFETY; SPATIAL ATTENTION; FREQUENCY; OSCILLATIONS;
   DYNAMICS; NETWORK; COMPREHENSION; CONNECTIVITY; SPEED; AREA
AB Developmental dyslexia (DD) is characterised by lower-than-average reading abilities and is diagnosed in approximately 10% of individuals. The societal barriers may limit professional fulfilment and psychological wellbeing of individuals with DD, calling for the development of effective interventions to counteract them. As DD is associated with challenges in both phonological and visuo-attentional domains, different longitudinal training approaches were developed to strengthen them. However, they require a considerable amount of personal, social and economic resources and the outcomes may vary depending on individual differences in behavioural and neurophysiological functionality. Hence, predicting training outcomes might help in developing personalised treatment protocols and optimising the use of resources. In the present work we applied machine learning to resting-state EEG to predict longitudinal training outcomes in adults with DD enrolled in a randomized clinical trial. In particular, one group received a visuoattentional training combined with transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), another group received visuo-attentional training with sham/placebo stimulation, and the third group received a phonological training with sham/placebo stimulation. The improvement in text reading speed was associated with spectral power in low-beta and individual frequencies in the alpha (IAF) and beta (IBF) bands, while the improvement in pseudoword reading was associated with IBF. The findings highlight the potential of capturing neural markers of treatment responsiveness in DD. Future studies should focus on the generalisability of predictive models to realworld settings, while investigating whether specific EEG markers predict responsiveness to distinct remediation protocols, thus supporting the development of personalised interventions.

TI Dissociation between cognitive deficits and reading mechanisms in
   Chinese children with comorbid dyslexia and ADHD
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Chinese reading; ADHD; Developmental dyslexia; Comorbidity; Rapid
   automatized naming; Morphological awareness
ID ATTENTION-DEFICIT/HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER; AUTOMATIZED NAMING RAN;
   MORPHOLOGICAL AWARENESS; DEVELOPMENTAL DYSLEXIA; HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER;
   ORTHOGRAPHIC KNOWLEDGE; GENDER-DIFFERENCES; VISUAL-SEARCH; PREVALENCE;
   DISABILITY
AB Background: Developmental dyslexia (DD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often co-occur, but the cognitive profile of their comorbidity and the mechanisms supporting reading performance remain unclear. This study aimed to characterize cognitive profiles associated with DD, ADHD, and their comorbidity, and to determine whether different cognitive mechanisms support reading performance across diagnostic groups. Methods: A matched sample of 200 Mandarin-speaking children was selected from a screened cohort of 2003 students, including four groups: typically developing (TD), DD-only, ADHD-only, and comorbid DD and ADHD (n = 50 per group). Participants completed assessments of reading fluency and accuracy, orthographic knowledge, phonological awareness, morphological awareness, rapid automatized naming (RAN), visual attention, and processing speed. Results: Children with DD showed broad impairments in reading-related measures compared with TD and ADHD-only children. Discriminant analyses revealed that phonological and morphological awareness primarily differentiated DD, whereas non-linguistic measures distinguished ADHD. Notably, RAN uniquely differentiated comorbid DD and ADHD from DD-only, with the comorbid group showing the greatest impairment. However, regression analyses revealed a dissociation between core cognitive deficits and reading mechanisms: the contribution of RAN to reading fluency was reduced in the comorbid group, whereas morphological awareness was a stronger predictor of character reading accuracy in the comorbid group. Conclusions: These findings suggest a distinct cognitive profile in comorbid DD and ADHD, with altered RAN-reading associations and greater reliance on morphological awareness. This pattern highlights the need for assessment and intervention approaches that address both core deficits and compensatory resources.

TI Does a task-based test promote TBLT test preparation materials? The case
   of Hong Kong
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Task-based language teaching; Materials analysis; Washback; Second
   language learning; English as a second language textbooks
ID TEXTBOOK; REPRESENTATIONS; IMPLEMENTATION; CULTURE; ENGLISH
AB Despite the growing popularity of task-based language teaching (TBLT) and assessment, the extent to which task-based tests promote TBLT preparation materials remains unexplored. To fill this gap, this study examines the alignment between East's (2021) four-criterion definition of task and materials designed for preparing learners to complete a task-based high-stakes exam in Hong Kong. Three sets of widely used test preparation English language textbooks were analysed in terms of task criteria. We found that less than thirty percent of the textbook activities fully met the definition of task across the series. However, forty percent satisfied three out of four task criteria, with communicative outcome being the least achieved criterion. In addition, more than half the sections provided language-related and exam-related information, indicating the existence of washback from the exam. We interpreted the overemphasis on examination strategies and information provision as negative washback. However, absence of explicit grammar instruction in the textbooks could be seen as a source of positive washback. Our findings highlight the challenge of introducing task-based materials, even where TBLT is the recommended pedagogic and testing approach.

TI To bot or not: Do chatbots make better planning partners than humans for
   EFL group discussions?
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE TBLT; FLSA; FLE; WTC; Task planning; Artificial intelligence; Chatbots
ID LANGUAGE ANXIETY; 2ND-LANGUAGE; WILLINGNESS
AB While conversational AI is increasingly used in language classrooms, little is known about how different chatbot modalities compare with human partners in shaping learners' Foreign Language Speaking Anxiety (FLSA), Foreign Language Enjoyment (FLE), and Willingness to Communicate (WTC). Prior research has focused primarily on in-task interaction, leaving pre-task planning underexplored. This within-subject classroom study investigated how three planning partners-human peers, text-based chatbots, and voice-based chatbots-were associated with Japanese EFL learners' self-reported anxiety, enjoyment, confidence, motivation, and communicative readiness during pre-discussion planning and subsequent group discussions. These indicators were interpreted in relation to FLSA, FLE, and WTC. Eighty-four university students participated in a six-week intervention. Data were analyzed using repeated-measures MANOVA and thematic analysis of open-ended responses. Human partners received the highest ratings for enjoyment and self-reported participation but were also associated with higher evaluative-anxiety ratings. Text-based chatbots received the lowest ratings on several anxiety-related items and the highest ratings for perceived thinking time, indicating greater perceived affective and cognitive comfort. Voice-based chatbots were generally rated less positively, with qualitative responses highlighting technical limitations such as lag and recognition errors. Findings revealed distinct patterns of self-reported affective and communicative experience across the three planning partner conditions. Rather than identifying a universally optimal partner, the results highlight the potential value of integrating human and AI-supported planning to balance authenticity, engagement, and affective support. The study contributes to CALL and TBLT research by identifying differences in learners' experiences across human-peer, text-chatbot, and voice-chatbot planning conditions.

TI Evaluating effect of implementing Gibbs' reflective model on quality of
   nurses' documentation in emergency departments: a clinical trial
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Emergency nursing; Documentation; Models; Educational; Thinking;
   Education
ID NURSING DOCUMENTATION; INTERVENTIONS; EDUCATION; THINKING; RECORDS; CARE
AB Background Emergency nurses are responsible for providing and documenting immediate patient care. Documentation is a fundamental component of their professional practice; however, evidence indicates that documentation standards are often not adequately met. Therefore, innovative training approaches should be employed to improve the quality of nurses'documentation.The present study aims to evaluate the effect of implementing Gibbs'reflective model on the quality of documentation by emergency department nurses. Methods This cluster-randomized clinical trial was conducted on 68 nurses working in the emergency departments of two hospitals in the south of Fars Province, Iran, in 2024. Randomization was performed at the hospital level, with one hospital assigned to the intervention group and the other to the control group using simple random sampling. All eligible nurses in each hospital were then invited to participate (34 nurses per group).The intervention group participated in a documentation training program based on Gibbs'reflective model (four45 to 60 min sessions over four weeks).The control group received only the hospital's routine documentation training. Data were collected using a validated checklist to assess documentation quality before and one month after the intervention. Due to significant baseline differences between groups, change scores (post-test minus pre-test) were calculated and compared using appropriate statistical tests based on the normality of the data distribution. Results In the intervention group, structural quality changed from 12.28 +/- 1.54 to 15.47 +/- 0.89 (p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.65), content quality from 45.06 +/- 8.70 to 61.11 +/- 3.28 (p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.70), and overall quality from 57.47 +/- 9.51 to 76.58 +/- 3.61 (p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.82). In the control group, structural quality changed from 9.76 +/- 1.12 to 10.27 +/- 1.20 (p = 0.020, Cohen's d = 0.36), content quality from 34.53 +/- 3.89 to 38.29 +/- 3.80 (p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.68), and overall quality from 44.29 +/- 4.69 to 48.57 +/- 4.34 (p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.69). The mean change scores for overall documentation quality were 19.11 +/- 10.53 points in the intervention group versus 4.27 +/- 6.19 points in the control group (r = 0.67). For structural quality, the change was 3.19 +/- 1.93 vs. 0.51 +/- 1.41 points (r = 0.65), and for content quality, it was 16.05 +/- 9.45 vs. 3.76 +/- 5.51 points (r = 0.63). All between-group differences in change scores were statistically significant. Conclusion This study provides preliminary evidence that a Gibbs' reflective model-based training program may improve the quality of emergency nurses' documentation. However, given the baseline differences between groups and the cluster design, these findings should be interpreted with caution. Further multi-center studies with larger sample sizes and longer follow-up periods are recommended to confirm these results and establish generalizability of this educational approach.

TI Creating digital twins awareness in African higher education
   institutions: Bibliometric analysis from top influential countries
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital twins; Digital twin technologies; Higher education institutions;
   Africa; Bibliometric
ID TECHNOLOGY
AB Despite the proliferation of digital twin technology since its inception in the 1960s across engineering, aerospace, and business sectors, its adoption within higher education remains nascent. The transformative potential of digital twins in academic contexts is still evolving and not yet fully conceptualised by educators and administrators. This study addresses this gap through a bibliometric analysis of research trends from 2011 to 2025, drawing on 3463 articles from the Web of Science core collection. The findings delineate a global research landscape dominated by China, the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom in both publication volume and citation impact. This limited engagement underscores a substantial research disparity. The study concludes by advocating for strategic research collaborations between African higher education institutions and both these continental pioneers and global leaders, urging administrators to champion the integration of the digital twin paradigm to catalyse the development of Africa's digital educational ecosystem.

   mobilisation des habiletés reliées au processus d'enquête en milieu
   minoritaire francophone au secondaire

LA English
DT Article
DE Culture scientifique; processus d'enqu & ecirc;te; milieu minoritaire
   francophone; didactique des sciences au secondaire
ID TEACHERS CONCEPTIONS; INQUIRY; SCIENCE; TECHNOLOGY; VIEWS; INSTRUCTION;
   ENGAGEMENT; CHALLENGES; ATTITUDES; GAMES
AB Within the context of pedagogical innovation, using a qualitative research intervention, this study examined the effects of an intervention on the application of scientific inquiry skills. Such skills are essential for the acquisition of scientific literacy, deemed fundamental to the development of a 21st-century skill set. This intervention is necessary because PISA results show that francophone students in New Brunswick have significantly lower scientific literacy scores than other students in Canada. TI Groundwater Quality Assessment Using Indexing Approaches (WQI, MQI, and
   NPI) in the Meknes Region (Morocco)
SO CASE STUDIES IN THE ENVIRONMENT
LA English

ID DRINKING PURPOSE; RIVER-BASIN; GIS; AQUIFER; GEOCHEMISTRY; IRRIGATION;

AB In the Meknes region, groundwater is essential for drinking and irrigation. Facing growing agricultural and urban pressures, this study applies three complementary indices (Water Quality Index [WQI], Microbiological Quality Index [MQI], and Nitrate Pollution Index [NPI]) to provide an evidence-based environmental diagnosis. From December 2016 to November 2017, 14 wells were sampled. Physicochemical and bacteriological analyses followed standardized protocols. The assessment combined the WQI, MQI, and NPI with multivariate statistical analyses. Physicochemical quality complies with Moroccan standards, except at well W13. Systematic microbiological contamination (fecal coliforms, streptococci) was detected at all sites. The WQI ranged from 26.57 to 191.26 (high spatial variability), while the MQI (3.33-4.0) confirmed widespread fecal pollution. The contrast between good chemical quality and extensive bacterial contamination demonstrates that compliance with physicochemical standards does not guarantee water safety. Well W13, located near a landfill, illustrates the impact of point pollution sources. This study identifies priority sites (W7, W13), establishes a multi-index baseline, and proposes transferable tools for other semi-arid regions. It recommends preventive measures: well protection, improved waste management, and regular bacteriological monitoring.

TI Digital Competence and Learner Engagement in AI-Mediated Higher
   Education: A Mixed-Methods Study of the Moderating Role of Cognitive
   Load in EFL Contexts
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-mediated EFL learning; cognitive load; digital competence;
   engagement; higher education; mixed-methods design
ID INSTRUCTIONAL-DESIGN; ARCHITECTURE
AB With the growing integration of artificial intelligence into higher education, digital competence has become central to learners' meaningful engagement in AI-mediated learning environments. However, its role may be constrained by the cognitive load generated when students navigate complex digital tools, resources, and learning tasks. This study, therefore, adopted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design to examine whether digital competence was associated with learners' engagement and whether cognitive load moderated this relationship. Quantitative data were collected from 339 Chinese university EFL learners through a questionnaire measuring digital competence, cognitive load and engagement. Regression analysis showed that cognitive load was negatively associated with engagement and significantly moderated the relationship between digital competence and engagement. In contrast, the direct effect of digital competence became non-significant after these factors were considered. In the subsequent qualitative phase, interviews with 10 learners were used to explain and extend these findings, showing that digital competence supported engagement through richer resources, personalised learning, autonomy, and interaction, whereas information overload, distraction, AI dependence, unequal access, and privacy concerns constrained meaningful engagement. These findings suggest that digital competence should not be understood as a stand-alone predictor of engagement, but as a conditional educational resource whose value depends on learners' ability to regulate cognitive load in AI-mediated learning contexts. The study contributes to current discussions on digital transformation in higher education by highlighting the need for pedagogical support, critical AI literacy and equitable learning conditions that help students engage meaningfully with emerging technologies.

AB Background The transition to adulthood for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ID) is a complex process marked by significant challenges for families.Method Using semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis with 17 parents of individuals with ID, this qualitative research examined transition obstacles, support systems, and emotional responses impacting family reorganization and life projects (LP) definition.Results Parents reported difficulties in planning and implementing LP due to standardized approaches, a lack of structured employment pathways, and challenges navigating fragmented services. Emotionally, parents exhibited resilience, pride, and hope, alongside anxiety, frustration, and powerlessness regarding their children's future and the adequacy of support.Conclusions The findings emphasize the need for holistic, family-centered support systems addressing practical and emotional needs. The LP framework is promising, but successful implementation requires bridging systemic gaps, enhancing service coordination, and empowering parents to improve outcomes for individuals with ID.

TI Unveiling the "Gray Zone": Characterizing Young People's Moderate STEM
   Identities
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SCIENCE TEACHING
LA English
DT Article
DE cluster analysis; gender; high school; STEM identity
ID SCIENCE; EXPERIENCES; PERFORMANCES; STUDENTS
AB Understanding how students identify with STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics) is crucial for fostering broader and more equitable participation within these fields. While existing research has focused on students who either strongly identify with STEM or disengage from it, this study explores the moderate STEM identities of students who occupy a "gray zone" between these extremes. These students, aged 12-16, exhibit moderate STEM identities configured through varying degrees of interest, competence, self-efficacy, and aspirations across STEM and non-STEM domains, and further modulated by patterns of perceived recognition. Using data from a sample of 1004 students across 64 schools in Catalonia, Spain, we conducted a hierarchical cluster analysis to explore patterns in self-identification and related constructs. The analyses revealed three clusters of students with moderate STEM identities. Cluster 3, predominantly male, displayed strong interest and recognition in mathematics and physical education but leaned toward non-STEM aspirations. Clusters 4 and 5, mainly female, showed high academic performance in STEM subjects but reported lower self-efficacy, recognition, and STEM-related aspirations. In particular, Cluster 4 displayed a strong alignment with the arts, while Cluster 5 preferred languages and social sciences. These patterns suggest that while these students have the potential to pursue STEM pathways, their broader interests and perceived lack of recognition in STEM hinder their identity development. The study highlights the critical role of recognition in shaping STEM identities, particularly for girls, whose achievements in STEM are often overshadowed by their strengths in other domains. Additionally, mathematics plays a pivotal role in boys' moderate STEM identities, albeit often viewed instrumentally rather than as a career pathway. We discuss implications for educational practice, including the potential of STEAM approaches that integrate arts and creativity, along with more tailored forms of recognition in STEM teaching.

AB There is evidence to support that the diverse linguistic repertoire of emergent bilingual students enhances learning and development. TI Learning for Resilience: Embedding Ecosystem Services Literacy Across
   Disciplines to Support Sustainable Urban Futures

DT Article
DE urban green infrastructure; urban forest; ecosystem services;

ID BIODIVERSITY; INFRASTRUCTURE; CHALLENGES
AB Cities face increasing pressures from climate change, biodiversity loss, and accelerating urban expansion, making informed management of urban green infrastructure (UGI) essential for climate adaptation, public health, and long-term urban resilience. While UGI provides vital ecosystem services (ES), stakeholders, particularly university students as future planners, administrators, and civic actors, often have uneven understandings of their contributions to urban well-being and to evidence-based environmental governance. This case study examines how students from diverse academic disciplines perceive ES in B & abreve;neasa Forest, an urban forest in Bucharest exposed to development pressures, and engage in sustainability-related decision-making within a contested urban land-use context. In doing so, it positions universities as active intermediaries at the science-policy-society interface, contributing to more resilient and participatory urban environmental governance.

TI Parental support and its relationship with primary school children's
   science self-concept and interest: the mediating effect of growth
   mindset
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Parental Support; Motivation; Growth Mindset; Interest; Self-Concept;
   Science
ID INVOLVEMENT; MODEL; INTELLIGENCE; ACHIEVEMENT; GRADES
AB Students' motivational characteristics, such as growth mindset, self-concept, and interest are significant for their academic outcomes. Previous research shows that parental support plays a crucial role. Children who perceive parental support through homework assistance and encouragement show a more positive self-concept and subject-related interest. However, little is known about the mechanism underlying these relations, particularly the mediating role of children's growth mindset. As children's growth mindset is linked to both parental support and self-concept and interest, we assume that it might play an important role in the outlined relationships between parental support and both children's science self-concept and science interest. In order to address this research gap, children's growth mindset is examined as a mediator and thus as an explanation for the expected relations. We collected cross-sectional survey data from 401 primary school students (mean age 10.97 years; 46.88% female, 52.87% male, and 0.25% non-binary). We conducted structural equation modelling and mediation analysis. The results show significant relationships between parental support and primary students' science self-concept and interest, respectively. Growth mindset fully mediates the relation between parental support and science self-concept and partially mediates the relation with science interest. The present study reveals how parental support relates to children's science self-concept and science interest, highlighting children's growth mindset as a mediator. These findings show parental support as an important resource for children's growth mindset which is linked to other motivational characteristics that benefit their academic outcomes.

TI Gender disparities among general surgery residents' ACGME case logs
   develop over the course of training
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Surgical education; Gender disparities; Resident operative experience;
   Case logs; General surgery; Graduate medical education
AB Background Gender disparities in operative autonomy and case volume persist in general surgery residency training. Compared to their male counterparts, female trainees graduate with lower ACGME case log totals and perceive lower intraoperative autonomy. While prior studies of resident case logs have relied on summary level data from graduating residents, this study utilizes individual case level data to better elucidate when these disparities emerge in training, and how factors such as PGY level and faculty gender might also influence these differences.Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis of 569,761 ACGME case log entries from 473 general surgery residents and 415 attendings at six university-based programs from July 2016 to June 2023. Resident and attending gender were obtained via self-reported SIMPL data. We examined total case volumes and case roles (First Assistant, Surgeon Junior, Surgeon Chief, Teaching Assistant) stratified by resident gender, attending gender, and post-graduate year (PGY). A multilevel logistic regression was performed to understand the association between resident gender, attending gender, and case logging trends.Results Female residents logged 8.1% fewer cases on average (1153 vs 1255, p = 0.04). When cases were stratified by operative role and PGY level, female residents were more likely to log cases as "first assistant" with the disparity widening as PGY level increased: PGY3 OR 1.57, 95% CI [1.14, 2.16]; PGY4 OR 2.76, 95% CI [1.97, 3.88]; and PGY5 OR 3.72, 95% CI [2.42, 5.70]. There were no differences in primary surgeon case logging trends. Overall, cases involving female faculty were less likely to be logged as "first assistant" OR 0.79, 95% CI [0.59, 0.91], however, among senior residents this association was reversed: PGY4 OR 1.68, 95% CI [1.09, 2.59] and PGY5 OR 2.46, 95% CI [1.22, 4.99]. There were no significant differences identified in case logs for residents operating with concordant versus discordant attending gender dyads.Conclusion This study reveals how gender-based differences in case logging behavior and operative roles develop over the course of residency training, with female senior residents logging cases as first assistant significantly more than their male counterparts. Additional research-particularly using EPA-based assessment data and qualitative methods-is needed to determine whether these trends reflect true differences in operative opportunity, or merely differences in perception, or case logging practices. Local program-level monitoring of case log data may offer a pragmatic step toward identifying and addressing disparities in real time.

TI Artificial Intelligence in Primary Mathematics Education: A Systematic
   Review of Pedagogical Applications, Benefits, and Challenges
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Pedagogical challenges; Primary mathematics
   education; Teacher professional development; Technology integration
ID LEARNING-SYSTEM; GAME
AB This systematic literature review examines current research on the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in primary mathematics education, focusing on bibliometric patterns, pedagogical applications and outcomes, as well as implementation challenges and teacher-related considerations over the past five years. By analysing 30 peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2020 and 2024, the review examines bibliometric patterns, research aims, methods, educational settings, perceived benefits, implementation challenges, and professional development needs. Findings indicate a growing interest in AI-enhanced learning, particularly through intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive platforms, and AI-based diagnostics. Key benefits include improved conceptual understanding, personalised feedback, and increased learner engagement, while major challenges involve technical limitations, pedagogical misalignment, and infrastructural disparities. The review highlights a predominance of experimental studies conducted in face-to-face classroom settings alongside the emerging use of blended and online models. Notably, teacher readiness and policy flexibility are pivotal for effective implementation. This review contributes a field-specific synthesis that informs researchers, educators, and policymakers of the evolving landscape of AI in primary mathematics education, offering insights for evidence-based design and sustainable integration.

TI Stereotypes concerning first-generation university students and
   correlates in higher education
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE First-generation students; Stereotypes; Social identity threat;
   Well-being
ID SUBJECTIVE SOCIAL-STATUS; ACHIEVEMENT; PERFORMANCE; THREAT; MAINTENANCE;
   PSYCHOLOGY; COMPETENCE; ATTITUDES; HEALTH; SENSE
AB First-generation students are no longer a minority in higher education. However, their experience differs from continuing-generation students in several ways: For example, many of them report a lower sense of belonging and lower study satisfaction. Research has suggested different explaining mechanisms for these findings, one of which are negative stereotypes about the competence of students with lower social status, which, in turn, may lead to social identity threat. However, it is not clear whether and to which extend findings about social status related stereotypes translate to the group of first-generation students - especially not outside of the U.S. In this study, N = 459 German university students reported stereotypes about first-generation students, continuing-generation students, and students in general. Based on a mixed methods approach using qualitative and quantitative data, results indicated that other than expected, first-generation students were perceived as more competent than continuing-generation students and were also ascribed attributes like resilient, independent, and brave. Yet, first-generation students expected the competence of their group to be perceived as lower by others than continuing-generation students did. Furthermore, social identity threat was not related to sense of belonging in first-generation students and sense of belonging was not stronger related to study satisfaction for first-generation students either. However, first-generation students reported a lower sense of belonging than continuing-generation students. Limitations and practical implications are discussed.

TI The relationship between contract cheating and faculty member turnover
   intention in the United Arab Emirates
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL FOR EDUCATIONAL INTEGRITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Contract cheating; Higher education; Faculty perspectives; United Arab
   Emirates; Structural equation modeling
ID WEIGHTED LEAST-SQUARES; REASONED ACTION; SAMPLE-SIZE;
   MAXIMUM-LIKELIHOOD; SATISFACTION; PERFORMANCE; COMMITMENT; MODELS
AB This study investigates contract cheating (CC) in higher education institutions in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in relation to staff turnover intentions. Grounded in the theories of reasoned action and social responsibility, it aims to investigate the relationship between students' contract cheating-outsourcing assignments to other parties in exchange for money-and its effects on faculty members' inclinations to quit their jobs. A survey was distributed in six public and private universities in the UAE and completed by 259 participants. A structural equation model was used to examine the relationships between faculty members' turnover intentions and their recognition of CC, their perceptions of its long-term effects, and the current CC-related policies of their institutions. The results showed that recognition and long-term effects were positively related to CC, while institutional policy was negatively related. These components of CC are, in turn, positively related to faculty turnover intention. The paper concluded with relevant theoretical and practical recommendations for faculty, and higher education administrations and institutions.

TI Twice-Exceptional Students' Lived Experiences of Social-Emotional
   Autonomy Support in Primary School
SO ROEPER REVIEW-A JOURNAL ON GIFTED EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ADHD; autonomy support; gifted; well-being
ID ACADEMIC SELF-CONCEPT; GIFTED STUDENTS; BENEFITS; LEARNERS
AB The importance of centering twice-exceptional students' voices has been acknowledged by researchers, yet there remains a gap in lived experience research with gifted children who have ADHD. This doctoral study begins to close this gap, centering the voices of five young boys, identified as twice exceptional (gifted with ADHD), and their lived experiences of autonomy support in the social-emotional domain. Honoring the phenomenological methodology, the authors present the findings through four existential themes: lived corporeality (body), lived spatiality (space), lived temporality (time), and lived relationality (human relations). Results indicated that gifted students with ADHD were empowered to navigate affective challenges with a high level of self-awareness when they perceived social-emotional autonomy support. Recommendations for professional practice include greater teacher awareness and understanding, inclusion of student voice, and positive student-teacher relationships.

TI An Exploratory Pilot Evaluation of a Blended Virtual Reality and
   Mannequin-Based Educational Program for Teaching the Initial Management
   of Postpartum Hemorrhage to Midwifery Students
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE virtual reality; simulation-based education; midwifery education;
   postpartum hemorrhage; educational technology; pilot study
AB Background/Objectives: Opportunities for pre-service midwifery students to manage postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), a high-risk, infrequent emergency, are limited. Virtual reality (VR) can provide contextual decision-making practice, whereas mannequin training provides tactile psychomotor practice. Evidence on combining these modalities and their instructional sequence remains limited. This exploratory pilot study examined implementation and preliminary outcomes of a blended lecture-VR-mannequin program. Methods: Ten final-year midwifery students were allocated by drawing lots to lecture-VR-mannequin (L-VR-M; n = 5) or lecture-mannequin-VR (L-M-VR; n = 5). Performance was assessed using an Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) before and after the program; motivation was assessed using the Course Interest Survey after the program. Analyses were exploratory, with effect sizes and Hodges-Lehmann confidence intervals reported alongside p values. Results: No statistically significant between-sequence differences were found. Across all participants, the median OSCE score increased from 34.5 (IQR, 31.0-35.0) to 44.0 (IQR, 41.0-45.0); the paired median difference was 10.5 points (95% CI, 9.0-15.5; p = 0.005; r = 0.89). This change cannot be attributed solely to the program because there was no no-intervention control and the same scenario was repeated. Uterine fundal massage showed a relatively large exploratory effect favoring L-VR-M (r = 0.54), but the confidence interval included no difference. Conclusions: The program was deliverable within one approximately 4 h session and was associated with higher post-program OSCE scores in this small cohort. The design does not establish effectiveness or an optimal sequence because of the very small sample, baseline imbalance, non-blinded assessors, and possible testing and practice effects. A larger controlled study using alternate OSCE scenarios, blinded assessors, and delayed follow-up is required.
