TI Exploring core competence in first-year medical students through
   narrative medicine and peer-assisted learning: a mixed-methods study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Narrative medicine; Peer-assisted learning; Core competence;
   Competency-based medical education; Mixed-methods research
ID EDUCATION; MODEL
AB Background Early development of core competencies is essential in medical education, yet traditional medical curricula often struggle to bridge the gap between biomedical knowledge and humanistic application. Drawing on social constructivism, this study examines an integrated Narrative Medicine (NM) and Peer-Assisted Learning (PAL) model designed to facilitate the transition from foundational knowledge to contextualized professional application. Methods An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed. A 19-indicator Knowledge-Skills-Attitude (KSA) scale was developed via a Delphi process and evaluated for preliminary psychometric properties. Following a 10-month intervention with 128 first-year students (Experimental n = 64; Control n = 64), hybrid thematic analysis of 14 in-depth interviews explored the underlying pedagogical mechanisms. Results The experimental group reported significantly higher self-reported core competency scores than the control group (77.42 +/- 7.45 vs. 68.00 +/- 7.31; p < 0.001; Cohen's d = 1.28). At the item level, critical thinking and empathy-driven awareness did not reach statistical significance. Qualitative findings suggested that participants perceived narrative features of the integrated package as a catalyst for meaning-making, while peer-assisted elements were viewed as providing social scaffolding necessary for skill development. Conclusion This exploratory study provides preliminary evidence that the integrated NM-PAL model may support students' self-reported development of contextualized clinical competence and early professional identity. By providing a low-pressure collaborative environment, the model may support early reflective engagement that could be foundational to professional development, warranting further longitudinal and confirmatory research.

TI Authenticity of academic lecture passages in high-stakes English tests:
   interrelations among temporal fluency features
SO LANGUAGE TESTING IN ASIA
LA English
DT Article
DE Authenticity; Temporal fluency; Listening assessment; Domain analysis;
   Corpus
ID L2; LANGUAGE; SPEECH; TEXTS
AB In listening assessment, a domain definition inference of temporal fluency features remains under-researched, posing a challenge for test developers in creating authentic listening texts. To address this issue, this paper reports two studies. Study I examined interrelations of temporal fluency features (e.g., articulation rate) in lecture settings. Lecture passages in TOEFL iBT and IELTS were compared to real-world data (Fluency Corpus of Academic English Lectures [FCAEL]). Results showed both similarities (e.g., positive association between articulation rate and end-clause silent pause frequency), and dissimilarities (e.g., correlations between articulation rate and mid-clause filled pause frequency and between repetition frequency and mid-clause filled pause frequency) among the three. Since correlations do not necessarily indicate that disfluencies co-occur, Study II investigated co-occurrences of two disfluency features that indicated high correlations in Study I (i.e., repetitions and filled pauses) in FCAEL and TOEFL. IELTS was excluded because of zero observations of repetitions. Results from generalized-linear mixed-effects models showed proportional similarities between the two, while paired-sample t-tests found significantly lower frequency of both co-occurrences and non-co-occurrences in TOEFL compared to FCAEL. The study proposes thresholds of co-occurrences of repetitions and filled-pauses in academic English lecture texts. The study also argues that variability should be considered construct-relevant, instead of noise.

TI Leading from Outside the 'Hierarchical Box': Enacting the Educational
   Leader Role in Early Childhood Teams
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE early childhood education and care; educational leader; discourse
   analysis; discursive practices; decision-making; quality; leadership and
   teamwork; roles and responsibilities
ID POLICY; CARE; AUSTRALIA; WORK
AB Early childhood education and care (ECEC) is significantly shaped by policy and an enduring focus on quality. While policy governs service provision, it is teams of educators who transform policy into practice, defining and enacting understandings of policy and quality through shared decision-making. In Australia, central to the ECEC quality agenda is the educational leader, a role positioned to guide teams of educators in decision-making. This paper examines how the educational leader role is interpreted in centre documents by services and then enacted in practice by individuals, drawing on Foucauldian-informed discourse analysis of a textual archive comprising policy documents, centre documentation, and focus group data from four Queensland long day care centres. Findings indicate a disconnect between policy intentions of the educational leader and centre-level enactment, where the role is both enabled and constrained in various ways. The educational leader is identified as enacted through five discursive practices: the educational leader as an 'add-on' role, no degree required, outside the 'hierarchical box', compliance officer, and guide and mentor. By making visible the ways centres interpret and individuals enact the role, this study presents pathways forward to revisit policy and reconsider the positioning of the educational leader in centre staffing structures.

TI Staying or leaving after graduation? Factors shaping international
   students' decision to remain in South Korea
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Two-step migration; Edugration; International student mobility; Skilled
   migration; Migration decision; Theory of planned behavior
ID MIGRATION; INTENTIONS; DESTINATION; ASPIRATION
AB South Korea increasingly relies on international students to sustain higher education and supplement its shrinking labor force, but stay rates after graduation remain low. Drawing on a survey of 2033 international students, this study examines factors associated with post-graduation intentions to remain in South Korea. Building on the theory of planned behaviour and the three-stage edugration framework (motivations, study experiences, and post-study opportunities) we show that work experience and the recognized value of students' degree are positively associated with their intentions to stay. Financial autonomy, particularly when supported by scholarships, also increases the likelihood of remaining. In contrast, unmet language-support needs reduce the likelihood of staying after graduation. By linking educational migration with post-graduation settlement, this study contributes to research on student mobility and highlights policy levers for retaining skilled migrants in new destination countries.

TI Code-switching in Cantonese-English bilingual adults who stutter
SO JOURNAL OF FLUENCY DISORDERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Bilingualism; Stuttering; Code-switching; Adults
ID LEXICAL TONE; FREQUENCY; CHILDREN; STRESS; SPEECH; MODEL
AB Purpose: Code-switching is a common phenomenon in bilinguals, but its study in the context of bilinguals who stutter (BWS) remains limited. This preliminary study aims to investigate whether code-switching behaviors contribute to the moment of stuttering in adult bilinguals who stutter. Method: 23 Cantonese-English bilingual adults who stutter participated in the study. Natural conversational speech was elicited through a standardized series of questions. The utterances were categorized into 4 types: fluent Cantonese only, stuttered Cantonese only, fluent codeswitched utterance and stuttered code-switched utterances. Results: The results showed that 78% of the utterances contained code-switching, all of which was intrasentential code-switching. Stuttering was statistically more likely to occur in code-switched utterances than in Cantonese-only utterances. Within code-switched stuttered utterances, 90.57% of stuttering moments occurred in Cantonese words and only 9.43% in English words that were code-switched. Conclusion: Stuttering was more likely to occur in code-switched utterances than in Cantoneseonly utterances. Interestingly, stuttering is predominantly associated with the base language, Cantonese, and not with the switch points (English), indicating increased cognitive-linguistic demands during speech planning, not just during production.

TI Longitudinal case study of syntactic, lexical and articulation rate
   development at stuttering onset in a young japanese child
SO JOURNAL OF FLUENCY DISORDERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Stuttering; Language development; Syntax; Lexicon; Articulation rate
ID PHONETIC COMPLEXITY; SPEECH-MOTOR; PRESCHOOL-CHILDREN; SENTENCE LENGTH;
   LANGUAGE; FLUENCY; MODEL; DISFLUENCIES; ACQUISITION; DIFFICULTY
AB Purpose: This study investigated the relationship between syntactic, lexical and articulation rate development and the onset of stuttering in a young Japanese child from the pre-onset stage. We also examined the linguistic factors influencing stuttering-like disfluency (SLD) immediately after stuttering onset. Methods: The case was a female child aged 1 year 11 months at the beginning of the study. Twenty free-play sessions were video-recorded over approximately two years and four months to analyze SLD, physical concomitants, predicate-argument structures, mean length of utterances (MLU), lexical diversity (VocD), and articulation rate. The influence of sentence-level factor (utterance length), and word-level factors (bunsetsu length, and syllable weight) on SLD was also assessed immediately after onset. Results: SLD frequency was near zero until the sixth session, and prior to the emergence of predicate-argument structures, SLDs were rarely observed. Stuttering onset occurred two days before the seventh session, at which point SLD frequency increased rapidly alongside the appearance of physical concomitants. During this period, predicate-argument structures and VocD values increased sharply, though MLU and articulation rate did not. Additionally, no significant influences of utterance length, bunsetsu length, and syllable weight were observed immediately after onset. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that, at least for the present case, rapid syntactic and lexical development can be associated with stuttering onset. Furthermore, the results imply that selected sentence- and word-level factors might not influence the occurrence of stuttering immediately after onset in this case.

TI Pictures or texts: Eye gazing patterns of preschoolers with ASD in
   picture book reading
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Children with ASD; Eye-tracking; Picture book reading; Orthographic
   awareness
ID AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDERS; ELECTRONIC STORYBOOK; CHILDREN; LANGUAGE;
   SKILLS; HYPERLEXIA; ATTENTION; STUDENTS
AB This study aimed to compare the eye-gazing patterns of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) during picture book reading, based on their distinct reading profiles. Eighty-one children with ASD were divided into three groups based on reading assessments: ASD with imbalanced reading profile (high word reading but low comprehension; n = 32), ASD with average reading profile (n = 25), and ASD with low reading profile (n = 24). A control group of 32 TD children was matched on age and Chinese orthographic symbols (i.e., character) recognition to the imbalanced and average reading profiles groups. Eye-tracking was used to measure fixation duration, fixation numbers, and fixation density on pictures and texts while participants read a picture book under three orthographic symbol conditions: common, rare, and foreign characters. Children with ASD and imbalanced reading profiles demonstrated statistically significantly longer fixation duration on text and shorter fixations on pictures compared to all other groups (ASD average, ASD low, and TD). All children exhibited similar fixation durations, fixation numbers, and fixation densities for rare and common characters but had fewer fixations on foreign characters. The findings underscore the critical importance of subgrouping children with ASD by their reading profiles in research, as their cognitive-linguistic profiles significantly influence visual attention during reading. The results highlight the role of orthographic awareness in character recognition and suggest that imbalanced reading profiles in ASD are characterized by a unique visual attention preference for text over contextual images.

TI Interpreting AI text detection outputs: Empirical evaluation and a
   threshold-based framework
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Academic integrity; Text detection; Educational
   assessment; Measurement
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has prompted widespread use of AI detection tools in higher education assessment, despite limited evidence regarding their validity, reliability, and interpretation. This study evaluates five detection tools across 500 academic text excerpts representing fully human-written, fully AI-generated, humanized AI, and hybrid human-AI conditions. While tools demonstrated near-perfect discrimination between fully human-written and fully AI-generated text (AUC = 0.994-1.000), performance declined substantially for hybrid and humanized texts. Inter-detector agreement was high (ICC = 0.92), indicating consistent ranking despite variability in absolute scores. These findings highlight important limitations in current evaluation practices that treat probabilistic outputs as definitive classifications. Building on these empirical findings, we develop and operationalize a threshold-based framework that aligns interpretation with decision context by distinguishing between screening and high-specificity diagnostic uses. This framework contributes to evaluation methodology by providing a structured approach to interpreting imperfect classification tools in high-stakes assessment settings.

TI Evaluating the use of an escape game to reinforce foundational pathogens
   recall among first-year student pharmacists
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Escape game; Immunology; Pathogen; Active learning; Gamification
ID ROOM; SCIENCE
AB Introduction: The objective of this study was to implement an escape game in a first-year basic-science lab and evaluate item-mapped outcomes immediately and at six weeks, including subgroup analyses and cohort-level GPA context. Methods: First-year student pharmacists (n = 49) worked in groups to "escape" in 50 min. One week prior, students received a list of 14 fungal and parasitic pathogens, were given a lecture over them, and told to memorize them. On the lab day, students completed an individual pre-quiz, the escape game activity, a post-quiz, and a reassessment six weeks later. Results: Post-quiz scores exceeded pre-quiz scores (86.59% +/- 2.7 vs 92.13% +/- 1.67; p < 0.05). Over half of the participants earned a perfect score on the pre-quiz. On mapped exam items at six weeks, the experimental year outperformed the control year (94% +/- 4.04 vs 85% +/- 4.16; p < 0.05) despite lower incoming GPAs (total 3.17 +/- 0.011 vs 3.44 +/- 0.007; math/science 3.00 +/- 0.012 vs 3.26 +/- 0.009; p < 0.05). Conclusions: The escape game activity was associated with higher immediate and six-week item-mapped performance with larger gains among students who did not find initial success with rote memorization.

TI Comparing the problem-posing competence of high school students with
   different cognitive styles: An epistemic network analysis study
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Problem-posing competence; Cognitive style; Epistemic network analysis;
   Information technology teaching
ID FIELD DEPENDENCE-INDEPENDENCE; QUESTION-GENERATION; ABILITIES;
   DEPENDENCE/INDEPENDENCE; PERFORMANCE; CREATIVITY; STRATEGIES; ATTITUDES;
   DESIGN
AB Innovation often comes from posing unconventional problems, while disciplinary integration requires formulating interdisciplinary problems. Although studies have investigated the association between cognitive style and general academic achievement, the influence of cognitive determinants on domain-specific problem-posing competence (PPC) remains underexplored. This study used the Embedded Figures Test to categorize students as having either a field-dependent (FD) or a field-independent (FI) cognitive style. Over a 16-week course, we collected generative text-based problems from 90 high school students aged 15-17 years (M = 15.94, SD = 0.63) across eight learning topics. Epistemic network analysis (ENA) was conducted to explore the characteristics and development trajectories of PPC. Results showed that the problems posed by FD students exhibited stronger connections between fluency and elaboration, typically targeting factual knowledge at the cognitive level. By contrast, the problems posed by FI students exhibited greater associations with flexibility and originality, including more open-ended and integrative problems. Furthermore, as the course progressed, FD students benefited more from the learning materials, which led to significant improvements in their cognitive level and the originality of their problems compared to FI counterparts. These findings indicate that PPC is a dynamically evolving competence throughout the learning process. Educators should design adaptive instructional scaffolds tailored to cognitive styles, and encourage learners to engage in continuous metacognitive reflection on their thinking habits and problem-posing processes.

TI Reconfiguring University Missions in the Knowledge Society: The Case of
   Portuguese Universities in European Alliances
SO HIGHER EDUCATION QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE discursive institutionalism; knowledge society; mission; Portugal;
   relationship with society; university
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; INSTITUTIONAL ISOMORPHISM; POLICY;
   INTERNATIONALIZATION; NETWORKS; PROGRAM
AB This paper examines how European Knowledge Society policy scripts, amplified by the European Universities initiative, are appropriated in the strategic plans of Portuguese public universities. Focusing on nine universities participating in European Universities Alliances, it asks how they position the 'relationship with society' in mission narratives, whether they prioritise commercial or civic/socially responsive engagement, and what patterns of convergence, local translation and decoupling emerge. The paper argues that these hybrid narratives reflect adaptive responses to multiple legitimacy pressures rather than inconsistency or failure.

TI The Impacts of Using a Gamified Intelligent Tutoring System on Students'
   Mathematical Self-Efficacy: A Mixed-Method Study
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gamification; ITS; K-12 students; Mathematical self-efficacy;
   Mixed-method design
ID LEARNING-SYSTEM; SCHOOL; MODEL; ENGAGEMENT; GAME
AB Gamification has emerged as an effective strategy to enhance student learning through intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs). This explanatory mixed-methods study examined the impact of a gamified ITS-Toc-toc MET-on second-grade students' mathematical self-efficacy (MSE) and learning achievement in a South Korean elementary school. Ninety students were divided into an experimental group (n = 45), which received instruction integrated with Toc-toc MET, and a comparison group (n = 45), which received conventional teacher-led instruction. Findings suggest that a gamified ITS can effectively enhance early elementary students' MSE and offer guidance for optimizing its implementation in mathematics education.

   teacher education; South Africa; Germany
AB This study employed Norman Fairclough's three-dimensional approach to critical discourse analysis to investigate the potential of defamiliarisation, supported by collaborative online international learning, to help pre-service teachers in South Africa and Germany challenge neoliberalism and promote critical global citizenship. A group of pre-service teachers in South Africa and Germany (N = 54) were prompted to critically analyse capitalism's global influence and articulate their ideas using creative illustrations inspired by the short online film Marx and I. The resulting artwork of a sub-sample of the South African student teachers (n = 7) shows their individual and collective reflections on global injustice, capitalism and human rights abuses, while that of the German student teachers (n = 7) emphasises the refugee crisis in Europe, environmental degradation and social exclusion. The research highlights the usefulness of defamiliarisation in producing context-specific criticisms and transforming student teachers' perceptions of global socio-political environments. The authors found that defamiliarisation promotes a transdisciplinary approach to teacher education and is valuable for contesting neoliberal beliefs and prevailing narratives, thereby encouraging student teachers' critical engagement with global challenges.
   Cultiver une & eacute;ducation & agrave; la citoyennet & eacute; mondiale critique par la d & eacute;familiarisation et l'apprentissage collaboratif international en ligne - La pr & eacute;sente & eacute;tude utilise l'approche tridimensionnelle de l'analyse critique du discours de Norman Fairclough pour examiner le potentiel de la d & eacute;familiarisation. TI Professional Role, Access to Digital Educational Resources, and the
   Appraisal of Digitalization in Anesthesia and Intensive Care: A
   Single-Centre Cross-Sectional Survey of Staff Perceptions
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE education; medical; continuing; nursing; computer-assisted instruction;
   simulation training; critical care; health personnel; medical
   informatics
ID INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; BIG DATA; HEALTH; ACCEPTANCE; SIMULATION;
   MEDICINE; IMPACT; TIME
AB Background and Objectives: Digital tools are now embedded in anesthesia and intensive care, but access to them, and in particular to digital educational resources, is distributed unevenly across professional groups. This study describes how nurses, residents, and specialist physicians in one department appraise the contribution of digital technologies to continuing education, patient safety, and clinical and managerial decision-making, and how they report using the digital educational resources available to them. The study is descriptive and exploratory. It does not evaluate an educational intervention and does not measure learning. Methods: We conducted an anonymous, paper-based cross-sectional survey of all 198 clinical staff of a tertiary anesthesia and intensive care department between 2 June and 31 July 2025; 161 questionnaires were analyzable (81.3%). The instrument was investigator-developed and has not been validated, and it is therefore treated as a set of individual items rather than as a scale. Four trichotomous items (Yes/No/Cannot appraise) covering continuing education, patient safety, clinical decision-making, and managerial decision-making were designated primary outcomes and are reported as proportions with Wilson 95% confidence intervals, together with between-group differences and their confidence intervals; overall comparisons used the chi-square or Fisher exact test with Cram & eacute;r's V as the effect size. Reporting follows STROBE and the CROSS checklist for survey research. Composite indices, regression models, and correlation analyses were devised after data inspection, are labelled exploratory, and are not reported in this manuscript. Results: Daily use of at least one digital tool was reported by 98.1% of respondents. An educational contribution was affirmed by 56.4% of nurses (95% CI 43.3-68.6), 91.9% of residents (82.5-96.5), and 93.2% of specialists (81.8-97.7); the difference was 35.5 percentage points between residents and nurses (95% CI 20.1-49.4) and 36.8 points between specialists and nurses (20.1-50.7). Response distributions differed by professional category on all four items (p < 0.001 for education, patient safety, and clinical decisions; p = 0.005 for managerial decisions; Cram & eacute;r's V 0.22-0.31). Explicit disagreement was very rare (1 to 4 respondents per item), so the differences consist almost entirely of the "Cannot appraise" category, which is reported descriptively because the reason for that response was not measured. Reported use of digital educational resources followed the same ordering: e-learning 50.9% of nurses, 98.4% of residents, 93.2% of specialists; simulators 18.2%, 72.6%, 50.0%; webinars 65.5%, 67.7%, 86.4%. These proportions correspond to documented differences in institutional access, since simulation rotations were mandatory for residents only and the e-learning platform was opened to physicians in 2021 but to nursing staff only in October 2023. Conclusions: In this single department, response distributions on all four appraisal items differed by professional category, and reported use of digital educational resources was lowest in the group with the latest and most restricted institutional access. Because the groups used different technologies under different access conditions, these differences cannot be attributed to professional role itself, and because no learning outcome was measured they are not evidence of educational benefit.
   The findings are exploratory and support the hypothesis that equalizing access to digital educational resources deserves prospective evaluation.

TI Listen and Learn! Enhancing Construction and Engineering Education with
   AI-Assisted Podcasts
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE active learning; audio-learning; multimedia learning; podcasts;
   student-centred learning
AB Emerging technologies provide promising opportunities to improve learning in construction and engineering education. In the current study, the interaction between students and AI-enhanced educational podcasts in undergraduate and postgraduate modules offered by two South African universities is analysed. Using a quantitative research design, the study noted a considerable increase in class average scores at the postgraduate level. However, the undergraduate class average scores remained at baseline, indicating no apparent improvement; therefore, no causation can be established based on these results. Furthermore, guided by the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning, the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), student perceptions were assessed across learning effectiveness and engagement, accessibility and satisfaction, and motivation and intent to continue using podcasts. Rankings showed high satisfaction across all dimensions. Although access challenges were infrequent, PLS-SEM revealed a significant negative relationship between technical barriers and motivation and willingness to expand podcast use, highlighting human-technology interaction constraints. Findings underscore the importance of seamless access and curriculum alignment and conclude with strategies to strengthen adoption, engagement, and learning outcomes in AI-assisted podcast-based education.

TI The Influence of Culture and Identity on Motivation in the
   English-as-a-Second-Language Acquisition Process: A Quasi-Experimental
   Study with Ecuadorian University Students
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE L2 motivation; culture; identity; English as a foreign language;
   quasi-experimental design; Ecuador
AB Motivation is a key predictor of success in second language (L2) acquisition, yet how culture and identity shape it among Latin American learners remains under-examined. This study used a quasi-experimental design with non-equivalent control and experimental groups (n = 100) to test the effect of an eight-week culturally responsive pedagogical intervention on the motivation of intermediate-level English-as-a-second-language learners at a public university in Ecuador, measured with the validated Spanish version of Gardner's Attitude/Motivation Test Battery (AMTB). An independent-samples t-test revealed a statistically significant difference in post-intervention motivation scores between the experimental group (M = 156.1, SD = 31.2) and the control group (M = 134.5, SD = 28.4), t(98) = 3.91, p = 0.002, Cohen's d = 0.72. The intervention was associated with a medium-to-large increase in motivation, consistent with sociocultural theory, the socio-educational model, the L2 Motivational Self System, and identity-investment theory; because the control group did not receive an equally novel activity, this finding should be read as preliminary evidence for the cultural/identity component specifically. Implications for culturally sensitive language teaching in diverse Hispanic contexts are derived.

TI Toward Safer Learning Environments in Creative Higher Education: A
   Capabilities-Informed Multimethod Study of Misconduct Prevention
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE creative higher education; misconduct; prevention; capabilities
   approach; thematic analysis
ID MIRACLE QUESTION; OUTCOMES
AB Students at creative higher education (CHE) institutions frequently report boundary violations and other forms of misconduct, while prevention efforts have been described as insufficient. Drawing on a capabilities-informed perspective attentive to the environmental and institutional conditions of flourishing, we examine what structural and cultural conditions stakeholders consider necessary for misconduct prevention in CHE. Using a complementary multimethod qualitative design, we report two studies: 16 interviews with stakeholder groups analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis, and 228 open-ended responses from a national student survey analyzed through structured tabular thematic analysis. Interview participants identified three interconnected areas of transformation: community, institutions, and knowledge and norms. Seven themes generated from the survey responses were classified as confirmatory, and one theme as expanding, foregrounding material stability and students' aspirations for cultural and institutional reform, a dimension addressed only implicitly in the interviews. Two themes had no direct counterpart, foregrounding students' skepticism about the possibility of change and the societal recognition of artists. Across both studies, participants described prevention efforts as often reactive and insufficient, and called for systemic approaches in which institutions recognize their societal role and prioritize students' flourishing. Our findings identify participant-informed starting points for developing and evaluating prevention strategies.

TI Socially Just Assessment in Initial Teacher Education: Analysis of a
   Participatory Co-Construction Experience in Chile
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE educational assessment; participatory assessment; Initial Teacher
   Education; social justice
ID JUSTICE
AB University assessment processes tend to prioritize testing of rote knowledge over critical thinking and the common good. Socially Just Assessment (SJA) aims to subvert these traditional logics; however, its implementation in Initial Teacher Education (ITE) remains scarce. This qualitative study, exploratory in scope, analyzes a participatory experience within an initial practicum course of a Language and Literature Education program in Santiago, Chile. The methodological design enacted the principles of SJA through a pedagogical sequence consisting of five sessions of co-design and collective validation between a teacher and her students. The results demonstrate that the exercise inverted traditional roles and redistributed pedagogical power. Furthermore, strengthening autonomy and teacher identity. In conclusion, assessment co-design constitutes an empirical practice of justice that transforms the classroom into a democratic space.

TI Individual and System Factors Involved in First-Generation College
   Students' Risk and Resilience: Qualitative Student Perspectives and
   Recommendations
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE first-generation college students; resilience; university programming;
   ecological systems theory; college preparation; college adjustment; risk
   factors; teachers
AB Since the term 'first-generation college student' (FGCS) garnered increased attention in the 2000s, many institutions have implemented programming specifically for FGCS (e.g., bridge programs, first-year seminars). FGCS should be key stakeholders who inform programming. As such, qualitative research is needed to elevate FGCS voices. To date, little research has examined adjustment and well-being in FGCS. This study included qualitative interviews (approximately 30 min) concerning adjustment and well-being in FGCS (N = 24; 79% female, M age = 19, 92% White), defined as students whose parents have not completed a four-year bachelor's degree. Participants' responses were coded according to Bronfenbrenner's Ecological Systems Theory levels, to account for the multi-layered systems (e.g., family, high school, university, peers) that impact their risk and resilience before and during college. One central theme was how seeking help from family, peers, and university resources promoted resilience. Conversely, individual risk factors (e.g., low socioeconomic status; insufficient guidance) interacted with the high school environment and economic landscape of higher education to confer risk. Overall, many challenges (e.g., mental health) improved over time. Students made recommendations for both high school and university staff about how to best support FGCS, which have implications for programming at the high school and university level.

TI Examining the Preparation-Efficacy Relationship Through Program Learning
   Outcomes in Traditional Teacher Preparation
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE traditional teacher preparation; alternative certification; preservice
   teacher education; practice-based education; teacher beliefs
ID SELF-EFFICACY; INDUCTION; EDUCATION; NOVICE; IMPACT; ENTRY
AB As schools navigate widening achievement gaps, learning recovery demands, and increasingly complex teaching contexts, understanding how educators are prepared to enter the profession has become increasingly important. Using end-of-program survey data from 473 completers of a large traditional teacher preparation (TTP) program in the southwestern United States collected across three post-pandemic semesters, the purpose of this study was to examine the relationship between program completers' perceived preparation adequacy and their self-efficacy during the transition from program completion to the first year of teaching. Implications for educator preparation and workforce development are discussed.

TI The IDEA framework for metacognitively regulated GenAI use in higher
   education: Development and exploratory pilot evidence
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; Metacognitive regulation;
   Self-regulated learning; Prompt engineering; Higher education
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can enhance students' efficiency and the apparent quality of academic work, yet its fluent outputs may encourage learners to outsource cognitive activities central to learning. This creates the risk of "performance without learning", whereby successful task completion does not necessarily reflect meaningful understanding or learner regulation. To address this concern, this article develops the Intent, Deconstruction, Expression, and Adaptation (IDEA) framework, a theory-informed metacognitive scaffold for GenAI-supported academic work. IDEA guides learners to articulate goals and constraints, decompose tasks into essential processes, communicate requirements through structured prompts, and critically evaluate and iteratively refine AI-generated outputs. By embedding prompting within a cycle of planning, monitoring, and regulation, IDEA provides an actionable approach for preserving learner agency in GenAI-supported work. An exploratory quasi-experimental pilot study with 42 undergraduates examined the feasibility and preliminary educational value of IDEA-based instruction relative to structured prompt-engineering instruction. Across immediate GenAI-assisted academic tasks, IDEA-trained students produced higher-quality prompts and final AIgenerated outputs, and their interaction records showed observable enactment of the framework's core activities. On unaided tasks completed five days later, the IDEA group demonstrated advantages on selected tasks. Together, the conceptual framework and pilot findings position IDEA as a practical instructional approach for transforming GenAI use from passive content outsourcing into deliberate, evaluative, and learner-regulated interaction. Future research can examine its operation across disciplinary contexts and its longer-term implications for learning.

TI Robotic Integration Without Laparoscopic Displacement: Protecting Basic
   Cases in Surgical Training
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE robotic surgery; laparoscopy; surgical education; residency; entrustable
   professional activities; competency-based training
AB Robotic surgery is now an essential part of general surgery practice and general surgery training. The educational risk is not robotic adoption itself but unmeasured substitution: the replacement of foundational laparoscopic experience in common operations before robotic proficiency can be defined, assessed, and entrusted. This Perspective argues for platform-balanced training in which robotics expands resident capability without consuming the basic laparoscopic case pool. TI Integrating Citizen Science into Advanced Practice Nursing education: a
   contemporary challenge
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nurse education; Advanced Practice Nursing; Nursing research; Citizen
   Science
AB Advanced Practice Nursing is internationally recognised as an innovative model of practice that expands the traditional scope of nursing by integrating specialised knowledge, advanced clinical skills, and greater autonomy in clinical decision-making. Within this model, research competence is recognised as a strategic pillar for consolidating Advanced Practice Nursing practice. Citizen Science, in turn, represents an innovative approach that promotes the active involvement of citizens throughout the research process, strengthening the alignment between research priorities and community needs. This paper discusses the integration of Citizen Science into postgraduate nursing curricula for Advanced Practice Nurses as a strategy to strengthen their capacity to generate context-sensitive and socially relevant evidence. It examines the potential contributions of Citizen Science to evidence generation and knowledge co-creation and proposes pathways for curricular integration. These includes curriculum review, the implementation of Citizen Science pilot projects, capacity building for faculty members and clinical mentors to support research based on Citizen Science principles, the development of partnerships across academic, healthcare, governmental, and community settings, and the strengthening of science communication initiatives. The paper also discusses key implementation challenges, including institutional resistance, ethical and legal considerations, and the need to prepare educators and students for participatory research approaches. Integrating Citizen Science into postgraduate Advanced Practice Nursing education represents a contemporary and strategic opportunity to better prepare nurses to generate context-sensitive evidence, engage citizens as partners in knowledge production, and promote more responsive, equitable, and socially accountable healthcare.

TI Cultivation of Aesthetic Experience as the Aim of Environmental Art
   Education: A Deweyan View
SO EDUCATIONAL THEORY
LA English
DT Article
DE John Dewey; environmental art education; environmental education; art
   education; aesthetic experience
ID ECOLOGY
AB Challenging the dichotomy of nature and culture is broadly seen as a key aim of environmental art education. Some of the literature on the topic focuses on the question of what metaphor for the relationship between nature and culture environmental art educators should adopt and attempt to convey to their students. In this article, I argue that such a focus reflects a problematically instrumental conception of art education, a conception that seems to partly stem from confusion about the epistemological status of art. To bring clarity to this matter, I will examine John Dewey's ideas about the nature of aesthetic qualities and aesthetic experience. According to Dewey, aesthetic qualities are culminations of human-environment transactions. He believed that art, contrary to science or other forms of declarative knowledge, operates indirectly, qualitatively, and imaginatively. In light of this, it seems implausible that the arts could be used to convey a specific metaphorical worldview to students. I argue that the aim of environmental art education should rather be to cultivate students' ability to experience the world aesthetically.

TI The Application of Augmented Reality for the Understanding of Chemistry
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION

AB This research was developed in response to the need for new ways of teaching Chemistry in order to improve the understanding of molecular geometry. This work was carried out using an action-research methodology, and both quantitative (statistical) and qualitative (ideas or opinions) data were analyzed. Such investigations are especially valuable in STEM disciplines, since they allow the students to enjoy lessons while staying in touch with new technologies that are already native to them.

TI Transition From Preservice to In-Service Teaching: The Impact of
   Personal Attributes and Social-Environmental Factors on Well-Being and
   Perceived Teaching Quality
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE early career teacher; cognitive attributes; non-cognitive attributes;
   social-environmental support; teaching-related outcomes
ID TEACHERS; MOTIVATION; VALIDATION; INTENTIONS; COMMITMENT; EFFICACY;
   FUTURE; SENSE
AB The transition from preservice to in-service teaching is a critical period for early career teachers, often presenting challenges that affect their occupational success and well-being. Identifying factors that influence key outcomes-such as transition difficulties, perceived teaching quality, well-being, and intention to quit-is essential for providing timely support. This longitudinal study examined how preservice teachers' cognitive attributes (Grade Point Average, pedagogical knowledge, practicum grades), non-cognitive attributes (personality, teaching motivation), and social-environmental support before graduation relate to their teaching outcomes after entering the profession. The sample comprised 1,711 preservice teachers; 206 reported being teachers 10 months after graduation and completed follow-up surveys. Structural equation modeling revealed that cognitive attributes and social-environmental support were not significantly associated with teaching outcomes. Instead, higher conscientiousness, greater openness, and stronger teaching motivation predicted fewer transition difficulties, greater perceived teaching quality, and better well-being. These findings underscore the importance of cultivating non-cognitive skills during teacher training to better prepare future educators.

TI The Intention-Implementation Gap: Micro-Cycles and Contextual Factors in
   First-Year STEM Students' Self-Regulated Learning
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE self-regulated learning; performance phase; first-year students; STEM
   education; plan implementation; intersecting factors
AB First-year students in STEM programs face significant academic and personal challenges that can undermine retention and success, particularly for those navigating new institutional environments without prior college experience. While self- regulated learning (SRL) theory offers a well-established framework for understanding how students plan and reflect, less attention has been paid to the performance phase, the stage where students must translate plans into action amid real academic and social demands. This qualitative study examines the experiences of 15 first-year life science students across three institution types, a Hispanic-Serving Institution, a predominantly white institution, and a liberal arts college, to investigate what plans students formed at the end of their first semester and what factors facilitated or hindered implementation during their second semester. Using thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews, three major plan themes emerged: help-seeking, internal academic adjustments, and managing social and emotional well-being. Facilitating factors for these plans included small class sizes, anonymized participation tools, approachable instructors, peer and family support, counseling services, and structured planning tools, while hindering factors included fear of judgment, high instructor-student ratios, scheduling conflicts, academic burnout, and unsupportive living environments. The findings reveal that plan implementation depended on the interplay of intersecting psychological, social, and structural factors, which created unique conditions that influenced whether students were able to enact their plans. Importantly, the findings reveal that plan implementation unfolded not as a linear process but through nested micro-cycles of forethought, performance, and reflection within the performance phase, triggered by specific events throughout the semester. These findings have implications for how institutions design learner-centered support for STEM students not only at key transition points, but also throughout the semester, to address the conditions that influence whether students are able to successfully implement, adapt, or abandon their regulatory efforts.

TI Discrepancies Between Self-Reported and Peer-Attributed Frequencies of
   AI-Assisted Academic Cheating Among Undergraduate Students
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE generative artificial intelligence; AI-assisted academic cheating;
   academic integrity; self-reported cheating; peer-attributed frequencies;
   higher education
ID DISHONESTY
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has intensified concerns about academic integrity, yet little is known about discrepancies between students' self-reported frequencies in AI-assisted academic cheating and the frequencies they attribute to their peers. Using an anonymous cross-sectional survey, this study collected responses from 863 undergraduates at a science and technology university in Vietnam. Participants rated ten AI-assisted academic cheating behaviors from two perspectives: the frequency they attributed such behaviors to their classmates, referred to as perceived peer cheating (PPC), and the frequency they reported such behaviors for themselves, referred to as self-reported cheating (SRC). Split-plot ANOVAs were conducted to compare PPC and SRC ratings and to examine whether the magnitude of the discrepancy varied by gender and student seniority. The results show that PPC ratings were significantly higher than SRC ratings for all ten behaviors, with partial eta-squared values ranging from 0.060 to 0.196. Cheating perspective & times; gender interactions and cheating perspective & times; student seniority interactions were each significant for three behaviors; however, all interaction effects were small (eta p2 <= 0.025). Overall, the study reveals a consistent discrepancy between self-reported and peer-attributed frequencies of AI-assisted academic cheating. This discrepancy highlights the limitations of using either direct self-reports or peer-attributed frequencies alone to estimate the actual prevalence of AI-assisted academic cheating.

TI On Stupidity as a Pedagogical Commitment A Constructive Engagement with
   Derek R. Ford
SO CRITICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
AB This paper undertakes a sustained engagement with Marxism, Pedagogy, and the General Intellect by Derek R. Ford (2021). The pedagogical form of stupidity, as developed by Ford, is given particular attention as one that is actually not pedagogical, but should rather be understood as a tactical force utilized by capital and the state in making subjects legible to it. I propose that stupidity is a potentially violent and dangerous suspension of thought that leaves a subject bare to the forces of capital self-valorization and state power. My analysis braves stupidity in order to bear the pedagogical form of intuition as one that can sustain life, that can provide relief, and alternate tactics for confronting both capital and state power. Stupidity is a fundamental technique used in the making of corpses. Intuition cultivates life in our children and does so with the aid of Karl Marxs' articulation of a 'social brain'. My hope is that my engagement be a call to begin a consensual contract with the general social forces that produce and sustain all of our lives in common.

TI Effects of Privatization Policies on Education in Türkiye Equity,
   Access, and Public Voices Against the Marketization of Education
SO CRITICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
AB Education privatization has increased globally in the past two decades, and T & uuml;rkiye is no exception. After the implementation of neoliberal policies in education following the 1980s, particularly in class-based societies, children from families with low socioeconomic status are faced with issues such as exclusion from education, barriers to accessing quality education, and violations of their educational rights. This research aims to analyze the process and effects of the privatization of education in T & uuml;rkiye based on the views of students and parents regarding privatization policies in education. A mixed-methods approach has been adopted in the study. Findings reveal that parents generally oppose direct privatization policies but are more accepting of indirect ones. Most parents believe education should be provided by the state, while some support a dual system involving both public and private schools. This perspective is supported by concerns about the inadequacy of public education, the perception that private schools better address family needs, and the diversity they offer. However, participants do not endorse the exclusive provision of education by private institutions. Additionally, the research highlights a negative sentiment towards policies requiring parents to finance education directly, with concerns that privatization exacerbates social inequalities.

TI The Marketization of "Quality" Academic Capitalism and the
   Contradictions of Accreditation in Turkish Higher Education
SO CRITICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID NEO-LIBERALISM; AUDIT CULTURE
AB This study critically examines how accreditation in Turkish higher education system functions as a tool of marketization and commodification within the framework of academic capitalism. Under the influence of neoliberal policies, accreditation carried out within the discourse of "quality assurance" restructure universities as entrepreneurial institutions open to global competition, leading to the commercialization of knowledge and the commodification of academic labor. Findings specific to T & uuml;rkiye reveal concrete manifestations of these processes: (1) The accreditation process creates a competitive arena among universities where financial capital becomes the determining factor. (2) The standards imposed by national and international accreditation bodies subject universities to a continuous regime of surveillance and performance. (3) The overwhelming majority of accredited programs being in engineering fields reflects a "market-oriented higher education" model tied to industrial needs while simultaneously reinforcing interdisciplinary hierarchies. In conclusion, this study argues that accreditation processes, serve to deepen the marketization of higher education and reproduce social inequalities. As an alternative, it proposes the urgent development of an evaluation model centered on the principle of public responsibility, one that preserves academic autonomy and does not produce inequalities.

In this manuscript, the authors narrativize their experiences as students at a large public urban university who organized for decolonial educational interventions in a school of education. We demanded that the school of education create curricular interventions that teaches future teachers, scholars, and researchers about the long struggle for Palestinian liberation, and how to be in solidarity as educational praxis. We envision methods for building radical study in alignment with principles of self-determination, courageous will-building, and anti-indoctrination pedagogy across K-20 educational settings.

TI Empowered Resistance Explains the Relationship Between Historical
   Knowledge and Support for Palestine Among College Students
SO CRITICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID RACISM; EXPERIENCE
AB College students' calls and demonstrations for Palestine Liberation in universities across the United States have increased exponentially after October 7, 2023. However, little is known about the dynamic relationship between historical knowledge and support for Palestine. We use critical consciousness theory to frame our study and hypothesize that students' knowledge of the history of occupied Palestine will predict college students'support for Palestine Liberation. In addition, this relationship between historical knowledge and support will be explained by college students' experiences of empowered resistance against oppression. Mediation analyses suggest that college students' (N = 250; Mage = 20.45, SD = 4.07) historical knowledge about the occupation and colonization of Palestine increased their empowerment and resistance, which increased their support for Palestine Liberation. We conclude with recommendations to support college students during times of crisis, fostering their education of Palestine, supporting other oppressed peoples, and resisting oppressive and racist systems.

TI Playing to become literate: Teachers' evolving roles during digital
   game-based learning in a Malawian childcare centre
SO SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF CHILDHOOD EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital game-based learning; teacher adaptation; early childhood
   education; focused ethnography; Malawi; community-based childcare
   centres; cultural mediation; multi-age classroom
ID TECHNOLOGY; CLASSROOMS; IPADS
AB Background: Integrating digital game-based learning in early childhood education poses challenges for teachers, particularly in resource-constrained settings where traditional methods predominate and educators often lack formal pedagogical training. Aim: To explore how teachers adapt their roles and pedagogical practices in a multi-age classroom where children aged 3-6 years engage with digital learning games. Setting: A community-based childcare centre in rural Malawi where volunteer teachers with limited formal education facilitate digital game-based learning. Methods: Ethnographic participant observation was conducted over one month (34 h across 17 sessions), using a developmental research sequence and focused ethnographic analysis of teacher practices, classroom interactions and adaptation patterns. Results: Four interconnected themes were identified: (1) teachers moved from restrictive control to selective intervention, developing 'adaptive oversight'; (2) technical challenges persisted, with teachers continuing to rely on external support; (3) embodied practices such as physical guidance and native language instruction remained stable, providing essential scaffolding; and (4) teachers gradually recognised and facilitated productive peer learning in the multi-age setting. Conclusion: Given the absence of mother-tongue content and culturally relevant materials, teachers' adaptation involved essential yet institutionally invisible cultural mediation work, creating hybrid approaches that bridged global technologies with local pedagogical traditions and children's lived experiences. Contribution: The study shows how teachers navigate digital learning through simultaneous adaptations: developing selective intervention strategies, managing persistent technical dependencies, sustaining embodied pedagogical practices and facilitating emergent peer learning, all while performing institutionally invisible cultural mediation work.

TI Knowledge, attitude, and practice of antifungal resistance and
   stewardship among pharmacy students in Zambia: a cross-sectional study
   to inform antifungal stewardship programs
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE antifungal resistance; antifungal stewardship; antifungal stewardship
   programs; antimicrobial resistance; fungal infections; pharmacy
   students; Zambia
ID FUNGAL-INFECTIONS; DRUG-RESISTANCE; MECHANISMS; AGENTS
AB Background: Antifungal resistance (AFR) is a growing global health threat, particularly in low-and middle-income countries such as Zambia, where antifungals are often accessed without prescription. Antifungal stewardship (AFS) programs aim to optimise antifungal use, yet limited data exist on pharmacy students' knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) toward AFR and AFS. This study evaluated pharmacy students' knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) toward AFR and AFS in Zambia. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional survey was conducted among 288 randomly selected pharmacy students between August and September 2024 using a structured questionnaire. Descriptive statistics summarised demographics and KAP responses. Associations were analysed using Chi-square and Fisher's Exact Tests, while multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of good KAP (p < 0.05). Results: Among respondents (55.2% female; 76.7% aged 18-25 years), most students (94.1%) knew how to define AFR, and 90.3% recognized antifungal misuse as a factor driving resistance. Nevertheless, only 18.1% showed good knowledge, 67.7% held positive attitudes (especially among fourth-year students, p < 0.001), and merely 2.4% practiced appropriately. Multivariable analysis found that being a fourth-year student increased the likelihood of a good attitude (aOR = 5.10, 95% CI: 2.28-11.43). Married students were more likely to demonstrate good practices (aOR = 2.75, 95% CI: 1.13-6.68) towards AFR and antifungal stewardship (AFS) compared to unmarried ones. Additionally, age above 33 years was not significantly associated with better knowledge (aOR = 1.29, 95% CI: 0.32-5.18). Conclusion: Pharmacy students in Zambia demonstrated positive attitudes towards AFR and AFS, but significant gaps in knowledge and practice remain. Strengthening AFR and AFS-related content and experiential training within the pharmacy curriculum is urgently needed to improve preparedness for clinical practice.

TI Automating language input: investigating the effect of AI-generated
   contextual flashcards delivered via Anki on EFL learners' sentence-level
   fluency
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adaptive learning; AI-assisted language learning; communicative
   competence; contextualized input; spaced repetition
AB The present research explored whether AI-powered contextual flashcards facilitated through Anki had a positive impact on learners' sentence-level fluency in EFL settings. This research employed a quasi-experimental pre-test-post-test control-group research design. Sixty EFL learners from the University of Zawia participated in the study and were allocated into either an experimental or control group where they received six weeks of AI-generated contextual flashcards or traditional instruction, respectively. The experimental group exhibited significant improvements from pretest to posttest (M = 10.45, SD = 2.11 to M = 17.82, SD = 1.95; t(29) = 14.52, p < .001), while the control group showed only marginal improvements (t(29) = 4.21, p < .01). Additionally, a significant difference was found between groups on the posttest (t(58) = 9.63, p < .001), d = 2.48. These results were discussed in relation to theories of second language acquisition and cognitive theory of learning. Findings suggest contextualized input combined with retrieval practice and spaced repetition can help learners develop fluency. Moreover, this study adds to the growing body of work related to AI-assisted language learning by showing its efficacy in developing fluency for communicative competence.

TI Making teaching visible: video-based dialogic feedback conversations and
   lecturers' interpersonal communication. An action research study in
   Israeli higher education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE action research; dialogic feedback; higher education; interpersonal
   communication; lecturers' professional development; reflective practice;
   video-based dialogic feedback
AB This study examines how higher education lecturers' interpersonal communication can be supported and developed through a cyclical, video-based dialogic feedback process. Conducted as qualitative action research in an academic college in Israel, the study involved ten lecturers who participated in a semester-long developmental process consisting of three video-recorded lessons, three dialogic feedback conversations, written summaries, and semi-structured interviews before and after the intervention. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis and thematic analysis. The findings indicate a developmental sequence across the three feedback cycles, moving from awareness of communicative difficulties, through experimentation and refinement, to consolidation and transfer of change to subsequent teaching. Participants described the video-based dialogic feedback conversations as enabling them to see, reinterpret, and better understand their own teaching practices. Reported and observed patterns of change were identified across five dimensions of interpersonal communication: lesson organization, clarity of messages, contact with students, creation of interest, and creation of value. Participants experienced the process as professional, concrete, supportive, and complementary to student evaluations. The findings suggest that formative, video-based dialogic feedback can strengthen academic development by providing lecturers with practice-based guidance, supporting reflective professional learning, and enabling gradual pedagogical change. The study highlights the value of moving beyond reliance on student evaluations alone toward developmental feedback processes that help lecturers examine concrete teaching situations, reinterpret their practice, and transfer new insights to subsequent teaching contexts.

   education; IEP goal quality; mixed methods; pre-service practitioners
ID SMART
AB Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT may help support special education practice, but evidence on their usefulness for IEP goal writing remains limited.Methods This mixed-methods study used a counterbalanced, scenario-based design with 111 participants from undergraduate and graduate programs across four universities. Participants wrote IEP goals in two conditions: participant-only and participant plus AI. TI Affective engagement across metaphor-related discourse moves in
   statistics education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE affective engagement; arousal trajectory; discourse analysis; metaphor;
   skin conductance response; statistics education
ID ACHIEVEMENT; EMOTIONS; STUDENTS
AB Introduction Statistics education faces the challenge of sustaining engagement with abstract material. Although metaphorical instruction is common, the discourse mechanisms shaping moment-to-moment affective engagement remain poorly understood. This study examines how metaphor-related discourse moves are associated with learner arousal during one-on-one statistics tutoring.Methods Fine-grained discourse analysis was combined with continuous psychophysiological measurement. Six discourse move categories were identified through qualitative coding, including Metaphor Construction, Metaphor Scaffolding, Affective Framing, Metacognitive Prompting, Learner Response, and Boundary Cues. Skin conductance response data from 30 novice learners were aligned with coded events and analyzed using event-triggered linear mixed-effects modelling.Results Metaphor Construction (Cohen's d = 1.33) and Learner Response (d = 1.26) were associated with the strongest sustained arousal. Affective Framing was associated with a rapid spike (d = 0.73) with steep decay, while Metaphor Scaffolding (d = 0.62) and Metacognitive Prompting (d = 0.31) were associated with slower cumulative growth. Boundary Cues were associated with declining arousal (d = -0.23). Discourse features explained 19.9% of SCR variance, increasing to 31.2% with learner-level differences.Discussion The findings suggest instructional metaphor as a temporally dynamic interactional process. Pedagogical effectiveness may depend on how discourse moves are sequenced within coherent metaphor episodes.

AB Introduction Large language models can produce fluent tutoring dialogue, but their educational use remains limited by weak grounding, uneven pedagogical control, and the risk of unsupported content.    Analytics-Driven Framework for Strategic Management and Functional
   Integration in Higher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE strategic management; Data Analytics; Higher Education Institutions;
   core function integration; evidence-based decision-making; modified
   Delphi; continuous improvement; institutional governance
AB Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) face increasing challenges in effectively integrating their core functions of Teaching, Research, and Community Engagement (TRCE) while responding to growing demands for quality, accountability, and data-informed governance. This study aimed to design and refine the Integrated Strategic Management and Functional Integration Model (MIGEAS, from its Spanish acronym: Modelo Integral de Gesti & oacute;n Estrat & eacute;gica y Articulaci & oacute;n Sustantiva), a Data Analytics (DA)-driven conceptual framework intended to strengthen strategic management and the articulation of core university functions. The framework was developed through a design-oriented process combining theoretical synthesis with exploratory diagnostic evidence obtained from specialized institutional informants, semi-structured interviews, focus-group discussions, documentary analysis, and Force Field Analysis. The diagnostic evidence was used to identify institutional conditions and design requirements rather than to support population-level statistical inference. These findings informed the dimensions, components, relationships, and six implementation phases of MIGEAS. The resulting framework was subsequently refined and evaluated through a three-round modified Delphi procedure involving five purposively selected experts. Expert judgments showed moderate but statistically significant agreement during the first two rounds and strong convergence in the final round (Kendall's W = 0.921, p < 0.001), following successive modifications based on expert feedback. The findings support MIGEAS as an expert-refined conceptual framework that integrates strategic management, Data Analytics, functional integration, organizational change, and continuous improvement within a unified institutional architecture. The framework provides a structured basis for future implementation and evaluation in diverse higher education contexts.

TI Localizing International Accreditation in Teacher Education: Evidence
   from CAEP Implementation in Kuwait
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE teacher education; international accreditation; CAEP; quality assurance;
   policy transfer; organizational learning
AB International accreditation frameworks increasingly influence teacher education and quality assurance worldwide, yet limited research has examined their implementation in non-Western higher education contexts. This study used an explanatory sequential mixed methods design to explore faculty perceptions of how well the teacher education programs at Kuwait University's College of Education align with the Council for the Accreditation of Educator Preparation (CAEP) standards. The study also explained the institutional factors that shaped these perceptions. In the quantitative phase, a questionnaire was distributed to all eligible College of Education faculty members, and 38 faculty members completed the survey. In the qualitative phase, seven faculty members were purposively selected because of their direct experience with accreditation, quality assurance, and program evaluation. In addition, historical accreditation reports were analyzed to provide a broader institutional context. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics. The integrated findings demonstrate that successful implementation of international accreditation standards extends beyond technical compliance and depends on organizational readiness, institutional commitment, and sustained quality assurance processes within the local context. The study recommends strengthening institution-wide quality assurance systems, improving leadership coordination, and promoting evidence-based decision-making to support sustainable accreditation and the continuous improvement of teacher education programs.

TI A Game-Based Eye-Tracking Task for Inclusive Educational Assessment in
   Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder and Dyslexia: An Exploratory
   Study
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE eye-tracking; game-based assessment; autism spectrum disorder; dyslexia;
   inclusive education; Universal Design for Learning; neurodiversity
ID JOINT-ATTENTION; PREVALENCE
AB Background: Inclusive educational assessment requires tools that capture how learners with diverse cognitive profiles engage with tasks. This study examines whether a game-based, gaze-contingent eye-tracking task can generate relevant indicators for inclusive assessment of autistic children and children with dyslexia. Methods: Forty-five children (15 autistic, 15 with dyslexia, 15 neurotypical) completed a Unity 3D eye-tracking task assessing implicit joint attention, inhibitory control, and task engagement. Six gaze-based metrics were analyzed alongside standardized measures of joint attention, theory of mind, working memory, and processing speed. Group differences in the eye-tracking metrics were examined using permutation-based analysis of covariance controlling for chronological age and Full-Scale IQ, and associations with clinical measures were examined using a small set of pre-specified, Holm-corrected Spearman correlations. Results: Significant group differences were observed for five of the six metrics (partial eta 2 = 0.33-0.81). The autistic group showed the highest values on difficulty-related metrics and differed significantly from both the neurotypical and dyslexia groups on nearly every measure, while the neurotypical and dyslexia groups did not differ significantly from each other. One correlation remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons: task efficiency in the autistic group was linked to a behavioral correlate of theory of mind. Conclusions: Gaze-based indicators within a game-based task can differentiate autistic children from neurotypical and dyslexic peers and show a preliminary behavioral correlate of theory of mind in autism specifically. These findings offer narrow, preliminary support for the value of process-oriented tools for inclusive educational assessment. Future research should examine feasibility, validity, and psychometric stability in larger, matched samples and in authentic school contexts.

TI Evaluation of Inductive Coding with LLMs
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative artificial intelligence; GenAI; large language model; LLM;
   ChatGPT; mixed methods; prompt engineering; educational technology;
   geography education
ID MODEL; AI
AB Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT are reshaping qualitative research by offering data-driven analysis. Recent studies focus on labeling and classifying qualitative data, yet the generative process behind code system development is underexplored. This study investigates how ChatGPT constructs coding systems from interview data under iterative code engineering. The resulting code system is systematically compared to an inductive coding framework derived by content analysis-quantitatively by SBERT analysis, Jaccard index, and network analysis, and qualitatively. The results of NLP-based analysis show that there are mostly high cosine similarities in the one-to-one mapping between ChatGPT codes and content analysis. The overall Jaccard index is low, indicating limited overlap between the coding units and, consequently, that the two coding systems often did not refer to the same content. However, the mapped codes showed substantial variation: while nearly half exhibited high overlap, others showed no overlap. Network analysis shows that network density is comparable across the two systems, indicating a similar level of interconnectedness among codes despite differences in network size. Finally, iterative prompt engineering could create a stable code system, but ChatGPT lacks in domain-specific coding addressing the research questions adequately, warranting further investigation across larger datasets.

   INTROSPECTION; AUTONOMY; DESIGN; ORGANIZATIONS; GIFTEDNESS; EXPERIENCE
AB For a long time, research on creativity has focused more on cognitive aspects ("minds") rather than the production side ("actions"). This paper examines the creative practice as a subjective experience, using researcher introspection as a qualitative methodology. Through in-depth reflection on the creative development of an Ikebana artist, this study captures the complexity of creative practice, and offers detailed insights into its embodied and procedural dimensions, including experimentation and flow. Drawing on the theory of deliberate practice, the study challenges the notion that creativity is purely spontaneous and demonstrates how improvisation emerges through disciplined practice and deliberate experimentation. We propose a three-stage, practice-based model for training creativity: mastering fundamentals, exploring variations, and ultimately breaking free from established forms.

TI Scaling Professional Development with a Diverse Early Childhood
   Workforce
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE early childhood education; professional development; train-the-trainer;
   early childhood workforce; cascade model
ID EARLY CARE; METAANALYSIS; EDUCATION; QUALITY; TEACHERS
AB This qualitative phenomenological study examines how CDI teachers and community mothers in Colombia experienced the implementation of a professional development program structured as a cascade model. Semi-structured interviews were used to explore participants' accounts of implementation and the conditions they described as facilitating or constraining their engagement with the program. Participants' accounts suggest that the cascade model operated within a workforce already differentiated by institutional roles, professional trajectories, and working conditions, with these differences being reflected in participants' experiences of training and pedagogical appropriation. Participants also described drawing on motivation, professional judgment, and peer networks, some of which supported the continued circulation of program-related knowledge beyond the formal training structure. Together, these findings suggest that cascade models can extend the reach of professional development but may also reproduce pre-existing structural inequalities unless workforce heterogeneity and the capacities educators already bring to implementation are explicitly considered in program design.

TI Citizenship Education in Engineering Degree Programs: An Analysis of the
   Academic Literature
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE engineering education; citizenship education; sociotechnical; higher
   education
ID DESIGN; TECHNOLOGY; UNIVERSITY; THINKING; CONTEXT; MODELS; ETHICS;
   SCHOOL
AB Citizenship education in engineering programs has become a topic of growing concern due to the social, environmental, and technological impacts of engineers' professional practice. However, there is a lack of systematized information about trends and gaps in the academic literature in this area, which hinders the work of researchers, educators, and academic administrators. Therefore, this study examined the academic literature of the last thirty years (1996-2025) in four major scientific databases (WoS Core Collection, Scopus, SciELO, and Dialnet Plus). A systematic review was conducted using the PRISMA method, which allowed the selection of the articles (n = 74). These articles were then examined through qualitative thematic analysis. Additionally, descriptive frequencies of the corpus were identified, allowing for more precise contextualization. The results show a growing, albeit concentrated, field amidst an incipient transition from a dominant individualistic approach to a critical-democratic one. Furthermore, several significant gaps in the literature were identified, pointing to new research directions. Finally, the implications of these results for engineering schools are presented.
