TI Supporting ChemistryStudents' Satisfactionthrough Physical and Virtual
   Laboratories
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Audience: Second-Year Undergraduate; Domain: ChemicalEngineering;
   Pedagogy: Virtual Laboratories; Topic:Analytical Chemistry
ID AUGMENTED REALITY; SCIENCE
AB This study investigates the effectiveness of a virtual reality (VR) laboratory in enhancing student engagement, confidence, and preparedness for real laboratory work. This resulted in three interrelated aims essential for an effective VR learning experience: content relevance, instructional design, and technical feasibility. Therefore, a simple pedagogical framework for designing VR learning materials was developed to meet these multidisciplinary goals. Following this framework, we developed and built a 360-VR version of a chemistry laboratory exercise. Data regarding its effectiveness were obtained through a laboratory course for over 250 first- and second-year chemical engineering students. Students performed the same laboratory exercise as a virtual laboratory and then as an authentic student laboratory. Since some of these exercises serve as learning aids for collaborative student practice, and since there is no actual physical experience in a virtual laboratory, students stated in the subsequent evaluation that virtual laboratories would not replace the experience in a real laboratory and do not directly increase student motivation. The students also had a very positive attitude about virtual learning materials and asked for more activating materials, such as quizzes and interactive videos, to be included in the learning materials. A small number of students commented on negative points in the virtual laboratory exercise. In summary, it was demonstrated that our design principles hold in practice, as students reported a number of true benefits upon completing a virtual lab exercise prior to the real-life laboratory exercise. These advantages consisted of understanding the proper sequence by which physical laboratory exercises are conducted and the way to conduct certain duties correctly.

LA English
DT Article

AB Direct methanol fuel cells (DMFCs) face two major challenges: slow methanol oxidation reaction (MOR) kinetics and catalyst poisoning by CO. These challenges limit their efficiency and lifetime, creating a need for better anode catalysts. This paper describes an undergraduate laboratory experiment on the soft-template synthesis of mesoporous palladium nanoparticles (mesoPd NPs). TI Educational content features of screen media for preschoolers: links
   with later language, literacy and maths ability
SO EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE Screen media; Television; Early childhood; Language development;
   Mathematics
ID TELEVISION PROGRAM; SOCIOECONOMIC-STATUS; VIEWING BEHAVIORS;
   CHILD-DEVELOPMENT; SCHOOL READINESS; BLUES-CLUES; GROWING-UP;
   VOCABULARY; TODDLERS; COMPREHENSION
AB An increasingly prominent environmental influence for young children is their screen media exposure. For preschoolers (children aged 2-5 years), television and video viewing remains the most common type of screen media consumed. In this research we aimed to examine children's natural television viewing habits (i.e., the television shows most frequently watched) at age 2 in relation to later language, literacy, and maths skills prior to school entry (age 4.5). Content viewed by children was coded for inclusion of language, literacy and maths instructional features. Data was collected as part of the longitudinal Growing Up in New Zealand study, with data available for 5,338 children and their mothers. Literacy instructional features were not associated with child outcomes. Our results indicate that for some children, exposure to educational media may help support the development of language and maths skills, highlighting the importance of high-quality educational media for preschool-aged children.

TI Developing educational trajectory indicators to fulfill stakeholder
   needs: Using data for dropout prevention in Uruguayan public schools

LA English

DE Educational trajectories; Dropout; Uruguay; Dashboard; Mixed methods;
   Joint display
ID MIXED-METHODS; GRADUATION; MATTER; TIME
AB With one of the lowest Latin-American secondary school completion rates, Uruguay aims for continuous and complete educational trajectories. To support this national goal, we set up a sequential multi-stage mixedmethods study to propose and discuss the incorporation of educational trajectories' indicators in the national public school dashboard. Interviews, focus groups and workshops were conducted to understand principals and teachers' data needs to support students' trajectories. Stakeholders' concerns on the relation between students' dropout risk, their trajectories and academic performance guide the design of a follow-up quantitative study. The rationale for choosing a mix methods study design as a way to integrate stakeholders input, foster evidence-based data usability and disseminate study findings is also discussed.

TI Time pressure and its impact on PhD success: A case study from Hungary
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Education policy; Education reform; Productivity; Success
ID PERFORMANCE; UNIVERSITIES; PRODUCTIVITY; INDICATOR; PUBLISH; CAREER
AB A significant portion of academic discourse examines how national doctoral training systems balance efficiency and scholarly impact. This paper presents a single-country policy analysis of how regulatory time constraints are associated with the performance and productivity of PhD students in Hungary. In Hungary, the government implemented a new structure, introducing a 4+1 year time limit for doctoral training, which replaced the previous open-ended system. Utilizing bibliometric and regression methodologies, we analyzed a comprehensive dataset comprising 2,454 individuals from 18 doctoral schools in economics, business, and regional science. Descriptive pre-post comparisons indicate lower average international publication intensity and citation visibility among post-2016 doctoral cohorts. However, these raw differences do not translate into a statistically significant conditional level difference in the multivariate models once individual characteristics, supervisory capital, and institutional context are accounted for. Instead, the regression and pre-post interaction results indicate selective periodspecific differences in the associations between doctoral research outcomes, broader-output productivity, field-adjusted citation efficiency, and selected supervisory characteristics. Research-year exposure shows specification-dependent associations and does not provide a uniform explanation for differences in international research performance. The findings therefore suggest a reweighting of the observable determinants of doctoral research outcomes rather than a uniform regression-adjusted decline in performance levels. The model results, therefore, point to an efficiency-impact trade-off in doctoral training design: more structured timelines may support short-horizon efficiency and more immediate output, whereas more flexible horizons may better accommodate the accumulation of scholarly returns over longer research cycles - an important consideration for policymakers designing doctoral training reforms in similar institutional contexts.

TI Generative ArtificialIntelligence in Medicinal ChemistryEducation:
   Student Engagement, Confidence Calibration, and
   Safety-RelatedUncertainty in Case-Based Learning
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative Artificial Intelligence; Medicinal ChemistryEducation;
   Case-Based Learning; Metacognition; Confidence Calibration; Student
   Judgment; Safety-RelatedUncertainty; AI Validation Literacy
ID JUDGMENTS
AB The current study focuses on the function and use of generative artificial intelligence in teaching medicinal chemistry, with particular emphasis on learning process dynamics, decision-making power, and confidence estimation. A total of 101 undergraduate students in pharmacy schools were assigned to work on four case-type medicinal chemistry issues with optional artificial intelligence help. The variables in this research included task-specific AI use, confidence (pre/post), agreement with AI-generated outputs, and perceived certainty regarding chemical correctness and safety. Findings include that while there was considerable variation in usage patterns depending on the task type, there was considerable usage for explanatory tasks, with reduced reliance for higher-stakes decision-making tasks (structural modification/ADMET). Confidence recalibration was also found to vary: while most participants showed increased confidence after interacting with AI, many showed little or no confidence. Notably, there was considerable agreement with the output of AI, even in situations of doubt about its correctness or safety. The qualitative results showed that students mainly viewed AI as an entity for conceptual scaffolding, and their experiences within the disciplines influenced conditional trust and challenges in the process of verification. In general, the research indicates that generative AI is a high-fluency cognitive aid that alters traditionally assessed metacognitive control and monitoring and not just improves it. AI can help students understand medicinal chemistry concepts but also highlights the weaknesses of their capacity for the process of verifying the correctness and safety of the results.

TI Closing the Gap in Ostomy Care: A Structured Curriculum Improves General
   Surgery Resident Competence in Preoperative Stoma Site Marking

DT Article
DE stoma site marking; simulation-based education; quality improvement;
   WOCN
ID COMPLICATIONS
AB OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether a structured, simulation-based multidisciplinary teaching session could improve general surgery resident self-reported confidence and knowledge in preoperative stoma site marking. DESIGN: Prospective pilot quality improvement initiative using a pre-/postintervention design. Resident confidence and knowledge were assessed immediately before and after the intervention using an investigator-developed 10-item instrument scored on a 5-point Likert scale (maximum composite score 50). Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used for comparison. SETTING: Community-based general surgery residency program at a single institution in California. CONCLUSIONS: A single, brief, multidisciplinary teaching session incorporating didactic instruction and simulation-based practice significantly improved resident confidence and knowledge in preoperative stoma site marking. Formal incorporation of this curriculum into general surgery residency training represents a practical, low-resource intervention with potential to reduce stoma-related complications and standardize care in settings where Wound, Ostomy, and Continence nurse (WOCN) expertise is unavailable. TI Executive control network efficiency and interactive creativity:
   Moderating the relationship between individual and paired performance
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Co-creativity; Executive control network; Graph theory; Divergent
   thinking; Remote associates test
ID FUNCTIONAL CONNECTIVITY; COGNITION
AB This study examined whether resting-state functional connectivity efficiency of the executive control network (ECN) moderates the relationship between creative performance in individual and paired contexts. A total of 151 adults completed the Alternative Uses Task (AUT) and the Chinese Radical Remote Associates Test (CRRAT) in single and paired modes and then underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Graph-theoretical analyses were used to estimate the local, global, and nodal efficiency of the ECN. The results showed that both local and global ECN efficiency moderated the relationship between flexibility in the single and paired modes. Specifically, under lower ECN efficiency, single-mode flexibility more strongly predicted paired-mode flexibility, indicating a moderating effect of ECN efficiency on the continuity of flexibility across solitary and paired contexts. No comparable moderating effects were found for fluency, originality, or CRRAT performance. These findings suggest that ECN efficiency plays a selective moderating role in the transfer of divergent-thinking flexibility from solitary to interactive contexts.

LA English
DT Article
DE reading; COVID-19; early development
ID ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; SCHOOL; COMPETENCE; SKILLS; COMPREHENSION;

AB COVID-19 disrupted early reading development, especially for under-resourced students. Few studies have evaluated early reading skill recovery after the return to in-person instruction. This study tracked reading achievement among 236,701 kindergarten through second-grade students from the academic year 2019-2020 to 2023-2024 (48.7% female; 69.8% Latine). TI Early mathematics interventions in pre-primary education: A three-level
   meta-analysis of intentional teaching and exploratory play approaches
SO EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Intentional teaching; Exploratory play; Early mathematics intervention;
   Preschool; Kindergarten; Three-level meta-analysis
ID NUMBER-SENSE INTERVENTION; CHILDRENS EARLY NUMERACY;
   LEARNING-DISABILITIES; KINDERGARTEN-CHILDREN; SECONDARY STUDENTS;
   PRESCHOOL; PROGRAM; MATH; RISK; CURRICULUM
AB Early mathematics interventions in pre-primary education are generally effective, but prior syntheses rarely distinguish the dominant pedagogical approach used and provide limited evidence on which study or implementation features are associated with effects within each approach. This three-level meta-analysis synthesized 74 studies (2000-2025) of early mathematics interventions in preschool and kindergarten, focusing on two broad pedagogical approaches: intentional teaching and exploratory play. Studies were classified by dominant pedagogical emphasis as intentional teaching (k = 56) or exploratory play (k = 18), yielding 566 effect sizes. Both approaches were associated with positive effects on children's learning (intentional teaching: g = 0.32; exploratory play: g = 0.21), and the difference between approaches was not statistically significant. Moderator analyses examined heterogeneity by program design, intervention conditions and outcome evaluation. For intentional teaching, effects were larger for advanced numeracy outcomes (quantitative comparison: g = 0.42; calculation: g = 0.45) than for foundational number and counting skills (g = 0.21). Effects also attenuated over time, with smaller follow-up than immediate post-test effects (post-test: g = 0.34; follow-up: g = 0.20), suggesting partial fadeout. For exploratory play, interventions incorporating contextual scenarios showed larger effects (g = 0.47) than those without (g = 0.13), and effects were stronger for mathspecific outcomes (g = 0.26) than for non-math outcomes (g = -0.01). Overall, the findings support the use of both pedagogical approaches in early mathematics programs and highlight the need to align instructional design with targeted numeracy goals and to sustain learning gains over time.

TI Towards family-friendly conferences: results from a first survey in the
   geosciences
SO GEOSCIENCE COMMUNICATION
LA English
DT Article
ID WOMEN; WORK; MOTHERHOOD; CONFLICT; ROLES
AB Building an academic career requires a high level of dedication to research, frequent publishing, and maintaining visibility within the academic community. Scientific conferences are the central platforms for networking and knowledge exchange, making them keystones of an academic career. However, the early stages of an academic career often coincide with family planning considerations. Many young researchers face the challenge of balancing professional responsibilities with family obligations. A balancing act that becomes particularly difficult during non-routine work events such as conferences. Such occasions tend to pose significant organizational challenges for families. As mothers still provide most of the care, they are disproportionately affected. This conflict is an important factor contributing to the "leaky pipeline" by inhibiting the progression of women through academic ranks. Increasing the family-friendliness of conferences has the potential to diversify the scientific community, allowing more parents to participate, while reducing the tension between academic work and family obligations.Here, we present the results of an online survey among researchers in the geoscientific field, primarily based in Europe. The required support of parents at scientific conferences is analyzed and the acceptance for the implementation of new support offered by researchers without children is examined. Our key findings are that (1) parents wish for more support at conferences, (2) the majority of non-parents welcome family-friendly measures, and (3) conference organizers can accomplish a lot in this respect, even with small adjustments. The responses we received from parents paint a qualitative picture of measures that can be considered to create a family-friendly conference experience, ranging from increased transparency and awareness for the challenges of parents to tangible offers such as childcare and financial support.Our findings are distilled into guidelines for conference organizers, allowing them to better address the work-family conflict and transform their conferences towards more equity, diversity, and inclusion.

TI STEM immersions plus pedagogical PD drives multi-domain growth in
   multi-disciplinary teachers: qualitative findings from the Kenan Fellows
   Program for Teacher Leadership
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF STEM EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE STEM experiences for teachers; Teacher professional development; Teacher
   professional growth; Industry experiences for teachers; STEM Education
ID PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; RESEARCH EXPERIENCES
AB Background Preparing students for evolving science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) careers requires teachers who understand workforce skills and pathways, yet most professional development (PD) and STEM Experiences for Teachers (SETs) are studied in isolation. This study examines the effects of the Kenan Fellows Program for Teacher Leadership (KFP) on teachers' professional growth. KFP is a year-long model that integrates a 120h summer industry or research immersion with 80h of pedagogical and leadership PD spread across summer, fall, and spring institutes. We conducted a secondary analysis of transcripts from 56 interviews and 3 focus-groups from 73 teachers who participated in KFP between 2018 and 2024. The data were originally collected for the purpose of program evaluation. We employed inductive coding and then mapped emergent categories to Clarke and Hollingsworth's () Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (IMPG) to examine professional growth in the participating teachers' personal domain, domain of practice, and domain of consequence. The IMPG accounts for the complex and multi-faceted nature of teacher professional growth that flows from PD experiences, providing a useful lens for examining the effects of KFP on teacher growth.Results Our findings indicate that the participating teachers most frequently reported changes in their personal domain (n = 371), with more references to knowledge (n = 160) than beliefs (n = 128) or attitudes (n = 69). Growth in their domain of practice (n = 211) centered on pedagogy (n = 136) and forming new community connections (n = 54). Reported changes in their domain of consequence (n = 241) highlighted teacher outcomes (n = 162) and new student opportunities (n = 95). Co-occurrence analyses linked knowledge gains to professional development and industry connections (72 co-occurrences) and belief change to program infrastructure/values and brand recognition (52 co-occurrences). A salient pathway traced increased self-efficacy -> agentic action -> new community connections -> opportunities for students.Conclusions The results of this study highlight how integrating SETs with sustained pedagogical and leadership PD drives multi-domain teacher growth and bridges the "knowing-doing gap" often seen in professional learning. Findings show that KFP's SET + PD model enhances teachers' knowledge, self-efficacy, and networks, which in turn catalyze agentic actions that expand classroom opportunities for students (e.g., classroom projects connected to apprenticeship programs). Through the lens of Clarke and Hollingsworth's IMPG, the study demonstrates that external supports-such as industry experiences, high-quality PD, and program infrastructure-produce personal growth that translates into new pedagogical practices, leadership roles, and student engagement. This study positions the KFP model as a replicable framework for workforce-aligned teacher professional development and offers design and policy recommendations for scaling SET + PD initiatives to strengthen K-12 STEM education and career readiness.

AB Background Dementia is highly prevalent globally with a fivefold increased risk in individuals with intellectual disabilities, particularly those with Down syndrome. AB Background: The Therapeutic Greenhouse Program, located at an elementary school in an underserved community, offers a sustainable and reproducible model for school-based garden programming. TI Examining the associations between quality of interactions children
   experience in child care learning environments and their developmental
   outcomes
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Child development; Early childhood education and care; Interactions;
   Quality
ID LOW-INCOME CHILDREN; CLASSROOM QUALITY; ACHIEVEMENT; SENSITIVITY;
   VALIDATION; TEACHERS; PATHWAYS; LANGUAGE; INFANT
AB Early childhood is a critical developmental period. During this time, children spend significant amounts of time in early childhood education and care (ECEC) learning environments. High-quality ECEC learning environments have been associated with positive developmental outcomes. However, emerging research suggests that aggregating quality assessments mask important variation based on the unit (e.g. classroom, educator, child) and time (e.g. throughout the morning) of assessment. This study examines the variation in the quality of interactions individual children experience from their educators across time using a novel "person-centred" longitudinal analysis, a group-based multi-trajectory model analysis. This analysis was employed to examine the observational changes in the interactions children experienced from their educators (i.e. warm interactions, negative interactions, and language that explicitly promotes language development) over six time points. The relationship between interaction quality children experience and their academic competence, interpersonal relationships, temperament, and learning style was examined. The sample included 610 children from 94 classrooms in Toronto, Canada; however, demographic information was provided by parents for only a subset of the sample (n = 228). The average age of children was 45.52 months (SD = 10.89). We found that most children received little-to-no interactions from their educators. The group-based multi-trajectory model analysis found three subgroups based on the frequency of each interaction type they experience and how that frequency changes: None to Some Quality (37%), Decreasing Quality (29.7%), and Consistently Low (33.3%). Children who were in the Consistently Low profile were more likely to not speak English as their first language at home and were more hostile and less considerate (based on the Classroom Behaviour Inventory) than those who experienced decreases in quality across the morning. Implications for policy, practice, training, and future research are discussed.

DT Article
DE Approaches to studying; Cluster analysis; Higher education; Learning
   environment; Occupational therapy; Study performance

AB Little is known about how learning environment (LE) perceptions cluster within student populations and how such profiles relate to study behaviors and performance. This study aimed to identify clusters of Norwegian occupational therapy students based on their LE perceptions and to examine sociodemographic, study behaviors, and performance covariates associated with cluster allocation. Data were drawn from a national longitudinal investigation (2017-2020) including 233 students from Norway. The present study used a cross-sectional analysis of averaged measures collected across the three-year study program. A two-step cluster analysis was conducted on six LE dimensions, followed by ANOVAs, chi-square tests, and multinomial logistic regression analyses. Students can be meaningfully grouped into LE perception profiles which were associated with study approaches, effort, and academic performance. LE positive students showed a favorable pattern of study approaches, particularly in comparison with LE negative students. Targeted educational strategies addressing LE dimensions and promoting effective study approaches may help improve students' learning outcomes.

TI Exploring subject-specific variations in teachers' promotion of
   self-regulated learning: insights from classroom observations, teachers'
   self-reports, and students' perceptions
SO METACOGNITION AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-regulated Learning; Strategy instruction; Classroom observation;
   Teachers' self-reports; Students' perceptions; School subjects
ID MATHEMATICS; MOTIVATION; FRAMEWORK; QUALITY; CONTEXT
AB Teachers play a crucial role in fostering students' self-regulated learning (SRL) skills in the classroom. Previous research indicates that teachers adopt diverse approaches to promoting SRL, but empirical evidence on subject-specific differences remains limited. This study examines the extent to which native language and science teachers promote SRL and whether their approaches differ. To explore teachers' SRL promotion, we analysed video recordings of their classroom behaviour, their self-reported SRL promotion, and students' perceptions of their teachers' SRL promotion. The study involved 28 teachers and 515 students, with data collected at two measurement points. Analyses of observational and questionnaire data revealed that teachers of both subjects promoted SRL predominantly implicitly, focusing mainly on metacognitive and cognitive strategies, while emotional regulation strategies were largely neglected. Overall, SRL promotion was implemented only to a limited extent and occurred similarly across subjects. Although comparisons of several direct and indirect SRL promotion approaches indicated some variation, no systematic subject-specific differences emerged. Moreover, correlations between the three perspectives, observations, teachers' self-reports, and students' perceptions, were generally low, suggesting that each perspective captures distinct and complementary aspects of SRL promotion. Taken together, these findings indicate that variation in SRL promotion may be more strongly related to individual teacher characteristics, task characteristics, or lesson type than to the subject domain. Future research on potential differences in SRL promotion would benefit from adopting multi-perspective approaches to gain a more comprehensive understanding of SRL in classroom practice, as well as from incorporating systematic variation in the observation of SRL over longer periods.

TI Types of self-regulated learners matter in the association between
   instruction quality and digital reading performance
SO METACOGNITION AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE instruction quality; digital reading; self-regulated learning; reading
   metacognition; reading motivation
ID AGE-DIFFERENCES; STUDENTS; CLASSROOM; METACOGNITION; ADAPTATIONS;
   MOTIVATION; ACHIEVEMENT
AB Many studies have found an association between instruction quality and digital reading performance. This study aims to investigate whether this association varies across self-regulated learning (SRL) profiles and whether instruction quality is indirectly associated with digital reading performance through SRL profiles. Participants were 12,058 fifteen-year-old students from Mainland China who participated in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2018. Latent profile analysis was conducted to identify SRL profiles and examine their roles in the association between instruction quality and digital reading performance. Four SRL profiles emerged. Profiles High SRL and Low SRL represented the best and the weakest levels of all SRL variables, respectively. Profile High Metacognitive Knowledge was characterized by high metacognitive knowledge of reading strategies but low motivation. Profile Strong Motivation-Low Feeling of Difficulty was characterized by high motivation and low levels of feeling of difficulty and metacognitive knowledge. Stimulation of engagement, disciplinary climate, and teacher enthusiasm were positively associated with profiles exhibiting higher motivation, while teacher-directed instruction and teacher feedback were negatively associated with profiles exhibiting higher metacognition. Adaptive instruction and teacher support showed weak associations with SRL profiles. The association between instruction quality and the performance varied significantly across SRL profiles. No instruction quality variable was consistently associated with performance across all profiles. For teacher-directed instruction, stimulation of engagement, and disciplinary climate, both direct associations with digital reading performance and indirect associations via SRL profiles were statistically significant. For teacher enthusiasm, only the indirect association was significant. For adaptive instruction, teacher support, and teacher feedback, no significant indirect association was found. The findings suggest the potential moderating and mediating roles of SRL profiles in the association between instruction quality and digital reading performance, but they should be interpreted as statistical associations rather than causal effects.

DT Article
ID GENERATION
AB The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) marks a potential inflection point in the way academic information is accessed, raising fundamental questions about the evolving role of search in student learning. This study examines this shift by analyzing longitudinal trends in physics-related search and page-view activity, using declines in traditional search behavior as a quantitative proxy for changes in independent information-seeking practices. We analyze Google Trends data for core concepts in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and optics across three academic years (2022-2025) in more than 20 countries and complement this analysis with Wikipedia page-view data across seven major languages to establish platform independence. The results reveal a substantial, systematic, and persistent global decline in search and page-view activity across most examined physics topics. The magnitude of this decline is domain-dependent, with mechanics-related content showing sharper and more consistent reductions than content related to electromagnetism and optics. Pronounced geographic and linguistic heterogeneity is observed: while English-speaking regions show relative stability or only moderate declines, non-Englishspeaking regions exhibit substantially larger reductions in traditional, search-based information-seeking activity. Despite the overall decrease in volume, the seasonal structure characteristic of academic activity remains robust. Taken together, these findings indicate a redistribution of physics-related informationseeking behavior in academic contexts where generative tools are increasingly available.

TI From Relevant to Publishable in TESOL Research: Contribution, Access,
   and Accountability
SO TESOL QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
ID ENGLISH
AB Many manuscripts sent to TQ are recognizably TESOL, carefully written, and ethically serious. The harder editorial question is what moves a manuscript from relevant to publishable. In this editorial, we argue that publishability rests on three connected expectations. The article needs to make a contribution that changes how TESOL researchers, teachers, teacher educators, or policymakers understand a problem. It needs to make knowledge accessible beyond a narrow group of specialists, including through clearer writing and the continued use of OASIS summaries for accepted articles. It also needs to make its claims accountable, through responsible data practices, transparent methods, careful use of AI, and authorial ownership of the argument. These expectations have consequences for authors deciding where to send their work, for reviewers deciding what deserves space in the journal, and for us as editors of a journal that helps shape what the field recognizes as valuable TESOL research.

TI Teaching Mathematics to Autistic Students: Findings From an Online
   Multicomponent Video Modeling Intervention
SO EDUCATION AND TRAINING IN AUTISM AND DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE autism; mathematics; video modeling; self-monitoring; online

AB The aim of this study was to examine the effects of an online multicomponent video modeling intervention which included self-monitoring supports and a system of least prompts when teaching mathematics to three autistic students using a multiple baseline design across participants of a single-case experimental methodology. Three autistic children, 8-12 years old, participated in a synchronous, online intervention focused on teaching single-digit subtraction, negative integers, and double-digit by single-digit multiplication. Math goals for the study were determined based on parental input followed by a brief, informal assessment. Following the intervention, participants showed greater accuracy in solving target math problems. The findings highlight the effectiveness of the online multicomponent intervention in teaching math skills to autistic children.

TI Relational Work in Higher Education: University Staff Perspectives on
   Institutional Responsibility for Student Well-Being
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION

ID PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTRESS; FACULTY INTERACTIONS; COLLEGE-STUDENTS;

AB As concerns about student mental health have intensified, responsibility for supporting student well-being is increasingly negotiated in everyday interactions between students and staff. This study aims to foreground the relational and caring dimensions of academic practice. It does so by examining how university staff understand and navigate their professional role in relational work to support students, and how this work is shaped by structural and emotional conditions. Drawing on five focus group interviews with 27 teaching and student-support staff across multiple campuses and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, the study shows that care, trust, and accessibility are integral to everyday pedagogical and support practice. TI Women's Experiences of Discrimination and Their Success Expectations in
   Higher Education: Evidence from Gendered Fields of Study
SO RESEARCH IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Discrimination experiences; Gender; Success expectations; Higher
   education; Horizontal gender segregation
ID ACADEMIC-PERFORMANCE; UNDERGRADUATE WOMEN; RELATIONAL VICTIMIZATION;
   COLLEGE; PERCEPTIONS; FEMALE; STUDENTS; SCIENCE; CLIMATE; MODEL
AB Women's underrepresentation in male-dominated fields of study is often attributed to a gender gap in success expectations. Prior research shows that female students report lower confidence in their academic abilities and future success than men, not only in male-dominated but also in female-dominated and gender-integrated fields. These lower success expectations can negatively affect women's academic paths, making it important to understand the factors that shape them. Although existing studies highlight the positive role of social experiences in shaping women's success expectations, particularly in male-dominated fields, women are also more likely than men to experience discrimination, which may undermine these benefits. However, the role of discrimination experiences in shaping success expectations in higher education remains underexplored. This study examines how female students' discrimination experiences contribute to the gender gap in students' success expectations and investigates whether the relationship between discrimination experiences and success expectations among female students varies across fields of study with varying gender ratios. Using data from 9,512 students collected as part of the Student Survey in Germany (SiD), we analyze female students' discrimination experiences and their associations with success expectations in male-dominated, female-dominated, and gender-integrated fields of study. The results show that women, particularly in male-dominated fields, report higher levels of discrimination than men. These experiences contribute to the overall gender gap in success expectations. However, detailed analyses reveal that only relational discrimination experiences, such as social exclusion or unfair treatment, are significantly associated with female students' success expectations, revealing a seeming paradox: this association emerges primarily in female-dominated rather than male-dominated fields, even though female students experience more discrimination in the latter. This suggests that the consequences of discrimination for success expectations are context-dependent and may reflect different coping strategies across disciplines. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between types of discrimination and contexts when examining gender disparities in success expectations. Furthermore, they underscore the need for targeted interventions addressing relational discrimination to support women's academic confidence in higher education.

SO CHEMISTRY TEACHER INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE teachers' training course; high school teachers; conceptual maps;

AB The study of preservice teachers' ideas and understanding of various aspects of chemistry is an important topic in chemistry education. In this work, the results of an activity performed with 71 preservice high school teachers in the framework of a training course for the national qualification in Italy are described and discussed. The activity consists of the building of hierarchic conceptual maps concerning the key concepts in chemistry starting from a provided list of 31 words. These maps were built by teachers during a collaborative activity; a collective discussion followed this cooperative work to discuss with future teachers the core concepts in chemistry and eventual misconceptions. The effectiveness of the conceptual maps and their main uses in teaching and learning chemistry were discussed with preservice teachers during the collective discussion. The analysis of conceptual maps and further collective discussion revealed several difficulties in explaining the connections among several key concepts in chemistry. Moreover, alternative ideas, for instance concerning the concepts of 'compounds' and 'mixtures', were observed among preservice teachers. The findings reported in the present paper are useful to reflect on some aspects of chemistry education and of the training of future high school teachers.

TI How leading a math circle fosters personal growth: a multiple case study
   of undergraduates conducting STEM outreach
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE math circles; mathematics education; service learning; STEM identity;
   STEM outreach; undergraduate instructors; university-community
   engagement
ID UNIVERSITY; ENGAGEMENT; KNOWLEDGE
AB This study examines a university-community engagement initiative through which undergraduate STEM students lead math circles, afterschool enrichment programs that welcome children of all mathematical abilities in Grades 4-6 (U.S.A.) to engage in mathematics-focused games and hands-on activities. In particular, we sought to generate an in-depth understanding of how the undergraduates describe their experience in the program and how it shapes their own personal and professional growth. Using a multiple case study approach, we collected and analyzed data from weekly reflections, observations, and end-of-semester interviews for three of the undergraduates in the program. Qualitative analysis consisted of iterative rounds of inductive coding to generate themes pertaining to teaching beliefs and strategies, identity, and personal and professional development, amongst others, followed by a cross-case analysis. Case narratives revealed unique journeys throughout the program for each participant, though all three expressed positive sentiments about the experience and its impact on them. Four cross-cutting themes were identified: the central role of relationship-building as an effective engagement strategy, the influence of prior beliefs about authority and their role on instructional decisions, the importance of reflective teaching to challenge prior assumptions, and the function of the program overall as a space for personal growth and identity affirmation. These shared experiences and positive impacts highlight the potential of math circles as an effective model for embedding service learning and community engagement within the undergraduate curriculum while supporting students' personal and professional development. They also underscore the importance of providing ongoing training and support to undergraduate leaders as they navigate new scenarios throughout the semester.

TI "TheyAre Students Just Like Me" - AnalyzingGeneral Chemistry Student
   Perspectives on Senior Undergraduate StudentLearning Assistants as
   Laboratory Instructors
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE First-Year Undergraduate/General; Curriculum; Laboratory Instruction;
   Mentorship; TA Training/Orientation
ID EDUCATION; BENEFITS; SCIENCE; IMPACT; SKILLS; SENSE
AB Senior undergraduate student learning assistants (LAs) have been utilized as instructors in the General (Introductory) Chemistry laboratories at a primarily undergraduate institution. We investigated what the students liked and disliked about senior undergraduate student LAs as laboratory instructors. Student (n = 102) responses to open-ended survey questions were thematically coded. The most important conclusion was that the General Chemistry students expressed an overwhelming preference for senior undergraduate LAs as laboratory instructors rather than for a staff member. Student responses were primarily positive toward LAs rather than negative toward staff. The most common themes that drove this preference for LAs as laboratory instructors were (1) a feeling of connection with the LAs, (2) liking that LAs are student peers, (3) feeling less (perceived) stress/intimidation with the LAs, and (4) appreciating that LAs have completed the same lab experiments themselves and thus have similar lab experiences. We also tested for significant differences in the frequency of responses between traditionally marginalized student groups vs their nonmarginalized counterparts. Tests for differences between students grouped according to gender (female vs male), race (nonwhite vs white), and access to learning accommodations revealed only a single difference: white students were more likely to identify imperfections in the LAs than their nonwhite counterparts. This suggests that implementation of LAs as general chemistry laboratory instructors is viewed as an equitable practice by students.

TI Folklore-based pedagogy for literacy and critical thinking in Sepedi
   classrooms
SO READING & WRITING-JOURNAL OF THE READING ASSOCIATION OF SOUTH AFRICA
LA English
DT Article
DE critical thinking; culturally responsive pedagogy; indigenous knowledge
   systems; literacy development; Sepedi folklore
AB Background: South African primary schools continue to face significant literacy challenges, with PIRLS 2016 finding that 78% of Grade 4 learners were unable to read for meaning. In Sepedi-speaking communities, the gap between indigenous oral traditions and formal education deepens these challenges, as culturally significant folklore resources remain underutilised. Objectives: This study examined the pedagogical potential of Sepedi folklore including folktales [dinonwane], proverbs [diema], and riddles [dithai] as culturally responsive tools for developing literacy and critical thinking among Grade 7 Sepedi home language learners in the Lebowakgomo Circuit, Limpopo. Method: A qualitative design used semi-structured teacher interviews, non-participant classroom observations and document analysis of learners' folklore-based activities. Participants were purposively selected, and data were analysed thematically using inductive coding. Results: Sepedi folklore functioned as an effective medium for vocabulary acquisition, figurative language, narrative competence and oral proficiency. It engaged culturally familiar schemas, reducing cognitive load and promoting higher-order analytical engagement. Dialogic folklore instruction improved learner engagement, inferential reasoning, and evaluative understanding. Conclusion: Sepedi folklore is a valuable tool for addressing literacy challenges and promoting critical thinking. Successful implementation requires ongoing professional development, curriculum alignment and community collaboration. Contribution: The study provides empirical evidence linking folklore-based pedagogy, literacy development and critical thinking in indigenous African language classrooms, supporting the integration of indigenous knowledge systems into formal literacy instruction.

TI Future orientation as a moderator of the association between bullying
   and cyberbullying victimization and perceived academic performance
   during adolescence
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adolescent agency; bullying victimization; cyberbullying; future
   orientation; perceived academic performance; school context
ID SELF-EFFICACY; SCHOOL; METAANALYSIS; RESILIENCE; PROGRAM; IMPACT
AB Introduction Peer victimization, in its traditional and cyber forms, is increasingly recognized as a relational and contextual process associated with multiple domains of adolescent development, including engagement with learning and academic self-perceptions. This study examined how traditional and cyberbullying victimization relate to perceived academic performance in a sample of Italian upper secondary school students, and tested whether future orientation, understood as a core dimension of adolescent agency, moderated these associations. Methods The final sample included 876 students (51.4% female, age range 14-17 years) who completed self-report measures of traditional and cyberbullying victimization and perpetration, future orientation, and perceived academic performance, assessed through self-reported grade ranges. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were conducted, complemented by bootstrap resampling with bias-corrected and accelerated confidence intervals. Results Both traditional and cyberbullying victimization were independently and negatively associated with future orientation and with perceived academic performance, even after controlling for perpetration and sociodemographic covariates. Traditional and cyberbullying perpetration also showed independent negative associations with perceived academic performance, though smaller in magnitude. Future orientation moderated the association between victimization and perceived academic performance in both models (both p < .001), attenuating the negative association at higher levels of future orientation across both traditional and cyber contexts. Discussion These findings situate peer victimization within a broader developmental and relational ecology and point to future orientation as a promising correlate of preserved academic self-perceptions among adolescents facing peer adversity. Because all measures were self-reported and the design was cross-sectional, causal or protective effects cannot be established. Implications for school-based educational and prevention practices are discussed.

TI Joy of moving: feasibility and fidelity of a child-led setup for mobile
   'phygital' play
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE children; feasibility study; mobile body tracking; mobile exergaming;
   phygital play
ID PHYSICAL-ACTIVITY; GUIDELINES; BEHAVIOR
AB Introduction: Fundamental movement skills (FMS) are an important foundation for children's confident participation in physical activity and sport, but many children spend substantial time engaged in sedentary screen-based activities. Phygital play, defined here as digital experiences that require real physical activity with gross motor skills, offers one possible way to create more active forms of screen time. However, before such experiences can be evaluated for broader developmental or movement-related effects, it is necessary to establish whether young children can access them successfully and whether they deliver the intended active gameplay experience. Methods: This implementation-focused pilot evaluated the mobile movement-tracking game Joy of moving in 182 children aged 4-7 years from Irish primary schools. The study examined whether children could independently complete a child-led setup process to reach gameplay and, once gameplay began, whether sessions delivered the intended dose of movement under adequate tracking conditions. An iterative three-phase design was used. Feasibility was defined as successful independent setup and access to gameplay. Fidelity was defined as "dose with quality" during gameplay. Results: Across three iterations of the setup flow, independent setup success increased from 42.6% to 77.4% (chi & sup2;(2, N = 182) = 16.41, p < .001). Among children who successfully completed setup, gameplay completion remained consistently high (92.3%-94.9%), while implementation fidelity ("dose with quality") improved from 66.7% to 91.1% as refinements to the setup guidance resulted in more reliable body positioning and tracking during gameplay. Discussion: These findings suggest that many children aged 4-7 years were able to access gameplay independently and that, following optimisation of the setup process, the intended movement experience could be delivered with high implementation fidelity.

TI The role of school management teams in monitoring and evaluating
   teachers' self-regulated learning implementation in primary school in
   the Lejweleputswa District, South Africa
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE evaluation; instructional leadership; learner autonomy; monitoring;
   school management teams; self-regulated learning; teacher support
ID LEADERSHIP; KNOWLEDGE
AB This study investigates the role of school management teams in monitoring and evaluating teachers' implementation of self-regulated learning in South African primary schools. Self-regulated learning is increasingly recognised as a critical factor for learner autonomy, motivation, and academic achievement. However, limited attention has been given to school management teams' role in supporting and quality-assuring its classroom implementation. Using a qualitative research design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with fifteen school management team members who were purposefully sampled across five primary schools. Thematic analysis revealed that school management team members' value self-regulated learning. However, monitoring practices are often inconsistent, compliance-focused, and constrained by limited self-regulated learning knowledge, time pressures, and administrative demands. Collaborative classroom observations and reflective discussions emerged as practices that enhance self-regulated learning integration. The study concludes that strengthening school management teams' capacity, formalising self-regulated learning evaluation frameworks, and providing systematic feedback mechanisms are crucial for improving self-regulated learning implementation. The findings contribute to educational leadership literature by identifying organisational conditions and capacity-building priorities necessary for effective self-regulated learning oversight.

TI Design guidelines for educational chatbots: supporting international
   students' acculturation in higher education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE acculturative stress; belongingnesss; chatbots; education; international
   students; study migration
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE AI; SOCIAL SUPPORT; ACADEMIC-PERFORMANCE;
   STRESS; UNIVERSITY; TRANSITION; ADJUSTMENT; TESTS; NEED
AB This study explored acculturative stressors experienced by HE international students studying in the UK and investigated their views on the potential of chatbots in supporting acculturation. To achieve these objectives, a two-phased mixed methods study design was designed. Firstly, 45 postgraduate international students participated in a longitudinal study across six months completing the Acculturative Stress Scale for International Students, ( Sandhu and Asrabadi, 1994), the Social Connectedness Scale, ( Lee and Robbins, 1995), and a demographics questionnaire including a measure of self-perceived English Proficiency. A key assertion of this work is that belongingness and acculturative stress are strongly linked, and that belongingness relates to three levels: social, academic and institutional, all important for acculturation. As a result of these findings, this article presents recommendations on how chatbot technology can be applied as a complementary resource to HEI's current services to assist the facilitation of social connections, academic support and collaborative learning.

TI Educational stress, anxiety, and academic success among Palestinian
   university students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic success; anxiety; educational stress; Palestine; university
   students
ID HEALTH; PERSPECTIVE
AB Background Student success is a complex concept that combines personal engagement with measurable performance. Within the specific educational environment of Palestine, unique contextual challenges are frequently linked with elevated levels of educational stress and anxiety, which are in turn inversely associated with academic outcomes. This study investigates the relationship between academic success, educational stress, and anxiety symptoms among Palestinian university students.Methods A cross-sectional design was employed with a sample of 1,397 students. Data were gathered using translated Arabic versions of the Academic Success Inventory for College Students (ASICS) and the Educational Stress Scale for Adolescents (ESSA), alongside the Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) scale. The analytical framework utilized descriptive statistics to characterize the sample and a four-step hierarchical regression analysis to determine the relative predictive power of demographic, social, and psychological factors on academic success.Results Descriptive findings indicated that the majority of students experienced moderate to severe symptoms of educational stress, with over half the sample reporting elevated anxiety symptoms. Hierarchical regression analysis revealed that the final model was statistically significant, explaining 23.2% of the total variance in academic success. Anxiety symptoms emerged as the factor most strongly associated with lower academic success, followed by symptoms of educational stress. Conversely, high baseline GPA, robust teacher student relationships, female gender, earlier years of study, a medical and health field of study and good sleep quality were significantly associated with higher success. Demographic factors, including family income, participant age, and geographical governorate, were not independently associated with academic success once psychological, health, and relational factors were controlled.Conclusions The results underscore the critical need for comprehensive mental health support, sleep hygiene awareness, and targeted educational interventions within Palestinian university environments. Institutional strategies should prioritize reducing academic anxiety and stress while actively fostering supportive teacher student relationships.

TI "Should I tell my teacher?" Student AI disclosure practices,
   stigma, and self-regulated learning in higher education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic integrity; AI in education (AIED); concealing AI use;
   generative artificial intelligence; help-seeking; higher education;
   self-regulated learning; student AI disclosure
ID HELP-SEEKING; MOTIVATION; LITERACY
AB As generative artificial intelligence (GAI) tools become popular in education, questions about when and whether students disclose their AI use have emerged as a critical concern for academic integrity and self-regulated learning (SRL). Using SRL as an interpretive lens, we examine undergraduate students' AI disclosure practices, investigating how their worries about negative consequences, AI usage behaviours, and demographic factors relate to their willingness to disclose AI use in academic settings. Drawing on survey data from 78 undergraduate students enrolled in an online education course, we developed study-specific survey items addressing worry, disclosure, and AI use. Given the developmental status of the instrument, we retained two preliminary composite indicators, worry and disclosure to teachers, and analyzed less internally consistent peer-disclosure and AI-use items individually. Our findings reveal a pattern of co-occurring worries: fear of teacher judgment and fear of social stigmatization are strongly correlated, and both are associated with students' active concealment of AI use. Interpretively, we describe two contrasting response patterns among students: a transparent-disclosure pattern, in which disclosing AI use to instructors appears to reflect part of SRL processes, and an anxious-concealment pattern, in which heavier AI users report less transparency with teachers. A further finding is that anxiety is not associated with reduced disclosure to teachers directly, but is associated with increased peer-only sharing and complete secrecy. Exploratory analyses also suggest demographic patterns worth further study, with academic discipline showing the largest association with disclosure and a marginal indication that monolingual students may disclose less than multilingual students. Given the sample size, we reserve our interpretations and treat these as hypotheses for future work rather than established effects. These findings suggest that institutional AI disclosure frameworks may benefit from addressing both policy compliance and the affective and disciplinary dimensions of students' SRL decision-making.

TI The Socratic Challenger: a structured GenAI-assisted workflow for
   undergraduate research inquiry
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE generative artificial intelligence; higher education; inquiry-based
   learning; instructional design; research-question formulation;
   scaffolding; undergraduate research
ID INFORMATION-SEEKING; QUESTION
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are increasingly used during early stages of academic inquiry, yet their role in supporting research-question development remains unclear. This mixed-methods study evaluated an eight-step GenAI-assisted workflow implemented in an undergraduate ecology course. The workflow alternated AI-supported exploration with literature verification, revision, and human feedback. The study population comprised students enrolled in the course, and all 45 students who consented to research use of their coursework were included; therefore, no sample-size formula was applied. Quantitative data consisted of ordinal ratings of the perceived contribution of each workflow step, while qualitative data consisted of students' written reflections. The rating items corresponded directly to the eight implemented workflow stages, and qualitative themes were independently reviewed and refined by two researchers. Quantitative results showed that perceived usefulness differed modestly across steps (Friedman chi 2 = 14.53, p = 0.0426; Kendall's W = 0.046), although the median rating for every step was "Helped a lot," and no pairwise comparison remained significant after correction. The ratings showed acceptable internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.745). Qualitative analysis indicated that students viewed AI primarily as a thought partner that helped them narrow and refine ideas, while the broader scaffolded workflow supported progress through literature engagement, structured pacing, and feedback. Together, the findings suggest that GenAI can support undergraduate research inquiry when embedded within a structured process that requires students to verify evidence, evaluate suggestions, and retain responsibility for the final research question.

   the sfera.BOT Project in Italian Schools

DE educational robotics; teacher professional development; technology
   integration; pedagogical innovation; Italian education system
ID DESIGN; IMPACT
AB Educational robotics is increasingly recognized as a promising tool for innovation in teaching and learning. However, its successful integration in schools often depends on the availability of targeted professional development programs that support educators with no prior experience in this field. This study addresses this gap by presenting and evaluating the development and implementation of a training program specifically designed to equip educators with the knowledge, skills, and confidence to integrate robotics into early and primary education. TI Enacted and Unaddressed Pedagogical Opportunities During Play Sessions:
   A Case Analysis of Early Childhood Education Pre-Service Teachers'
   Professional Vision
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE early childhood education; guiding play; mobile eye-tracking;
   pedagogical goal; professional vision
ID METHODOLOGY; CONTEXT
AB In early childhood education (ECE), eye-tracking research has primarily investigated in-service teachers' visual gaze and reflective practices in pedagogical settings. However, little is known about how pre-service ECE teachers' visual information-processing is oriented by their pedagogical goals, particularly in authentic play-based contexts. This paper addresses this gap by examining how pre-service ECE teachers adapt their professional vision during children's play. The study involved two pre-service ECE teachers with work experience. The data consisted of video recordings and mobile eye-tracking data collected during authentic play situations involving children aged 3-5, participants' written pedagogical plans, and cued retrospective recall interviews with mobile eye-tracking recordings as interview stimuli. Integrating these data sources enables a process-oriented analysis of professional vision by linking observable gaze patterns with participants' retrospective accounts of what they attended to and why. The data demonstrate that professional vision is a goal-oriented process in which pre-set goals guide pre-service teachers' gaze allocation, shaping their interpretations of children's play in pedagogically relevant ways. The analyses also reveal instances of unaddressed pedagogical opportunities. These instances restrict teachers' ability to reorient their attention in response to children's initiatives. The study conceptualizes visual information-processing in play-based contexts as a dynamic relationship between pre-set pedagogical goals and ad hoc adaptation, thereby offering insights into emerging aspects of developing adaptive expertise.

TI Gamification and Active Learning in Agricultural Engineering: Evaluating
   the Impact of an Interactive Response System on Academic Performance and
   Stress Reduction
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE gamification; agricultural engineering; active learning; student
   response systems; peer instruction; learning analytics
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; MATH ANXIETY; ENGAGEMENT; CLICKERS; SCIENCE; STYLES;
   POWER
AB The transition towards active-learning pedagogies represents an important challenge in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) education, particularly in Agricultural Engineering courses characterised by mathematically demanding content and complex engineering problem solving. Although gamification and Student Response Systems (SRSs) have shown promising educational potential, empirical evidence regarding their combined application in Agricultural Engineering remains limited. This quasi-experimental repeated-measures study evaluated an Educational Innovation Project integrating the Wooclap Student Response System with structured gamification activities-including educational escape rooms, forensic engineering simulations, collaborative challenges, and peer discussion-in two undergraduate Agricultural Engineering courses at the University of Almer & iacute;a. Academic performance was assessed through short-term (one week) and medium-term (one month) knowledge-retention tests, while students' perceptions were explored using repeated questionnaire administrations throughout the intervention. Quantitative analyses included descriptive statistics, assessment of normality, paired-samples Student's t-tests, 95% confidence intervals, and Cohen's d effect sizes. The intervention was associated with statistically significant improvements in short-term and medium-term academic performance, with medium to large effect sizes, while students also reported high levels of engagement, perceived knowledge retention, technological usability, and reduced academic stress. These findings suggest that integrating a Student Response System with structured gamification may support active learning and knowledge retention in technically demanding Agricultural Engineering courses. Nevertheless, because of the quasi-experimental repeated-measures design and the absence of a parallel control group, the findings should be interpreted as evidence of an association between the instructional approach and the observed educational outcomes rather than as proof of causal effectiveness. Further controlled studies involving larger and more diverse engineering cohorts are warranted.

TI Designing for Circularity: A Gamified Deck of Cards for Sustainability
   Education in the Textile and Fashion Industry
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE design education; circular design; gamification; pedagogical tool;
   sustainability; lifelong learning
AB The transition to a circular economy requires professionals to adopt new strategies and a systemic approach to product development. This shift demands continuous learning and the development of new competencies to understand and apply circular economy principles. In this context, innovative educational approaches that foster engagement and lifelong learning (LLL) are essential. Gamification can support this process by enhancing motivation, creativity, problem-solving, and knowledge retention, while interactive tools help learners critically examine and operationalise circular economy principles. This article discusses the design and application of the "Circularity Deck of Cards," a learning resource developed as part of a European-funded project Be@t, to facilitate the circular design of products and services. The study follows a mixed-methodological approach encompassing three phases: a systematic mapping of international tools and methodological approaches; the conceptual and visual development of the resource; and its implementation and evaluation through a workshop involving undergraduate, master's, and doctoral students and researchers in fashion design and textile engineering in Portugal. The data were collected using a questionnaire that combined quantitative and qualitative questions, designed to assess the receptiveness to, challenges of, and opportunities arising from gamification in the teaching of circular design. The findings indicate that participants responded positively to the tool, recognising its value as both a pedagogical resource and a professional instrument for promoting sustainability and circularity in the textile and clothing industry. Ultimately, gamification catalyses training students, designers, and industry professionals to address the challenges of circularity, fostering new perspectives on circular design in professional practice.

TI The IMAGINE Programme: Inspiring Innovative Practice for Intercultural
   and Democratic Teacher Education in Europe
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE intercultural and democratic competences; human diversity; innovative
   teacher education; non-formal education pedagogy; criticality
AB In increasingly multicultural societies, preparing teachers to engage effectively with human diversity and to foster inclusive, equitable, and democratic learning environments has become a central priority for teacher education. This study examines (1) how a human diversity perspective contributes to the conceptualisation and development of intercultural and democratic competences in teacher education, and (2) how non-formal, participatory, dialogical, experiential, and heritage-based pedagogies support the development of these competences among pre-service and in-service teachers through participation in the IMAGINE programme. Moving beyond approaches that primarily frame diversity in terms of cultural difference, minority status, or racialised identities, the study conceptualises human diversity as an inherent condition of contemporary democratic societies and explores its potential as both a conceptual framework and a pedagogical resource for competence development. Drawing on established international frameworks, particularly Deardorff's model of intercultural competence and the Council of Europe's Reference Framework of Competences for Democratic Culture (RFCDC), the study adopts a qualitative longitudinal case study design to examine IMAGINE, an annual residential teacher education seminar implemented since 2021. The analysis explores participants' understandings of human diversity and examines how participatory, dialogical, experiential, and heritage-based pedagogies create the conditions that support intercultural and democratic competence development across successive editions of the programme. The findings highlight the relevance of a human diversity perspective for teacher education and identify a set of interconnected pedagogical conditions that support competence development. These include engagement with minority narratives and lived experiences, dialogical and collaborative learning, emotional and experiential engagement, critical reflection, the creation of safe spaces for dialogue, and heritage-based educational experiences. Rather than operating independently, these conditions appear to reinforce one another by enabling participants to encounter different perspectives, critically examine assumptions, engage emotionally with experiences of diversity, and negotiate meaning collaboratively. The study contributes to research on intercultural and democratic teacher education in two main respects. First, it provides empirical insights into the potential of human diversity as a broader conceptual lens through which diversity may be understood as constitutive of democratic societies, thereby opening discussion on the possibility of moving beyond predominantly culture-centred understandings of diversity towards a more encompassing human diversity perspective. Second, it provides empirical insights into the pedagogical conditions through which intercultural and democratic competences can be fostered, demonstrating the potential of dialogical, experiential, collaborative, and heritage-based learning environments for the professional development of both pre-service and in-service teachers.

TI Effects of Instructional Guidance on Modeling Causal Loop Diagrams in
   Climate Change Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE climate change education (CCE); education for sustainable development
   (ESD); systems thinking; instructional design; simulation-based
   learning; digital literacy; causal loop diagram (CLD); cognitive load
   (CL)
ID COMPUTER-SIMULATIONS; SYSTEMS THINKING; KNOWLEDGE; SKILLS
AB Climate change education requires learners to understand complex systems and dynamic interdependencies, making systems modeling an important competence within education for sustainable development. This study investigated how instructional guidance influences students' modeling of causal loop diagrams when working with the climate simulation En-ROADS. In a two-phase design, 242 secondary school students first explored En-ROADS and constructed an initial diagram representing their intermediate knowledge, then refined it while receiving conceptual guidance, procedural guidance, both, or none. Structural complexity of the causal loop diagrams and cognitive load were assessed after each phase. Structural complexity increased significantly in all four conditions, eta 2 p = 0.22. Procedural guidance was associated with a smaller increase, eta 2 p = 0.02, located primarily in the branching structures of the diagrams, and with higher germane cognitive load, eta 2 p = 0.02. Conceptual guidance showed no overall effect but interacted with intermediate knowledge, beta = 0.23; as the conditional effects were not significant, this indicates that its influence differed across levels of intermediate knowledge rather than that it benefited either group. The structural complexity of the initial diagram was by far the strongest predictor of that of the refined one, underlining the importance of aligning instructional guidance with learners' intermediate knowledge in complex digital modeling environments.

TI Management course design quality, feedback literacy, and
   judgment-oriented learning in AI-rich business school classrooms:
   Evidence from Taiwan
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Management education; Feedback literacy; Deep management learning;
   Managerial judgment; Responsible management; Generative AI
AB Business schools are redesigning courses as generative AI becomes routine, employer scrutiny intensifies, and responsible management gains prominence. Drawing on Biggs' Presage-ProcessProduct (3P) model, this study examines management course design quality (MCDQ) as a course-level presage condition, feedback literacy and deep management learning as processes, and managerial judgment transfer, responsible management judgment, and perceived professional readiness as products. The study uses data from 792 students nested within 27 courses at nine Taiwanese institutions, where AI adoption, bilingualization, and workforce relevance are salient pressures. Two independent coders assessed MCDQ using 108 course documents (ICC (2,1) = .770), while student data were collected in two waves. MCDQ was positively associated with feedback literacy, which was positively associated with deep management learning; deep management learning, in turn, was positively associated with all three outcomes. Indirect associations between MCDQ and the outcomes through feedback literacy and deep management learning coexisted with retained direct associations from MCDQ and feedback literacy to downstream outcomes. Findings concerning professional readiness warrant caution because its average variance extracted was .466. Taiwan and generative AI are treated as contextual conditions rather than tested explanations.

TI Is covert articulation impaired in developmental stuttering?
SO JOURNAL OF FLUENCY DISORDERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Stuttering; Short-term memory; Phonological loop; Individual-level
   analyses
ID NONWORD REPETITION ABILITIES; SHORT-TERM-MEMORY; WORKING-MEMORY; PHONEME
   ELISION; YOUNG-CHILDREN; ADULTS; SPEECH; IMPAIRMENTS; REHEARSAL;
   DYSLEXIA
AB Adults who stutter (AWS) have been reported to show difficulties in nonword repetition tasks, where covert articulation supports the maintenance of phonological information during the retention interval. However, it remains unclear whether these difficulties reflect impaired covert articulation, auditory-phonological encoding, overt articulation, or aspects of executive function/ attention. It is also unknown whether such difficulties characterize any, some, most, or all AWS. To address these questions, we administered spoken and written versions of a phonological memory task-both using printed nonwords during encoding-alongside a visuospatial memory task, to twenty AWS and forty matched controls, and conducted both group-level and individual-level analyses. As a group, AWS underperformed controls on all three tasks, but their difficulties were more pronounced on the two phonological tasks, suggesting impaired covert articulation. However, substantial heterogeneity emerged at the individual level, highlighting the importance of individual-level analyses and conclusions.

TI Third grade students' spatial structuring of rectangular arrays: A
   constructive replication study with eye-tracking data
SO JOURNAL OF MATHEMATICAL BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE Spatial structuring; Area; Multiplicative reasoning; Eye tracking
ID 3 INTERVENTIONS
AB Children's spatial structuring is a critical aspect of their understanding of both area and multiplicative reasoning. Since Battista et al.'s (1998) and Outhred and Mitchelmore's (2000) studies over 20 years ago, spatial structuring of rectangular arrays have been examined with a wide variety of tasks and protocols. Despite observations that tasks can affect such reasoning, there has been little specific focus on examining how task and protocol structure affect students' spatial structuring. AB Background Planetary Health (PH) content is increasingly recognized as essential for medical education. PH content was integrated into courses by a subset of participants. Beyond the workshop, ongoing networking may further support sustainable PH content integration into the curriculum.
