TI LLMs do not grade essays like humans
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Automatic essay scoring; Large language models; Natural language
   processing; LLMs in education
AB Large language models have recently been proposed as tools for automated essay scoring, but their agreement with human grading remains unclear. In this work, we evaluate how LLM-generated scores compare with human grades and analyze the grading behavior of several models from the GPT and Llama families in an out-of-the-box setting, without task-specific training. Our results show that agreement between LLM and human scores remains relatively weak and varies with essay characteristics. In particular, compared to human raters, LLMs tend to assign higher scores to short or underdeveloped essays, while assigning lower scores to longer essays that contain minor grammatical or spelling errors. We also find that the scores generated by LLMs are generally consistent with the feedback they generate: essays receiving more praise tend to receive higher scores, while essays receiving more criticism tend to receive lower scores. These results suggest that LLM-generated scores and feedback follow coherent patterns but rely on signals that differ from those used by human raters, resulting in limited alignment with human grading practices. Nevertheless, our work shows that LLMs produce feedback that is consistent with their grading and that they can be reliably used in supporting essay scoring.

TI Education intention profiles: Perceived teaching support as a predictor
   and associations with school completion
SO CONTEMPORARY EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Education intentions; Academic engagement; Teaching support; School
   completion
ID STUDENT ENGAGEMENT; MISSING DATA; EXPECTATIONS; MOTIVATION; ASPIRATIONS;
   VARIABLES; MODEL
AB Students' education intentions lay a foundation for the pathways they go on to choose. In the present study, we examined school and postsecondary education intentions among Year 10 secondary school students: intentions to complete school, intentions to attend university, and intentions to undertake vocational education and training (VET). We were interested in determining how the different intention variables combine for different types of students, and whether these patterns differ for students from rural, regional, and city locations. Among 40,815 Australian secondary school students, we used latent profile analysis to identify intention profiles. Next, we examined perceived teaching support in Year 9 as a predictor of membership in the intention profiles. We also examined the extent to which profile membership was associated with school completion in Year 12. Results showed that five broadly similar profiles were evident in each of the three locations (with some differences in sizes): Completer-University (40-57% across the locations), Completer-VET (8% across the locations), Completer-Undecided (18-22%), Uncertain-VET (10-17%), and Noncompleter-VET (10-12%). Results also showed that higher levels of perceived teaching support predicted membership in the three "Completer" profiles over the remaining two profiles in all locations. The proportion of students who completed school was highest for the Completer-University profile and lowest for the Noncompleter-VET profile in all locations. There was some nuance in differences between the remaining profiles across locations. Findings hold relevance for efforts aiming to boost school completion rates across different geographic locations and better support students with their postschool decision making.

TI When infrastructure collapses: Collective resilience and digital
   learning among Palestinian university mathematics students during the
   war on Gaza
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Collective academic resilience; Emergency remote mathematics education;
   Assumption gap; Collective crisis creativity; Palestinian higher
   education; War on Gaza; Conversational AI in crisis education
AB Few educational crises have exposed the structural vulnerabilities of digital learning with the severity witnessed in Gaza following the October 2023 escalation. This qualitative interpretivist study examines how twelve undergraduate mathematics students at Al-Aqsa University experienced digital learning amid active armed conflict, with particular attention to the epistemological demands of mathematics - a discipline requiring sequential scaffolding, dialogic reasoning, and immediate feedback that asynchronous crisis modalities fundamentally cannot sustain. Data were generated through semi-structured WhatsApp audio interviews and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Four analytically distinct themes emerged: structural and psychosocial precarity, including recurrent displacement within the academic semester itself; subject-specific epistemic barriers, including the loss of what participants termed the "collective clarity moment"; adaptive strategies spanning peer learning networks, multi-platform appropriation, and AI tools deployed as interactive substitutes for absent faculty by eight of twelve participants; and diverse meaning-making practices in which academic persistence was reframed as cultural resistance (Sumud), collective commitment, or - in deviant cases - silent exhaustion. Theoretically, the study introduces three conceptual contributions: collective crisis creativity, documenting how severe resource scarcity intensifies pre-existing collaborative practices into structured survival systems; assumption gap, critiquing the uncritical transfer of COVID-era materials to war contexts; and collective academic resilience, extending Sumud scholarship into contemporary higher education. Findings offer evidencebased recommendations for conflict-responsive mathematics curriculum design and AI governance in crisis education.

TI Unpacking the link between entrepreneurial education and intention: A
   moderated mediation model of self-efficacy and university
   entrepreneurial climate
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Entrepreneurial education; Entrepreneurial intention; Entrepreneurial
   self-efficacy; University entrepreneurial climate; GUESSS; Moderated
   mediation
ID STUDENTS; GENDER; IMPACT
AB This study examines the extent to which Entrepreneurial Education is associated with Entrepreneurial Intention, focusing on the mediating role of Entrepreneurial Self-Efficacy and the moderating effect of University Entrepreneurial Climate. Integrating the Theory of Planned Behaviour and Social Cognitive Theory, we test a moderated mediation model using a large dataset from the 2023 GUESSS Spain project. This research provides an empirical extension of the associations underlying the relationship between Entrepreneurial Education and Entrepreneurial Intention by applying a moderated mediation framework. The results underscore that a dynamic University Entrepreneurial Climate is as relevant as formal curricula for stimulating students' intentions, with implications for managers of higher education institutions.

TI Integrating Generative AI Into Clinical Reasoning Education for Medical
   Students: Mixed Methods Study
SO JMIR MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE large language models; clinical reasoning; AI literacy; prompt
   engineering; medical education; generative AI; diagnostic
   decision-making
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; GUIDE
AB Background: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into clinical learning and practice. However, medical students often lack the competencies required for safe and critical use, including prompt design, output verification, and recognition of limitations. Educational interventions that integrate GenAI with clinical reasoning frameworks remain limited. Objective: This study evaluated a structured, theory-informed workshop integrating GenAI, prompt engineering, and clinical reasoning education to enhance medical students' self-perceived AI literacy and collaborative learning attitudes, and to assess whether patient-centered orientation changed following intensive AI exposure. Methods: We conducted a single-group, pre-post, explanatory sequential mixed methods study with fifth-year medical students enrolled at an academic medical center between April 2024 and May 2025. The 3-hour workshop comprised 6 modules integrating clinical reasoning, cognitive-bias awareness, verification-oriented GenAI use, and hands-on prompt engineering and centered on ChatGPT (OpenAI). Quantitative outcomes were self-reported measures from a 20-item self-report AI-literacy questionnaire adapted from the Meta AI Literacy Scale and were examined with exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, the 6-item Patient-Practitioner Orientation Scale-Short, and a modified Collaborative Learning Attitude Scale (CLAS). Pre-post change was assessed using 2-tailed paired t tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction and Cohen d; the Patient-Practitioner Orientation Scale-Short and CLAS were available for a subsample (n=46). Qualitative data from 6 interviews and 17 reflective narratives were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and integrated with the quantitative findings. Results: Among 150 eligible students, 139 (92.7%) completed paired AI-literacy assessments. Self-perceived AI literacy improved across all domains (Cohen d=0.69-0.93, all P<.001; all remaining significant after false discovery rate correction), and collaborative learning attitudes increased substantially (d=0.94, P<.001). Patient-centered orientation showed no significant change (d=0.03); however, baseline scores were concentrated at the favorable end of the scale (a floor/restricted-range effect), and the subsample analysis was underpowered (minimum detectable dz=0.42), so this null result is inconclusive rather than evidence of unchanged orientation. Gains did not differ by sex or across the sequential cohorts. Reflexive thematic analysis (interviews: n=6; reflections: n=17) identified five themes and one emergent theme describing a shift toward verification-oriented GenAI use: (1) understanding GenAI capabilities and limitations, (2) prompt-engineering skill development, (3) calibrated trust through verification, (4) GenAI-supported communication and collaboration, and (5) ethical considerations, with emerging reconceptualization of professional identity. Conclusions: A brief, theory-informed educational intervention integrating GenAI with clinical reasoning was associated with medium-to-large improvements in self-perceived AI literacy and collaborative attitudes. No detectable change in patient-centered orientation was observed; however, this finding should be interpreted as inconclusive, given measurement and power constraints. Embedding verification practices within clinical reasoning frameworks may offer a scalable approach for preparing physicians for responsible human-AI collaboration.
   Future studies should incorporate comparative designs, performance-based assessments, and longitudinal follow-up.

   teachers: A Q methodology approach
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION

   methodology; Pre-service teachers
AB This study explores pre-service social studies teachers' perspectives on climate change education using Q methodology. TI Robotic ATLAS: adapting advanced laparoscopic suturing training to a
   robotic platform with proficiency benchmark scores
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Education; Robotics; Laparoscopy; Training
ID FUNDAMENTALS; PERFORMANCE; CURRICULUM
AB Purpose Robotic-assisted surgery is increasingly incorporated into surgical training; however, structured curricula for advanced robotic suturing remain limited. The Advanced Training in Laparoscopic Suturing (ATLAS) curriculum established proficiency benchmarks for laparoscopic suturing but has not been adapted for robotic platforms. This study aimed to adapt the ATLAS curriculum to robotic surgery (R-ATLAS) and establish expert-derived proficiency benchmarks for robotic suturing tasks. Methods The six ATLAS tasks were adapted for robotic instrumentation using the Intuitive Abdominal Dome Trainer, and a non-dominant forehand suturing task (3ND) was introduced. Four expert robotic surgeons performed five repetitions of each task using a da Vinci Xi system. Performances were video-recorded and independently scored. Outliers ( > +/- 2 standard deviations) were excluded prior to benchmark calculation. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize expert performance and establish proficiency benchmarks following removal of predefined outliers. Results Of 140 total attempts, six were excluded as outliers, leaving 134 for analysis. Proficiency benchmarks were established for all seven tasks. Mean performance varied among surgeons for Tasks 1-5 and Task 3ND, whereas Task 6 demonstrated relatively similar performance across surgeons. NASA-TLX scores ranged from 15.5 to 30, with the highest workload for Task 3ND and the lowest for Task 4. Conclusions R-ATLAS provides a structured robotic adaptation of the ATLAS curriculum with expert-derived proficiency benchmarks. Variability in expert performance across most tasks suggests that expert-derived thresholds may reflect heterogeneity in robotic suturing performance rather than a single consensus standard. These benchmarks provide preliminary reference standards for robotic simulation training.

TI When coping is not inclusion: Practitioner assessment narratives and the
   sustainability of autistic participation in mainstream schools
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE autism; autistic burnout; inclusive education; masking; school-home
   discrepancy; sustainability of participation
ID SPECTRUM; EDUCATION; OUTCOMES; CHILDREN
AB Inclusive education is often evaluated through visible indicators such as classroom engagement, behaviour, attendance and academic participation. For autistic learners, however, visible functioning may not fully reflect the accessibility of the educational environment or the regulatory effort required to sustain participation. This paper examines a purposively selected set of cases in which autistic learners were described as coping or participating in mainstream education while assessment documentation also recorded evidence of strain, environmental dependence or difficulty sustaining participation across contexts and time. TI Why ethics, relationality and meaning-making matter to resilience
   education: Initiatives from global disaster contexts
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE disaster contexts; education for resilience; relationality;
   socialisation
ID ENVIRONMENTAL-EDUCATION; HIGH-SCHOOL; COMMUNITIES; CURRICULUM; GEOGRAPHY
AB Education is widely positioned in international policy frameworks as a mechanism for fostering agency in young people to promote resilience in their communities, including in the United Nation's Sendai Framework on Disaster Risk Reduction. However, educational responses to disaster risk, emanating from natural hazards, frequently emphasise technical preparedness over attention to the socially contextualised and ethical dimensions of education. Drawing on Gert Biesta's distinctions between three core functions of education (qualification, socialisation and subjectification), and Paul Ricoeur's understanding of relational identity as 'Oneself as Another', we propose novel socialised forms of education that foster meaningful resilience. Data were obtained through deliberative discussions with disaster education programme implementers and education scholars in Japan, Indonesia and the United States and analysed through interpretive phenomenological analysis. Three core themes are identified as framing a socialised form of resilience education: (1) orienting education towards communal experiences of disaster, (2) fostering a critical consciousness grounded in empathy and (3) honouring culturally situated interpretations of disaster. Our findings show that socialised approaches to education offer unique insights into how concepts of risk, resilience and agency are interpreted across social and cultural contexts. We argue that attending to these socialised conceptualisations enable a higher quality of resilience education: promoting ethically grounded, culturally responsive and socially situated forms of agency more akin to a 'futures thinking' approach that also serves to reposition education's core functions beyond standardised 'technical fixes'.

TI High school coping patterns and emerging adult mental health across
   COVID-19: A latent profile transition analysis
SO CHILD DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE COVID-19; coping; adolescence; emerging adulthood; longitudinal; latent
   profile analysis
ID ADOLESCENCE; CHILDHOOD
AB Using latent profile transition analysis, this study identified patterns and developmental changes in adolescents' coping across high school prior to COVID-19 and examined whether pre-pandemic coping differentiated depressive symptom trajectories across the pandemic years as youth transitioned into emerging adulthood. Participants were a diverse cohort (N = 940; 51% female; 34% White, 26% Latinx, 15% Multi-racial and multi-ethnic) assessed annually in Grades 9-12 on 5 coping indicators (internalizing, externalizing, social support seeking, problem solving, and avoidance). Distinct coping profiles reflected relatively approach-oriented coping (Balanced; Regulated Approach) and more avoidant or reactive coping (Reactive Approach; Self-Directed). With this later stability, Grade 12 coping patterns differentiated depressive symptom trajectories across the COVID-19 pandemic (2021-2023). Specifically, Balanced and Regulated Approach (i.e., approach-oriented) profiles had fewer depressive symptoms, whereas Reactive Approach and Self-Directed (i.e., avoidant, reactive) profiles had more depressive symptoms. Findings highlight both continuity and early reorganization in coping across adolescence and show that coping pathways foreshadowed depressive symptom trajectories during the pandemic as youth transitioned into emerging adulthood.
   This study examined how adolescents coped with stress across high school before the COVID-19 pandemic and whether these coping patterns shaped symptoms of depression across three years of the pandemic (2021-2023). Following a diverse group of 940 adolescents from 9 to 12 grades and into early adulthood, we identified four coping patterns: balanced, active coping with strong emotional control, active coping with higher emotional reactivity, and inward, self-directed coping without support-seeking. Coping patterns changed most early in high school and became more consistent in later years. Adolescents with balanced coping or stronger emotional control in twelfth grade reported fewer symptoms of depression and improved earlier during the pandemic, whereas reactive and self-directed copers reported higher and more persistent symptoms.

TI How Cognitive Factors and Motivation Shape Learners' Engagement in
   AI-Supported Language Learning?: Insights From the Combined SEM and

LA English
DT Article
DE AI-supported language learning; cognitive factors; learner engagement;
   motivation and self-efficacy; social cognitive theory
ID CRITICAL THINKING
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been integrated into both classroom-based and informal language learning, with tools such as AI chatbots, automated feedback systems and generative AI applications offering personalised, interactive and adaptive learning experiences. However, little is known about how learners' cognitive factors and psychological mechanisms are associated with engagement in AI-supported learning environments. Guided by Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), this study investigated the roles of AI literacy, growth mindset and critical thinking disposition in predicting learners' motivation, self-efficacy and engagement. DT Article

ID ASSESSMENTS; STUDENTS
AB Foreign language classroom anxiety remains a central construct in applied linguistics, but brief instruments require context-specific evidence before their scores are used for substantive interpretation. This study examined the eight-item Short-Form Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale (S-FLCAS) with 826 Japanese university learners of English as a foreign language. The study provides internal-structure and item-functioning evidence for a provisional, low-stakes interpretation rather than a complete validation or formal replication. Thus, one-factor fit should not be equated with broad construct coverage or fully independent indicators. The present data provisionally support descriptive group summaries of a continuous S-FLCAS score within this sample.

TI How reading comprehension and age at arrival predict achievement among
   1st generation immigrant students in Germany: evidence from PISA
   2012-2022
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE International large-scale assessment; Educational policy; Immigrant
   students; Age at arrival; Educational equity; Reading competence;
   Teacher ratings
ID SCHOOL SEGREGATION; IMPUTATION; EDUCATION; LANGUAGE
AB Background Germany consistently shows one of the largest achievement gaps between immigrant and non-immigrant students across countries in PISA, with disparities persisting even after adjustment for socioeconomic factors. Yet international large-scale assessments typically treat immigrant students as a homogeneous group, potentially obscuring within-group heterogeneity-particularly regarding varying stages of second language acquisition-that could inform targeted intervention.Purpose Based on these considerations we investigate which migration-related factors-age at arrival, teacher-rated reading comprehension, and home language-predict academic achievement among 1st generation immigrant students in Germany, and whether these relationships remain stable across a decade of changing migration contexts.Methods Using German PISA data from four PISA cycles (2012-2022; N = 1,189 1st generation immigrants), we estimated multilevel models with students nested within assessment cycles. Achievement was measured across mathematics, reading, science, and a composite domain using 100 plausible values per student derived from IRT models. Exploratory analyses include arrival-age categories which were derived through recursive partitioning.Results Teacher-rated reading comprehension-a classroom-based functional literacy indicator distinct from PISA's standardized reading score-was the strongest predictor of achievement across all domains. This measure predicted not only reading (R2 = .506) but also science (.290) and mathematics (.217), indicating that reading comprehension is an essential prerequisite for understanding the text-heavy PISA tasks in science and mathematics. While teacher-rated reading comprehension emerged as the strongest predictor, age at arrival proved robust across all model specifications (beta = -0.03 standard deviations per year), with cumulative effect of d = 1.15 between earliest and latest arrivers. Among socioeconomic indicators, only home possessions contributed significantly; parental education and occupational status showed no significant associations.Conclusions Reading comprehension and migration timing emerge as substantially stronger predictors of immigrant student achievement than socioeconomic background in German PISA data, while home language use shows negligible effects. These findings highlight limitations in current reporting practices: aggregating immigrant students into broad categories obscure the heterogeneity that actually drives achievement gaps. Disaggregating results by arrival age and reading comprehension would provide educators and policitymakers with more actionable insights.

TI AI literacy won't save us: a reply to Bannister (2025)
SO HIGHER EDUCATION RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; AI literacy; academic integrity; higher education;
   academic writing
AB In a recent article, Bannister [2025. ParadAIse L0st? Higher Education Research & Development, 1-10] makes a compelling argument that a point of no return has been reached with generative AI (genAI) and that a focus on genAI literacy and human stewardship of writing represents a positive way forward. In this article, we broadly agree with this position, but argue that genAI literacy is insufficient to mitigate the harms of genAI. To do so, we make three claims. First, the 'witch hunt' framing of responses to genAI is often a straw man. Second, early evidence suggests that genAI is negatively impacting academic literacy. Third, genAI is already having negative impacts on academic writing, discourse, publishing and peer review. We conclude that while literacy is important, it should not distract from the potential harms of AI.

TI AI-Enabled Virtual Patients as Part of Clinical Skills Training: A
   Cross-Sectional Program Evaluation of Student Perspectives on the
   McMaster Virtual SP Tool
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; virtual patients; standardized patients;
   clinical skills; simulation; deliberate practice; medical education
ID EDUCATIONAL ALLIANCE; FIDELITY; FEEDBACK; FEATURES
AB Large language model-enabled virtual patients may expand access to clinical skills practice by supporting explicitly defined practice tasks. This program evaluation examined medical students' awareness, use, and perceptions of the McMaster Virtual SP Tool, a custom generative artificial intelligence tool developed to supplement clinical skills practice. We conducted an anonymous, single-institution cross-sectional survey of students across three cohorts at McMaster University. Quantitative responses were summarized descriptively, and free-text responses were analyzed using qualitative content analysis informed by task-aligned fidelity, deliberate practice, learner-centred feedback, and simulation instructional design. Thirty-five students responded; 23 (65.7%) were aware of the tool and 16 (45.7%) had used it. Among the 16 users, 15/16 (93.8%) found the tool at least somewhat easy to navigate; 13 (81.3%) would use it again; and 13 (81.3%) would recommend it. Across all respondents, 14/35 (40.0%) reported using AI-enabled virtual patients for OSCE preparation. Users valued its accessibility, independent low-stakes rehearsal, and usefulness for focused history-taking, question wording, and clinical reasoning. Perceived limitations included reduced human connection, nonverbal and emotional realism, physical examination practice, and feedback specificity. AI-enabled virtual patients may therefore be considered as adjuncts for selected cognitive and structural rehearsal tasks. Objective educational outcomes were not assessed.

TI The Impact of AI-Powered Robots on Speaking Skills: Exploring the
   Mediator Role of Foreign Language Enjoyment and Self-Efficacy in Higher
   Education
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-powered robots; ANCOVA; enjoyment; higher education;
   self-determination theory; self-efficacy; speaking skills
AB Practicing speaking has remained a permanent difficulty for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students, mainly due to the limited chances to engage in meaningful speaking interaction in supportive settings. AI-powered robots, in response, emerged as a successful speaking interaction in language teaching. Grounded in self-determination theory (SDT), this study examined the effects of AI-powered robots on EFL learners' speaking performance, with enjoyment and self-efficacy as mediating variables. We used a pretest-posttest design and conducted the intervention over 10 weeks. The sample included 224 learners from a Chinese university, where 123 participants were assigned to the experimental group and 101 to the control group. While the former participated in robot-based speaking tasks, the latter got involved in traditional teaching, such as textbook-based communication activities, description, drill practice and pairwise work. The results showed that while both groups confirmed significant improvements in speaking scores over time, the experimental group had significantly higher achievement compared to the control group. These findings indicated that AI-powered robots can create a structured, interactive and supportive learning atmosphere that more effectively improves learners' speaking ability. As for the indirect effects, running a parallel mediation analysis revealed that both self-efficacy and enjoyment mediated the effect of the treatment, jointly accounting for 28.6% of the total intervention effect. Uniquely, enjoyment accounted for 15.5% of the total effect, and self-efficacy for 13.3% of it. These results indicated that self-efficacy and enjoyment serve as partial mediators in improving speaking performance through AI-powered robots. Accordingly, these results underscore the pedagogical potential of robot-assisted language learning in EFL instruction and highlight that integrating the robots significantly improved the learners' self-efficacy, boosted their enjoyment and enhanced their speaking performance.

TI From Basic Fuchsin to Mixed Dyes: Teaching ElectrocatalyticAdvanced
   Oxidation and Digital Image Colorimetry via a
   Knowledge-TransferFramework
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Electrochemistry; Hands-On
   Learning/Manipulatives; Catalysis; EnvironmentalChemistry
ID ELECTROCHEMICAL REMEDIATION; LABORATORY EXPERIMENTS; DESTRUCTION;
   ENVIRONMENT; REMOVAL; WATER
AB This article presents an upper-level undergraduate laboratory activity that integrates electrochemistry and environmental chemistry through the electrocatalytic oxidative degradation of the organic dye basic fuchsin (BF). Students assemble a simple two-electrode electrolysis system, operating it under both constant-voltage modes. At the three-dimensional porous nickel-foam cathode, dissolved O2 is reduced via a two-electron pathway to generate H2O2. This H2O2 is subsequently activated at the nickel surface via a reversible Ni2+/Ni3+ redox cycle to yield highly oxidative hydroxyl radicals (center dot OH), which rapidly degrade BF. Reaction progress is initially monitored qualitatively through time-lapse decolorization. Students then translate these visual changes into semiquantitative trend information using digital image colorimetry. By extracting RGB values from standardized photographs and applying the complementary color principle, students calculate an RGB-derived equivalent absorbance as an operational optical metric, which is compared with UV-Vis spectroscopy to evaluate the degradation trend. Crucially, to foster knowledge transfer, students complete an independent extension task evaluating alternative emerging pollutants to validate the broader applicability of this analytical method. Emphasizing experimental design and variable control, this mechanism-supported, data-driven platform successfully equips students with practical skills in advanced water treatment technologies and accessible analytical techniques.

SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE classroom pedagogy; deictic expressions; descriptive statistics; EFL

AB This study investigates the effects of deductive and inductive grammar instructional approaches on Jordanian fifth-grade EFL learners' acquisition of English deictic expressions. Sixty-six Arabic-speaking students participated in a quasi-experimental pre-test-post-test design to assess their knowledge before and after instruction. TI Debating for persuasion versus debating for deliberation: the effect of
   differing communicative goals on disciplinary knowledge construction
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE argumentation; debate; deliberation; higher education; learning;
   persuasion
ID ARGUMENTATION
AB Introduction Learning disciplinary knowledge is a complex process and a challenge for university education. Although it is argued that active methodologies, such as debate, are a means of promoting learning, there are few studies that measure this effect. There are good reasons to think that debate does promote learning, since it promotes argumentation, a type of dialogue that would be key to the construction of knowledge. However, it is not clear what effect different types of debate objectives would have on disciplinary learning. The purpose of this study was to determine the effect of two debate designs (with persuasive and deliberative objectives) on the construction of disciplinary knowledge of psychology students.Methods A mixed repeated measures design was conducted with 43 students who were randomly assigned to the debate designs. Interviews were conducted to assess disciplinary knowledge before and after the intervention, and the argumentative moves used by each participant in the debates were identified with a pattern of argumentative moves.Results A Principal Component Analysis identified two configurations of argumentative moves: deliberative component and persuasive component. A Kruskal-Wallis test with these components showed that students use significantly more deliberative moves in the deliberative debate, but there were no significant differences in persuasive moves between the debates. A Mixed ANOVA showed that students advance in disciplinary knowledge in both designs. Finally, a Linear Mixed Model is presented showing that change of position significantly predicts advancement in disciplinary knowledge.Discussion The findings are discussed from the relationship between objective, argumentative language and learning.

TI The social and emotional dynamics of teachers' peer relationships
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION

   LEADERSHIP; RESOURCES; KNOWLEDGE; CULTURE
AB Introduction Teachers' relationships with colleagues are a crucial aspect of professional activity in schools but can often be overlooked as a by-product of teachers' working lives. Extant literature indicates that research on these relationships and the role they play in teachers' professional lives, wellbeing, and retention is a developing field. The purpose of this study was to examine variations in teachers' peer relationships to develop a theory to explain this phenomenon.Methods Using a critical realist grounded theory approach, and adopting an equal status, sequential, mixed-method design, the study combined a focus on individual experiences, alongside an exploration of the accumulative, contextual issues relating to the role of collegial relationships for primary and secondary schoolteachers in England. Results suggest that enhancing the quality of professional relationships could potentially lead to improved school cohesion, offering insights for policy and practice.

TI The raw gap misleads: conditional conversion from environmental
   familiarity to action is small and development-gradient-patterned
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE cross-national heterogeneity; Education for Sustainable Development;
   environmental action; perceived environmental familiarity (PEF); PISA
   2018; value-action gap
ID CLIMATE-CHANGE; COMPETENCE; RESPONSES; EDUCATION; VALIDITY; GENDER
AB Background Education for Sustainable Development assumes that environmental understanding converts into action, but the "value-action gap" literature warns that this conversion is uneven.Methods We analysed PISA 2018 data from 612,004 students across 80 countries, using BRR-Fay replicate weights, country fixed effects, and a 999-iteration country-cluster bootstrap.Results A one-standard-deviation increase in perceived environmental familiarity is associated with a 0.12 standard deviation increase in reported action. Raw familiarity-action gaps and residual action shortfalls move in opposite directions across socio-economic terciles, demonstrating that raw gaps are not valid measures of conversion deficit. Country slopes are heterogeneous (standard deviation = 0.07) and load on a development/governance gradient (the first principal component explains 67.5% of country-context variance).Conclusion Raw cross-national gaps misdiagnose the effectiveness of Education for Sustainable Development. The conditional conversion from familiarity to action is modest, developmentally patterned, and inseparable from response-style heterogeneity in this design.

TI From prediction to prescription: profile-aware prescriptive analytics
   for student dropout in a Latin American Public University
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE algorithmic recourse; counterfactual explanations; explainable AI;
   higher education; prescriptive analytics; retention; SHAP; student
   dropout
ID EXPLANATIONS
AB Introduction Student dropout in higher education remains a persistent challenge, particularly in developing contexts where structural disadvantage intersects with academic readiness. This study proposes a prescriptive analytics framework that integrates supervised learning, unsupervised profiling, and explainable artificial intelligence to move beyond prediction toward actionable interventions.Methods Using anonymized records from 2,500 entrants (2020-2024) at a Latin American public university, the analysis combines data from a foundation (pre-university) program with early bachelor's indicators and socioeconomic profiles. A Random Forest classifier was evaluated under stratified cross-validation, while student profiling and explainable AI techniques (SHAP, ALE, DiCE, CARLA, and Alibi) were used to characterize risk patterns and generate actionable recommendations.Results The Random Forest classifier achieved strong discrimination, with ROC-AUC values between 0.95 and 0.97 and an Expected Calibration Error of 0.031. Student profiling revealed three coherent segments with observed dropout ranging from less than one percent to approximately one quarter. Global and local explainability consistently identified foundation GPA, early credit progress, socioeconomic index, and residential Internet access as the primary drivers of predicted dropout. Counterfactual explanations identified minimal, feasible changes that reclassified high-risk cases as lower predicted risk, providing recourse over the model's decision.Discussion The proposed framework extends predictive modeling by generating interpretable, profile-aware, and actionable recommendations that can support equitable student success through targeted interventions.

TI Governing generative AI in digital education: how institutional guidance
   becomes course-level policy
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI governance; AI literacy; assessment; course syllabi; digital
   education; generative AI; instructor discretion; policy enactment
ID SUBJECT-MATTER; ORGANIZATIONS
AB Introduction As generative artificial intelligence becomes embedded in digital education, universities face a governance problem that institutional guidance alone cannot resolve: how should acceptable AI use be defined within particular courses and assessments? This study examines syllabi as formal governance texts through which university principles become student-facing rules.Methods Using qualitative comparative document analysis, the study analyzed 35 syllabi collected from a large U.S. public research university, including 22 from Education and 13 from other fields. Course-level statements were compared with the institutional governance framework. The analysis distinguished primary governance stances and examined institutional alignment, policy rationales, discourse registers, and variation across course contexts.Results The institutional framework delegated substantial authority to instructors while emphasizing communication, attribution, verification, and student responsibility. Course-level enactment was highly heterogeneous: 11 syllabi were silent on student AI use, 11 were prohibitive, five permitted specified uses, two broadly permitted AI with responsibility safeguards, and six treated AI or machine learning as an object of pedagogical or professional learning. Six syllabi were explicitly aligned with institutional guidance, seven implicitly aligned, eight elaborated the institutional framework, three provided minimal guidance, and 11 remained silent; none directly contradicted a specific institutional requirement. Authentic or independently produced work was the most common rationale, appearing in 18 of 24 non-silent syllabi. Governance patterns crossed disciplinary boundaries, while all pedagogical cases were concentrated in AI-adjacent courses.Discussion The findings challenge simple disciplinary explanations and show that course-level AI governance is shaped by the interaction of assessment design, authorship expectations, course purpose, AI adjacency, and instructor discretion. Variation is best understood as an outcome of delegated digital governance whose educational value depends on clarity, justification, and alignment with the intellectual work students are expected to perform.

ID MATHEMATICS; RESOURCE
AB Background: Mother Tongue-based Bilingual Education (MTBBE) aims to strengthen learners' home language while developing English as an additional language. Limited research has examined how language choices in African-language classrooms shape learners' early mathematical understanding. TI Exploring challenges of integrating Afghan returnee children into
   schools in Afghanistan
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational barriers; educational integration; refugee education;
   returnee children; torkham omari camp
AB This study investigates the challenges of educational integration for refugee children returning from Pakistan to Afghanistan, specifically within the Torkham Omari Refugee Camp. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach involving 143 participants and targeted interviews, the research identifies a significant disconnect between parental aspirations and structural realities. Findings reveal that while 98.6% of parents are willing to support their children's education and 95.8% maintain high trust in Afghanistan's formal education system, approximately 76.3% of children experience incomplete educational trajectories. Poverty emerges as the most fundamental barrier, with economic constraints and a lack of identification documents (12.6%) hindering enrollment. Furthermore, one-third of returning children experience significant language barriers due to the shift from Urdu or English to instruction in Dari or Pashto. Qualitative analysis confirms that inconsistencies in curriculum and a lack of systematic integration programs exacerbate these challenges. Crucially, these integration deficits are profoundly gendered; the de facto authorities' formal prohibition on female secondary education transforms reintegration into an absolute legal barrier for girl returnees above grade six. The study concludes that successful integration requires targeted government interventions, including free quality education and specialized linguistic support.

TI Evidence, context, and pedagogy: rethinking ELT practice in Turkey
   through a contextual validity lens
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE contextual validity; evidence-informed pedagogy; Global South ELT;
   pedagogical transfer; teacher agency; Turkish ELT
ID TEACHERS
AB In English language teaching (ELT), pedagogical evidence rarely transfers intact across educational systems, a challenge particularly salient in Turkish ELT. This perspective article introduces contextual validity as an analytical and evaluative framework for judging whether a research-supported pedagogy remains educationally appropriate, institutionally feasible, sociolinguistically legitimate, and ethically defensible in a given teaching ecology. Unlike context-sensitivity, which describes variability, contextual validity issues a verdict: a practice is appropriate, appropriate with adaptation, or inappropriate for the given context. Building on postmethod critiques and extending them through ecological and complexity perspectives on teacher agency and language learning, the article specifies six analytical dimensions with measurable indicators, a provisional normative hierarchy for weighing dimensions that may conflict, and a staged workflow for professional judgement. Translanguaging pedagogy in multilingual Turkish classrooms serves as the case example, demonstrating the framework's discriminating, analytical use. The more productive question for Turkish ELT is not which method the field should adopt globally, but whether, by what evidence, and at what level of decision-making, a given pedagogy can be justified locally.

TI Is theoretical training enough? Effects of a university course on
   disability and health in physical activity and sport science students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic self-concept; adapted physical activity; disability; higher
   education; inclusion
ID TEACHERS ATTITUDES; PARTICIPATION; INCLUSION; IMPACT
AB Introduction: The preparation of future physical activity and sport professionals to promote inclusive and health-oriented practices for people with disabilities remains a persistent challenge in higher education. This study examined the effects of the course Physical Activity for the Health of People with Disabilities on students of a Bachelor's Degree in Physical Activity and Sport Sciences. Methods: Fifty-eight fourth-year students participated in a pre-post mixed-methods design combining questionnaires with open-ended questions. Results: Quantitative analyses revealed improvements in perceptions of theoretical training (p < 0.001; r(b) = -0.71, large), methodology (p = 0.041; d = -0.27, small), and community participation (p = 0.044; r(b) = -0.35, moderate). Conversely, decreases emerged in academic self-concept (p = 0.002; r(b) = 0.47, moderate) and self-efficacy (p < 0.001; r(b) = 0.62, large). Qualitative findings provided a nuanced interpretation of these results. Students reported acquiring a more structured conceptual framework and greater awareness of social, environmental, and attitudinal barriers affecting participation in physical activity. However, this increased cognitive understanding was accompanied by heightened recognition of the complexity of inclusive practice. The absence of authentic practical experiences and direct interaction with people with disabilities emerged as a recurrent theme, limiting perceived preparedness and confidence for real professional contexts. Discussion: Overall, the integration of findings suggests that predominantly theoretical training enhances knowledge and critical awareness but may simultaneously expose perceived competence gaps. Incorporating structured experiential learning opportunities appears essential to strengthen professional self-efficacy and facilitate effective transfer to inclusive practice settings.

SO READING & WRITING-JOURNAL OF THE READING ASSOCIATION OF SOUTH AFRICA

DT Article

   Education; language and literacies; teacher educator engagement;
   linguistic repertoires; translanguaging
AB Background: In 2016, the South African Department of Higher Education and Training initiated a project to develop standards to guide English and Mathematics teacher educators in curriculum design and implementation. Objectives: The investigation aimed to identify key affordances and limitations of the Primary Teacher Education (PrimTEd) knowledge and practice standards for the teaching of English, and to identify directions for their refinement and take-up. The article traces the conceptual foundations of the draft standards, examines their alignment with current language and literacies education scholarship, with South African directions in language education, and with conceptions of teacher knowledge. It also explores how the standards are being interpreted in teacher educator practice. Method: Using the frame of reflection-on-action, reflection-in-action, and reflection-for-action, the study makes use of documentary sources and vignettes to provide a literature and practice-informed account of the standards. Furthermore, the standards need to be more accessible to the community of teacher educators. Conclusion: The standards provide a valuable benchmark against which teacher educators of English can reflect on their own practice and develop their curricula. Some revisiting of the standards is needed to foreground emerging directions in research and practice. Contribution: Greater clarity, accessibility, and official endorsement of the standards are recommended to strengthen implementation and enhance teacher education in language and literacies.

AB This study examined cognitive and affective outcomes observed following an interdisciplinary project-based STEM intervention framed by a socially relevant humanitarian challenge. Cognitive analyses used 78 complete pretest-posttest pairs from two ordinary-classroom analytical groups (MG1, n = 29; MG2, n = 30) and a Curricular Diversification group (CDG, n = 19). Affective results were analysed descriptively at the item level for students in the ordinary classrooms and in the CDG. Difference scores did not depart significantly from normality, and paired-samples t-tests with Holm correction showed higher posttest cognitive scores in all three groups (all adjusted p < .001; Cohen's dz = 0.93-1.62). Descriptive affective patterns included higher motivation, confidence, and positive evaluations of teamwork, together with lower reported frustration and concern. Open-ended self-assessments provided limited exploratory context for these patterns. Because there was no non-intervention control group and the affective instruments differed across educational settings, the findings are interpreted as within-group changes associated with the study period rather than as causal or cross-group evidence of inclusion.

TI Who Are the Actors Involved in the Chinese Government Scholarship
   Council's (CSC) Policy Implementation? A Mapping Analysis of Policy
   Documents
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE scholarships; higher education policy; institution management; sponsored
   students; international student mobility
ID RETURNEES; DIASPORA
AB International student mobility (ISM) is one of the most important and widespread features of international higher education today. One factor affecting ISM is the range and increase in scholarship providers, of which the China Scholarship Council (CSC) scholarship, is among the most influential and impactful globally. While many existing studies have focused on the national economic motivations of scholarship programmes, the research presented in our paper adopts a broader perspective, emphasising some of the organisational and political complexities in scholarship policy implementation. We use and build upon a framework that explains how scholarship policy is implemented. In it, scholarship organisations are mapped alongside the students as scholarship recipients as well as the universities as policy actors. The principal aim of this paper is to map out the roles and relationships of different actors in the implementation of scholarship policies, showing the importance of multi-level governance and stakeholder collaboration. The findings show that CSC scholarship policy involves multiple interconnected actors whose roles and relationships can be systematically identified through policy documents. By extending the framework, this study identifies not only scholarship organisations, universities, and sponsored students, but also local education departments and employers as important actors in the policy process. The analysis further shows that CSC scholarship policies have evolved over time, with changes in priorities, requirements, and selection criteria reflecting broader national development strategies. Given that fact that the complex structures and workings of the CSC are still little understood and under-researched in anglophone literature, our analysis provides practical insights as well as additional guidance for promoting effective, inclusive, and sustainable transnational higher education. The discussions offer valuable insights for policymakers and institutions committed to enhancing international scholarship programmes and global higher education capacity building.

TI "Everything Depends on Yourself": Freedom, Hidden Competition and
   Student Self-Management in Sino-British Transnational Higher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE transnational higher education; Sino-British universities;
   institutionalised autonomy; student self-management; hidden competition;
   English-medium instruction; generative AI
ID FRAMEWORK; QUALITY; MARKET; SIZE
AB Freedom and choice are often presented as benefits of transnational higher education, but participants in this study also described freedom as something they had to learn to manage. This article examines that tension through a qualitative case study of one Sino-British university. It draws on 12 Chinese-language semi-structured interviews analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, together with a separate qualitative analysis of public institutional materials. Participants valued having room to make their own decisions, although some recalled early uncertainty when direct supervision was reduced. Competition did not disappear; it became harder to read and extended beyond grades to internships, research experience, postgraduate applications and employment. Participants generally knew that support existed, but it often became useful only after they recognised a problem and asked for help. Their accounts therefore described academic, linguistic, relational and career self-management. Several participants also described using generative artificial intelligence (AI) to understand course content, translate material and prepare for assessment, although AI-related material was uneven across the interviews and included concerns about accuracy, disciplinary fit and independent judgement. We use institutionalised autonomy to describe how arrangements that widen discretion can also shift planning, help seeking and risk judgement towards students. The concept is offered as a context-specific specification of responsibilisation rather than a general theory. This single case is not statistically representative, but it identifies a mechanism that can be examined in other transnational settings.

TI Neuro-symbolic pedagogical alignment (NSPA) for long-horizon classroom
   discourse analysis: Mitigating dialect bias via counterfactual
   preference optimization
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Neuro-symbolic pedagogical alignment (NSPA); Natural language
   processing; Educational data mining; Direct preference optimization;
   Algorithmic fairness; Classroom discourse
ID LANGUAGE MODELS
AB Automated analysis of classroom discourse has traditionally relied on discriminative Transformer architectures like RoBERTa to classify isolated utterances, an approach that inherently struggles with long-horizon dependen cies and exhibits significant algorithmic bias against speakers of non-standard dialects of American English. Off-the-shelf models, however, often fail to align with pedagogical frameworks such as Dialogic Instruction and Asset-Based Pedagogy. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a Neuro-Symbolic Pedagogical Alignment (NSPA) framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) within a Judge-Critique-Refine Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) loop to quantify high-inference educational constructs like Student Reasoning and Teacher Uptake. We specifically propose a novel Dialect-Invariant Contrastive Learning objective that utilizes style-transfer data augmentation to decouple semantic reasoning from surface-level linguistic variation, thereby mitigating the deficit framing often encoded in standard models. Evaluated on 1660 elementary mathematics lessons from the National Center for Teacher Effectiveness transcript corpus, our framework improves the detec tion of complex reasoning chains by 14.2 percentage points, measured by the macro-averaged harmonic mean of precision and recall, compared to state-of-the-art discriminative baselines. Furthermore, the proposed debiasing mechanism reduces the false-negative rate for contributions voiced in African American Vernacular English by 18.4 percentage points, ensuring a more equitable measurement of epistemic agency across diverse student de mographics. Finally, we validate the ecological utility of these metrics by establishing a statistically significant Pearson correlation (p = 0.10) with value-added models of teacher effectiveness, confirming that automated, equity-aware discourse analysis can serve as a rigorous proxy for learning outcomes.

TI Qualitative analysis of a hands-on activity for urinary incontinence in
   a pharmacy therapeutics course
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Urinary incontinence; Qualitative research; Reflection; Active learning
AB Introduction: Absorbent products for urinary incontinence (UI) are accessible in community pharmacies and commonly used in the hospital and long-term care settings. Little has been reported on how use of these products is taught in pharmacy schools. The objective of this study was to analyze the self-reported impact of a hands-on learning activity featuring UI absorbent products. Methods: Students in a clinical therapeutics course were asked to use UI absorbent products outside the classroom and submit a written reflection. Three investigators reviewed the reflections and developed a codebook with categories related to the physical and emotional impact of the products, clinical application, and pedagogical utility. Consensus was reached on application of codes, and themes were generated based on patterns in the data. Results: Three themes and ten sub-themes were identified within 98 reflections. Themes identified were 1) risks of stigmatization, 2) reflections on the value of the experience, and 3) transferability of didactic learning to practical healthcare experiences. Students experienced the products in various ways, including by wearing and using them. They described both the physical and emotional aspects of the activity and reflected heavily on the value it added to their classroom learning and their ability to provide effective patient care. Sixty-six percent of students (65 out of 98) self-reported increased knowledge and/or confidence regarding the use of absorbent products after participating in the activity. Conclusion: A hands-on activity related to the use of UI absorbent products as part of a clinical therapeutics course enhanced students' learning experience.

TI Grading Comparison of Standardized Patients and Pharmacist Faculty
   During a Mental Health Simulation
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Simulation; Standardized patients; Mental health
ID STUDENT; COMMUNICATION; IMPACT
AB Objective: To analyze concordance between pharmacist evaluators and paid actor standardized patient (SP) evaluators when grading student pharmacists' performance in a simulated mental health patient interaction. Methods: A mental health telehealth simulation was developed for second-year student pharmacists. Performance was concurrently assessed by an SP and a pharmacist evaluator. Conclusion: This study found strong concordance between SP and pharmacist evaluators for assessing observable communication behaviors and professionalism but identified significant differences in ratings for items requiring clinical judgment.

TI From Anxiety to Action: Mental Health Education Transforming Pharmacy
   Students' Self-Care and Resilience
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacy students; Cognitive behavioral therapy; Role modeling;
   Reflective writing; Psychological resilience
AB Objective: Pharmacy students experience alarmingly high rates of mental health challenges, with 18% to 60% reporting depressive symptoms, 21% to 50% experiencing anxiety, and up to 17% reporting suicidal ideation. Despite recognizing the importance of self-care, students struggle to prioritize their well-being, creating a critical knowledge-behavior gap, while professional resilience declines throughout training. Methods: This study examined how a 2-session mental health educational intervention was associated with reported shifts in pharmacy students' cognition of stress, self-care, and professional resilience, exploring mechanisms that bridge the knowledge-behavior gap. Qualitative thematic analysis examined 39 reflective assignments from students completing a 2-session mental health educational intervention integrating 7 evidencebased components grounded in cognitive-behavioral therapy and role modeling theory: young pharmacist instruction, data-driven education, case-based analysis, action-oriented recommendations, safe reflection, cognitive restructuring, and behavioral change strategies. Results: Six interconnected themes emerged, demonstrating a transformation from anxiety to action: (1) anxietydriven learning to intrinsically motivated growth; (2) validating suffering and legitimizing help-seeking, thereby reducing stigma; (3) reframing stress as normative and manageable; (4) reconceptualizing self-care as a professional competency; (5) building resilience through realistic role modeling; and (6) transformation through psychologically safe pedagogy. Students demonstrated metacognitive awareness, sought support, and developed adaptive professional identities integrating well-being with competence. Conclusion: Comprehensive mental health education combining role modeling with psychologically safe pedagogy facilitated transformative cognitive-behavioral shifts, successfully bridging the knowledge-behavior gap by reconceptualizing well-being as professionally essential. However, individual interventions must be complemented by organizational changes addressing structural stressors. Mental health literacy represents a foundational competency in pharmacy education, essential for thriving during training and providing quality patient care.

TI Teachers as reflective regulators of cognition: Understanding cognitive
   offloading in AI-augmented practice
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Cognitive offloading; Reflective practice; Teacher cognition; Generative
   artificial intelligence
AB This study investigates how teachers perceive, manage, and reflect on the cognitive implications of integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into their professional practice with a focus on the evolving interplay between human judgment and automation. Using a collective case-study design, we conducted interviews with 18 in-service teachers selected from mainland Chinese and Hong Kong educational settings. We employed the cognitive offloading framework to guide data collection and thematic coding, aiming to capture teachers' reasoning within AI-supported teaching and administration. Results revealed three interrelated processes: recognising and evaluating the need of using GenAI, redistributing cognition between human and machine systems, and reflectively re-engaging after use. The participating teachers generally framed GenAI not as a substitute for thinking but as a partner in cognitive regulation shaped by institutional and ethical contexts. Building from the findings and Risko and Gilbert's cognitive offloading framework, the study later proposes metacognitive ecology as a discussion-level interpretive lens for understanding how participating teachers' cognitive monitoring, pedagogical interpretation, ethical boundary-setting, and institutional-technological conditions shaped GenAImediated cognitive redistribution.

TI The readiness of pre-service teachers to teach Coding and Robotics
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Coding and robotics; Pre-service teacher education; Behavioural
   intention; Teacher readiness
ID UNIFIED THEORY; TECHNOLOGY ACCEPTANCE; INTENTION
AB This study explores pre-service teachers' engagement with Coding and Robotics within a teacher education programme. It aims to determine their readiness through their behavioural intention to teach this new subject in South Africa. A quantitative analysis of behavioural intention predictors was conducted on data collected from 235 pre-service teachers through a structured 5-point Likert survey. The research was grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) framework, focusing specifically on three core constructs: Performance Expectancy (PE), Effort Expectancy (EE), and Social Influence (SI), and their influence on Behavioural Intention (BI). The lack of alignment between curriculum reform and teacher education policies raises concerns about the readiness of pre-service teachers to implement Coding and Robotics effectively in a classroom setting. This study contributes to the growing body of research around educational robotics and coding by highlighting its role and pre-service teachers' preparedness by examining possible factors affecting their readiness to teach the subject.

TI Accept, elaborate, modify, or no uptake?: Which peer feedback features
   matter?
SO CONTEMPORARY EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Peer feedback features; Peer feedback uptake; Peer feedback
ID STUDENTS; QUALITY; PERCEPTIONS; LEVEL
AB Despite the recognized importance of acting on peer feedback to support learning, there has been limited research on how students take up received feedback. This research explored how feedback features (cognitive, affective, and metacognitive features) differentially predict various types of students' feedback uptake behaviors (accept, elaborate, modify, and no feedback uptake). Seventy-four graduate students from a Dutch university participated in this study, providing a total of 476 implementable peer feedback comments focusing on high-level comments. These comments were coded using two coding schemes: (1) feedback features and (2) peer feedback uptake. Analysis revealed patterns in both feedback features and uptake behaviors. Two-level binary logistic regression analyses, controlling for first-draft quality, explored the predictive relationships of feedback features on uptake behaviors. When providing peer feedback, students included more cognitive features (i.e., identifications, explanations, suggestions) and more affective features (i.e., mitigating praise). Students were much more likely to elaborate on feedback or show no uptake. Only cognitive features were significant predictors of uptake behaviors. This study extends the types of feedback uptake behaviors previously considered and provides critical insights into different reactions to feedback, in terms of which reactions are common and what kind of feedback supports those reactions. These expansions are central to developing unified accounts of learning from peer feedback across contexts.

TI Similarities in mother' and fathers' toddler interactions and links with
   school readiness
SO EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE Observational; School readiness; Reciprocity; Warmth; Family systems
ID INVOLVEMENT; FAMILIES; PLAY; DETERMINANTS; ASSOCIATION; FOUNDATIONS;
   BEHAVIOR; RISK
AB Despite the evolving role of fathers, studies rarely examine the development of mother- and father-toddler interactions in tandem. In addition, evidence of how these preschool family interactions support children's school readiness is also heavily focused on mothers. We respond to this via two studies. In a sample of 185 two-parent families, Study One examined similarities, differences and longitudinal links between displays of warmth and reciprocity in home-based play observations of mother-toddler and father-toddler dyadic interactions at two timepoints (14- and 24-months). At 14-months, mothers displayed higher average levels of warmth than fathers, but there were no mean differences by parent gender in dyadic reciprocity. Within-family associations strengthened over time, and by 24 months, average levels of warmth and dyadic reciprocity were similar for mothers and fathers. Mother-toddler reciprocity and maternal warmth at 14-months each predicted fathertoddler reciprocity at 24-months, controlling for fathers' behaviour at 14 months. Expanding the developmental scope of these findings, Study Two involved an age 48-months follow-up of 77 children, for whom teachers rated school-readiness, including subscales of language and cognition, daily living skills, behavioural regulation, and family support. Tentative findings with this reduced sample indicate potential contrasts in associations between mother- and father-toddler interactions and domains of school readiness. Father-toddler reciprocity at 24-months was associated with children's language and cognition skills and teacher-rated family support, while mothers' warmth at 24-months was associated children's daily living skills. Findings highlight tandem developmental processes in mother and father-toddler dyadic interactions and the potential importance of fathers in supporting school readiness.

TI Child development post-COVID-19 school closures in Ghana: The roles of
   remote learning experiences
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Post-COVID-19; Remote learning experiences; School closure; School
   reopening; Sub-Saharan Africa; Ghana
ID QUALITY; SUPPORT; IMPACTS
AB In 2020-2021, the COVID-19 pandemic led to school closures worldwide and created significant learning losses for children around the world, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, a region with pre-existing wide learning gaps. Little is known about how remote learning experiences during school closures predict academic performance after school reopenings, or how these relations vary by children's demographic characteristics and pre-pandemic achievement levels. Using longitudinal data from the Greater Accra region of Ghana (N = 1604) and controlling for pre-pandemic (2018) outcomes, this study examined the associations between children's remote learning experiences during school closures in 2020 and subsequent academic achievement one, two, and four years after such closures (2021, 2022, and 2024). Moderation by child, household, and school characteristics was also examined. Results showed that remote learning experiences during school closures - especially engagement in and resources for remote learning - were positively associated with children's academic outcomes in 2021 and 2022, but not in 2024. Subgroup analyses revealed that children with average or above-average pre-pandemic math scores benefited from remote learning during school closures at the trend-level, but not students with below-average scores. Household socioeconomic status, economic shocks, and school type did not significantly moderate the relation between remote learning experiences and post-pandemic learning outcomes.

TI The hidden curriculum of generative AI in business schools: Power,
   identity, and the reconfiguration of management learning
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; Hidden curriculum; Management education; Epistemic
   authority; Identity formation; Institutional norms; Responsible
   management education
AB Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping management education, influencing how students access information and construct their professional identities. Existing research highlights opportunities and risks of AI-mediated learning, but pays little attention to the implicit messages and assumptions AI systems introduce into educational environments. This paper focuses on generative AI - large language models and similar systems - whose fluent, conversational outputs produce hidden curricular effects distinct from analytical AI. Drawing on hidden curriculum theory, the paper develops a conceptual framework for understanding generative AI as an algorithmic actor shaping learning through three interconnected domains: epistemic authority, identity formation, and institutional norms. The paper makes four contributions: a theoretical framework identifying the three domain pathways through which AI shapes implicit learning; eleven formally stated, empirically testable propositions providing a research agenda; pedagogical strategies for surfacing and counteracting AI's hidden curriculum; and practical implications for assessment, faculty development, and institutional governance. The conceptual analysis suggests that AI can reinforce dominant managerial ideologies, narrow epistemic diversity, and shift expectations around productivity, authorship, and professional competence - though these tendencies operate conditionally and are not deterministic. The paper contributes to debates on responsible management education and provides a foundation for future empirical research.

   research priorities of adults who stutter and perceived supports to

DT Article
DE Stuttering; Research priorities; World Cafe; Research partnerships
ID QUALITY-OF-LIFE; NONPHARMACOLOGICAL INTERVENTIONS; PARTICIPATORY
   RESEARCH; THE-ART; PEOPLE; WORLD; PART; EXPERIENCES; ACCOUNTS; IMPACT
AB Background: Stuttering research tends to be researcher-led and there is minimal engagement with adults who stutter to ascertain their research priorities. Results: Eleven adults who stutter (male: n = 7; female: n = 4) participated in the World Cafe. Seven themes relating to the participants' research priorities, and three themes relating to actions that researchers can take to support future partnerships with people who stutter were identified. Conclusion: Findings of this exploratory study will inform the methodology of a larger study on research priority setting and partnership between researchers and adults who stutter.

TI From organisational visions to professional actions: Teachers' agency
   for equitable education for autistic students
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism; Teacher agency; Teacher self-efficacy; Equity-oriented
   education; Neurodiversity; Special didactics
ID QUALITATIVE CONTENT-ANALYSIS
AB This study examined how teachers reflect on the organisational and educational changes needed to achieve equity-oriented education for autistic students following professional development. Drawing on special didactics and the neurodiversity paradigm, it explored how teachers' reasoning reveals the interplay between professional agency, self-efficacy and structural conditions. The data were drawn from open-ended questionnaire responses (N = 53) to a post-intervention questionnaire completed by Swedish primary school teachers who took part in a professional learning programme on neurodiversity and accessible learning. TI Feasibility and Effectiveness of an Adolescent Glass-Analysis Reading
   Intervention Delivered Online by Lay Tutors
SO DYSLEXIA
LA English
DT Article
DE analytic phonics; decoding; dyslexia; fluency; literacy
ID COMPONENT; READERS
AB Many adolescents do not have the basic reading skills needed to successfully comprehend increasingly complex academic texts, and the COVID-19 pandemic has further disrupted reading achievement. These concerns motivate the present pilot study, which adapts the Glass-Analysis programme, a theoretically distinctive analytic phonics intervention, for online delivery by lay tutors. Fifth- and sixth-grade students (N = 34) with poor reading skills were alternately assigned to an intervention or waitlist control group. Intervention participants completed individualised sessions over 11-19 weeks. The Woodcock Reading Mastery Test (WRMT-III) and Test of Word Reading Efficiency (TOWRE-2) were used to measure changes in reading skills. Tutors reached high fidelity at the end of training; technological barriers were minimal, and tutor and participant retention was high. Moderate effect size differences between the intervention and waitlist control group were observed for measures of decoding and rapid automatised naming, but the study was designed with low statistical power and none of the observed group differences were significant. We conclude the Glass-Analysis programme holds promise as a scalable and accessible reading intervention for adolescent struggling readers and that future work to more definitively test its effectiveness is warranted.

TI Conceptualising Ideologically Bounded Equity in Japan: A Document
   Analysis of Curriculum Governance, High-Stakes Transitions and Shadow
   Education
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE curriculum governance; document analysis; educational equity;
   high-stakes transitions; Japan; policy enactment; shadow education
ID REFORM; POLITICS; JUSTICE
AB This study examines how responsibility for educational fairness is represented across curriculum governance, reform cycles, selective transitions, supplementary education and values and moral education in Japan. It uses thematic document analysis of a criterion-based purposive corpus of 43 documents: six Japanese official documents, five OECD publications and 32 academic or scholarly sources. The analysis identifies a substantive public guarantee of common curricular provision, meaningful but uneven recalibration across the Yutori and Post-Yutori periods, socially differentiated conditions for converting provision into valued pathways and heterogeneous functions of shadow education. Ideologically Bounded Equity is retained as a qualified, revisable middle-range interpretation: public commitment, institutional guarantee and differentiation are strongly supported; the boundary of public responsibility is partial and contested; and ideological legitimation remains tentative.

TI Food Colorantsas a Context-Based Approach for HighSchool Chemistry: From
   Natural Sources to Marketing Practices
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Food Safety; Food Colors; Azo dyes; Chemistry Education; Inquiry-Based
   Learning; FoodLabeling; Marketing; Student Engagement
AB This study presents an inquiry-driven teaching approach that draws on students' everyday experiences with colored foods and beverages. The activity synergistically integrates areas of organic and analytical chemistry to develop students' experimental and problem-solving skills while supporting their informed decision-making in everyday life. Student engagement was fostered through guiding questions framing two central dilemmas - colorful versus uncolored foods and natural versus artificial colorants - providing an authentic context to address issues related to food safety, current legislation, and environmental sustainability. Following the experimental work and in line with active citizenship goals, students shared the outcomes of their educational research through public outreach events involving the local community.
