TI Editorial: Understanding, designing, and teaching the curriculum to
   incorporate the cultivation of thinking skills
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Thinking skills cultivation; Creativity development; Curriculum design;
   Curricular space; Designing learning environments; Teacher professional
   capabilities; Teaching practices
AB The purpose of this special issue is to advance understanding of how thinking skills can be effectively cultivated within educational curricula. Drawing on 33 papers selected from more than 160 submissions, this Editorial synthesizes the collection's principal theoretical, research, and practical contributions. Collectively, the papers demonstrate that thinking skills can be developed through the deliberate design of coherent learning environments that make thinking visible, support its development through interaction and feedback, and promote its continual refinement and application. The Editorial first examines how the papers extend theoretical perspectives on thinking skills development, curricular space, and the broader capabilities that underpin effective thinking. It then considers methodological advances that strengthen the investigation and evaluation of thinking-related processes and outcomes. Finally, it synthesizes practical approaches for integrating thinking skills into curricula, scaffolding learners' thinking, designing effective learning activities, and strengthening teachers' professional capabilities. Together, these contributions demonstrate that the cultivation of thinking skills is not merely an educational aspiration but a realistic and achievable goal, while providing researchers, educators, curriculum developers, and teachers with a comprehensive resource for advancing thinking skills education across diverse educational contexts.

TI The Nguluway of Knowledges Framework: weaving together Indigenous
   Institutional Theory and the 8 Aboriginal Ways of Learning
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Indigenous Institutional Theory; 8 Aboriginal Ways of Learning;
   Indigenous theory; Curricula; Conceptual framework; Pedagogy
ID CURRICULUM
AB There is a push for Australian educational institutions to meaningfully weave together Indigenous and Western pedagogical approaches. Ideally, this synergy of pedagogical approaches would be reflected in curricula that authentically integrates Indigenous ways of learning and Community-informed content. Despite this educational push, few frameworks exist to guide meaningful integration of Indigenous pedagogy in Western institutions. Similarly, there is a need for Indigenous-designed theoretical underpinnings that are tailored to the interface between university education and institutional research contexts. The authors address gaps in educational theory by presenting an innovative conceptual framework, the Nguluway of Knowledges Framework. Nguluway, a Wiradjuri word meaning "meeting each other", positions authentic Indigenous pedagogical approaches within Western educational structures. The conceptual framework weaves Indigenous ways of learning in Westernised institutions, such as universities, by bringing together Indigenous Institutional Theory (Coates et al., ) and the 8 Aboriginal Ways of Learning Framework (Yunkaporta, ). The authors aim to; (1) consider the application of Indigenous Institutional Theory (IIT) and the 8 Aboriginal Ways of Learning Framework in university education; (2) present and describe the new conceptual framework, the Nguluway of Knowledges Framework; and (3) discuss the application of the conceptual framework for embedding Indigenous knowledges in Western university institutions, specifically within an Australian medical degree program. The framework serves both as a theoretical underpinning for education and research and as a practical tool to facilitate stakeholders in designing curricula with Indigenous people in Westernised institutions. A key strength of the framework lies in its capacity to shape Indigenous pedagogical approaches, guide curriculum design, and inform institutional practice within Western education systems.

TI An exploration of VET in Schools programs and contributions to the STEM
   careers pipeline
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE STEM education; VET in Schools; Careers; Gender; Socio-economic status;
   Remoteness
ID STUDENTS; GENDER
AB STEM-based employment is projected to grow at almost twice the rate of other occupations; yet, there are persistent difficulties in meeting the demands for a STEM-skilled workforce. Further, there are well-established issues in STEM education that impact the pursuit of STEM careers by equity groups including girls, low-SES and non-metropolitan students. Attrition among these groups has been described as the "leaky pipeline", characterised by students from such equity groups withdrawing from educational pathways that lead to STEM careers. A potential contributor to the STEM careers pipeline is STEM-aligned Vocational Education and Training (VET) programs delivered within secondary schools. The current study explores publicly available VET in Schools data to determine the participation of school-age students, including among equity groups (i.e. girls, low SES, and non-metropolitan students), in STEM-aligned programs. Overall, less than 5% of VET in Schools program completions were aligned to STEM careers; however, the completion of STEM-aligned programs has more than doubled in the last five years. Increases in STEM program completions were observed for girls within this sample; though, their participation in these programs were observed to be lower overall as a group. Descriptive analyses suggested there were increases in STEM participation across all SES quintiles and remoteness categories, but lower completion rates for more disadvantaged and non-metropolitan students. It appears that the potential for STEM-aligned VET in Schools programs to contribute to the STEM careers pipeline is not yet fully realised.

TI Beyond a Standardized Energy Justice Model: Culture, Context, and
   Community Agency in a Student-Led Comparative Case Study of Community
   Solar in Los Angeles and Medellín
SO CASE STUDIES IN THE ENVIRONMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE community solar; community energy; renewable energy; international
   studies; climate change; energy justice; student-led research;
   environmental science; climate justice; energy communities; solar
   energy; solar panels; environmental justice; environmental policy;
   energy policy
ID UK
AB Through a student-led comparative analysis of community solar initiatives in Los Angeles, California, and Medell & iacute;n, Colombia, this study examines the assumption that energy justice can be achieved through a replicable model. This case study examines two divergent systemic structures: a top-down, utility-sponsored framework in California optimized for economic efficiency and passive participation, and a bottom-up, collectively owned system in Colombia centered on technical literacy and social empowerment. Initial attempts to derive a replicable implementation template revealed that project "success" is not necessarily a product of technical design but is determined by unique social infrastructures and cultural norms regarding collectivity. While the California case successfully provides financial relief to disadvantaged households through institutional management, the Medell & iacute;n case demonstrates how community energy can catalyze civic engagement, collective empowerment, and environmental stewardship. By moving beyond techno-optimistic narratives that treat social contexts as variables to be adapted, this research emphasizes the necessity of localized, socio-technical frameworks. By engaging with this case, readers will be able to identify the limitations of a standardized policy framework in energy justice and evaluate how social frameworks affect the context-specific outcomes of renewable energy projects.

TI FROM CRITICAL THINKING TO d-CRITICAL THINKING: RECONSTRUCTING
   DEWEY'S SENSE OF CRITICAL IN HOW WE THINK
SO EDUCATIONAL THEORY
LA English
DT Article
DE Dewey; critical thinking; induction and deduction; metacognition;
   educational theory
AB In this article, I reexamine John Dewey's original sense of critical in How We Think (first published in 1910), arguing that contemporary discourse about critical thinking reveals a process of lexicalization through which the term critical has lost its meaning. This article finds that Dewey's original sense of critical (which I term d-Critical) functions operatively (as a set of regulating procedures that fine-tune bounded inquiry) and normatively (as an assessment of how safeguarded inferences made during an act of thinking are). Through a close reading and analysis of Dewey's explanatory analogies, I show that Dewey's sense of critical avoids the four dangers outlined in Johnson and Hamby's critique of current definitions of critical thinking: a) failure to capture the sense of the term critical; b) conflation with related constructs; c) sublimation of the concept; and d) ignoring the role of belief maintenance. The result is a clarification of Dewey's meaning that distinguishes reflective thought from critical thought and portrays criticality as a property of safeguarded acts of thinking.

TI From the Practical to the Sapient: Curriculum Judgment Beyond Schwab
SO EDUCATIONAL THEORY
LA English
DT Article
DE Schwab; curriculum; practical; sapience; judgment; epistemology
AB Joseph Schwab's "practical turn" remains a defining moment in curriculum theory. His practical papers of the late 1960s and early 1970s sought to restore professional judgment to a field dominated by technical rationality and policy prescription. Yet, despite its democratic intent, Schwab's conception of the practical rests on an empiricist epistemology that reduces deliberation to procedural coordination. This article revisits Schwab's framework through the philosophical lens of sapience. Drawing on Sellars, Brandom, Gadamer, Murdoch, and Arendt, we reconstruct curriculum deliberation as a form of reasoning that is inferential, ethical, and temporal rather than merely instrumental. Our analysis proceeds as an immanent critique, acknowledging Schwab's historical achievement while showing that his model of the practical cannot sustain the conditions of knowledge or judgment it presupposes. The article concludes that educational practice requires not the restricting but the deepening of theory, toward a sapient understanding of teaching as participation in the space of reasons. A sapient curriculum reclaims time for reflection, moral attention, and the interpretive labor of understanding qualities that procedural deliberation cannot provide but upon which education depends.

TI From Policy to Practice: School Stakeholder Perspectives on Alternative
   Breakfast Implementation in Utah
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE alternative school breakfast; implementation science; school breakfast
   program; school policy
ID FREE KIDS ACT; FOOD INSECURITY; PARENT PERCEPTIONS; DIETARY QUALITY;
   CONSUMPTION; HEALTHY; PARTICIPATION; ASSOCIATION; OUTCOMES; CHILDREN
AB Background The School Breakfast Program (SBP) provides academic and nutritional benefits to U.S. children. In Utah, the Start Smart Utah policy requires schools with higher proportions of students from low-income backgrounds to adopt alternative breakfast models. Research suggests policy adoption does not guarantee effective implementation. This study examined school stakeholders' perspectives on implementing Start Smart Utah.Methods This qualitative study recruited Utah school stakeholders (n = 32) whose schools were required to implement an alternative breakfast model under Start Smart Utah. A semi-structured interview guide explored implementation experiences and perceived support. Interviews were analyzed using reliability thematic analysis.Results Five themes were constructed: (a) supporting students through school breakfast, (b) initial implementation: shifting strategies and support, (c) student participation in school breakfast, (d) tensions among quality, choice, and waste, and (e) recommendations for strengthening alternative breakfast models.Implications for School Health Policy, Practice, and Equity Findings show that clear communication, adequate resources, and stakeholder engagement are essential for policy success. Embedding funding, training, and feedback mechanisms can improve implementation and equity.Conclusions SBPs remain vital to student well-being and academic success. Start Smart Utah shows that expanding access through policy can yield benefits, but success depends on implementation realities.

TI Children's metacognitive awareness and self-correction of their own
   spelling mistakes
SO METACOGNITION AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Metacognition; Spelling consciousness; Spelling; Self-correction; Answer
   changing
ID INSTRUCTION; PERFORMANCE; CONFIDENCE; ANSWERS; ACCURACY; SKILLS;
   JUDGMENTS; STUDENTS; TIME
AB This paper examines how children identify and correct spelling errors in their own writing. Our research focused on two questions: (a) how accurate primary school children are in their metacognitive monitoring of their own writing of a dictated text, and (b) whether they are able to translate their spelling performance monitoring into regulatory behaviour such that they revise and correct detected spelling errors. A total of 318 German-speaking primary school children wrote a continuous text that was dictated to them by an instructor in their language of instruction (German). In order to differentiate between the processes of monitoring and control, children were first instructed to underline words they were unsure about (Review Phase). After this initial monitoring process, children were told that they could change their initial spellings (Revise Phase). Our results demonstrate that the primary school children were accurate in identifying their correctly spelled words (high specificity), whereas their error detection rate was poor (low sensitivity). Furthermore, only about 24% of the words selected in the Review Phase were then actually changed in the Revise Phase. When children did revise the spelling of a word, they were more likely to correct an initial spelling mistake than change a correct spelling. Children's difficulties in identifying and correcting their own spelling mistakes seem to be related to their low sensitivity to spelling errors (spelling awareness deficit) and their reluctance or inability to correct misspelled words (implementation or knowledge deficit).

TI COVID-19-related school closures and students' achievement and
   motivation: Did teacher support make a difference
SO NPJ SCIENCE OF LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
ID SELF-CONCEPT; CLASSROOM
AB Most effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on student outcomes were negative, though school systems varied in their ability to mitigate learning losses. In this study, we examined teacher-student contact as a key factor for buffering pandemic-related risks to achievement and motivation. We analyzed multicohort data collected at the beginning and end of the school year from 2740 first-grade students in Baden-W & uuml;rttemberg, Germany. Against expectations, no overall decline in achievement emerged under pandemic schooling; however, high teacher-student contact was associated with higher math achievement compared with regular schooling. Motivational outcomes showed negative average effects for interest and self-concept in language domains, particularly under low teacher-student contact and low family socioeconomic status. Owing to its timing at the start of formal schooling during the first wave of the pandemic, this study provides unique evidence of the role of teacher-student contact in students' achievement and motivation during crisis conditions.

TI A systematic scoping review on cyberbullying involving ethnic minority
   and Indigenous youth: toward culturally sensitive research and
   interventions
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Ethnicity; Indigeneity; Migrants; Online bullying; Online racial
   discrimination; Young people
ID RACIAL IDENTITY; MENTAL-HEALTH; SCHOOL; VICTIMIZATION; ADOLESCENCE;
   STRESS; PEOPLE; RACE; CONCEPTUALIZATION; RACE/ETHNICITY
AB Ethnic minority and Indigenous youth represent particularly vulnerable populations for involvement in cyberbullying. The existing literature is marked by conceptual confusion and methodological heterogeneity, highlighting the need for a scoping review to map current research in this area. This systematic scoping review provides an overview of empirical research conducted worldwide on cyberbullying involving ethnic minorities and Indigenous children and adolescents, with the goal of informing future research and offering relevant implications for interventions. The review was conducted in accordance with JBI guidelines, and results were reported following the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews). The following databases were searched: Academic Search Premier, ERIC, PsychINFO (OVID), PubMed, Scopus, SocINDEX, Web of Science, Medline, and ProQuest. The review included peer-reviewed studies published in English, involving children and adolescents (participants' mean age below 18 years) identified as ethnic minorities or Indigenous, and reporting data on cyberbullying related to ethnicity or indigeneity. Following a two-stage screening process, 166 articles were selected for inclusion. Findings suggest that research on this topic is expanding. However, literature remains characterized by limited geographical coverage, underrepresentation of ethnic and Indigenous groups, scarce contextual and theoretical positionality, and a predominance of quantitative approaches. A lack of intervention studies and of research addressing identity-based cyberbullying and perpetration is evident. By disentangling and focusing on the role of ethnicity and indigeneity in cyberbullying, this scoping review represents a crucial step toward guiding future research focusing on the development of contextually responsive prevention and intervention strategies.

TI Examining Behavioural Intentions, Metacognitive Regulation, and
   GenAI-Assisted EFL Writing Performance
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE behavioural intentions; GenAI-assisted writing performance;
   metacognitive regulation; social cognitive theory of self-regulation;
   theory of planned behaviour
ID PLANNED BEHAVIOR; REGULARIZATION; EFFICACY
AB Despite the growing use of GenAI in English as a foreign language (EFL) writing, research on the interplay between learners' behavioural intentions and GenAI-assisted writing performance remains scarce. To address this gap, the present study integrates the theory of planned behaviour with social cognitive theory of self-regulation to examine how behavioural intentions relate to writing performance and the mediating role of metacognitive regulation. A total of 174 participants completed instruments assessing metacognitive regulation and behavioural intentions before engaging in GenAI-supported writing tasks. Data were analysed via structural equation modelling (SEM) and Elastic Net regression in R. Moreover, evaluation emerged as the strongest predictor of learners' intentions and GenAI-assisted writing performance. These findings advance a theoretical integration, providing empirical insights into how metacognitive regulation can optimize the effective use of GenAI in EFL writing contexts.

TI Capturing language teachers' work engagement in online EFL classes: a
   questionnaire development and validation study
SO LANGUAGE TESTING IN ASIA
LA English
DT Article
DE English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers; Factor analysis; Online
   EFL classes; Questionnaire development and validation; Teacher work
   engagement
ID EMPLOYEE ENGAGEMENT; SELF-EFFICACY; INTERPLAY; RESPONSES; BURNOUT
AB Given the growing importance of teacher work engagement for instructional quality and student learning, the availability of valid and context-sensitive measurement instruments has become increasingly important. Although several instruments have been developed to assess work engagement, they were primarily designed for general occupational or educational settings and do not adequately capture the distinctive pedagogical, technological, and interactional demands of online English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction. To address this gap, this study developed and validated the Teacher Work Engagement Questionnaire (TWEQ), specifically designed to assess EFL teachers' work engagement in online instructional settings. The study employed Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) to examine the factor structure, reliability, and construct validity of the TWEQ, which was administered to a sample of 225 EFL teachers. The instrument also demonstrated strong internal consistency and satisfactory convergent and discriminant validity, providing robust evidence of its psychometric quality. These results indicate that the TWEQ is a reliable and valid instrument for assessing teacher work engagement in online EFL contexts. By offering a context-specific measure of teacher work engagement, the TWEQ extends the existing literature and provides a valuable diagnostic and research tool for investigating teacher engagement in online EFL education. It may also assist teacher educators, administrators, and policymakers in identifying engagement-related strengths and areas requiring targeted professional support.

TI Embodied Learningfor Abstract Concept Teaching inChemistry: Insights
   from a Textbook-Based Analysis
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Embodied learning; Seniorhigh school chemistry; Textbook coding;
   Submicroscopicconcepts; instructionaldesign
ID REALITY; PREVALENCE; BIAS
AB To address persistent challenges in teaching abstract concepts in senior secondary chemistry-particularly the gap between macroscopic manipulation and submicroscopic explanation-this study conducted a textbook-based content analysis of Senior Secondary Chemistry (Compulsory Modules 1-2) published by the People's Education Press and the accompanying teachers' guides. A four-dimensional coding framework was developed, encompassing concept type, level of bodily engagement, action-concept alignment, and degree of contextual immersion. Nineteen analytical units were independently coded by two raters, yielding high interrater reliability (Cohen's kappa > 0.80). The results indicate a pronounced structural imbalance in the distribution of embodied learning opportunities. Embodied support is predominantly concentrated at lower levels, mainly in observation-based activities (A1) and macroscopic experimental operations (A3-1). In contrast, higher-level embodied designs-including gesture-based action chains (A2), activities supporting structural mapping at the submicroscopic level (A3-2), and immersive simulations (A4)-are markedly underrepresented. Although topics amenable to direct macroscopic manipulation, such as solution preparation and energy transformation, receive relatively strong embodied support, representations that explicitly account for submicroscopic particle mechanisms and symbolic relationships, such as atomic structure and chemical bonding, are largely absent. This pattern suggests that current textbook designs emphasize macroscopic "doing" without sufficiently scaffolding students' understanding of how submicroscopic interactions give rise to observable phenomena and symbolic representations. Based on the analyzed textbook and teacher-guide materials, these findings suggest that future textbook design may benefit from moving beyond simply increasing embodied activities and instead providing targeted embodied support for concepts that require students to connect macroscopic experience, submicroscopic models, and symbolic representations.

TI Energy transitions and the C3 inquiry arc: modeling an inquiry-driven
   unit for rural elementary preservice teachers
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE classroom discourse; energy transitions education; inquiry-based
   learning; place-conscious pedagogy; primary sources; rural education;
   social studies; teacher preparation
AB University-based teacher educators in teacher preparation programs (TPPs) are tasked with preparing preservice teachers (PSTs) to design meaningful and engaging learning experiences for diverse elementary students. In rural contexts, this work often involves supporting PSTs in making instruction more relevant through place-conscious approaches that connect classroom learning to students' local communities, experiences, and identities. However, engaging students in locally relevant topics, particularly complex and potentially contentious environmental issues such as energy transitions (ETs), requires PSTs to navigate multiple perspectives and community tensions, which can challenge their teaching confidence and self-efficacy. Despite this need, TPPs often lack explicit models that demonstrate how to design and facilitate inquiry-based, place-conscious instruction around difficult topics. In response, this article outlines the development and implementation of a College, Career, and Civic Life (C3) Framework-aligned instructional sequence used by a rural teacher educator to model for PSTs how they can: (1) locate place-conscious primary sources and materials, (2) design inquiry-driven activities for elementary students, and (3) implement inquiry driven tasks alongside place-conscious materials to encourage classroom discourse around complex environmental topics such as ETs. Implications are discussed for how discourse-driven, place-conscious instructional sequences can be used within TPPs to support PSTs' development of teaching self-efficacy and confidence, as well as directions for future research on preparing teachers to engage elementary students in meaningful inquiry around difficult, locally relevant issues.

TI What is the relationship between sports psychology and educational
   attainment: exploring the moderating and the mediating relationship
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational attainment; goal setting; self-motivation; self-efficacy;
   sports psychology; students; Sustainable Development
ID SELF-EFFICACY; MOTIVATION; AUTONOMY; ESTEEM; PERFORMANCE; LEVEL;
   PERSPECTIVE; SCALE; LIFE
AB Decision-makers in most countries are recognizing the importance of sports in education. Sports are important because they help improve a person's performance at both the individual and professional levels. Despite this established importance, the specific explanation for how these psychological factors jointly influence educational attainment among sports students remains insufficiently articulated in existing literature. This study investigates how sports psychology enhances educational attainment through the integration of goal setting, self-motivation, self-esteem, self-autonomy, and self-confidence. A quantitative research design and a purposive sampling technique were used. The study's respondents were KSA-based students who participated in sports. The researcher distributed 350 questionnaires to KSA students. The number of usable questionnaires was 242, with a response rate of 69.14%. The instrument's reliability was greater than 70%. Structural equation modelling in AMOS was used to analyze the data. The results of the study demonstrated the positive effects of goal setting, self-esteem, self-autonomy, and self-confidence on self-motivation. Self-esteem had a significant positive effect on self-motivation (beta = 0.88, p <= 0.01). Similarly, self-autonomy (beta = 0.35, p <= 0.01), goal setting (beta = 0.36, p <= 0.01), and self-confidence (beta = 0.58, p <= 0.01) had significant positive effects on self-motivation. Self-motivation positively influences educational attainment (beta = 0.68, p <= 0.01). The measurement model exhibited high reliability because all model fit indices met the necessary standards (CFI = 0.92, RMSEA = 0.02, and CMIN/DF = 1.25). Results also showed a significant mediating role for motivation and a moderating role for self-efficacy. These findings are vital for policy developers and strategists, enabling them to focus on students' psychological motivational traits to improve their academic performance. In this study, a cross-sectional research design was used; future research may include a longitudinal study or a cross-cultural or cross-country analysis.

TI From trainee to colleague: REM scholars' experiences transitioning from
   postdoctoral fellow to faculty within the same biomedical department
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE faculty diversification ecosystems; faculty hiring; postdoc-to-faculty
   conversion programs; postdoc-to-faculty programs; URM postdocs; racial
   and ethnic minority postdocs; biomedical postdocs; URM faculty diversity
ID COLOR
AB Introduction Postdoctoral-to-faculty pathway initiatives have increased within biomedical higher education as strategies intended to broaden participation within the professoriate. Earlier scholarship identified disparities in biomedical faculty representation and positioned postdoctoral training as a critical stage in academic career trajectories. Institutions developed structured postdoctoral-to-faculty pathways to intentionally connect postdoctoral training with faculty opportunities. Although studies have examined the implementation and diversification goals of these initiatives, less attention has been given to how scholars experience these career pathways.Methods This descriptive phenomenological study examined the experiences of racialized ethnic minority (REM) postdoctoral scholars who transitioned into tenure-track faculty roles through the AGEP PROMISE Academy Alliance (APAA), a National Science Foundation-funded train-and-retain (T-RT) postdoctoral initiative operating across a Mid-Atlantic public university system. Semi-structured interviews with four REM scholars, between 2018 and 2022, revealed five interconnected themes shaping transition into faculty roles.Results The themes that emerged included: (1) encountering varying mentorship and advocacy; (2) navigating unclear expectations and institutional processes; (3) managing uneven resources and expanding workload expectations; (4) sustaining research productivity during transition; and (5) negotiating belonging and faculty identity. Participants described the transition as simultaneously familiar and uncertain, as they navigated evolving collegial relationships, shifting expectations, perceptions of legitimacy, and departmental environments where past trainee identities remained visible. Mentoring relationships often provided support and advocacy while also complicating independence and faculty identity formation.Discussion Findings distinguish this phenomenon from early-career faculty experiences typically examined after the faculty appointment. Within T-RT pathways, participants' experiences began during the postdoctoral period and continued across tenure-track positions, as prior trainee identities, relationships, and recognition carried into faculty roles within the same departmental context. Professional legitimacy, collegial integration, mentoring, racialized visibility, belonging, and faculty identity were gradually negotiated across the formal transition.

TI Making professional learning pathways visible: student-generated
   curriculum visualization and rubric-based self-checking in a landscape
   architecture bridge course
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE curriculum visualization; landscape architecture education; professional
   learning pathways; rubric-based self-checking; single-case study
AB In high-participation higher education contexts, students in professional programs may complete individual courses without clearly understanding how those courses form a coherent learning pathway or relate to future professional roles. This exploratory single-case study examines student-generated curriculum visualization and rubric-based self-checking as a bridge-course strategy in a junior-year landscape planning theory course in Taiwan. The course was positioned at a curricular threshold between foundational design learning and more integrative planning-oriented and professionally situated learning. Students used fishbone diagrams to map vertical and horizontal relationships among courses, concepts, competencies, and future applications. Rubrics were used as formative self-check tools to help students evaluate the completeness, coherence, and professional relevance of their maps, while problem-based guidance and teaching assistant facilitation provided additional scaffolding. The study drew on three-wave questionnaire data, reliability analysis, exploratory paired comparisons, student fishbone outputs, rubric records, institutional course evaluation, student feedback forms, teaching assistant review records, and group learning logs. Questionnaire results showed stable positive responses across the course sequence. Descriptive paired-comparison patterns suggested a possible later-stage increase in perceived career linkage and application, but this pattern was interpreted cautiously because of the small matched sample and multiple exploratory comparisons. Process-based evidence indicated that students used the fishbone task to move from course-by-course recall toward more relational interpretations of curriculum hierarchy, cross-course linkage, learning gaps, and professional application. The study does not claim statistical generalizability or causal effectiveness. Instead, it contributes an analytically transferable pedagogical model showing how student-generated visual mapping, rubric-supported self-checking, and guided facilitation may help make professional learning pathways more visible and discussable at a critical curricular transition point.

TI Navigating uncertainty: strategy formulation in higher education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational leadership; higher education management; strategy
   formulation; strategy-as-practice; university strategy
AB This exploratory interpretative study delves into the strategic formulation processes and practices at higher education institutions (HEIs) in a developing country. Drawing on Mintzberg's strategic schools and the strategy-as-practice (SAP) perspective, this research examines the actors involved, methodologies employed, and the influence of the pandemic on strategic planning within these institutions. The study utilises semi-structured interviews with key figures from both public and private universities, coupled with strategic document analysis, to investigate strategy formulation. The study highlights a general paucity of external stakeholder involvement across the HEI spectrum, with limited engagement from employers and alumni in strategic development. The findings also show that public universities in the sample remain strongly shaped by state-directed planning, prescribed performance indicators, and formal reporting requirements, while some private universities display greater use of positioning, broader strategic direction, annual review, and delegated planning. At the same time, deliberate and emergent strategies coexist across the sector, as formal plans are supplemented by situated managerial responses to changing conditions. The study contributes to strategy-as-practice and higher education strategy research by offering a context-sensitive account of how regulation, ownership, stakeholder participation, and managerial action interact in strategy formulation.

   YOUTH
AB In the United States, approximately one in 31 children is identified as autistic, and research indicates that autistic individuals complete bachelor's degrees and secure employment at lower rates than their non-disabled peers. Expanding access to STEM may help address these disparities, which often emerge during the transition to adulthood. Although autistic college students often pursue STEM majors, low degree completion rates highlight the need for stronger preparation and support in these high-demand fields. TI Enabling a professional learning community in Malaysian rural primary
   schools: the role of collegial trust
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE collegial trust; constructs; Malaysia; professional learning community;
   rural primary schools
ID LEADERSHIP PRACTICES; CULTURE; CHINA
AB Purpose This study examines how different dimensions of collegial trust are associated with teachers' engagement in Professional Learning Communities (PLCs) practices within rural primary schools. Although PLCs are widely recognized as mechanisms for teacher learning, limited attention has been given to understanding which dimensions of collegial trust function as relational resources that sustain collaboration in geographically isolated and resource-constrained educational contexts.Methods A cross-sectional correlational survey design was used to collect data from 310 teachers selected through proportional cluster random sampling across 57 rural Malaysian primary schools. Descriptive analyses and structural equation modelling (SEM) were conducted to examine relationships between collegial trust dimensions and PLC practices.Results The strongest dimensions of collegial trust among rural teachers were reliability, competence, and openness. However, because this study was cross-sectional, these findings should be used only to describe the relationship between these variables, rather than to suggest causal relationships.

   Grade 1 classrooms

AB Background: Structured pedagogy programmes are increasingly implemented in low-and middle-income countries, including South Africa, to address poor early-grade literacy outcomes. These programmes combine structured lesson guidance, teaching materials and teacher coaching to strengthen classroom instruction. Despite their widespread implementation, limited research has examined how teachers use these materials in rural indigenous African language classrooms such as Sepedi. Conclusion: Structured Sepedi teaching materials supported organised reading instruction aligned with the Sepedi Home Language CAPS in rural Grade 1 classrooms. TI When Schools Are Equal but Children Are Not: A Multilevel Analysis of
   Home-Driven Variance and Cumulative Disadvantage in Early Childhood
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE IELS 2025; Flemish Community; print-focused home literacy; executive
   function; multilevel modelling; educational equity
ID EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; SKILLS; METAANALYSIS
AB Early childhood education and care (ECEC) systems in equitable welfare states are designed to provide comparatively standardised institutional inputs, yet substantial developmental gaps among children persist. This study examined this configuration-descriptively labelled the "Flemish Paradox"-using data from the OECD's International Early Learning and Child Well-being Study (IELS 2025) for the Flemish Community of Belgium (2363 five year olds in 200 ECEC centres; parent-questionnaire data were available for a subset of the sample, and missing parent-report data were addressed through multiple imputation). Children's cognitive and executive skills were measured with standardised direct tablet-based assessments, while home environments were reported by parents, separating measurement sources. Two-level hierarchical linear models with design-based weighting (child weight and 92 BRR replicate weights), pooled across five plausible values and 20 multiply imputed datasets, showed comparatively limited between-centre outcome variation (ICC approximate to 23% for foundational learning, approximate to 11% for executive function). Within centres, family socioeconomic status (B = 25.11, p < 0.001) and a print-focused home literacy index (PHLI; B = 16.60, p < 0.001) were positively associated with foundational learning, and centre-mean PHLI showed an independent contextual association (B = 24.11, p < 0.001). A positive within-centre indirect association through children's executive function skills was estimated (3.60, 95% Monte Carlo CI [1.83, 5.40]); a secondary exploratory analysis indicated a parallel between-centre pattern (8.40, 95% CI [1.16, 15.65]). Centre socioeconomic composition was strongly associated with outcomes (B = 36.38, p < 0.001); the analysis did not provide evidence that it modified the within-centre PHLI-learning association (p = 0.219). The findings are consistent with cultural-capital perspectives and indicate that family resources, print-focused home literacy, and EFs are jointly associated with early learning within a multilevel ECEC context. However, the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal or causal mediation, and the results should not be interpreted as evidence regarding the effectiveness of particular family-or centre-based interventions.

A cross-sectional survey design was used, and participants were categorized into three age groups (<= 30 years, 31-50 years, and >= 51 years). Associations between age and didactic preferences were analyzed using chi-square tests, adjusted standardized residuals, and ordinal and multinomial logistic regression models. Significant age-related differences were identified for didactic approach (chi(2)((4)) = 14.67, p = 0.005, V = 0.063), teaching style (chi(2)(4) = 15.25, p = 0.004, V = 0.064) and methodological-organizational form (chi(2)(8) = 21.71, p = 0.006, V = 0.076), although effect sizes were small. Teachers aged <= 30 years had higher odds of preferring a technical rather than combined approach than teachers aged 31-50 years (OR = 1.958, 95% CI = 1.344-2.852, p < 0.001) and teachers aged >= 51 years (OR = 1.563, 95% CI = 1.019-2.399, p = 0.041). Teachers aged 31-50 years showed stronger preferences for practical rather than command teaching styles than both younger (OR = 1.455, p = 0.018) and older teachers (OR = 1.386, p = 0.023). Pearson's chi-square test did not identify significant associations with teaching-unit duration (p = 0.052); however, ordinal logistic regression indicated significant overall age-group effects (p = 0.022). No significant age-related association was observed for preferred game activity (p > 0.05). The findings indicate that teacher age is associated with selected didactic preferences in team sports instruction. Although the observed associations were small, they may reflect variation in professional socialization and teaching experience and may have implications for PE teacher education and professional development.

AB Self-determination is critical in promoting classroom engagement among students with autism spectrum disorder. TI From Exploration to Facilitation: The Affective Journeys of High School
   Math Teachers Adopting Project-Based Learning
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE project-based learning; affective domain; teacher identity; narrative
   inquiry; mathematics teacher education
ID NARRATIVE INQUIRY; EDUCATION; STORIES; ACHIEVEMENT; LIVE
AB Project-based learning (PBL) holds significant promise as a student-centered instructional approach in secondary mathematics, yet teachers' capacity to leverage it for diverse learners is deeply shaped by their affective experiences during implementation. This narrative inquiry examines the affective journeys of three high school mathematics teachers as they adopted PBL in classrooms characterized by varied student readiness levels and engagement profiles. We document teachers' affective journeys as they experience initial PBL awareness, participate in active experimentation, and work toward forming emerging commitments and facilitator identities. Analysis of focus groups and interviews reveals three affective tensions: comfort versus transformative reflection, epistemic ideals versus ontological school realities, and career risk versus identity change. The findings demonstrate how teachers can navigate iterative methods of trial, how teacher educators can better support future teachers' use of student-centered pedagogies, and how administrators can be aware of the impact that teacher affect can have on performance and pedagogy. Implications address how this broader education community can support differentiated, inquiry-based mathematics instruction. This support can be advanced through scope-controlled projects, micro-evidence portfolios, and incremental adoption pathways. These approaches honor teachers' emotional labor while supporting their sustained use of student-centered learning strategies intended to broaden opportunities for participation and learning in mathematics classrooms.

TI Strengthening the Teaching Profession: Evaluating Cambodia's
   Implementation of SDG-4.c Targets
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Cambodia; SDG-4; teacher training; pre-service training; CPD
ID DOCUMENT ANALYSIS; EDUCATION; QUALITY
AB The Cambodian Ministry of Education Youth, and Sport (MoEYS) has, over time, made noticeable progress toward Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG-4) to ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all. However, the pace and extent of that progress remain uneven, particularly in the area of teacher training, which is central to achieving inclusive and quality education. Utilising a document analysis framework, this study draws upon national policy reform documents including the Teacher Policy Action Plan to examine the extent to which the MoEYS's policy commitments to professionalise the teaching workforce are meeting SDG-4.c goals. Changes to pre-service programmes including the 12 + 4 programme, investments in teacher training centres, and continuous professional development (CPD) frameworks have strengthened the system. Yet, significant challenges persist. Limited access to effective CPD, high student/teacher ratios, teacher shortages, especially in rural locations, and resource constraints continue to undermine the consistency and quality of instructional practice. A contention of this paper is that for Cambodia to fulfil its SDG-4.c target relating to teacher preparedness, progress is contingent upon sustained investment, targeted support for rural and remote regions, and stronger implementation capacity to ensure all learners benefit from well-trained and effectively supported educators.

TI Generative AI in Higher Education: Student Perceptions and a Teaching
   Framework for Creative Interactive Content Design
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE education; higher education; research; generative artificial
   intelligence; creativity; digital literacy
AB This study examines the role of generative artificial intelligence in higher education, focusing specifically on creative degree programs and students' perceptions of its academic and creative value. Employing a mixed-methods design, data were collected from 555 university students enrolled in communication- and design-related degrees in Spain. By combining an online survey with focus groups, the research analyzed the frequency, purposes, and meanings of AI use in academic tasks. The results show that students primarily use generative AI to clarify concepts, develop ideas, review literature, and support academic production. Although they acknowledge its utility as a learning tool, participants also raised concerns regarding overreliance, reduced creative effort, unreliable outputs, and potential threats to originality and authorship. Consequently, the study concludes that while generative AI is already influencing learning practices in higher education, its educational potential relies heavily on clear pedagogical guidance, ethical implementation, and active teacher mediation. Based on these findings, the article proposes a ten-step teaching framework for AI-supported creative interactive content design, aimed at fostering pedagogical innovation while preserving critical thinking, creativity, and student authorship.

TI Contextualizing Mental Health Support in Engineering Education:
   Evaluating a Brief Classroom-Based Presentation
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE students' mental health; integrating well-being into curriculum design;
   culture of well-being on campus; help-seeking; engineering students;
   engineering education; mental health literacy; integrated behavioral
   model; intention; attitude
ID COLLEGE-STUDENTS; ACADEMIC-PERFORMANCE; SUICIDE-PREVENTION; UNIVERSITY;
   IMPACT; INTERVENTIONS; UNDERGRADUATE; OUTCOMES; PROGRAM; HELP
AB In higher education, there is growing recognition that mental health support should be responsive to students' lived experiences, educational contexts, and disciplinary norms. For instance, engineering students report high levels of distress and underutilize professional mental health services when compared to students in other disciplines, reflecting a culture that normalizes excessive workload, self-reliance, and academic rigor. Therefore, this case study examined the impact of a 15-min contextualized, classroom-based mental health presentation tailored to undergraduate engineering students at a large Southeastern U.S. university. Grounded in the Integrated Behavioral Model of Mental Health Help-Seeking, the presentation integrated findings from the literature on engineering culture and its influence on student well-being. Across two years, the presentation was delivered to nearly 4500 engineering students, reaching an average of 82% of enrolled engineering students. The study evaluated this impact by comparing presentation and non-presentation groups among students who completed surveys in Spring 2023 (n = 431) and Spring 2024 (n = 132). The presentation group showed significant improvements in perceived and objective knowledge of mental health and help-seeking resources, whereas help-seeking beliefs, mechanisms, and intention did not significantly change, likely due to the deeply culturally ingrained nature of these constructs. These findings underscore the value of contextualized approaches to mental health promotion and provide support for scalable, classroom-embedded presentations and other interventions within engineering education and higher education more broadly.

TI An Exploratory Survey of Adult Perceptions Regarding Childhood Cursive
   Writing Requirements and Later Literacy Skills
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE cursive writing; manuscript writing; print writing; literacy; reading
ID MANUSCRIPT; ACCURACY; LANGUAGE; CHILDREN; MODES
AB Purpose: The purpose of the current study was to evaluate adults' retrospective recollection regarding childhood cursive writing requirements and their view of their current reading-writing abilities, efficiency, speed, confidence, accuracy, and the perceived ease in and value of learning to read and write print and cursive. Method: An online survey, consisting of 24 questions, was administered to adults. A total of 190 participants without any history of speech, language, or reading disorders were included in the current analysis. Results: Of the 190 respondents, 70.53% were required and 29.47% were not required to learn cursive. Mann-Whitney U test revealed no significant differences between the two groups in the ratings for reading print, writing print, or communication. All participants reported poorer ability and ease, higher stress levels, and lower perceived value of learning to read and write cursive compared to print. Participants' beliefs regarding their reading efficiency, speed, accuracy, or confidence levels did not differ based on whether they recalled having a childhood cursive requirement. Some of the participants (56.25%) with cursive requirements found it beneficial and worth the effort. Conclusions: Overall, adult perspectives provide little subjective justification for requiring young children to learn cursive to enhance reading and writing skills.

AB Deep learning and social-emotional learning (SEL) are increasingly recognized as essential for preparing children to thrive in an increasingly complex and interconnected world. This study investigated the association between SEL and deep learning during inclusive play among 13 children with ASD (IQ <= 50; 2 females and 11 males; Mage = 6.23 years, SD = 0.60). TI Interdisciplinary IoT-Enhanced Project-Based Learning in Pre-Service
   Teacher Education: Exploring Computational Thinking and Collaboration
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Internet of Things (IoT); IoT-enhanced teacher training; computational
   thinking; collaborative learning; STEM education; digital-age
   competencies
ID STUDENTS
AB As educators are increasingly expected to integrate technology into meaningful learning experiences, higher education institutions face growing demands to prepare digitally competent STEM teachers. This study examines an interdisciplinary IoT-enhanced project-based training involving pre-service teachers from the Computer Education and Instructional Technology (CEIT) and Science Education programmes, focusing on pre-post changes in computational thinking, collaborative processes, project development experiences, and participants' perceptions of how the training contributed to their professional development. The study involved 36 pre-service teachers from CEIT and Science Education programmes and employed an embedded mixed-methods design combining computational thinking assessments with qualitative analyses of project and collaboration processes. Results showed statistically significant pre-post increases in decomposition in both groups and in algorithmic thinking among Science Education pre-service teachers. Furthermore, active participation in collaborative meetings was associated with stronger teamwork practices, while limited engagement was associated with reported implementation challenges. Because attendance was self-selected, these associations cannot be interpreted causally. Participants perceived their IoT learning experience as making a positive contribution to their professional development and future teaching practice. Taken together, the findings suggest that interdisciplinary IoT-supported project-based learning (PBL) may provide a promising framework for supporting selected dimensions of computational thinking and collaboration in pre-service teacher education, while also offering an accessible instructional model that supports participation among learners with different levels of prior technical expertise.

TI Teacher Leadership Under the School Renewal Approach: Conceptual
   Differentiation, Theoretical Elaboration, and Empirical Illustration
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES

   integrated leadership; professional agency
ID COLLABORATIVE LEADERSHIP; DECISION-MAKING; PRINCIPALS; ORGANIZATIONS;

AB Teacher leadership has gained increasing attention since the 1980s. With the various operationalizations of teacher leadership in research and practice as well as mixed results of effects of teacher leadership, we sought to investigate the difference in teacher leadership under the school reform and renewal approaches. TI Automatic discourse relation classification and feedback optimization in
   English teaching based on transformer BERT model
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE English teaching; Discourse relation classification; Automatic
   assessment; Feedback optimization; Bidirectional encoder representations
   from transformers
AB To address the limitations of existing automatic evaluation systems that rely on surface features and fail to provide actionable feedback for improving discourse coherence, we propose a Transformer model based on BERT to classify discourse relations (causal, contrastive, progressive, or incoherent) between adjacent sentences, thereby identifying coherence defects at the sentence-pair level and supporting precise feedback generation. TI Voice-interactive virtual simulated patients as a complement to
   standardized patient training in pharmacy education: A pilot evaluation
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING

DT Article
DE Virtual simulated patient; Pharmaceutical interview; Voice recognition;
   Standardized patient; Pharmacy education
ID USER ACCEPTANCE; TECHNOLOGY
AB Introduction: Standardized patients (SPs) are widely used in pharmacy education for communication skills training, but high resource demands limit practice frequency. Voice-interactive virtual simulated patients (VSPs) powered by generative artificial intelligence may serve as a scalable complement, yet evidence supporting their use in pharmacy education remains limited. Methods: We conducted a single-center, cross-sectional pilot evaluation of a voice-interactive VSP system among 62 fourth-and fifth-year pharmacy students who had previously completed traditional SP-based training. Conclusions: Students found the voice-interactive VSP system usable and perceived it as educationally meaningful, primarily as a complement to rather than a replacement for SP training. Findings inform a planned three-year multi-cohort evaluation using objective competency assessment based on the objective structured clinical examination (OSCE).

AB Introduction: Mental illness is prominent throughout higher education and even more so amongst healthcare professionals and those of Hispanic descent. The purpose of this study was to assess the state of mental health amongst a Doctor of Pharmacy cohort with a large Hispanic representation and compare their specific barriers to care and mental health care needs to other graduate health professions. Methods: This prospective, university-wide, survey of graduate health profession students investigated barriers to mental health resource utilization as well as key social determinants of mental health between Doctor of Pharmacy Students and other graduate health professions. TI "No boundaries to inclusion": Narrow realities and broad ideals in
   Sharjah's private schools
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Inclusive education; Inclusive practices; Sharjah; Policy enactment;
   Inclusion ideals; Special educational needs
ID EDUCATION; POLICY; TEACHERS; PERSPECTIVE
AB Inclusive education represents a critical challenge in contemporary educational systems, where policy intentions often diverge from classroom realities. Based on in-depth interviews with a range of staff in four private schools in the Emirate of Sharjah in the UAE, this study explored the intricate landscape of inclusive education, revealing a nuanced narrative that challenges conventional understandings of policy enactment. Contrary to typical narratives of the top-down policy-practice relationship, this research uncovered a more complex dynamic: school staff actively implementing federal inclusion policy requirements while simultaneously holding broader, more expansive ideals of inclusion. However, these ideals are reshaped through an intersection between institutional context, cultural expectations (especially when it comes to parental views and cultural understandings), and macro-policy environment which influence school leaders and teachers' inclusive practices. Our findings demonstrate that while schools successfully adhere to formal policy guidelines, school leaders and teachers envision inclusion as a more comprehensive concept that extends beyond current implementation. Thus, the enactment of inclusive education policy in Sharjah's multicultural, privatized and largely resource-rich private schools is not a mere adoption but rather a recontextualisation that responds to culture, local logics, and marketdriven education. This research illuminates the gap between policy compliance and transformative educational practice, offering insights into the dynamic relationship between policy directives and the ideals of inclusion. The findings taken together point to a greater need for context-sensitive policy frameworks, culturally responsive preparation of school leaders and teachers, and inspection processes that value ethical leadership, relational practices, and adaptive decision-making-not just procedural compliance.

TI Remote tutoring for learning recovery: Experimental evidence from a
   low-tech intervention in Peru
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Peru; Randomized controlled trial; Remote tutoring; Learning recovery
ID GROWTH MINDSET
AB The COVID-19 pandemic worsened educational inequalities globally, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where prolonged school closures disrupted learning continuity. In Peru, these disruptions led to significant declines in students' mathematics performance. This paper evaluates the impact of Desaf & iacute;a-T a aprender, a remote tutoring program implemented in the Peruvian highlands to address pandemic-related learning losses. The program provided eight phone-based math tutoring sessions to all participants (Group A) and three additional growth mindset sessions for female students (Group B). The study was conducted in 60 high schools in the Ayacucho region of Peru, randomly assigned in equal parts to treatment and control conditions. Among students who received at least one session, the effect sizes were 0.14 SD in mathematics and 0.27 SD in the growth mindset index. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of low-tech, scalable interventions in bridging learning gaps and promoting educational equity. The study provides evidence that can inform policymakers seeking cost-efficient solutions to mitigate learning losses and enhance student outcomes in resource-constrained contexts.

DT Article

ID SELF-DETERMINATION
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming increasingly embedded in art and design education, making students' AI-assisted creative experiences an important research issue. Existing studies have rarely explained group heterogeneity and differences in creative cognition in GenAIassisted creation from the perspective of psychological need satisfaction. Grounded in Basic Psychological Need Theory (BPNT), this study surveyed 560 art and design students with experience in GenAI-assisted creation. TI Students' day-to-day experiences of basic psychological needs and their
   relation to variability in emotional well-being
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Emotional well-being; Self-determination theory; Basic psychological
   needs; Primary school students; Positive/negative affect; Within-person
ID AUTONOMY SUPPORT; NEGATIVE AFFECT; BETWEEN-PERSON; CHILDREN;
   ADOLESCENTS; SCHOOL; COMPETENCE; TEACHERS; MOOD
AB According to Self-Determination Theory, the basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and social relatedness are considered essential for students' emotional well-being. However, little empirical evidence addresses how the daily satisfaction and frustration of these needs each relate to emotional well-being in primary school children's everyday classroom experiences. This study examined how daily need satisfaction and frustration relate to day-to-day variability in students' emotional well-being at school. To this end, we conducted an intensive longitudinal study with 322 children in grades 3 and 4 at primary schools in Germany (Mage = 8.58; SDage = 0.73). Over 15 consecutive school days, students made daily reports on their need satisfaction and frustration, as well as on their positive and negative affect at the end of lessons with their class teacher. Hierarchical linear models showed that each need satisfaction was positively related to positive affect and negatively associated with negative affect at the within-person level. Each need's frustration was positively related to negative affect at the within-person level. However, only autonomy and relatedness frustration with peers and teachers were negatively related to positive affect, while competence frustration was not. At the between-person level, only autonomy and peer relatedness were significantly associated with affect throughout the analyses. Overall, variation in emotional well-being was explained by stable differences between students, but also by day-to-day fluctuations in individual experiences. These findings point to the dynamic nature of emotional well-being at school, emphasizing that within-person variability in daily need experiences accounts for variance that between-person approaches may overlook.

TI Which Teachers Adopt AI in Teaching? An Interpretable Machine Learning
   Analysis of East Asian Data from TALIS 2024
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE TALIS 2024; Artificial Intelligence; LASSO; Machine Learning
ID TECHNOLOGY ACCEPTANCE; USER ACCEPTANCE; ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE;
   EDUCATION; SCHOOL; MODEL; RESOURCES
AB Against the backdrop of generative AI reshaping the global education ecosystem, identifying predictors of teachers' artificial intelligence (AI) adoption has become an important issue. Most existing studies focus on single variables or traditional acceptance models, this study adopts a broader perspective, aiming to simultaneously examine multiple potential predictors. Guided by socio-ecological theory, this study employs machine learning methods (LASSO and AutoML) to predict and analyze factors associated with teachers' AI adoption across 25 factors at the individual, microsystem, and mesosystem levels in four East Asian economies (Singapore, Shanghai (China), Korea, and Japan). Results indicate that, in the overall East Asian sample, teaching self-efficacy, age, and perceived risk were the top three predictors; higher teaching self-efficacy was generally associated with a greater likelihood of teachers adopting AI, whereas higher age categories and perceived risk were associated with a relatively lower likelihood. These findings suggest that teachers' AI adoption can be advanced by strengthening teaching self-efficacy at the individual level through practice-oriented training to strengthen teachers' confidence; at the microsystem level, leveraging teacher professional collaboration to promote experience sharing and provide practical support through professional learning communities, peer modeling, and collaborative case development; and at the mesosystem level, further translating institutional support into accessible resources and technical support for teachers. Additionally, different economies can provide differentiated support tailored to teachers' age and experience.

TI Simulated Operations: Enhancing Environmental Familiarity and Confidence
   for Medical Students

DT Article
DE environmental familiarization; psychological safety; simulation;
   surgical education; transition to clinically based learning
ID THEATER; EXPERIENCES; EDUCATION
AB OBJECTIVE: Entering the surgical environment for the first time can be extremely daunting for medical students. Unfamiliarity with the layout and staff of operating rooms can be overwhelming and impact on a student's ability to learn in that environment. Our aim was to develop a teaching session to provide students with environmental familiarity prior to them attending an operating theatre. DESIGN: This study made use of high-fidelity mannequins, members of theatre staff and designing the simulation space to mirror that of an operating room. RESULTS: Students were more confident at scrubbing in after the session (M = 8.06, SD = 1.39) than before (M = 5.50, SD=1.41) p < 0.0001. They were more confident on the surgical safety checkpoints after the simulation (M = 7.56, SD = 1.71) pre-session (M = 2.81, SD = 1.47) p <0.0001. Students were more confident in the roles of the different healthcare professionals, p < 0.0001 (M = 8.56, SD = 0.89) (Pre-session M = 4.81, SD = 2.10).Students felt more comfortable being in a theatre environment after the session (M = 7.44, SD = 1.93) than before the session (M = 4.56, SD = 2.19) p <0.005. CONCLUSION: Simulation is often used in medical education to teach new aspects of medicine and surgery and allow learners to apply their clinical knowledge in a safe environment. This study shows that simulation improves student confidence while also providing environmental familiarity. Simulation is uniquely placed to provide Environmental familiarity, which enables students to focus on learning by reducing anxiety. Providing a teaching session, such as this, early in a medical student's journey lays valuable groundwork for their future learning opportunities.

ID AWARENESS; LITERACY
AB This study examines future teachers' normative ideas about linguistic heterogeneity in the classroom as expressed in their conversations about students. It uses membership categorization analysis (MCA), ethnomethodological conversation analysis (EMCA), and Goodwin's concept of "professional vision" to analyze videotaped conversations between small groups of student teachers about written, ethnographically inspired classroom observations. TI Immersive virtual reality vs. traditional instruction for short-term
   learning and follow-up outcomes in the Bobath concept: a randomized
   controlled trial
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Virtual reality; Physiotherapy; Education; Clinical skills; Bobath
   Concept
ID TEACHING PHYSIOTHERAPY; REHABILITATION; 360-DEGREES; SKILLS
AB Background Although virtual reality has increasingly been incorporated into health professions education, its effectiveness for teaching structured neurorehabilitation frameworks within physiotherapy remains insufficiently explored. Purpose: This study aimed to compare immersive virtual reality-based instruction with traditional education by evaluating theoretical knowledge and practical skills at short-term (2 days) and follow-up (2 weeks) assessments following Bobath concept instruction among physiotherapy students. Methods: In this assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial, 20 third-year physiotherapy students (mean age: 21.3 +/- 1.1 years) were randomly assigned to immersive virtual reality-based instruction or traditional instruction. Both groups received standardized 45-minute training on postural control strategies within the Bobath concept. Learning outcomes were assessed using a multiple-choice theoretical test and a practical examination at 2 days (short-term) and 2 weeks (follow-up) after instruction. Results: Both groups showed a decrease in theoretical scores from the short-term to the follow-up assessment, with no significant between-group difference in change scores (p = 0.817). In contrast, between-group comparison of practical change scores showed a significant difference favoring the virtual reality group (p = 0.017, r = 0.54), with a median difference of + 15 points (95% CI: +5 to + 30). Within-group analyses indicated a significant decline in the traditional instruction group (p = 0.011, r = 0.81), whereas no significant change was observed in the virtual reality group (p = 0.666, r = 0.14). Practical scores increased by approximately 3% in the virtual reality group but decreased by 17% in the traditional instruction group from short-term to follow-up assessment. Conclusion: These findings suggest that immersive virtual reality may support the preservation of practical performance over time in physiotherapy education and may represent a promising instructional approach for teaching complex neurorehabilitation skills.Clinical trial number ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT07270107 (retrospectively registered on December 8, 2025).

TI Attitudes and practices regarding volunteering among medical graduates
   from Romania
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Volunteering; Community health; Medical graduates; Medical school
ID SERVICE
AB Introduction The public health sector is among the most in need of volunteer engagement. The medical student community may participate in many voluntary activities, such as getting involved in public health programs, organizing community health awareness events, delivering administrative support to local health authorities, or engaging in emergencies or in disaster relief operations. Prior studies demonstrated that students' involvement in extracurricular activities such as volunteering and community service projects can lower burnout, develop stress management skills, and promote leadership, teaching, and soft skills like communication, decision-making, social skills, and empathy; also, volunteering positively impacts academic performance. Objectives This study focuses on the assessment of perspectives on the importance of volunteering and factors that influence student participation in voluntary activities as well as on identifying volunteering related behaviors among medical graduating students. The study aims to compare behaviors and attitudes related to involvement in voluntary activities between Romanian and international graduates and analyze these factors throughout time from 2021 to 2023. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted between 2021 and 2023 among 572 medical graduates at the Iuliu Hatieganu University of Medicine and Pharmacy (IHUMP) in Cluj-Napoca, Romania. Results The outcomes demonstrate that most graduates recognized the significance of volunteering. Factors promoting engagement in volunteering activities, as more strongly recognized by students, include valuing personal motivation, appreciating socializing opportunities, and recognizing the desire to offer community assistance. Over 70% of graduates reported volunteering, with significantly higher participation among Romanian graduates (> 80%) compared to international graduates (< 50%). Half of the graduates were interested in participating in voluntary activities after graduation, international graduates being statistically significant more interested in this. Romanian students were more engaged in student exchanges, student organizational and administrative activities, health education and medical support initiatives, as well as volunteering in emergency and medical assistance services, while international students were more inclined towards social and humanitarian volunteering activities. Conclusion This study indicates that enhancing educational and cultural strategies could improve voluntary participation among medical students. This study offers significant insights for mentors, policymakers, and graduates, promoting a collaborative approach to improve medical education and volunteer participation.

TI The effect of topic interest on children's understanding of
   informational texts
SO DISCOURSE PROCESSES
LA English
DT Article
ID READING-COMPREHENSION; EYE-MOVEMENTS; PRIOR KNOWLEDGE; DISCOURSE
   COMPREHENSION; INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; MOTIVATION; MODEL;
   REPRESENTATION; READERS; CONSTRUCTION
AB This study investigated the role of topic interest in comprehension processes and outcomes among elementary school children as a function of reading comprehension skill. Fifth- and sixth-graders (N = 50) were presented with 12 topics and asked to rank the three they found most interesting and the three they found least interesting. Each participant then received a customized set of six texts covering these high- and low-interest topics. Comprehension outcomes were assessed through literal and inferential questions after reading, whereas comprehension processes were assessed through eye-tracking measures collected during reading. Results indicated that topic interest positively impacts comprehension, especially for less-skilled comprehenders: They showed higher accuracy on both question types, longer reading times, and more fixations for high-interest texts, suggesting greater reader engagement. Skilled comprehenders showed higher accuracy on both question types as well, but their eye-movement metrics were not affected by topic interest. These findings highlight the dual role of cognitive ability and motivation, supporting the potential of interest-driven approaches for struggling readers.

TI Engagement and Achievement in Grade 9 Chemical Reactions:Classroom
   Demonstrations and Teacher-Curated AI-Assisted
   RepresentationalPresentations
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE chemistry education; chemical reactions; classroomdemonstrations;
   representational scaffolding; AI-assistedpresentations; scientific
   curiosity; learning motivation; achievement
AB Chemical reactions require learners to coordinate visible phenomena, particle-level explanations, and symbolic equations. This quasi-experimental study compared two teacher-led approaches in a grade 9 chemical reactions unit: classroom demonstrations organized through prediction, observation, and explanation, and teacher-curated AI-assisted presentations that kept macroscopic, particulate, and symbolic representations visible during interpretation. The study examined a representationally scaffolded classroom format rather than an autonomous AI intervention. Supplementary moderated mediation indicated that motivation and curiosity partially explained the association between instructional condition and achievement. The findings suggest that carefully reviewed visual sequences can support chemistry learning when they connect visible events, particle changes, and symbolic equations.

AB Previous studies of STEAM initiatives have often emphasized K-12 contexts; comparatively fewer reports describe their implementation and outcomes in undergraduate STEM education. TI Developmentof Interdisciplinary SynZyme CURE: A Bridgebetween Organic
   Synthesis, Protein Biochemistry, and Drug Discovery
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Interdisciplinary/Multidisciplinary;
   Organic Chemistry; Biochemistry; Inquiry-Based/DiscoveryLearning;
   Problem Solving/Decision Making; Synthesis; CURE; Bioinstrumental;
   Enzyme Inhibition
ID UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH EXPERIENCES
AB The SynZyme Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experience (CURE) was developed to immerse students in an interdisciplinary semester-long project integrating organic synthesis and enzyme biochemistry within the context of early stage drug development. Embedded within a bioinstrumental chemistry course, this CURE also emphasizes the practical use of instrumentation in chemical and biochemical research. Eight undergraduate students synthesized a series of five novel triazole-based compounds and performed detailed molecular characterization to confirm purity and identity. Students then performed ADMET analysis and molecular docking before evaluating the inhibitory activity of the compounds against two target bacterial protein tyrosine phosphatases. Student Assessment of their Learning Gains (SALG), along with the Undergraduate Research Student Self-Assessment (URSSA) instrument, was used to evaluate the gains and experiences of the participants. Data revealed increased confidence in conducting independent research and contributing meaningfully to a research project. It also highlights the potential to promote a deeper understanding, skill development, and research competency among undergraduate students. Overall, the SynZyme CURE demonstrates the effectiveness of course-based research in fostering scientific identity, strengthening interdisciplinary literacy, and preparing undergraduates for real-world research environments.
