TI Living effectively with stuttering: Narratives from voices of past and
   present as client-based evidence
SO JOURNAL OF FLUENCY DISORDERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Stuttering; Recovery; Client-based evidence; Narrative
ID QUALITY-OF-LIFE; ADULTS; SELF; PERCEPTIONS; DISABILITY; PEOPLE; IMPACT
AB This study explored how people who stutter define and experience recovery, aiming to understand what it means to "live effectively with stuttering" and to evaluate personal narratives as client-based evidence. Using narrative inquiry and thematic analysis, 30 publicly available recovery narratives from SLPs who stutter were analyzed. Narratives were drawn from ASHA convention panels (1996-2019) and examined holistically to identify shared themes and insights. Six themes captured the core dimensions of recovery: (1) the emotional and cognitive work of acceptance, (2) claiming voice through disclosure and visibility, (3) the lifelong and nonlinear nature of living with stuttering, (4) challenging dominant fluency-centered paradigms, (5) the healing power of relationships, and (6) therapy as a co-narrative process. Participants emphasized identity, resilience, and communicative agency over fluency. For this population, living effectively with stuttering was defined not by producing fluency, but by empowerment, authenticity, and connection. These narratives support a paradigm shift toward narrative-informed, clientcentered therapy that values lived experience as valid clinical evidence.

TI Effects of anodal transcranial direct current stimulation over the right
   primary motor cortex on a sequential motor finger tapping task in
   developmental stuttering
SO JOURNAL OF FLUENCY DISORDERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Anodal tDCS; Anodal transcranial direct current stimulation;
   Developmental Stuttering; Non-invasive Brain Stimulation; Finger Tapping
   Task; SEQTAP; Non-speech motor learning; Non-speech motor control
ID SPEECH; ADULTS; CHILDREN; IMPLICIT; SINGLE; BRAIN; TDCS; NONSPEECH;
   LANGUAGE; CONNECTIVITY
AB Introduction: This study investigates the impact of anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) on non-speech sequential motor practice in adults who stutter (AWS), compared to nonstuttering controls (ANS). Recent research has explored the effects of tDCS on speech fluency in stuttering. However, its effect on non-speech motor tasks has not yet been studied. Methods: 20 AWS and 30 ANS right-handed participants were randomly assigned to anodal or sham tDCS conditions, performing a sequential finger tapping task. We targeted over the right primary motor cortex, stimulating at 2 mA for 20 min. Sequence duration and reaction time were analyzed . Results: AWS analysis revealed that the anodal condition had significantly slower reaction times in the second half of the task compared to sham. For sequence durations, AWS in the anodal condition had slower overall sequence durations than the sham condition. However, there were no block-by-block differences in sequence duration. When comparing AWS and ANS, no significant differences were observed for sequence duration. However, there were significant differences in reaction time between AWS and ANS, specifically in earlier blocks. Additionally, there was no significant Group & times; Condition interaction. Discussion: The findings suggest that anodal stimulation impeded finger sequencing in AWS, showing overall slower sequence durations and a diminishing effect on reaction times in the second half of the experiment, suggesting anodal tDCS may interact uniquely with the neural mechanisms in stuttering. Future studies should explore the effects of anodal tDCS on non-speech motor tasks to gain a broader understanding of its impact on motor control and motor learning.

TI Exploring Gender, School Environment, and Reporting Barriers in
   Adolescent Cyberbullying: A Cross-Sectional Study from Qatar
SO JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGISTS AND COUNSELLORS IN SCHOOLS
LA English
DT Article
DE adolescents; cyberbullying; reporting; school environment; teacher
   support; peer support
ID SEEK HELP; STUDENT; BEHAVIOR; VICTIM; METAANALYSIS; WILLINGNESS;
   RESISTANCE; SUPPORT; CLIMATE; IMPACT
AB Cyberbullying is a concern among adolescents, with gender, age, and school environment shaping its prevalence. Although they affect victimisation and reporting, little is known about their operation in Qatar, where cultural norms and school structures may influence disclosure. This study examines gender, age, and school environment factors associated with adolescents' cyberbullying victimisation, reporting to school authorities, and barriers to disclosure in Qatar. A sample of 351 adolescents (aged 13-16 years; 49.9% boys) from five public schools completed a survey assessing demographics, school satisfaction, academic pressure, performance, teacher and peer support, cyberbullying experiences, reporting behaviours, and barriers. Data were analysed with two-way ANOVAs, multiple regressions, and Bayesian checks. Boys reported higher victimisation than girls, and early adolescents (13-14 years) experienced and reported more incidents than older peers. Peer support was negatively associated with victimisation, while teacher support and school satisfaction were associated with greater reporting, and peer support with lower reporting. Teacher support was associated with reduced doubts about responsiveness but greater concerns about retaliation and parental restriction, whereas peer support was associated with reduced social-cost concerns. These findings highlight the school environment's role in cyberbullying and reporting. Interventions should strengthen teacher-student trust and address barriers to formal reporting.

SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM

AB This study examines moderators of the communication outcomes for young preverbal children with autism who participated in a randomized control trial of a multicomponent communication intervention. AB The present study tracks the development of conversational implicature (CI) comprehension among adult Chinese L2 learners studying in the UK over an eight-month period and examines the extent to which learners' motivation and L2 interaction predict gains in CI comprehension. TI When AI enters the field: Reconfiguring academic and pedagogical
   practice in teacher education
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION

ID COMMUNITIES; SENSE
AB This study examines how teacher educators negotiate the meaning and implications of artificial intelligence (AI) within professional discourse. TI Against acceleration: Susan sontag, solitude, contemplation and the
   education of creative thinking
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Susan Sontag; Creativity; Solitude; Contemplation; Creative thinking;
   aesthetic education; Attention; Pedagogy; Silence; Performativity
ID HUMANIZING CREATIVITY
AB Creativity in education is frequently rendered visible through outputs, measurable skills, innovation agendas and collaborative problem-solving. This conceptual inquiry argues that such framings, valuable as they are, leave a crucial region of creative life in shadow: the interior conditions of attention, solitude, silence and aesthetic seriousness from which durable creative work arises. Drawing on Susan Sontag's essays, particularly Against Interpretation, On Style and The Aesthetics of Silence, together with her journals, the article develops a pedagogical re-reading of solitude and contemplation as educational conditions rather than as withdrawal or privilege. Sontag is not a theorist of the classroom, yet her insistence that criticism should help audiences see and feel more, rather than translate art into meaning that is paraphrased, offers education a vocabulary for the pre-productive field of perception that precedes any artefact. This reading is placed in conversation with cognitive, sociocultural and classroom-based accounts of creative thinking, and with the temporal critique of acceleration in contemporary schooling. The analysis neither romanticises the solitary genius nor rejects collaboration, assessment or skill; rather, it proposes that creative education requires both sociality and inwardness, both output and preparation. The article closes with a conceptual model and its implications for curriculum, pedagogy and assessment, arguing that protected time for slow perception and aesthetic judgment may be among the most important, and most endangered, conditions for meaningful creative thought.

TI Study on the prediction of prosociality through empathy and gratitude in
   the school context of Cartagena de Indias, Colombia
SO JOURNAL OF NEW APPROACHES IN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Prosociality; Empathy; Gratitude; School; Children and adolescents
AB Several studies show a relationship between empathy, gratitude, and prosocial behaviors. In some cases, these associations have been examined independently across different sociocultural contexts. However, these findings can be further extended to the educational field, especially considering the differences between public and private schools in cities with marked socioeconomic disparities, such as Cartagena de Indias (Colombia). In this regard, the present study aims to examine the relationship between empathy and gratitude as predictors of prosocial behaviors in children attending public and private schools in Cartagena de Indias. Using quantitative, cross-sectional, correlational design, the study assessed 318 children and adolescents (159 from public schools and 159 from private schools), aged 12 to 16 years, through validated measures of empathy, gratitude, and prosocial tendencies. These findings highlight that empathy and gratitude operate as consistent predictors of prosocial behaviors regardless of school context, offering a valuable foundation for developing salutogenic strategies to enhance interpersonal relationships and school coexistence.

TI Temporal Politics and discursive marginalization: neoliberal and
   neocolonial dynamics of English-medium instruction in Pakistan's higher
   education
SO LANGUAGE POLICY
LA English
DT Article
DE English-medium instruction; Temporal politics; Policy discourse
   analysis; Higher education internationalization; Multilingual
   marginalization
AB English-medium instruction (EMI) is widely promoted in non-Anglophone higher education as a route to internationalization, employability, research visibility, and institutional competitiveness. Yet EMI policy research has largely treated time as exposure duration, implementation chronology, or program length rather than as a governing mechanism. This article examines how time is produced, organized, and contested in EMI-related policy reform in Pakistan. Drawing on Torres's concept of temporal regimes and Koselleck's theorization of historical time, it analyzes 17 official Higher Education Commission (HEC) sources through critical qualitative document analysis, combining reflexive thematic analysis with theory-sensitized policy discourse analysis. The study asks how HEC policy documents operationalize time in English-driven internationalization and what neoliberal, neocolonial, and policy-discursive openings they contain for alternative multilingual academic rhythms. Findings show that HEC policy organizes higher education through five temporal mechanisms: calendarized compliance, degree-time corridors, audit-time cycles, transnational synchronization, and temporal stratification. These mechanisms align institutional quality, English-mediated academic legibility, and global competitiveness with deadlines, review cycles, completion rules, rankings, publication timelines, and eligibility thresholds. The analysis further shows that neoliberal temporalities of efficiency, audit, and measurable performance intersect with neocolonial temporalities of external recognition, English-dominant indexing, and globally benchmarked legitimacy. However, the corpus also retains limited openings through flexibility, contextualization, force majeure, local relevance, and alternative delivery provisions. The article argues that EMI-driven internationalization functions as chronopolitical governance and proposes a Temporal Equity in EMI (TE-EMI) framework for designing more time-sensitive, multilingual, and context-responsive higher education policies.

TI Uncovering the Landscape: A Closer Look at Internships in Educational
   Measurement
SO EDUCATIONAL MEASUREMENT-ISSUES AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE foundational competencies; internships; professional development
AB High-impact practices such as internships have long been recognized for enhancing student learning and development. Yet, in educational measurement graduate training, internships remain underexamined. The current three-part study explored the structure, expectations, and implications of graduate-level internships in educational measurement and assessment. Part 1 reviewed 19 internship calls from summer 2024, identifying trends in required skills, application materials, and internship logistics. Part 2 surveyed 22 internship mentors and organizers to better understand specifics pertaining to mentorship, project supervision, the application review/interview process, and internship logistics. Part 3 surveyed 28 current graduate students, examining the value of internships from the intern perspective. Findings suggest that graduate internships in the fields of educational measurement and assessment are valuable and impactful experiences that serve a variety of stakeholders. Study limitations and directions of future research are discussed. Implications are provided for graduate students, graduate programs/faculty, internship organizers/mentors, and the field.

TI Exploratory Evaluation of a Medical Student-Led Health Literacy Program
   Among High School Students
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE adolescent health; community engagement; health equity; health literacy;
   medical education; social determinants of health
ID BEHAVIORS
AB Background: Low health literacy is a barrier to positive health behaviors and outcomes among adolescents, especially in marginalized communities. Sustained, youth-centered interventions for high-risk populations are limited. Contributions: to Practice We implemented and conducted an exploratory evaluation of a year-long, medical student-led program for ninth- and tenth-grade students at two Detroit public high schools. The program demonstrated the feasibility of interactive school-based health literacy programming and identified practical considerations for future implementation. Using anonymous pre and postprogram surveys, we examined group-level response patterns in self-reported confidence on health-related knowledge and abilities (n = 71 baseline; n = 52 follow-up). Survey items reflected domains addressed during program sessions, including healthcare navigation, understanding medical terminology, identifying reliable health information, self-advocacy in healthcare settings, and emergency response skills. Postsurvey responses showed more favorable group-level response patterns across all domains. Implications for School Health Policy, Practice, and Equity: Near-peer, school-based health literacy interventions may represent a practical strategy to support adolescent engagement with healthcare concepts in under-resourced communities. Partnerships between medical schools and secondary schools may provide scalable opportunities for community engagement and health education. Conclusions: This exploratory evaluation supports the potential value of medical student-led health literacy programming as a community-centered model for adolescent health education.

TI Metacomprehension accuracy and regulation in multiple-document reading:
   On the effects of summary writing and external standards
SO METACOGNITION AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Metacomprehension accuracy; Regulation; Generative task; External
   standards; Multiple-document reading
ID IMPROVE; COMPREHENSION; MEMORY; ARGUMENTATION; JUDGMENTS; TEXTS; MODEL
AB Learning from multiple, partially conflicting documents places high demands on both comprehension and metacomprehension. This study examined how two instructional supports-a generative task and external standards-influence metacomprehension accuracy and regulation in multiple-document reading. Building on prior research showing that both supports can independently improve metacomprehension accuracy, we investigated whether combining them yields additive benefits. A total of N = 163 university undergraduates read multiple documents on a historical controversy and were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: generating forum posts and comparing them with external standards, generating forum posts only, or viewing external standards only. Participants' metacomprehension judgments and comprehension measures were assessed for essay performance, historical content knowledge, intertextual conflicts (contradictory information across documents), and source-content links (connections between claims and their sources). Regulation was measured via re-reading intentions. The results showed that generating forum posts alone did not improve metacomprehension accuracy. When external standards were added, learners judged their essay performance more accurately than learners who received external standards only, though no benefits emerged for the other comprehension measures. Similarly, learners in the combined condition demonstrated better regulation of source-content links than the expert-only group, whereas other regulation measures were unaffected. In addition, learners relied more strongly on their self-generated forum posts as cues to their comprehension when no external standards were provided. Together, these findings provide some support for the assumption that combining generative tasks with external standards can strengthen metacomprehension accuracy in complex writing tasks. Generative tasks alone can offer learners useful cues, but external standards appear necessary to foster more accurate metacomprehension and regulation.

AB Despite growing attention to access aesthetics in disability studies, its development for non-verbal communication preferences, particularly for learning-disabled audiences, remains underexplored. This study examines non-verbal access aesthetics in Tactile Talk (2022), a non-disabled participatory performance by Katrien Oosterlinck. TI Teacher growth mindset as a buffer against hukou-based stereotypes in
   relation to student academic resilience
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Growth mindset; Academic resilience; Teacher expectations; Migrant
   students; Hukou system; Educational equity
ID EXPECTATIONS; THREAT
AB To address persistent educational disadvantages among rural-to-urban migrant learners, this study examines whether teacher growth mindset is associated with weaker hukou-related differences in students' academic resilience. Using a multilevel cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 53 teachers and 1,428 primary school students in China. After controlling for prior academic performance and demographic covariates, migrant hukou status was negatively associated with academic resilience. Teacher growth mindset moderated this association: the estimated hukou-related gap was larger when teacher growth mindset was low and much smaller when teacher growth mindset was high. Multilevel moderated mediation analyses further indicated that teacher expectations statistically mediated the association between teacher growth mindset and student academic resilience, with a stronger indirect effect among migrant students than among local students. Although broader institutional reforms remain necessary, the findings suggest that growth-oriented teacher beliefs and high expectations may be associated with more equitable resilience-related experiences at the classroom level.

LA English
DT Article
DE Academic integrity; Generative AI; Optical character recognition;
   Transcription; Assessment policy; AI detection; False positives; Higher
   education; AI assessment scale; Assessment validity
AB Since 2023, universities worldwide have adopted policies restricting or prohibiting the use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in assessed work. In the United Kingdom, the Quality Assurance Agency (QAA) and the Russell Group have issued guidance, and many institutions now operate tiered assessment classification systems. Internationally, An et al. () report that ninety-four per cent of the top fifty US universities (by the ranking used in that study) had issued faculty-facing GenAI guidelines, and Luo () documents broadly similar structures across the world' s top twenty institutions by QS ranking. This paper argues that such policies frequently lack the technical precision necessary to distinguish between genuinely generative AI use-where a machine produces the assessed intellectual content-and non-generative uses of AI-powered tools, such as optical character recognition (OCR), voice-to-text transcription, and handwriting recognition, where the tool performs a clerical format-conversion function on content the student has already authored. The paper is a conceptual and policy analysis; it advances interpretive arguments and a proposed evidential framework, not empirical findings. Its principal limitations are stated in Section 7.4.

However, understanding this relationship among Asian Americans is critical given their unique U.S. history and distinct manifestations of IR, including endorsement of the model minority myth and colonial mentality. The current meta-analysis synthesized cross-sectional associations between IR and mental health among Asian Americans (k = 156; N = 12,480; 39 studies, 2006-2024). Results revealed statistically significant (p < .05) small and small-to-moderate positive correlations between IR and anxiety symptoms (r = .19), depressive symptoms (r = .26), psychological distress (r = .09), suicidal ideation (r = .23), and assorted poor mental health indicators (r = .17). IR was also weakly but significantly negatively associated with life satisfaction (r = -.06). IR was not significantly (p > .05) correlated with varied positive mental health indicators (r = -.06) or somatic distress (r = .03). Using a pooled mental health outcome, moderator analyses revealed stronger associations when IR was group-directed rather than self-directed, manifested as self-hatred or cultural and ethnoracial group inferiority rather than colonial mentality, and was negative rather than positive valenced. Tests of bias suggested that higher quality studies reported stronger associations with varied positive mental health, whereas smaller studies yielded larger effects for depression. Precision-Effect Test-Precision-Effect Estimate with Standard Errors and rank-correlation tests did not suggest bias across outcomes. These findings highlight that IR undermines psychological well-being among Asian Americans and underscore the need for culturally specific research to clarify causal mechanisms and inform clinical interventions.

TI Reframing the reluctant assessor: host-organisation supervisor
   experiences of assessment and feedback in placement-based
   work-integrated learning
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATION AND WORK
LA English
DT Article
DE Work-integrated learning; work-placement; internship; assessment;
   supervisor
ID PERFORMANCE
AB Despite growing attention to work-integrated learning (WIL) as a strategy for enhancing graduate employability and skill development, the perspectives of supervisors at host-organisations - key contributors to student learning - remain underexplored. Utilising a mixed methods design, and drawing on survey responses from 99 host-organisation supervisors across 24 programmes, this study offers rare empirical insights into how host-organisation supervisors experience and enact WIL assessment and feedback practices. Findings indicate that the experiences of these supervisors at the host-organisation were overwhelmingly positive and consistent across disciplines. This finding challenges common portrayals of host-organisation supervisors as reluctant or unprepared assessors. A comparison with analogous student survey responses exposes a statistically significant gap in perceptions, especially in relation to the relevance and transparency of assessment processes. Qualitative data further highlight host-organisation supervisors' strong emphasis on student development and feedback. The study highlights the need to reframe host-organisation supervisors as formative partners and suggests that triadic collaboration between students, universities, and host organisations, underpinned by tools such as negotiated learning plans, may enhance WIL assessment. These findings contribute to a more nuanced understanding of placement-based WIL assessment and offer practical implications for its future design and delivery.

   Model

ID CHEMISTRY
AB This study examined the effects of integrating the 9E Learning Cycle Model (9E LCM) with the Tetrahedral Multiple Representation Learning Model (TMRLM) on learning outcomes in hydrocarbons while also evaluating each model individually. TI Bringing LeadAwareness into the Classroom: A MultigradeCurriculum
   Connecting Environmental Chemistry and Public Health
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE lead poisoning prevention; soil lead contamination; environmental health
   education; childhood lead exposure
ID LEAD-EXPOSURE; PHYTOREMEDIATION
AB Lead poisoning, a legacy of industrial pollution, remains a serious public health risk in major industrial cities. Aging infrastructure, contaminated soil, and persistent environmental inequities contribute to ongoing exposure, disproportionately affecting low-income communities and children. Recognizing the urgent need for prevention strategies, a student-led research team at Marian University developed "The Lead Poisoning Prevention Program," an educational outreach initiative that addresses lead exposure risks through school-based learning. "The Lead Poisoning Prevention Program" is a four-session curriculum for students in Pre-K through eighth grade, incorporating hands-on activities, nutrition education, and environmental science. Instruction focuses on building knowledge and practical prevention strategies, including the TCTT method (Test soil, Cover the soil, Take off shoes, Test child). Other topics include sources of lead, the role of diet in reducing lead absorption, and sustainable remediation using phytoremediation techniques. To extend impact beyond the classroom, the program incorporates interactive activities, bilingual brochures, and take-home soil sampling kits that promote family engagement and community action. Across schools in Indianapolis, the program has consistently demonstrated student engagement, gained educator support, and fostered meaningful family participation. Soil analyses collected during implementation indicate that nearly 23% (n = 101) of student-submitted samples exceed the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) threshold screening level. This article describes the program's scientific background, curriculum design, pedagogy, implementation, and outcomes, highlighting the value of chemistry-based outreach for community health and STEM engagement.

TI Kuwait university students' perspectives on academic support-seeking and
   associated factors: a preliminary convergent mixed-methods study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic support; counselling services; faculty; family; mentorship;
   psychological factors
ID HELP; INTEGRATION
AB Introduction: Academic support-seeking is an essential issue addressed in educational contexts. It highlights the need for students to seek academic support at Kuwait University (KU). Seeking academic support at KU was not explored. Therefore, this study aimed to: (1) describe academic support-seeking engagement and its related constructs; (2) examine adjusted associations between engagement and demographic, academic, attitudinal, support-related, and barrier-related factors; and (3) characterize students' stated reasons for seeking or avoiding academic support. Methods: A convergent mixed-methods cross-sectional study was conducted among Kuwait University students using convenience sampling. Data were collected using a newly developed 39-item Academic Support-Seeking Questionnaire comprising demographic, quantitative, and qualitative sections. Exploratory factor analysis identified four quantitative domains. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, Kruskal-Wallis tests, and multivariable linear regression, while qualitative responses underwent inductive content analysis. Quantitative and qualitative findings were integrated using a joint display. Results: A total of 1,134 Kuwait University students participated. Higher academic support-seeking engagement was associated with greater perceived mentor support and accessibility and more positive support beliefs and future intention, whereas psychosocial and service-related barriers were lower (all p < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, positive support beliefs and future intention (beta = 0.34, p < 0.001) and perceived mentor support and accessibility (beta = 0.27, p < 0.001) were independently associated with greater engagement, whereas psychosocial and service-related barriers were inversely associated (beta = -0.09, p = 0.001). Conclusion: To our knowledge, this is the first mixed-methods study at Kuwait University to comprehensively examine academic support-seeking engagement and its associated factors. Positive support beliefs, perceived mentor support and accessibility, and lower psychosocial and service-related barriers emerged as key correlates of greater engagement. Universities should strengthen the visibility, accessibility, and responsiveness of academic support services while fostering a campus culture that normalizes help-seeking and reduces self-stigma.

SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article

   positive psychology; reliable alliance; undergraduate students
ID ADOLESCENTS
AB Background: While dispositional optimism is a critical psychological resource for university students navigating academic and developmental transitions, its social correlates particularly the specific dimensions of friendship quality in non-Western contexts remain underexplored. Objective: This study investigated the predictive power of distinct friendship quality dimensions on optimism among undergraduate students in a Middle Eastern context, controlling for demographic variables. Methods: A quantitative cross-sectional design was employed with a sample of 450 undergraduate students (63.3% female) from Jadara University, Jordan. TI A multicomponent model of faculty innovative activity in the context of
   career stages
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational innovation; higher education; inclusive education;
   innovation activity of teachers; institutional support; professional
   development; regression analysis
ID TEACHERS
AB Introduction: The development of university teachers' innovative activity is one of the key prerequisites for the digital transformation, quality enhancement, and sustainable development of contemporary higher education. Despite the substantial body of research on innovative behavior, innovation competencies, and innovative teaching practices, the mechanisms underlying the interaction of motivational-value, cognitive, behavioral, institutional-resource, and inclusive components of innovative activity remain insufficiently understood. Little attention has also been paid to how the roles of these components evolve across different stages of teachers' professional careers. The aim of this study is to develop and empirically validate a multi-component model of university teachers' innovative activity and to identify changes in the structure of relationships among its components depending on teaching experience. Methods: The study was based on a questionnaire survey of 55 university teachers in science and engineering disciplines from Kazakhstan. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and multiple regression analysis with verification of the underlying statistical assumptions. The reliability of the developed questionnaire was assessed using Cronbach's alpha, demonstrating a high level of internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.85). Results: The regression analysis revealed that the inclusive component (beta = 0.440, p < 0.001) and the institutional-resource component (beta = 0.404, p = 0.013) were the most robust predictors of innovative activity. The results also demonstrated that the structure of significant predictors changes across different stages of teachers' professional development. Discussion and conclusion: The proposed model conceptualizes innovative activity not as a set of isolated competencies or manifestations of innovative behavior, but as an integrative and dynamic system of interrelated components whose structure evolves throughout teachers' professional development. The findings suggest that professional experience is associated not with a linear increase in innovative activity, but with qualitative changes in the relationships among its components. The findings may be applied to the design of professional development programmes and institutional strategies aimed at fostering innovative activity among university teachers.

AB Importance: Neurodivergent students are at increased risk during disasters, yet school personnel often lack training to support them effectively. AB Scientific problem: Although Work-Integrated Learning (WIL) is widely recognised for enhancing graduate employability, limited empirical evidence exists on students' perceptions of WIL and the factors influencing its effectiveness within South African Universities of Technology. Aim: This study examined postgraduate students' perceptions of WIL as a skills acquisition programme by describing perceived WIL outcomes, identifying contextual factors associated with favourable WIL experiences and perceived job readiness, and documenting challenges affecting implementation. Method: A quantitative, descriptive-correlational design was adopted within a post-positivist paradigm and informed by Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory, Human Capital Theory, and Social Learning Theory. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire from 182 postgraduate students who had completed compulsory WIL placements at Durban University of Technology. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, selected Pearson correlations, and inductive thematic analysis were employed. Results: Postgraduate students reported favourable perceptions of WIL. Item-level results showed positive perceptions of practical skills development (item means 4.15-4.27), professional confidence (4.24-4.30), and communication and interpersonal skills (4.20-4.33). Programme structure, mentorship quality, workplace environment, and institutional support were positively associated with perceived WIL effectiveness and perceived job readiness (all p < .001). Thematic analysis identified workplace adaptation, financial and transport constraints, communication difficulties, workload pressures, limited coordination, task misalignment, technology barriers, and placement-related concerns. Conclusion: The findings suggest that postgraduate students generally view WIL as educationally valuable and relevant to their perceived workplace preparation. Strengthening programme design, supportive workplace learning environments, mentorship, institutional coordination, and equitable financial support may enhance the quality of WIL. Because overlapping questionnaire content precluded treating WIL effectiveness and perceived job readiness as fully distinct inferential outcomes, the findings are interpreted primarily as descriptive and contextual associations. Future research: Future studies should validate these findings across multiple higher education institutions using longitudinal and mixed-methods approaches.

   transferable curriculum framework using pandemic contexts

DT Article

ID SOCIOSCIENTIFIC ISSUES; SCIENCE-EDUCATION
AB This manuscript presents a conceptual, design-based curriculum framework for integrating socio-scientific issues (SSI) into undergraduate cell biology instruction. TI From self-regulated to self-determined learning: identifying the
   heutagogical gap and designing GenAI scaffolds in asynchronous higher
   education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE asynchronous learning; GenAI; heutagogy; pedagogical scaffolding;
   self-determined learning; self-regulated learning; teacher education
AB Introduction Asynchronous online courses require substantial learner independence, yet structural flexibility does not necessarily lead to self-determined learning. This study examines the transition from self-regulated learning (SRL) to self-determined learning and explores how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may scaffold heutagogical development.Methods We conducted a secondary qualitative analysis of 304 SRL-coded meaning units from 75 preservice teachers enrolled in an asynchronous course. The data were coded using a 0-3 heutagogical-gap scale. The resulting patterns were then translated into a GenAI prompt repository, presented as an empirically grounded design output rather than a tested intervention.Results The heutagogical gap was defined as the developmental space between learners' capacity to regulate learning within a predefined structure and their capacity to define learning goals, pathways, products, and evaluative criteria more independently. Overall, 86.8% of meaning units reflected some level of gap, while 37.5% showed substantive or critical gaps. Patterns included dependence on external feedback, limited knowledge transformation, help-seeking characterized by isolation or dependence, and coping without explicit emotional regulation. The findings informed an AI-Enhanced Heutagogical Cycle (AIHC) aligning SRL dimensions, heutagogical transitions, and pedagogically constrained GenAI roles.Discussion The study distinguishes effective regulation within a given structure from self-determined learning. It proposes GenAI as a differentiated scaffold for expanding learner agency rather than substituting for learners' cognitive effort, judgment, and responsibility. The framework and prompt repository require validation in future intervention studies.

TI Examining AI-assisted writing revision through assignment design and
   implementation in an undergraduate course
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI (artificial intelligence); higher education; pedagogy; reflection;
   writing revision
ID CHALLENGES; FEEDBACK; TEACHER
AB Introduction Although artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, poses challenges related to potential misuse in education, it also offers an opportunity to improve students' writing and revision skills when thoughtfully integrated as a pedagogical resource. To investigate AI use in undergraduate education and understand students' perceptions of its impact on their writing, we designed and implemented two consecutive writing assignments that incorporated AI-assisted revisions in a large-enrollment general education (GE) course.Methods For each assignment, students were required to compose an initial draft without AI assistance to promote critical thinking and writing proficiency. They then used AI tools of their choice to revise the drafts with the goal of improving grammar, clarity, and coherence. Assignment grading was based mainly on the initial drafts, and feedback was provided by the instructor and the teaching assistant to support students' learning. In addition, students completed reflection questions about their experiences with AI, particularly its effects on their writing process and outcomes.Results These reflections provided insights into how students selected and engaged with AI tools during the revision process as well as how they perceived the role of AI in assisting their writing development.Discussion By preserving traditional writing practices and strategically integrating AI-assisted revisions, this study can potentially inform pedagogical strategies that enhance student writing experience while maintaining academic integrity.

TI Teacher stress and support gaps: a mixed methods study of the resource
   paradox in K-12 schools
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE appraisals; demands; mixed methods; resources; teacher stress
ID DEMANDS
AB Introduction Teacher stress and wellbeing are influenced by how educators perceive and experience workplace demands and available resources. This study examined how teachers' appraisals of workplace demands and resources contribute to stress vulnerability and educator wellbeing.Methods Using a mixed methods concurrent nested design, the study triangulated quantitative data from the Classroom Appraisal of Resources and Demands (CARD) survey with qualitative reflections on teachers' lived experiences in schools. Participants included 131 public school teachers. Qualitative responses describing workplace demands and resources were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. Teachers were categorized by the CARD measure as either higher risk-for-stress (Demanded) or lower risk-for-stress (Resourced).Results Teachers classified as Demanded reported more workplace demands and less access to resources than Resourced teachers. Specifically, Demanded teachers more frequently described instructional demands, demand overload, and missing resources. However, when discussing available resources, both Demanded and Resourced teachers emphasized the insufficiency or absence of meaningful support. Findings revealed a resource paradox in which resources that are technically available may be perceived as inadequate or experienced as additional demands.Discussion The findings suggest a mismatch between available resources and teacher-identified needs, highlighting the importance of considering teacher perceptions when addressing workplace stress. Implications for educational leadership include prioritizing workload management, aligning resources with teacher-appraised demands, and incorporating teacher voice into decisions regarding resource allocation and support systems.

TI Climate change education in Thailand: from curriculum presence to system
   coherence and climate-smart schools
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE climate change education; climate-smart schools; green skills; school
   resilience; system coherence; teacher professional development;
   Thailand; TVET
AB Thailand faces a climate change education (CCE) challenge that is simultaneously pedagogical and operational: while national policy documents and curriculum frameworks establish meaningful entry points for climate learning, empirical evidence shows that implementation is fragmented, teacher preparation is inadequate, and climate hazards are already disrupting schooling at scale. A 2025 national survey of 329 schools found that every school had experienced at least one extreme weather event in the previous three years, that over 80 percent of teachers had never received formal training on CCE or climate preparedness, and that Thailand rose sharply to 17th place in the Global Climate Risk Index 2026. Drawing on a synthesis of policy documents, official survey data, and peer-reviewed implementation studies identified through a systematic, criteria-based search of the empirical literature, this article situates the Thai evidence within recent research on CCE in East and Southeast Asia and argues that the country's central challenge is not policy absence but system coherence. The Basic Education Core Curriculum, the National Education Plan 2017-2036, and emerging green skills frameworks in technical and vocational education and training (TVET) each provide institutional entry points for climate learning, yet these elements are not yet aligned across curriculum progression, teacher development, assessment, and school resilience planning. Analysis of implementation research across basic education, TVET, and higher education reveals that teacher training is the strongest predictor of effective CCE, that locally grounded and place-based pedagogies produce measurable gains in preparedness and knowledge, and that the rural-urban resource divide systematically disadvantages the schools most exposed to climate risk. These patterns mirror findings across the region, where legislative density and curricular presence coexist with shallow enactment, persistent student misconceptions, and a knowledge-behavior gap. The article proposes a five-priority systems agenda: establishing an explicit national climate learning progression; scaling professional development beyond science teachers; aligning assessment and quality assurance with climate competencies and school resilience; defining whole-school climate-smart standards; and targeting equity-based resource allocation toward climate-vulnerable and underserved schools.

TI Exploring approaches to measuring student engagement across
   computer-supported collaborative learning contexts
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE cognitive theories; computer-supported collaborative learning; embodied

ID FRAMEWORK; SCIENCE; SCHOOL
AB Introduction Supporting meaningful student engagement is an important goal of educators and educational researchers. However, there are many variations in definitions and measures of engagement, making it challenging to recognize and design for deep engagement. To address this challenge, the purpose of this work is to interrogate the ways that different theoretical and methodological choices impact how we describe student engagement.Methodology We applied two student engagement coding schemes to classroom video from two computer- supported collaborative learning (CSCL) contexts. We compare how each coding scheme made different types of engagement more or less visible and explore potential decision points and synergies.Findings The coding schemes differed in many ways, including their theoretical grounding, level of analysis, and inclusion of various dimensions of engagement. There are also substantial challenges that researchers may encounter when using engagement coding schemes outside of the contexts in which they were developed, including achieving reliability and the relevance of indicators of engagement to the novel context.Discussion This study contributes to our understanding of how to make sense of engagement in classroom video and the synergies between different coding choices and theoretical perspectives.

AB This study descriptively examines the implementation of a student-centered Project-Based Learning (PBL) approach in fluid mechanics and heat transfer laboratory courses at major university located in south India during the fall and winter semesters of the 2024-25 academic year. PBL promotes active participation, experiential learning, and real-world problem solving, aiming to strengthen conceptual understanding, critical thinking and practical skills beyond traditional lectures. Structured survey feedback was collected from 47 students from the fluid mechanics course and 38 students from heat transfer course and analyzed to assess learning outcomes. Students responses were strongly positive: 91.5% fluid mechanics and 97.4% heat transfer students values the project-based assignments, while classroom support was recognized by 100% and 94.7% respectively. All fluid mechanics students and 97.4% of heat transfer students reported an improved understanding of core concepts, and confidence increased to 95.7% and 100% of them, respectively. The main challenges were material collection (40.4% and 52.6%); team management caused minimal difficulty. Overall, the findings show that PBL significantly enhances comprehension, self-directed learning, teamwork and practical problem solving, highlighting its importance in modern engineering education.

SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE challenges; in-service training; mechanical technology; practical
   skills; teaching practice; technology education
AB In this empirical paper, we explore the challenges experienced by 4th year Mechanical Technology student teachers during teaching practice. Teacher training and development in South Africa is geared towards replenishing the aging and retiring teachers, replacing those lost through natural causes and keeping the teaching profession sustainable. Prospective teachers are inducted into the teaching profession through a programme of study at an institution of higher learning. Student teachers are exposed to Work-Integrated Learning (WIL) whereby they are deployed to schools to observe their mentors teaching for a specific period. Additionally, the student teachers have the chance to prepare lessons and instruct under the guidance of a mentor teacher. The purpose of this article was to identify the challenges that Mechanical Technology (MT) student teachers faced during WIL, also referred to as Teaching Practice (TP). The study included twenty (20) MT student teachers from a university of technology. The study used a qualitative case study design, and focus groups and questionnaires were used to survey participants. The qualitative data was analyzed and presented using Thematic Content Analysis. The findings demonstrated that a lack of teaching/learning media and resources, workshop overcrowding, practical skills content knowledge gaps, and workshop equipment were typical issues faced by the student instructors. We recommend the review of the nature of the Technology Teacher training programme from being a semester programme to a year programme, the training of Technology teachers to be in sync with industry and for the provision of adequate teaching/learning resources such as models, charts and access to electronic teaching/learning media.

AB Introduction AI adoption is growing rapidly across Chinese higher education, yet few studies explore local university stakeholders' perceptions of domestic generative AI (DeepSeek) for student administrative work. TI ChatGPT Use and Abuse: A 3 Year Look at Undergraduate Perceptions and
   Usage in the Classroom
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; AI; academic integrity; cheating behavior;
   ChatGPT
AB The release of ChatGPT, a generative artificial intelligence (AI) model, in November of 2022 marked a pivotal transition in how students use technology to learn. The ability of these models to process natural language inquiries and produce cogent, highly tailored answers has sparked serious concern among educators regarding its implications for academic integrity and the future of education. The current research surveyed (n = 845) college students in a cross-sectional design administered over the course of seven semesters and focused on students' use of ChatGPT in the classroom and their views on the appropriateness of these actions. Results indicated that students' awareness of ChatGPT rose rapidly following its release (Spring 2023: 58.5%; subsequent semesters: 81.8% to 100%). Cheating behavior (e.g., asking ChatGPT to write a final draft of a paper) increased over the course of data collection (r = 0.24, p < 0.001), with 33.9% of students reporting using the software sometimes to always to help with class assignments and 12.7% reporting using it to write essays/papers or parts of essays/papers due for class. The discussion focuses on key trends regarding student cheating behavior using ChatGPT over time as well as possible explanations for the changes in student usage.

AB In preservice chemistry teacher training courses at teacher education institutions worldwide, there exist common challenges such as misalignment between course content and secondary school curriculum standards, inflexible instructional models, and inadequate practical competencies. TI Teachers' Uses and Perceptions of Generative AI in North
   Rhine-Westphalia, Germany: A DigCompEdu-Informed Analysis
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative artificial intelligence; teacher digital competence;
   DigCompEdu; teacher perceptions; secondary education; North
   Rhine-Westphalia; teacher professional development
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE
AB The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence has moved educational debate beyond access to new tools, placing teacher work, pedagogical mediation, assessment, and digital competence under renewed pressure. This article examines teachers' perceptions, declared uses, and forms of engagement with generative AI in Gymnasien (academic-track secondary schools) and Gesamtschulen (comprehensive secondary schools) in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. The study is based on an anonymous and voluntary online questionnaire circulated through school leaderships. The operational database comprised 204 records, while the main analysis was based on 156 completed questionnaires. Closed-item responses were examined through descriptive statistics and interpreted through DigCompEdu and its AI-related supplement. The findings indicate an asymmetrical incorporation of generative AI across teachers' work. Its presence is stronger in preparation, organisation, professional reflection, and risk awareness than in direct classroom mediation, process-oriented assessment, and institutionally supported student use. The strongest contrasts concern perceived student overreliance on AI-generated answers, the need to adapt assessment practices, limited school-level guidance, and weak use of AI-supported process monitoring. Rather than interpreting this imbalance as a simple delay in adoption, the article argues that teacher competence in relation to generative AI is produced through the interaction between professional judgement, pedagogical purposes, and institutional conditions. It therefore cannot be reduced to an individual technical attribute.

TI A Knowledge-Scenario-Learner Framework for Target-Oriented Adaptive
   Sequencing: A Simulation-Based Proof-of-Concept Study
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE adaptive learning; target-oriented sequencing; prerequisite-aware
   sequencing; learner modeling; educational technology
ID SPACES
AB Adaptive learning systems need to sequence learning activities according to individual progress while respecting the prerequisite structure of the learning domain. This study proposes the Triadic Educational Knowledge Space (TEKS) framework for target-oriented adaptive sequencing in structured domains. TEKS integrates a prerequisite graph, a task-specific target set, and a recursively updated predictive distribution over prerequisite-consistent latent knowledge states. At each decision step, candidate items are evaluated using their predictive one-step acquisition probability, adjusted by graph-based target relevance. A simulation-based proof-of-concept study evaluated TEKS on an eight-node symmetric branching graph with two isomorphic target conditions, a six-node asymmetric converging graph, and a six-node linear prerequisite chain. Each condition involved 200 virtual learners, 90 interaction steps, and 30 independent repetitions. TEKS was compared with Prerequisite-Weighted Mastery Gap (PW-MG), a deterministic static schedule, and random selection under matched simulation conditions. In the branching structures, TEKS yielded higher final target mastery, mean target mastery over time, and final scope mastery than all three comparison strategies. In the linear prerequisite chain, TEKS and PW-MG showed similar target-level outcomes, whereas TEKS retained higher final scope mastery. Within the examined conditions, the difference between TEKS and PW-MG was most evident when multiple prerequisite-related candidates competed for selection. These results provide controlled proof-of-concept evidence for target-adjusted one-step acquisition scoring. Further evaluation is needed on larger and more varied prerequisite structures, under broader forms of model misspecification, and with authentic learner interaction data.

TI Evaluating Competency Transfer from Factory I/O to Real PLC Systems in
   Industry 4.0 Engineering Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English

AB The growing demand for engineers with practical competencies in industrial automation requires educational approaches that effectively integrate theoretical knowledge with hands-on experience. This study proposes and evaluates a hybrid virtual-physical learning framework for programmable logic controller (PLC) education by combining Factory I/O simulation with deployment on a physical PLC laboratory system. TI The Role of Agility in Shaping Perceived Service Quality in Higher
   Education Institutions: A Student Perspective
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE agility; higher education institution; perceived service quality;
   HEdPERF; students
ID SOCIAL-EXCHANGE THEORY; HEDPERF; SATISFACTION; PERCEPTION
AB This research investigated the relationship between agility and educational service quality in higher education. The prior literature has mainly studied such relations in production organizations, while service organizations, especially higher education organizations, have been examined less often. We extend prior knowledge by developing and analyzing a comprehensive model that explains how key internal and external organizational factors affect overall agility and, in turn, how overall agility influences perceived educational service quality in higher education institutions. The study draws on management, education, and quality theories and analyzes responses from final-year students in business and management studies. The results show that the main agility factors-namely, market forces, internal practices and processes, and human resource management-significantly affect the agility of higher education institutions. The study's findings also confirm that the agility of higher education institutions significantly affects the dimensions of Higher Education PERFormance (HEdPERF), the chosen model for assessing the quality of educational services. Considering the importance of agility in achieving objectives in an era of uncertainty and crises, we propose a model that may help improve the current higher education system by enhancing service provision to students and other stakeholders.

TI Hybrid Education Management and Ecological Sustainability in

LA English
DT Article
DE educational management; hybrid education; postgraduate psychopedagogical

ID USER ACCEPTANCE; TECHNOLOGY
AB This exploratory descriptive-correlational study analyses the perceptions of 257 adult students (doctoral, master's, and teachers) at DPPD, USV Iasi, during the 2025-2026 academic year regarding hybrid education, teaching quality, and environmental sustainability. Using a structured Likert-scale questionnaire, the analysis indicates good-to-excellent internal consistency, with Cronbach's alpha values ranging between 0.886 and 0.901, and a high overall global average score of 4.64. The model appears well suited to postgraduate programmes addressed to employed adults, although the ecological benefits should be read as partial and do not displace perceived teaching quality as the central factor.

TI Examining Equitable, Student-Centered STEM Undergraduate Instruction
   Across Three U.S. Institutions
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE STEM education; equity; student-centered learning; inclusion; belonging;
   antiracist; curriculum; instruction; classroom assessment; classroom
   environment
ID DESIGN-BASED RESEARCH; UNDERREPRESENTED STUDENTS; AFRICAN-AMERICAN;
   HIGHER-EDUCATION; PEER FEEDBACK; SCIENCE; PERCEPTIONS; ENGAGEMENT;
   EXPECTATIONS; ACHIEVEMENT
AB Student- and equity-centered instructional practices benefit student learning, motivation, and belonging; however, STEM higher education instructors may not be using them. In this concurrent mixed-methods descriptive study, we examined how STEM instructors (N = 21) across three U.S. higher education institutions understood and enacted student-centered and equitable instruction, and how students from their classrooms (N = 365) experienced learning-and the differences between students' and instructors' perceptions. Our qualitative analysis uncovered the instructional practices that students perceived instructors used the most, benefited their learning, and increased their belonging in the course/field. Moreover, we found that instructors tended to underestimate their students' experiences of student-centered and equitable practices. However, we found that aspects of students' social identities (e.g., gender) and the proportion of students who were male or White may have influenced how students experienced instructional strategies. We discuss how information generated from this study can be used to improve undergraduate STEM education.

TI Developing an Ethnoscience-Oriented Electrochemistry Worksheet Based on
   the Indigenous Practice of Metal Container Electroplating Used in
   Balinese Traditional Ceremonies
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE culturally relevant pedagogy; indigenous knowledge; ethnoscience;
   electrochemistry worksheet; chemistry learning; electrochemistry;
   Balinese traditional ceremonies
ID CONTEXT; CHEMISTRY; EDUCATION; KNOWLEDGE
AB Integrating culturally relevant ethnoscientific contexts into chemistry education has the potential to support more meaningful and culturally responsive learning. This study aimed to develop and evaluate an ethnoscience-oriented electronic worksheet based on the indigenous Balinese practice of electroplating bokor and dulang, metal containers used in traditional Balinese ceremonies. The study adopted an educational design research approach using the ADDIE model. The ethnoscientific reconstruction was conducted through document analysis and literature review to connect indigenous electroplating practices with electrochemical concepts. The developed worksheet was subsequently evaluated through expert validation involving five experts and a limited classroom implementation with 29 secondary school students to examine its educational feasibility. Data were collected using validation sheets and students' response questionnaires and were analyzed using Aiken's V coefficient and descriptive statistics. The expert validation indicated a high level of validity (Aiken's V = 0.86), supporting the scientific, pedagogical, and cultural appropriateness of the developed learning material. The limited classroom implementation showed positive student responses regarding the worksheet's contextual relevance, usability, and learning engagement. The findings provide preliminary evidence that the developed worksheet was appropriate for classroom use for contextualizing electrochemistry through indigenous knowledge and may serve as a practical reference for culturally responsive chemistry education.

ESD must extend beyond the transmission of knowledge; it must shape mindsets, behaviors, and systems. TI Interprofessional Communication in Surgical Residency: Insights for
   Training and System Improvement
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE interprofessional communication; surgical education; residency training;
   teamwork
ID SKILLS
AB OBJECTIVE: To characterize interprofessional communication challenges experienced by general surgery residents and identify modifiable factors to inform targeted training and system improvement. DESIGN: Prospective direct observational study with inductive thematic analysis of resident-reported communication encounters. SETTING: A general surgery residency program at a tertiary referral, level 1 trauma center. PARTICIPANTS: Thirty-one general surgery residents (PGY 1-5) participated. Research assistants observed residents during routine clinical activities over approximately 670 hours and recorded interprofessional communication encounters. RESULTS: A total of 624 encounters were recorded, with 240 (38.5%) rated below the highest score. Four major themes described communication challenges: emotional experience and professional growth (31.7%), internal team communication (31.7%), between-team communication (30.4%), and system and workflow barriers (14.2%). Emotional strain frequently occurred during vulnerable moments in training, including uncertainty and evolving responsibility, often in the presence of attending physicians. Communication challenges were observed both within and between teams, with overlapping issues such as relational strain and communication breakdowns, but with distinct manifestations across contexts. System-level barriers, including unreliable technology and unclear protocols, further contributed to inefficiencies and discomfort. Among the highest-rated encounters (61.5%), protective factors included supportive leadership, learner development, psychologically safe team environments, and effective communication. Notably, positive experiences occurred even in complex situations, suggesting that communication quality is influenced by modifiable interpersonal and system-level factors. CONCLUSIONS: Interprofessional communication challenges are a common and expected component of surgical training, shaped by emotional, relational, and system-level factors. Targeted interventions-including inter-professional communication training, leadership development for senior trainees and faculty, and system-level improvements-may enhance resident experience, team function, and patient care. TI AI-mediated cognitive divergence in built-environment education:
   Evidence from a mixed-methods study
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Cognitive divergence; Generative AI in design education; Process
   visibility; Faculty AI positivity; Mixed-methods
ID ALPHA
AB Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly integrating into design education, yet its effects on student learning processes remain empirically underexplored. This study reports a sequential mixed-methods investigation across a built-environment faculty at a research-intensive university, drawing on 24 faculty interviews, a survey of 32 instructors with regression modelling, and five clustered discussions involving 31 participants. Faculty accounts converge on a pattern in which AI amplifies existing differences in student readiness rather than producing uniform improvements. Consistent with cognitive offloading theory, students with stronger foundations use AI to extend reasoning and accelerate iteration, while those with weaker foundations delegate formative cognitive work to AI, producing coherent outputs without corresponding understanding. This divergence is compounded by a loss of process visibility, as AI-generated outputs no longer reliably indicate how students arrived at their work, and by the erosion of frictional learning stages through which competence is built. Faculty have responded with adaptive strategies including process-oriented assessment redesign and deliberate reintroduction of cognitive constraint, but report no scalable solution. Exploratory quantitative analysis (n = 32) identifies perceived pedagogical relevance rather than seniority or career stage as the primary predictor within the model of faculty AI positivity. A significant negative association between theoretical course orientation and AI positivity suggests that uniform integration strategies risk producing uneven outcomes across course types. Effective AI integration in design education requires differentiated strategies responsive to course epistemology and student preparation level, assessed through process-visible methods rather than output quality alone.

TI Does expanding access to high quality technical education induce
   participation and improve outcomes?
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Career and technical education; Postsecondary outcomes; College;
   Earnings
ID CAREER; EMPLOYMENT
AB Career and Technical Education (CTE) has expanded with the intention to meet a changing economy and broaden pathways to higher education and training. Using longitudinal administrative data from Massachusetts, we generate causal evidence on the impact of high-quality CTE expansion in comprehensive high schools. Leveraging the staggered rollout of these programs, we find that access to a new CTE program induces 5.4 percent of prior non-participants to enroll. On average, while CTE exposure decreases four-year college enrollment, initial earnings one-year post-graduation increase by 8.8 percent among those with in-state employment. Conversely, more collegealigned programs induce a 4.8 percent increase in quarters of employment through age 23 while experiencing a more muted decline in four-year college enrollment and completion.

TI Chemistry Instructors'Interpretations of AssessmentInstrument Data for
   Instructional Action
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE General Chemistry; Assessment; ResponsiveTeaching; Pedagogy; Instruction
ID BELIEFS; INSTRUMENT; KNOWLEDGE; BARRIERS; DESIGN
AB Assessment instruments enable instructors to collect valid and reliable data about students' content knowledge and support data-informed pedagogical decisions. Despite the widespread development of assessment instruments in chemistry education research, instructors' use of these data is often constrained by limited time, interpretive support, and integration into instructional practice. This study investigates how instructors engage with assessment instrument data to interpret student thinking, draw conclusions, and propose instructional actions. Semistructured interviews were conducted during which chemistry instructors interacted with visualizations of their students' responses, including representations of both correct and alternate conceptions. Instructors' conclusions and proposed actions were analyzed through the lens of Data-Driven Inquiry to characterize patterns in how assessment data are interpreted and used. This work identifies common trends and challenges in instructors' sensemaking of assessment instrument data and highlights opportunities for targeted supports. Of note, deficit framing of conclusions from assessment was found to be closely linked to proposal of ambiguous instructional actions, indicating that interpretive stance matters more than the specific conceptual issue identified within assessment data. Future work will focus on designing and evaluating supports that bridge the researcher-practitioner gap by facilitating instructors' integration of research-based assessments and data-informed instructional practices.

TI A Low-Cost BroadbandNanosecond Pump-ProbeTransient Absorption
   Spectrometer for Education and Research
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Graduate Education/Research; Physical
   Chemistry; Chemical Education Research; Laboratory Instruction; Hands-On
   Learning/Manipulatives; Problem Solving/Decision Making; Spectroscopy;
   Lasers; Instrumental Methods; Laboratory Equipment/Apparatus;
   Calibration; Dyes/Pigments; Photochemistry; UV-Vis Spectroscopy
ID ULTRAFAST TRANSIENT ABSORPTION; PHOTOINDUCED ELECTRON-TRANSFER;
   TIME-RESOLVED FLUORESCENCE; ZINC TETRAPHENYLPORPHYRIN; SPECTROSCOPY;
   DYNAMICS; METALLOPORPHYRINS; PHOTOPHYSICS; EXCITATION; STATES
AB Transient absorption spectroscopy offers an effective method to explore excited state dynamics, providing mechanistic insights into fundamental light-induced processes across diverse fields such as organic and inorganic photosystems, biology and medicine, and technological applications like material design and photocatalysis. Commercial transient absorption spectrometers, designed for research laboratories and user facilities, have excellent temporal and spectral capabilities but come at high costs. Alternatively, the affordable teaching kits that introduce advanced molecular photophysics into undergraduate and graduate education probe dynamics at single wavelengths and thus do not capture the full picture of the excited state dynamics. To monitor the overall excited state energy landscape, broad spectral coverage is crucial, revealing spectral shifts and the interplay between different states. We present a low-cost (similar to 20 000 EUR at the time of publication) transient absorption spectrometer that can be built from individual components or as an extension to an educational single wavelength kit. We validate the spectrometer using a well-characterized zinc tetraphenylporphyrin sample, providing high quality time-resolved spectra that track excited state dynamics in the ns to ms time range with a broad spectral coverage of 450-1000 nm. From an educational point of view, the spectrometer offers a platform for introducing lasers, optics, and time-resolved spectroscopy into the curriculum at both the undergraduate and graduate level. The spectrometer can be built as an introduction to basic optics and alignment, providing hands-on experience in instrument design and implementation, or it can be provided as a complete transient absorption instrument for capturing excited state dynamics of a variety of different samples.

TI Investigating causal constructions in academic writing: Integrating
   local grammar with construction grammar
SO JOURNAL OF ENGLISH FOR ACADEMIC PURPOSES
LA English
DT Article
DE Causal construction; EAP; Local grammar; Construction grammar
AB The challenges of English for Academic Purposes (EAP) lie not only in mastering vocabulary and grammatical rules, but also in acquiring discipline-specific patterned language. While causality is a core element of academic reasoning, the recurrent lexico-grammatical patterns expressing causality remain inadequately addressed. This study adopts local grammar and construction grammar approaches to explore causal expressions in academic discourse. By integrating the descriptive granularity of local grammar with the structural systematicity of construction grammar, the research provides a bottom-up method for identifying causal constructions. Using a self-constructed corpus of research articles in applied linguistics, the study systematically identifies 24 local grammar patterns that realize causal functions. These micro-level patterns are then abstracted into five meso-level causal constructions, which together form a hierarchically organized and interconnected constructional network. The findings reveal that causality in academic writing is instantiated through highly conventionalized pattern-function pairings and show how local grammar patterns can provide a data-driven basis for identifying causal constructions. Pedagogically, the resulting inventory supports the development of a more systematic and function-oriented approach to teaching causal language in EAP.

TI Differential visual attention in autism spectrum disorder: A
   meta-analysis of gaze duration across dynamic-static and
   social-nonsocial stimuli
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism spectrum disorder; Eye movement; Visual attention; Meta-analysis
ID INFANT SIBLINGS; SEX-DIFFERENCES; EYE-MOVEMENTS; CHILDREN; PERCEPTION;
   PATTERNS; TODDLERS; GENDER; INTEGRATION; COMPETENCE
AB Background: Current research on visual attention characteristics in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) predominantly focuses on single stimulus dimensions, with inconsistent conclusions regarding attentional modulation mechanisms. Aim: This meta-analysis aimed to quantify gaze duration differences in ASD across orthogonal stimulus dimensions (dynamic-static, social-nonsocial) and evaluate moderating effects of age, sex, and task type. Methods and procedures: In accordance with PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search strategy was adopted. First, 2805 records were identified through database searching; then, title-abstract screening led to the identification of 89 potentially relevant studies and, finally, after full-text screening, 26 studies were included. Outcomes and results: The meta-analysis revealed a complex, stimulus-dependent pattern of visual attention in ASD. For dynamic stimuli, individuals with ASD showed significantly enhanced gaze duration to non-social content (d = 0.75, p = .011) but a non-significant trend toward reduced gaze to social content (d =-0.58, p = .376). For static stimuli, a marked dissociation emerged: severely reduced gaze duration to social stimuli (d =-2.89, p < .001) contrasted with comparable performance on non-social stimuli (d = 0.04, p = .930). Moderator analyses revealed significant effects of age (dynamic: p = .022; static: p = .012), sex (dynamic: p = .049; static: p = .140), and task type (dynamic: p = .033; static: p = .015). Conclusions and Implications: ASD demonstrates stimulus-dependent visual attention patterns characterized by (a) severe differences in processing of static social stimuli, (b) enhanced attention to dynamic non-social stimuli, and (c) preserved performance on static non-social tasks. These patterns are differentially modulated by developmental stage, sex, and task demands. Findings support the dual-pathway processing theory (ventral social network difficulty / dorsal non-social network compensation) and provide empirical foundations for developing developmental-stage-and sex-specific attention interventions.

TI Job demands, resources, and teachers' work engagement: the multiple
   mediating roles of emotional exhaustion and self-efficacy
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Job demands-resources model; Work engagement; Emotional exhaustion;
   Self-efficacy; Teachers
ID ORGANIZATIONAL COMMITMENT; INTERPERSONAL CONFLICT; SCHOOL CONTEXT;
   BURNOUT; SATISFACTION; CONSERVATION; LEADERSHIP; STRESSORS; VARIABLES;
   VALIDITY
AB Based on the Job demands-resources model, this study examined the associations of workload, interpersonal conflict, and perceived organizational support with teachers' work engagement, with emotional exhaustion and self-efficacy adopted as mediators. A cross-sectional correlational design was utilized with a valid sample of 473 Chinese primary and secondary school teachers. Results revealed distinct associations of job demands and resources with teachers' work engagement.
