TI Generative AI as a conversational companion: A design-oriented
   post-draft framework for preserving authorial judgment and creative
   agency in scientific manuscripts
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; Academic writing; Critical thinking; Creative agency;
   Post-draft revision
ID REPORTING QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
AB Generative AI is increasingly used in academic writing, yet little guidance exists on how to integrate it without replacing the author's reasoning or diluting their scholarly voice. Accordingly, the paper is positioned as a design-oriented methodological framework that functions as a metacognitive scaffold by specifying an operational procedure for post-draft AI use rather than as an empirical study or a purely theoretical contribution. In this proposed framework, authors first produce a human-written draft and only then engage generative AI as a diagnostic conversational companion restricted to post-draft auditing of coherence, alignment, and reconstructability. In this revision stage, generative AI is used to perform specific, verifiable actions: checking coherence across sections, auditing alignment between research questions, methods, results, and conclusions, detecting ambiguous or overly abstract formulations, and verifying adherence to reporting conventions. Drawing on Maturana's concept of structural coupling, we argue that this boundary preserves the author's epistemic authority by ensuring that the meaning of the manuscript originates in the author's own distinctions, while AI contributes through perturbations that prompt clarity and refinement rather than generating content. The framework expands current guidelines by moving beyond general ethical prescriptions to define a practical, auditable procedure for post-draft AI use that preserves authorial voice and epistemic control. It offers a replicable workflow that integrates efficiency with transparency, helping researchers use generative AI to strengthen-not substitute-their scholarly reasoning, transforming the role of AI from a content generator into a catalyst for critical thinking and creative precision.

TI Dimensions and temporal stability of medical students' motivation:
   longitudinal evidence from a panel data survey
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Study motivation; Intrinsic motivation; Extrinsic motivation; Medical
   studies; Study
ID PROFESSIONAL IDENTITY FORMATION; SELF-DETERMINATION;
   ACADEMIC-PERFORMANCE; EDUCATION; EMPATHY; CURRICULUM; SELECTION; DECLINE
AB Background Motivation is a key determinant of students' engagement, learning strategies, and professional development in medical education. However, little is known about how different motivational dimensions change within individuals across training. The Hannover Screening of Study Motivation panel survey offers a unique opportunity to map how medical students' motives evolve over time.Methods Using the first five waves of data at Hannover Medical School, Germany (N = 1,218 subjects), we applied confirmatory factor analysis to validate three theoretically grounded dimensions of study motivation: extrinsic, autonomous, and prosocial. Female students display less extrinsic and higher prosocial motivation, compared to males. We find no meaningful associations between any motivational dimension and early academic outcomes.Conclusions The longitudinal patterns of study motivation suggest both pragmatic recalibrations, as students' idealized views of medical practice meet clinical realities, and the subtle influence of hidden curricula that may erode altruistic motives. TI AI-assisted, instructor-supervised grading and feedback in higher
   education: Design and evaluation of an end-to-end pipeline
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Automated grading; Large language models; GPT; Rubric-based assessment;
   AI feedback; Academic integrity
ID AGREEMENT
AB This paper presents the design, deployment and evaluation of a GPT-4o-based grading and feedback pipeline for a Master's-level Information Systems Project Management course, developed following the Design Science Research Methodology. The artefact orchestrates submission collection (Google Forms), rubric-based scoring with rubric-linked qualitative feedback (OpenAI GPT-4o via a Cloud Function) and analytics storage (BigQuery), across six consecutive case-study assignments. The AI grader supplemented rather than replaced instructor grading: official grades remained the instructor's, while AI grades and feedback served as a second-opinion signal and additional formative feedback. The evaluation followed a pre-specified analysis plan combining a quantitative comparison of AI and instructor grades, a voluntary student survey and an automated assessment of feedback quality on the full corpus. Across 362 submissions from 66 students, the AI reproduced the instructor's mark within the pre-specified tolerance of 0.5 points on a five-point scale in 83% of cases, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.31 points and a small systematic bias of-0.16 points (95% CI [-0.19, -0.12]). Chance-corrected agreement, measured by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), was moderate at best: ICC(2,1) = 0.49 (95% CI [0.33,0.61]), spanning the poor-to-moderate range. Among the 112 survey responses (31% response rate), about 80% rated the feedback useful and 77% accurate. The pipeline operated at EUR 0.55 per student per assignment and delivered feedback within 24 h. The findings support using LLMs as scalable assistants for formative assessment, as a supplement to rather than a substitute for instructor evaluation.

AB This study aimed to compare the pedagogical and content quality of AI-generated assessment tasks with those developed by humans in English language teaching, using a sequential-explanatory mixed-methods design. TI Capturing multidimensional engagement within small groups: A multimodal
   perspective
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Multidimensional engagement; Multimodal learning analytics;
   Human-centered analytics; Game-based cscl; Collaborative learning;
   Engagement measurement
ID ONLINE; SCHOOL
AB This study develops and validates a human-centered approach to measuring small-group, multidimensional engagement in a game-based Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) environment. Grounded in sociocultural perspectives, the proposed framework integrates multimodal data sources, including discourse, interaction logs, and linguistic indicators, to assess behavioral, collaborative, and disciplinary engagement through theory-informed human interpretation. Human-annotated engagement ratings serve as ground truth for evaluating whether supervised machine learning models can approximate multimodal interpretive judgments, establishing a pathway toward scalable assessment. Three supervised learning algorithms were compared to examine model performance across engagement dimensions, and multiple regression analysis was conducted to investigate associations between quest-level average engagement and group learning outcomes. Results indicate that average collaborative and disciplinary engagement ratings positively predict group performance, whereas behavioral engagement alone does not significantly relate to learning outcomes. Qualitative analysis of group responses further illustrates these associations. Methodologically and theoretically, the study advances multimodal learning analytics by proposing a generalizable, human-centered workflow that integrates multimodal interpretation with model-assisted scalability, emphasizing the essential role of human interpretation in producing valid and contextually grounded engagement assessments in collaborative learning environments.

TI The longitudinal interplay of mathematics self-concept of abilities,
   intrinsic value, cost, and performance - A random intercept cross-lagged
   panel model
SO CONTEMPORARY EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Motivation; Random intercept cross-lagged panel model; Self-concept of
   abilities; Intrinsic value; Cost
ID MOTIVATION; EXPECTANCY; STUDENTS; ACHIEVEMENT; GENDER; GRADES
AB The Situated Expectancy-Value theory suggests that students' expectancies for success, positive task values, costs and performance are interrelated, yet most empirical evidence reflects stable differences between students rather than motivational dynamics within individual students. Using a random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RICLPM), this study examined both between- and within-person longitudinal relations between self-concept of abilities, intrinsic value, emotional cost, and math performance across six time points among Finnish 10-12-yearolds (N = 584). Between-person results confirmed that self-concept of abilities and intrinsic value were positively related to each other and to math performance, while emotional cost was negatively related to all three. Within-person results showed that increases in intrinsic value predicted subsequent increases in self-concept of abilities and decreases in emotional cost. Self-concept of abilities and emotional cost were reciprocally linked, where a decrease in either predicted an increase in the other at the next time point. No longitudinal cross-lagged withinperson paths emerged between motivational beliefs and math performance, though within-person correlations indicated a concurrent relation between these constructs. In conclusion, intrinsic value appears as a promising intervention target among 10-12-year-olds, as interestsparking math education may strengthen ability beliefs and buffer against negative emotions at the next time point. High emotional cost seems to harm self-concept, highlighting the importance of also addressing negative emotions related to math already from 4th Grade.

TI Pizza Snack Rolls Go Digital: Teaching Real-World Cooking in Virtual
   Reality
SO EDUCATION AND TRAINING IN AUTISM AND DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE virtual reality; technology; intellectual disability; food preparation;
   middle school; single case
ID FOOD-PREPARATION SKILLS; DAILY LIVING SKILLS; SCHOOL-STUDENTS; VIDEO;
   DISABILITIES; PEOPLE; INDIVIDUALS; INSTRUCTION; SYSTEM
AB Virtual reality (VR), especially nonimmersive VR, offers an option to support secondary students with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) in learning life skills, such as food preparation. While an emerging research base exists to support nonimmersive VR in assisting secondary students with IDD in acquiring food preparation skills, the existing literature has paid limited attention to generalization in real-world settings. In this study, researchers employed a multiple-probe across participants' single case design study with three middle school students with IDD to explore how nonimmersive VR and the system of least prompts (SLP) supported their acquisition, maintenance, and generalization of learning to make pizza snack rolls in a microwave. All three students acquired the skill of making pizza snack rolls in a virtual microwave within the nonimmersive VR system (i.e., virtual environment) following receipt of the intervention package involving the nonimmersive VR and the SLP. The students also maintained their skills of making pizza snack rolls in a virtual microwave within the nonimmersive VR system at higher levels than baseline. However, generalization to making real pizza snack rolls in a real microwave was limited.

TI Do soft-skills courses pay for individuals? Evidence from German matched
   data
SO EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN VOCATIONAL EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
DE Soft skills; Training; Wages; Span of control; Leadership; Job
   satisfaction; Monopsony; Event study
ID LABOR-MARKET OUTCOMES; IMPACT; WAGES; PRODUCTIVITY; PERFORMANCE; TRAITS
AB Soft skills are widely promoted as levers for productivity and as enablers for digital and green transitions. Linking soft-skills training courses with German matched employer-employee records for 2010-2020, we examine whether participation in employer-financed non-formal soft-skills training is associated with subsequent labor market outcomes for full-time workers. A staggered event-study design finds no post-training changes in daily wages, span of control, leadership status, or job satisfaction for up to three years. TI From Biobased Materials to Flexible Functional Devices: An
   Interdisciplinary Innovative Experiment Design for Materials Science and
   Engineering Students
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Lignin; Natural rubber; Direct laserwriting; Flexible functional
   devices; Experimentdesign
AB To bridge the gap between materials synthesis and intelligent systems engineering, this article presents an interdisciplinary innovative experiment based on fully biobased flexible functional devices for undergraduate materials science and engineering students. Students prepare a flexible substrate through latex compounding and acid coprecipitation, using interfacial hydrogen bonding between plant-derived lignin and natural rubber latex to suppress lignin self-aggregation. Direct laser writing is then introduced, in which the photothermal effect of a CO2 laser beam converts the insulating lignin in situ into conductive, porous laser-induced graphene (LIG). On this platform, students construct and evaluate five types of functional devices: resistive strain and pressure sensors evaluated using a universal testing machine and digital multimeters; a serpentine temperature sensor that exploits polymer thermal expansion; a capacitive humidity sensor based on a graphene oxide/NaOH dielectric film, characterized across saturated salt solutions using an LCR meter; and an electrothermal Joule heating actuator evaluated using a DC power supply and an infrared thermal camera. Finally, students collect real-time resistance signals from their self-fabricated knee-joint strain sensors and use a deep-learning model for human motion recognition with over 97% accuracy. Implemented across two consecutive semesters with 58 students, this experiment helps students develop a systematic "Materials-Devices-Data-Applications" engineering perspective in green electronics.

TI Rethinking teacher professionalism through the capability approach:
   responding to superdiversity in education
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Capability approach; Teacher professionalism; Superdiversity; Agency;
   Capabilities; Conversion factors
ID SOCIAL-JUSTICE; ACCOUNTABILITY; STANDARDS; DIVERSITY
AB Recognition of increasing student diversity highlights the limitations of standards-based models of teacher professionalism. These frameworks often struggle to accommodate complexity, and risk reducing ethical and relational work to technical compliance and measurable outputs, thereby overlooking crucial qualities like care, autonomy, and situated judgement. This paper proposes the capability approach, initially developed by Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum, as a human-centred and justice-sensitive alternative for redefining teacher professionalism in superdiverse contexts. The capability approach shifts the evaluative focus from prescribed standards and outcomes to the real freedoms and opportunities (capabilities) teachers possess to be and do what they value as professionals. We argue for the normative and practical appeal of a capability-oriented model that would involve: (1) identifying valued professional functionings through participatory processes; (2) evaluating teachers' real capabilities; and (3) understanding the personal, social, and environmental conversion factors affecting whether resources translate into substantive freedoms. This article contributes a conceptual model of capability-oriented teacher professionalism that integrates the capability approach's normative and evaluative dimensions. The model offers a compelling theoretical shift away from universalising, outcomes-based models by centring teacher agency and reframing capability deprivation not as individual failure but as a result of interacting systemic barriers. Adopting this approach calls for policy and leadership to move away from standardisation towards plural, context-sensitive, and agency-enhancing professional trajectories.

TI Embedding Computational Thinking in Engineering and Energy Fundamentals:
   A PBL-Experiential Design Supporting Conceptual Engagement and Skill
   Development
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE computational thinking; design-based research; energy education;
   engineering education; experiential learning; information and
   communication technologies supported learning; problem-based learning
ID KNOWLEDGE
AB Introductory electrical engineering courses frequently emphasise procedural calculation rather than conceptual reasoning and systems-level problem solving. Although computational thinking (CT) has been recognised as relevant for engineering education, its explicit integration within undergraduate engineering practice remains insufficiently explored. This study investigates how CT can be embedded and analysed within an ICT-supported problem-based learning (PBL) environment aligned with Kolb's experiential learning cycle in undergraduate electrical engineering education. A design-based research approach was implemented during a 14-week intervention in electrotechnics and electrical machines courses. Custom-developed simulation tools were integrated into lecture and laboratory activities to support collaborative problem solving, parameter exploration and student-generated engineering problems. Data sources included student-generated artefacts, reflection reports, simulation-based activities and structured classroom observations. Analysis employed predefined coding rubrics aligned with five CT dimensions: abstraction, decomposition, algorithmic thinking, automation and generalisation. Inter-rater agreement exceeded Cohen's kappa > 0.80. Student-generated artefacts increasingly demonstrated explicit circuit decomposition, structured analytical procedures and transfer of reasoning strategies across DC and AC contexts. Simulation tools evolved from being used primarily for answer verification to supporting exploratory modelling and comparative analysis of alternative circuit conditions. Classroom observations indicated increased collaborative reasoning, engagement and autonomous problem formulation during later intervention phases. Descriptive coding frequencies across artefacts and observations provided convergent evidence of increased enactment of CT-related behaviours over time. The study demonstrates how CT can be operationalised within foundational electrical engineering education through the integration of ICT-supported simulation environments, PBL activities and experiential learning structures. The work contributes a replicable instructional and analytical framework linking CT dimensions with observable engineering problem-solving practices and technology-supported learning activities.

TI Affective and cognitive pathways linking connectedness to nature with
   academic burnout/engagement among adolescents: A daily diary analysis
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Connectedness to nature; Academic burnout; Academic engagement; Positive
   affect; Ego depletion
ID SCHOOL BURNOUT; SELF-DISCIPLINE; ENGAGEMENT; RELIABILITY; VALIDATION;
   EMOTIONS; LOVERS; SCALE
AB In the context of Chinese secondary education, learning is a central component of adolescents' daily lives. Academic burnout has been shown to undermine adolescent development, whereas academic engagement facilitates positive growth. However, existing studies have paid limited attention to the role of the natural environment and the underlying mechanisms through which it may influence these two learning-related psychological states in adolescents. Building on this foundation, the present study drew on stress reduction theory and attention restoration theory to investigate how connectedness to nature was associated with daily academic burnout and engagement among adolescents. We adopted a 14-day daily diary design and recruited 215 adolescents (M age = 12.72, SD age = 0.56, 40.5% female) to complete daily measures of connectedness to nature, academic burnout, academic engagement, positive affect, and ego depletion. Multilevel path analyses revealed that higher-than-average daily connectedness was associated with lower-than-average academic burnout and higher-than-average academic engagement, and that these associations were mediated by daily positive affect and daily ego depletion. These findings have important implications for the development of nature-based prevention and intervention strategies in secondary education.

TI Solving Repeating-Pattern Tasks in First Grade: an Eye-Tracking Study of
   Students With and Without Risk of Developing Mathematical Difficulties
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pattern recognition; Eye tracking; Mathematical difficulties;
   First-grade students
ID LEARNING-DIFFICULTIES; STRATEGY USE; CHILDREN; COMPETENCES; KNOWLEDGE
AB First-graders' patterning skills are a robust predictor of later mathematics achievement. This underscores the importance of fostering these skills in primary mathematics education, especially for students at risk of developing mathematical difficulties. Understanding students' errors, pattern-recognition processes, and process accuracy, defined as the success rate associated with specific solving processes, is essential to support students in developing their patterning skills. This study examines differences in error rates, pattern-recognition processes, and process accuracy between first-grade students with and without the risk of developing mathematical difficulties (RMD and nonRMD) using eye-tracking technology. A total of 224 first-grade students completed twelve repeating-pattern tasks while their eye movements were tracked to assess their pattern-recognition processes. The results show that RMD students had significantly higher error rates. Eye-tracking analyses revealed that RMD students were more likely to use pattern-recognition processes focused on a single unit of repeat compared to nonRMD students, while nonRMD students were more likely to use relational processes and validate the unit of repeat, along with lower error rates. Our findings identify validation processes as a potentially relevant focus for instructional support; however, intervention studies are needed to determine whether fostering these processes improves first-graders' conceptual understanding of repeating patterns.

TI Preschoolers' Self-Regulation and Engineering Skills During Play-Based
   Model-Building and Their Correlation to Mathematical Problem-Solving
   Skills
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Early engineering; Mathematical skills; Play-based model-building;
   Problem-solving; Self-regulation
ID EARLY NUMERACY SKILLS; YOUNG-CHILDREN; NUMERICAL SKILLS; 5TH GRADE;
   PERFORMANCE; THINKING; METACOGNITION; KNOWLEDGE; EDUCATION; ABILITY
AB Young children naturally explore the world, making early childhood an ideal time for foundational mathematical thinking and problem-solving abilities. This study investigated correlations between preschoolers' numeracy skills, mathematical problem-solving, engineering skills, and metacognitive and self-regulation skills during play-based LEGO (R) model-building. This study aimed to understand how these skills are correlated in early childhood. Data were obtained from 56 preschoolers (4-5 years old) during individual sessions with each child in their preschool classroom. The Mathematical Capabilities Test assessed number recognition, counting, and mathematical problem-solving skills. The model-building guided play involved building several LEGO (R) models according to pre-defined diagrams that the child was asked to reproduce using LEGO (R) bricks. The children attempted to build the models, starting with the one deemed easy and gradually progressing in difficulty. The interactions with the child-LEGO (R) model and the diagram were video-recorded and analyzed. Findings revealed rich evidence of interactions, engineering, and mathematical skills. Number recognition and counting skills correlated only with regulation of emotions, while mathematical problem-solving skills correlated with engineering skills, metacognitive strategic awareness, and self-regulation. Mathematical problem-solving skills significantly mediated the effect of number recognition on the regulation of cognition and regulation of emotions. However, they did not mediate the effects of counting skills, engineering skills, and metacognitive strategic awareness. These results highlight the interconnected nature of these skills in preschool children, suggesting that promoting mathematical problem-solving experiences in early childhood education may support the development of crucial self-regulation skills, laying the foundation for later learning in mathematics and related domains.

TI Semipinacol Rearrangement Enabled by Radical-Polar Crossover: An
   Undergraduate Laboratory Experiment
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Semipinacol Rearrangement; Allylic Alcohol; Radical-Polar Crossover;
   CobaltCatalysis; HydrogenAtom Transfer; Undergraduate organic chemistry
   experiment; Hands-On Learning.
ID PINACOL REARRANGEMENT; ALLYLIC ALCOHOLS; CHEMISTRY
AB Organic transformations are traditionally classified as either ionic or radical processes. Ionic reactions, which involve charged intermediates such as carbocations, often provide predictable selectivity but typically require specific conditions and show limited functional group tolerance. In contrast, radical reactions proceed under milder, neutral conditions with broader functional group compatibility, though controlling their selectivity can be challenging. The radical-polar crossover (RPC) reaction merges these two mechanistic paradigms through a single-electron transfer event, combining the mild nature of radical chemistry with versatile and highly selective capabilities of ionic chemistry. This hybrid strategy offers an effective pathway for the semipinacol rearrangement of allylic alcohols, avoiding the competing S(N)2 ' displacement and other side reactions commonly encountered under traditional acidic promotion. Despite its synthetic advantages, the RPC-enabled semipinacol rearrangement has not yet been incorporated into undergraduate organic chemistry laboratory instruction. Here, we present a hands-on experiment that demonstrates a cobalt-catalyzed semipinacol rearrangement via metal-hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT) and RPC. Students perform the reaction under an inert atmosphere, monitor its progress by TLC, purify the product by flash column chromatography, and characterize it using H-1 NMR, C-13 NMR and FT-IR spectroscopy. This experiment not only reinforces fundamental laboratory skills but also bridges textbook knowledge of ionic and radical mechanisms with a contemporary, selective synthetic methodology.

TI Conformity and Creativity in Conflict: Cognitive Pluralism and the
   Reimagining of Educational Aims
SO JOURNAL OF CREATIVE BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE cognitive pluralism; creativity and conformity; dual-pathway learning;
   institutional design in education; transformational creativity; wisdom
   in education
ID MODEL; ORGANIZATIONS; INNOVATION
AB Formal education is widely understood as a system for cultivating knowledge and human potential. Yet its structural logic often privileges conformity, standardization, and the efficient reproduction of established knowledge-paradoxically suppressing the very cognitive dispositions that underpin creativity, originality, and flexible thought. This paper revisits the tension between conformity and creativity from a philosophical perspective, examining how institutional designs systematically reward one mode of cognition while marginalizing others. We develop a pluralistic model of learning that distinguishes competence-oriented from creativity-oriented development-associated respectively with structural and Gestalt cognitive orientations-while treating these not as fixed learner types but as complementary tendencies that most learners combine and that a well-designed system should cultivate together. In response to the asymmetry of current systems, we propose a normative theory of cognitive pluralism, which reimagines education not as a mechanism of selection but as an ecosystem of developmental cultivation. Because creativity is not intrinsically benign, we further argue that its cultivation must be tempered by wisdom-directed toward transformative and ethically responsible ends rather than novelty for its own sake. We conclude by outlining implications for curriculum architecture, teacher formation, and institutional reform, and by identifying directions for interdisciplinary research bridging education, philosophy, and cognitive theory.

TI Developing Scientific Creativity in Digital Game Environments: A
   Framework and Tutorial for Application to Game Design
SO JOURNAL OF CREATIVE BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE creativity; game-based learning; STEM education
AB Wallas' model of creativity describes a continuous process by which an individual obtains relevant information (preparation), unconsciously processes said information (incubation), has a flash of insight (illumination), and builds upon an idea (verification or implementation). Per this model, technologies or methodologies looking to develop creative skills in individuals must find a way to nurture this four-step process. Regarding technologies, creativity research has shown that games and simulations meant to provide the tools and context needed to promote creative thinking may have significant developmental value. The goal of this paper is to detail a methodology for the design of games which promote the development of creative skills through the facilitation of all four phases of Wallas' model. The example we will be providing involves creative skills in a general chemistry context, but the design principles at play should apply to other domains as well.

TI Bridging local needs and global standards: a socio-cognitive validation
   study of Japan's EIKEN Pre-2 Plus Test
SO LANGUAGE TESTING IN ASIA
LA English
DT Article
DE Glocalisation; Local language tests; Test validation; Socio-cognitive
   framework; Expert judgement; CEFR alignment
AB The development of locally contextualised English proficiency tests that maintain global standards is a critical challenge in Asian language testing contexts. Japan's EIKEN Foundation exemplifies this through the development of EIKEN Grade Pre-2 Plus, designed to fill the proficiency gap between existing EIKEN Grades 2 and Pre-2 examinations. The EIKEN test suite, with over 4 million annual candidates, spans Grade 5 (A1) to Grade 1 (C1). Research shows progression from Grade Pre-2 to Grade 2 takes 18.8 months on average, which makes goal-setting and sustaining motivation challenging for the main candidate group of junior and senior high school students. The new Grade Pre-2 Plus enables the test suite to function more effectively within the local education system by providing yearly targets throughout secondary studies. This study addresses how locally-developed assessments can achieve contextual appropriateness while ensuring international credibility through rigorous validation. Employing a socio-cognitive framework approach, six international language testing experts conducted a comprehensive review and analysis of extensive test materials from EIKEN Grades 2, Pre-2 Plus, and Pre-2, including sample question booklets across all skills, test specifications, item writer guidelines, candidate performance samples, and rating scales. The analysis focused on features of context validity (i.e. content features), cognitive validity (i.e. cognitive processes), and scoring validity. The expert review confirmed that Grade Pre-2 Plus exam successfully occupies the intended intermediate position, demonstrating appropriate difficulty calibration. Context validity analysis revealed test content appropriately reflects real-world language use for Japanese learners of English while maintaining CEFR alignment. Cognitive validity analysis indicated test items engage intended cognitive processes at target proficiency levels. Scoring validity highlighted robust assessment procedures, statistically corroborated by post-test validation. This study demonstrates how systematic expert reviews can support locally-relevant tests which still strive to meet international standards. The findings suggest comprehensive validation frameworks can provide crucial quality assurance for glocalised test development initiatives in Asia and beyond. The study offers a fully worked example of how a socio-cognitive framework approach can effectively contribute to the validation process.

TI All you had to do was stay? Roles of personal and contextual factors in
   predicting novice teachers' intention to stay
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher retention; Intention to stay; Predictive modeling; Novice
   teacher; Resilience; Team collaboration; Principal support
ID I STAY; RESILIENCE; MODELS; LEAVE
AB Teacher retention remains a critical concern in many education systems, especially for novice teachers facing professional challenges, work stress, and burnout risks. This study examined personal and contextual factors associated with intention to stay among Thai novice teachers using a theory-informed machine learning (TiML) approach. Data were obtained from 1513 novice teachers, with a pilot external validation sample of 71 teachers used to provide preliminary predictive evidence. Eight theoretically derived predictors were examined. Latent class analysis identified two intention-to-stay profiles: Committed Stayers and Uncertain Stayers. These profiles were used as categorical outcomes for classification models, while continuous intention-to-stay scores were modeled through regression. Predictive performance was moderate across elastic net, random forest, and XGBoost models. Resilience, team collaboration, and principal support emerged as relatively consistent predictors. The findings show that TiML can examine retention-related intentions in novice teacher research, but not actual retention or attrition behavior.

TI Surrogate Model-Based Visualization Program for Groundwater Engineering
   Computation
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE dewatering; foundation pit; MODFLOW; surrogate model; visualization
   program
ID DEEP FOUNDATION PIT; LAND SUBSIDENCE; FLOW; OPTIMIZATION; WELL
AB In groundwater engineering practice, dewatering design and groundwater flow analysis are essential for the stability assessment of underground excavations, such as foundation pits and tunnels. Traditional groundwater engineering education often suffers from several limitations, including abstract theoretical concepts, complex modeling procedures, and insufficient experiential learning. To address these challenges, intelligent foundation pit dewatering prediction (IFPDP) simulation software was developed in this study, designed specifically for groundwater engineering education to enhance students' understanding of seepage mechanisms, dewatering processes, and groundwater numerical simulation. The IFPDP employed MODFLOW files generated in GMS and uses FloPy as a Python interface to enable model execution and repeated simulations. In addition, a surrogate model based on the BP neural network was integrated to enhance computational efficiency and supports parameterized teaching. The system was designed to integrate numerical simulation, visualization, and interactive learning with autonomous modeling and case-library expansion, thereby enabling students to complete the full workflow from theoretical learning to model construction and intelligent prediction. A teaching experiment and questionnaire survey were conducted involving 120 undergraduate students across different academic levels. The results indicate that the IFPDP significantly improves students' knowledge acquisition, learning motivation, and modeling practice skills. Students widely acknowledged the software's intuitive visualization, engineering relevance, and interactive experience, while also suggesting further expansion of the case library and enhanced parameter guidance. Overall, the study demonstrates that the IFPDP provides an efficient virtual simulation platform for groundwater engineering education and shows strong potential for future application.

TI Understanding the role of learning analytics and generative artificial
   intelligence on decision-making and learning design practice in higher
   education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning design; Decision-making; Epistemic network analysis; Generative
   artificial intelligence; Learning analytics; Creative problem solving
ID SELF-DETERMINATION; SATISFACTION; PERFORMANCE; FRAMEWORK; IMPACT
AB High-quality learning design is an important contributor to student success. Higher education institutions can leverage the combined potential of learning analytics (LA) and Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) to enhance instructors' learning design practices. However, the way LA and GenAI are being used in combination for learning design is not well understood. In this context, one theory that can provide valuable insights into instructors' technology integration into learning design (LD) practice is Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Using SDT as an interpretative lens, this study illuminates the factors in instructors' learning design practices when utilising LA and GenAI. For this purpose, we employed quantitative ethnography to explore how instructors utilise LA and GenAI for LD. Eleven focus groups were conducted with instructors from a large Australian university. Using thematic analysis, we created a codebook consisting of ten codes that were applied to our dataset and then analysed using Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA). Our results show that instructors' LA-informed LD discussions primarily revolved around course, contextual, and creative problem-solving considerations, as well as student support. The predominant GenAI factors were assessment design, contextual consideration, creative problem solving and design for student self-determination. Based on our results, we discuss the integration of LA and GenAI in LD practice and decision-making, highlighting the practical implications of our findings.

TI From Mediation to Independence: Writing a Research Seminar as a Case
   Study with Experienced Paraprofessionals in Teacher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE mediation; scaffolding; zone of proximal development; paraprofessionals;
   nontraditional students; first-generation students; teacher education;
   academic writing; self-regulated learning
ID SELF-EFFICACY; STUDENTS
AB This article traces how nontraditional preservice teachers experience the mediation of academic research writing, and how the transition from mediation to independence unfolds in their accounts when the supporting structure is withdrawn. The case centers on the first research seminar of a teacher education program in which 13 experienced paraprofessionals, most of them the first in their families to enter higher education and carrying long histories of academic difficulty, design and write a structured self-regulation intervention study with a pupil. From a qualitative analysis of three retrospective focus groups, five themes were constructed: (1) arriving with academic apprehension; (2) holding the standard as recognition; (3) the graduated scaffold of the first seminar; (4) concentric circles of mediation and support; and (5) the abrupt fading of the scaffold in the move toward independence. The findings highlight that participants valued scaffolding not only for the support it provided but for the way responsibility for the work was gradually handed over. Despite this gradual structure, the handover toward independence was experienced by some students as an abrupt, sudden transition, which provoked ambivalent feelings. The discussion proposes two participant-grounded sensitizing concepts, the effort ladder and the concentric circles of mediation, as interpretive lenses for scaffolding theory. We discuss the unresolved tensions that participants hold between the importance of high academic standards and the need for accommodations, and the implications for teacher education.

TI Ecological Factors Associated with Classroom Learning Outcomes in
   Inclusive Education: A Secondary Analysis of the Special Needs Education
   Longitudinal Study (SNELS)
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE inclusive education; classroom learning outcomes; peer relationships;
   special educational needs
AB This study examined teacher-, school-, and student-level factors associated with classroom learning outcomes among junior high school students with special educational needs in inclusive education settings. Data were drawn from the 2012 wave of the Special Needs Education Longitudinal Study (SNELS), part of a nationwide longitudinal research project in Taiwan. The analytic sample comprised 1479 students across multiple disability categories, with learning disabilities, intellectual disabilities, and physical disabilities among the largest groups represented. SNELS was selected because it provides large-scale data on students with special educational needs and their educational experiences, allowing factors across multiple ecological levels to be examined within a common analytical framework. Pearson correlation analysis and hierarchical multiple regression were conducted to examine associations among the study variables and incremental changes in explained variance. Peer relationships and disability-related impact showed relatively large bivariate associations with classroom learning outcomes, while teacher attitudes toward inclusive education, resource teacher support, and teacher collaboration were also associated with classroom learning outcomes. The full hierarchical regression model accounted for 21.6% of the variance in classroom learning outcomes. These findings highlight the value of considering factors across multiple ecological levels when examining classroom learning outcomes in inclusive education. By integrating teacher-, school-, and student-level factors using a nationwide dataset, this study provides historical baseline evidence regarding inclusive education in Taiwan prior to subsequent policy developments and offers an empirical reference point for future research examining changes in inclusive educational practices and support systems over time.

AB The Transformer project at TU Wien exemplifies how universities can act as initiators for sustainability education and STEM science communication. Addressing the urgent need for climate change adaptation and the strengthening of key competencies for sustainability, this paper examines the university's role in creating a temporary, participatory learning space. The Transformer bridges academic research and societal practice, demonstrating how higher education institutions can actively shape sustainable development. TI Longitudinal Associations Between Peer Support in Regular Education
   Settings and Emotional Intelligence Among Gifted Children
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE gifted children; peer support; emotional intelligence; regular education
   settings
ID STUDENTS
AB Using a non-experimental quantitative approach and a longitudinal design, this study included 234 gifted children (M age = 7.58) and 226 non-gifted children (M age = 7.61). First, we examined whether gifted children in regular education settings differed from their non-gifted peers in peer support and emotional intelligence. We then used a parallel latent growth model to examine the longitudinal associations between the developmental trajectories of peer support and emotional intelligence among gifted children. The results showed that, in regular education settings, (1) gifted children did not differ significantly from their non-gifted peers in peer support or emotional intelligence, providing no support for Hypotheses 1 and 2; (2) the initial level of peer support is positively associated with the initial levels of all dimensions of emotional intelligence, partially supporting Hypothesis 3; and (3) the growth rate of peer support is positively associated with the growth rates of all dimensions of emotional intelligence, supporting Hypothesis 4. These findings suggest that both the early foundation of peer support and its later development should receive attention to promote the continuous improvement and healthy development of emotional intelligence among gifted children.

TI Impact of MOOC-Based CME on General Practitioners' Knowledge of
   Early-Life Nutrition
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE online CME; massive open online course; general practitioners;
   knowledge; child nutrition
AB General practitioners (GPs) are at the forefront of stunting interventions, but only a few studies have examined their understanding of growth monitoring. Therefore, this study aims to assess the effectiveness of massive open online course (MOOC)-based Continuing Medical Education (CME) programs to increase GPs' knowledge of nutrition and early detection of growth abnormalities. The study procedures were carried out using a pre-and post-cohort approach involving 121 GPs, mostly working in primary care in Indonesia. The pre-and post-test scores were observed before and after the 12-week MOOC intervention, and the participants were asked for feedback. Participants reported high satisfaction and preferred a combination of synchronous and asynchronous learning. The feedback suggested improving parental education techniques, specifically in low-socioeconomic settings, and strengthening collaboration between GPs and nutritionists in managing feeding problems.

TI Assessment practices resistant to inappropriate AI use in Open Distance
   eLearning: insights from Zimbabwe Open University
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; assessment strategies; era; insights; Open
   Distance eLearning; Zimbabwe Open University; resistant
AB The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into educational practices has raised significant concerns among educators regarding the integrity and effectiveness of traditional assessment methods in the Zimbabwean education sector. This has raised concerns regarding the reliability of submitted assignments, research articles, research projects and other formative assessments, especially as some students use AI to write assignments and other academic tasks. Accordingly, this paper sought to identify assessment practices perceived as effective in promoting authentic student learning and minimizing the inappropriate use of artificial intelligence in Open Distance eLearning environments. A qualitative and instrumental case study design was employed with in-depth interviews and focus group discussions. Seven lecturers, fourteen students and a quality assurance coordinator were purposively sampled from the Masvingo Regional Campus of the Zimbabwe Open University. This study used Constructivist Learning Theory (Piaget, Vygotsky), as lens to understand effective assessment strategies that minimize inappropriate use of artificial intelligence. The findings indicate that in class tests/ assignments, presentations, creation of tasks that can be assessed by observation of student performance, interviews and engaging students in debates, panel discussions and seminars that require students to prepare their arguments and support them can be resistant to inappropriate use of Artificial Intelligence in Open Distance learning. The study suggests that efforts should be made to incorporate artificial intelligence into teacher training curricula in colleges and universities to maintain academic integrity.

TI Assessment of anxiety detection in students using machine learning and
   wearable sensors during virtual and in-person laboratory sessions
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE anxiety detection; control engineering; higher education; machine
   learning; wearable devices; educational innovation
ID AUTONOMIC RESPONSE; HEART-RATE; STRESS; PERFORMANCE; DISORDER; AROUSAL
AB Introduction Anxiety is an increasingly prevalent concern among graduate students, highlighting the need for objective approaches that complement conventional self-report assessments. Wearable sensing technologies combined with machine learning offer opportunities to characterize anxiety-related physiological patterns during authentic educational activities. This pilot study investigated the feasibility of multimodal physiological monitoring for participant-level anxiety screening in graduate engineering education.Methods Eleven graduate students completed virtual and in-person Control Engineering laboratory activities while electroencephalographic (EEG) and peripheral physiological signals, including electrodermal activity (EDA), skin temperature (TEMP), heart rate (HR), inter-beat interval (IBI), and heart rate variability (HRV), were recorded using wearable devices. Participant-level anxiety reference labels were derived from a context-adapted administration of the Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item questionnaire (GAD-7). Six supervised machine learning classifiers were evaluated using subject-independent Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) cross-validation. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, F1-score, ROC-AUC, and confusion matrices, complemented by feature importance analyses.Results Physiological differences were observed between participant anxiety groups and across virtual and in-person laboratory conditions, with EDA and temperature showing comparatively larger effect sizes than cardiovascular measures. Logistic Regression achieved the highest classification performance, although this result requires cautious interpretation given the limited sample size. All evaluated models identified anxiety-labeled participants without false negatives. Feature importance analyses further indicated that EEG-derived variables, particularly frontal and temporal Gamma and Beta activity, contributed substantially to discrimination.Discussion The findings provide preliminary evidence that integrating central and peripheral physiological signals with subject-independent machine learning evaluation may support anxiety screening during authentic educational activities. Rather than replacing established psychological assessment methods, wearable sensing may provide complementary objective evidence for wearable learning analytics and student well-being research. Given the small sample, single institutional context, and context-adapted GAD-7 reference labels, the results should be interpreted as evidence of feasibility rather than clinical validation.

Model robustness was evaluated using goodness-of-fit, multicollinearity, and bootstrap analyses, with statistical significance set at p < .05. Results The prevalence of psychological distress, major depression, and generalized anxiety was 49.80%, 23.29%, and 17.17%, respectively. In terms of the demographic characteristics, younger teachers (<= 35 years), those who were single, and those in the early years of their teaching career were at risk for psychological distress, major depression, and generalized anxiety. With regard to pandemic-related adversities, difficulty managing time and reduced social interaction, consistently predicted generalized anxiety, depression, and psychological distress. These findings demonstrate that both personal characteristics and pandemic-related stressors independently contributed to teachers' mental health vulnerability. Conclusion This study provides one of the largest empirical assessments of teachers' mental health conducted in the Philippines during the COVID-19 pandemic. The findings identify distinct demographic and pandemic-related risk factors that can guide the development of targeted mental health screening, prevention, and intervention strategies for vulnerable teacher subgroups. They also provide evidence to inform educational and public health policies aimed at strengthening psychological support systems and workforce resilience during future public health emergencies.

TI From ICT integration to digital transformation: perceptions and
   pedagogical innovations in Ivorian higher education-comparative study of
   UVCI and ISTC
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE C & ocirc;te d'Ivoire; digital transformation; higher education;
   pedagogical innovation; perceptions; UVCI and ISTC polytechnique
ID DIFFUSION; LESSONS
AB Digital transformation has become a major driver of higher education modernization in Africa. While the integration of Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) into teaching practices is widely documented, less attention has been paid to how this technological adoption evolves into broader processes of digital transformation capable of reshaping pedagogical practices and institutional models. This gap is particularly evident in Sub-Saharan African higher education, where empirical comparative studies remain limited. Drawing on Rogers' Diffusion of Innovation Theory and Huberman's work on educational change, this study examines how academic actors perceive digital transformation as a driver of pedagogical innovation in Ivorian higher education. A comparative case study was conducted between the Virtual University of C & ocirc;te d'Ivoire (UVCI) and ISTC-Polytechnique. The study addresses the following question: how do academic actors perceive the effects of digital transformation on pedagogical innovation? A mixed-methods approach was adopted, combining quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis. Quantitative data were analyzed using non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis) and regression models, while qualitative data were subjected to thematic analysis. The findings reveal significant institutional differences in the adoption of hybrid teaching practices, with higher levels observed at UVCI. Institutional context emerges as the strongest predictor of adoption, whereas individual characteristics exert only limited influence. Qualitative evidence further indicates that digital transformation extends beyond ICT integration by fostering pedagogical innovations that enhance accessibility, flexibility, interactivity, and learner engagement. These results highlight the pivotal role of institutional environments in enabling the transition from ICT integration to meaningful digital transformation in higher education. The study contributes to the literature by empirically distinguishing technological integration from broader digital transformation processes and by demonstrating how institutional conditions shape the emergence of pedagogical innovation in an African higher education context.

DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; educational digitalization; higher education;
   high-quality development; Shandong province
AB Against the backdrop of the ongoing technological revolution and industrial transformation, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a pivotal technological driver for advancing the high-quality development of higher education. As one of China's leading provinces in both higher education and manufacturing, Shandong faces a pressing need to integrate AI into its higher education system to facilitate educational modernization and support the broader transition from old to new growth drivers. DT Article
DE academic achievement; college; continuing-generation college student;
   first-generation college student; retention
ID TRANSITION; SUPPORT; MODEL
AB Introduction First-generation college students (FGCS) face unique challenges in higher education; however, research examining the specific mechanisms that affect their success remains limited. Methods This study analyzed pre-enrollment survey data and first-year transition experiences from students at a large midwestern university to investigate how first-generation status influences college adjustment and academic outcomes. Using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, we identified several important pre-enrollment and first-year transition factors. Results Multi-group structural equation modeling revealed that pre-enrollment characteristics differentially predict first-year transitions for FGCS versus continuing-generation college students (CGCS; Delta chi 2 = 84.658, Delta df = 54, p = 0.005). Conclusion Suggesting that unmeasured factors may be more consequential for FGCS academic success. These findings suggest that FGCS and CGCS follow distinct pathways to academic success, necessitating distinct forms of support.

TI Integrating AI-supported project-based inquiry to foster mathematical
   connections in elementary education: a learning innovation framework
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION

DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; elementary education; innovation framework;
   mathematical connections; project-based inquiry
ID DESIGN-BASED RESEARCH
AB This study investigates the effectiveness of integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) within a Project-Based Inquiry (PBI) framework to enhance elementary students' mathematical connections in geometry learning. AI functions as a cognitive scaffolding tool by providing adaptive prompts that support students' reasoning, representation, and reflection, while PBI engages learners in authentic problem-solving tasks such as designing classroom layouts and park environments.The indicators of mathematical connections assessed in this study include: (1) connections between mathematical concepts (e.g., area and multiplication), (2) connections across multiple representations (visual, symbolic, and verbal), and (3) connections between mathematics and real-world contexts. Data were collected at the elementary school level through classroom observations, students' project artifacts, short interviews, and AI-student interaction logs. AI-supported scaffolding facilitated this shift by guiding students from informal reasoning toward formal mathematical modeling. Interview data confirmed increased student engagement, metacognitive awareness, and confidence in problem-solving.These results suggest that AI-supported PBI effectively promotes interconnected mathematical understanding and meaningful learning experiences in elementary education.

TI Teaching embodied knowledge through narratives
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE class practice; embodied knowledge; learning; narrative inquiry;
   physical education; teaching
ID EXPERIENCE
AB Introduction This paper examines how embodied knowledge can be understood and taught across school subjects by dissolving the enduring body-mind dualism rooted in classical philosophy. Drawing on Dewey's critique of this dualism and his concept of a body-mind continuum, the authors situate physical education (PE) as a paradigmatic case for exploring embodied knowledge in teaching and learning. Historically, schooling privileged cognition, treating the body instrumentally and marginalizing bodily experience in curricula. Although PE eventually became institutionalized, its epistemic foundation remained conceptually split between bodily practice and abstract reflection. This paper addresses three key issues: (1) the historical and conceptual persistence of the body-mind divide in schooling, illustrated through the evolution of PE; (2) how embodied knowledge serves as a dynamic connector between body and mind, informed by pragmatism, phenomenology, and competence-oriented approaches; (3) the role of narratives and metaphors in articulating and transmitting embodied understanding.Methods This study combines discourse analysis and narrative inquiry to analyze the historical and cultural context of PE and sports. The research focuses on the concept of body-mind dualism in PE, utilizing data from two studies conducted in Swiss middle schools. The analysis explores how different individuals operate under varying rules within the body-mind dualism, examining embodied knowledge through narratives and thick descriptions.Results and Discussion A class practice vignette-the sea star example of a student learning the high jump-shows how learners draw on metaphors to express bodily insights that may not align with teachers' technical language, highlighting both the presence of embodied knowledge and the communicative gap hindering its pedagogical use. This paper concludes that narratives and metaphors function as a shared language for embodied knowledge, enabling dialogue between teachers and learners. Rather than abandoning technique-based teaching, embodied narratives can complement it, fostering reflective, democratic learning across subjects. Ultimately, dissolving the body-mind dualism requires integrating embodied knowledge not only in PE but in all educational practices.

AB This study examines engineering education as a learning ecosystem and investigates the role of the National Society of Black Engineers (NSBE) within that system.    programming education
ID CLASSROOM
AB This study examines lecturer-guided artificial intelligence (AI)-supported flipped learning in undergraduate Information Technology programming education. The study focuses on how multiple AI tools can be pedagogically orchestrated across pre-class preparation, in-class programming practice, and post-class reflection while maintaining lecturer guidance, student reasoning, and responsible AI use. A classroom-based non-equivalent groups quasi-experimental design was implemented with 120 undergraduate Information Technology students in a Programming Techniques course. One intact class participated in a lecturer-guided AI-supported flipped learning condition (n = 60), while another intact class participated in a traditional flipped classroom condition without planned AI-supported learning tasks (n = 60). Quantitative data included pretest and posttest programming scores and post-intervention self-reported measures of learning autonomy, reflective learning, and digital competence. Qualitative interview data from students and lecturers were used to contextualize participants' perceptions of AI-supported learning activities. The results showed that the AI-supported flipped learning group achieved higher posttest programming performance, showed a larger observed programming-performance gain, and reported higher post-intervention learning autonomy, reflective learning, and digital competence than the traditional flipped classroom group. Because the self-reported items referred explicitly to AI-supported activities, these differences are interpreted as condition-linked perceptions rather than as comparisons of general competence. Qualitative findings indicated that students and lecturers perceived AI as useful for preparation, debugging-related feedback, solution comparison, reflection, and lecturer-guided verification. The findings should be interpreted as classroom-based evidence of observed group differences rather than as definitive causal proof of AI tool effects. The main contribution of the study is to illustrate how multiple AI tools can be organized as a lecturer-guided pedagogical orchestration within the flipped programming learning cycle.

TI Exploring the professional challenges and opportunities of nursing
   faculty in India: a nationwide e-survey
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE challenges; education; nursing faculty; opportunities; professional role
AB Background Nursing faculty play a key role in preparing competent nurses, yet their professional challenges and opportunities remain underexplored in India. This study examined these challenges and opportunities among nursing faculty in India. Methods A quantitative cross-sectional exploratory study was conducted among 322 nursing faculty members across India using convenience sampling. Data were collected electronically using a self-structured questionnaire. Descriptive statistics, Mann-Whitney U test, Kruskal-Wallis test, and ordinal logistic regression were performed using SPSS version 23. Results Most participants were aged 31-40 years (51.6%) and held MSc Nursing qualifications (60.9%). Moderate professional challenges (66.5%) and opportunities (75.5%) were common. Age and educational qualification were significantly associated with both outcomes (p < 0.001). Educational qualification and academic designation were significant predictors. Conclusions Nursing educators in India experienced moderate professional challenges and opportunities. Strengthening faculty development and supportive academic environments may enhance professional growth, job satisfaction, and retention.

TI Measuring changes in learning outcomes through in-session assessments
   during progressive curriculum implementation
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE competency threshold; constructivism; flipped mode teaching; generative
   learning; mastery threshold; peer assessment; project-based learning
ID DEFINITIONS; CLASSROOM; SELF
AB This paper reports a four-year progressive implementation study of Embedded Mechatronic Systems, redesigned using Generative Learning Theory (GLT) within a flipped classroom and supported by studio- and project-based learning. The redesign modernised the curriculum, strengthened theory-practice integration, and aligned learning outcomes with industry expectations. The subject focuses on physical computing via digital circuit design and embedded systems, enabling students to interface sensors and actuators, while applying foundational digital signal processing. Teaching emphasises industry-relevant microcontroller platforms and direct industry collaboration, fostering authentic, practice-aligned skills that underpin advanced coursework in control, mechatronics, vibration, and environmental acoustics. To address fragmentation between lectures and labs, a session-long group project was introduced, transforming isolated experiments into cohesive engineering tasks. Students collaboratively design, implement, and demonstrate functional embedded systems within structured workshops, supported by reflective reports and demonstration videos that promote metacognition and peer-learning, consistent with GLT. Metrics were developed to track competency and mastery thresholds based on assessments during the session directly, to serve as a heuristic for estimation of learning outcomes. Evaluation using internal quantitative measures shows sustained improvement post-redesign, with estimates of improved learning outcomes increasing by 41% +/- 33% per year and similar to 96% +/- 7% overall from 2020 to 2025. Involving the cohort in assessment (self and peer) can help identify individuals who are not aware of their performance in a large class. The approach offers a scalable alternative to traditional examinations and performance metrics, which often require formalised entry and exit exams. It demonstrates that aligned pedagogy, authentic technology use, and reflective assessment can substantially enhance learning outcomes and bridge academic instruction with professional engineering practice.

TI Growing Crystals,Growing Minds: A STEAM Approachto Introducing
   Crystallography in Early Education
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Early Education; Chemistry Education; Inquiry-BasedLearning; Creativity;
   Crystallography
AB Crystallography is rarely introduced in early education despite its strong potential to foster inquiry-based chemistry learning through observation, experimentation, and model building. This work presents an STEAM-based educational intervention designed to introduce crystallographic concepts through the integration of experimental activities, narrative, and artistic expression. The proposal was implemented with approximately 420 students across preschool and primary levels, combining crystal growth experiments using sucrose and copper(II) sulfate with a literary framework based on O Veleiro de Crystal. Students engaged in hands-on crystallization activities with sucrose and teacher-guided observation of copper(II) sulfate crystal growth, together with systematic observation and creative production, including drawings and three-dimensional models. The results reveal high levels of student engagement and motivation, as well as the development of early scientific thinking, particularly in relation to crystal growth, material properties, and time-dependent processes. In addition, students demonstrated the ability to connect scientific observations with imaginative interpretation, while collaborative activities supported the development of socio-emotional skills such as teamwork, persistence, and empathy. These findings highlight the potential of crystallography as an effective interdisciplinary context within STEAM education capable of bridging science, art, and humanistic perspectives. The use of low-cost materials, detailed experimental procedures, and accessible methodologies further support the adaptability and reproducibility of this approach, providing a practical framework for introducing crystallography in early chemistry education across diverse educational contexts.

AB Organic chemistry instruction relies on graphically complex problem types, especially mechanism, synthesis, and bonding questions. These problems cannot easily be reduced to conventional digital input formats without conceptual loss. Because digitization remains essential for scaffolding, active learning, and remote instruction in large service classes, a variety of solutions exist that each introduce their own technical burden and cost. TI Exploring the mechanism of technology-enhanced formative assessment
   through students' behavioral and cognitive task engagement
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Computer-assisted learning; Behavioral engagement; Argumentation;
   Formative assessment
ID WRITTEN-CORRECTIVE-FEEDBACK; SCIENCE; TAXONOMY; SCHOOL; STATE
AB Due to advances in educational technology, students receive automated feedback on their writing, requiring understanding of its mechanism of effectiveness. Although it is assumed that behavioral and cognitive task engagement play a crucial role in the effect of feedback on writing outcomes, their impact remains partially understood. We conducted an experimental study, comparing two groups of secondary school students who completed a writing task and revised their drafts with or without feedback (automated feedback [n = 348] vs. no feedback [n = 227]). We assessed students' behavioral task engagement using a linguistic similarity measure (i.e., edit distance) and students' cognitive task engagement using self-reports. Our results indicate that behavioral task engagement mediated the effect of automated feedback on writing performance. We found no mediating effect of cognitive task engagement. The findings imply that in writing, performance gains due to automated feedback emerge when students show proactive behavior in text revision. Educational Relevance: Understanding how automated feedback supports students' writing skills allows educators to optimize learning environments. We provide evidence that automated feedback supports writing performance by engaging students in revisions of their texts. For educators, this underscores the importance of feedback that invites action and supports students in making revisions.

TI The Nature of Sibling Bullying Among Primary School Students
SO JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGISTS AND COUNSELLORS IN SCHOOLS
LA English
DT Article
DE sibling bullying; primary school students; perpetration; victimisation;
   childhood bullying
ID PEER; ASSOCIATION; BEHAVIOR; VIOLENCE; FAMILY; PERSONALITY; EXPERIENCES;
   AGGRESSION; CHILDHOOD; CHILDREN
AB This study examined the nature and extent of sibling bullying in terms of its frequency, perpetrators and victims, motives, and contextual characteristics. Participants were 356 Turkish fourth-grade primary school students (191 girls, 165 boys). Data were collected using the Revised Sibling Bullying Scale, the Motives and Reasons for Sibling Bullying Questionnaire, the Places and Times of Sibling Bullying Questionnaire, a sibling identification form, and a demographic information form. Findings indicated that the most common sibling bullying behaviours were name-calling, hitting, intimidation, and teasing. Older brothers were identified as the most frequent perpetrators, whereas younger brothers were the most frequent victims. Fun, revenge, and boredom emerged as the most common motives for perpetration, while victims reported joking, relieving boredom, scaring, and revenge as the most common reasons for victimisation. Sibling bullying occurred most frequently when siblings spent time together and in situations where parental supervision was absent. The findings suggest that sibling bullying is a significant problem within the home environment and highlight the importance of parental awareness and early intervention. Implications for the definition, prevention, and intervention of sibling bullying are discussed in light of the existing literature.

TI Precision Education: How Ready Are Obstetrics and Gynecology Clerkships
   for the Future of Medical Education?
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE precision education; learner assessment; technology; professional
   development
AB OBJECTIVES: Precision education has been heralded as the future of medical education, yet substantial barriers to realizing this future exist. We sought to explore the current state of precision education in obstetrics and gynecology clerkship settings including barriers to adoption of this approach and strategies to support clinical educators interested in accelerating the advancement of precision education in their educational programs. DESIGN: We designed a survey using an iterative approach informed by a literature review of principles and best practices for a precision education approach in clinical education settings. The survey queried about current adoption of technologies, resources, and approaches associated with precision education, as well as perceived barriers to further adoption of precision education. The survey was piloted among of subset of educators prior to distribution. PARTICIPANTS: Obstetrics and gynecology clerkship directors were identified through cross-referencing list from the LCME and from the national professional society supporting obstetrics and gynecology educators, to optimize our ability to capture one response from each MD granting program within the United States. RESULTS: About 95 clerkship leaders responded, for a response rate of 69.3%. Nearly one-quarter of clerkships use autonomously generated teaching materials, 17% use augmented-reality technologies, and 6% use artificial-intelligence teaching assistants. Factors such as grading system or clerkship director experience were not associated with readiness for precision education. Strategies identified as more practical to implement include automated generation of teaching materials, flexible scheduling of clerkship experiences, and inclusion of students and community members into curricular decisions. CONCLUSIONS: As with other technological advancements in healthcare and education, the adoption of precision education is occurring gradually and at varying paces at institutions across the nation. This work suggests strategies that may be more readily implemented into clerkships for institutions aiming to accelerate progress towards precision education. ( J Surg Ed 83:104119. TI Video Assessment of Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: A Validation Study to
   Develop a Criterion-Based Scoring Tool for Performance
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE laparoscopic cholecystectomy; scoring tool; surgical education; surgical
   training; video assessment
ID VALIDITY EVIDENCE; RELIABILITY
AB OBJECTIVE: Surgical education requires effective skill transfer and objective assessment. Existing competency evaluations often rely on subjective observations. This study aims to validate a quantitative video-based assessment rubric for laparoscopic cholecystectomy and formulate a criterion-based scoring instrument. DESIGN: A prospective cohort study at Northern Health, Melbourne. SETTING: De-identified performance of laparoscopic cholecystectomy videos collected from consultant surgeons and surgical trainees. The assessment framework included quantitative performance benchmarks and case difficulty variables. PARTICIPANTS: Four specialist general surgeons accredited as fellows of the Royal Australasian College of Surgeons (FRACS), comprising of 2 consultants and 2 fellows, alongside 4 trainee registrars enrolled in a formal surgical training program. Three hepatopancreatobiliary surgeons rated the videos. RESULTS: Analysis of 80 videos showed moderate (0.5-0.75) to good (0.5-0.9) interrater agreement. Trainees took longer to achieve critical view of safety (14.2 minutes versus 9.8 minutes for consultants; p = 0.014) and rotated the gallbladder more frequently (7.5 versus 4.0 times; p = 0.024). Subjective performance ratings correlated with poorer achievement of critical view of safety components, and lower counts of the number of Hartmann's pouch grasping, gallbladder rotation, incorrect clipping, lack of progress and perforation. A scoring system was derived, with a cut-off score of 9 for easier cases, and score of 7 for harder cases, and achieved a ROC AUC of 0.81 and 0.78 respectively, in performance assessment. CONCLUSIONS: This study validates a video-based assessment rubric capable of correlating with criterion-based assessment outcomes in laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The developed scoring instrument offers a structured, objective approach to surgical assessment, facilitating technical progress monitoring and identifying areas for improvement, thus supporting a more objective evaluative framework in surgical education.
