TI Reaching Beyond the Milestones: The Thresholds to Mastery in Obstetrics
   and Gynecology Training
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE threshold concepts; medical education; residency; professional identity
   formation; assessment frameworks
ID MEDICAL-EDUCATION; TRAINEES
AB BACKGROUND: Competency-based medical education aims to ensure that physicians develop the skills and knowledge necessary for independent clinical practice through graduated autonomy. Existing competencies in obstetrics and gynecology (OBGYN) residency often fail to capture higher-order transformations in clinical reasoning, professional identity, and emotional maturity. A more nuanced, applicable, and valid articulation of these developmental transitions is needed to better support resident growth and assessment. OBJECTIVE: To identify OBGYN-specific threshold concepts that represent transformative developmental milestones in training, as perceived by leaders in residency education. DESIGN: This qualitative study used a constructivist, inductive thematic analysis approach. Interviews explored moments of significant developmental transition, areas of learner struggle, and examples of transformative learning during residency. Audio-recorded interviews were transcribed, deidentified, and independently coded by 2 reviewers using line-by-line analysis. Codes were iteratively organized into themes through consensus, with thematic saturation reached after 9 interviews. Credibility was supported through expert review, member checking, and iterative refinement. SETTING: Semistructured, one-on-one interviews were conducted with 11 attending physicians holding formal educational leadership roles within OBGYN residency programs at 4 academic institutions in the New York City metropolitan area. RESULTS: Six threshold concepts were identified that characterize developmental transitions into OBGYN practice: recognition of clinical severity, anticipation and adjustment of surgical technique, ownership of patient care in dynamic settings, empathic collaboration and team management, confidence in independent decision-making, and advanced emotional regulation. These concepts reflected observable shifts in judgment, responsibility, teamwork, and emotional processing that educators consistently associated with readiness for independent practice. In a subsequent survey of n = 78 medical education leaders at a national conference, 90% of respondents endorsed incorporating these threshold concepts into resident assessment frameworks. CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies 6 threshold concepts that capture essential, yet under-recognized, developmental milestones in OBGYN residency training. These concepts offer a complementary framework to existing assessment systems by emphasizing transformative growth in clinical judgment, professional identity, and emotional resilience. Integrating threshold concepts into curriculum design and evaluation may enhance the ability of educators to support learners, identify developmental challenges, and promote readiness for independent practice.    Partnership, and Trainee Voice

LA English
DT Article
DE equity; global surgery; mentorship; reverse mentoring; surgical
   education; trainee voice
AB OBJECTIVE: To propose reverse mentoring as a practical educational framework for global surgical education, with emphasis on trainee voice, bidirectional partnership, and equity. DESIGN: Perspective article grounded in published literature on reverse mentoring, surgical mentorship, mentoring across difference, and global surgery education. TI LLMs in text linguistics teaching: an exploratory study with genAI
   novices in higher education
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE LLM; Text linguistics; Language education; Prompting; Metacognition
AB This study examines the use of LLMs in text linguistics education, focusing on novices in generative AI (genAI) and their ability to design prompts and evaluate AI-generated outputs. Employing an action research design in higher education, it investigates prompting strategies, student perceptions, and learning outcomes in text analysis tasks. Students' reports containing prompts and LLM outputs show that novices refine prompts through trial and error and occasionally use in-context examples or simplify complex instructions. End-of-term reflections indicate limited prompting competence but growing confidence in applying subject-specific knowledge, although students often attributed unsatisfactory results to the LLM's limitations rather than to their own prompt formulation. Challenges such as anthropomorphizing the models and overgeneralizing limited outcomes were also observed. The findings suggest that, in this specific classroom context, students reported engaging in metacognitive reflection while using LLMs, particularly when disciplinary knowledge was already well consolidated. However, limited knowledge of prompt design remains a major obstacle.

AB This paper presents an application of a framework for educational social justice-oriented digital transformation, providing an analytical examination of four case studies of community-led design and implementation of digital technology with marginalized populations. TI Heterogeneous growth mindset trajectories in middle school: Predictors
   and outcomes
SO CONTEMPORARY EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Implicit theory of intelligence; Sense of belonging; Guided inquiry;
   Academic achievement; Longitudinal study; Developmental trajectories;
   Person-oriented approach
ID STUDENTS IMPLICIT THEORIES; MOTIVATIONAL BELIEFS; LATENT GROWTH;
   ABILITY; INTELLIGENCE; ACHIEVEMENT; ADOLESCENTS; SELF; MATH; PERFORMANCE
AB Prior research often reports average declines in growth mindset during adolescence, typically attributed to increased academic pressure and social comparison. However, these mean-level trends may obscure important individual differences. This longitudinal study examined heterogeneity in growth mindset development by identifying distinct trajectory patterns and testing whether guided inquiry instruction and school belonging predicted trajectory membership. Additionally, the association between mindset trajectories and academic achievement was assessed. A sample of 1094 students was followed longitudinally from Grades 7 to 9. Latent growth modeling indicated minimal change in students' growth mindset on average. However, growth mixture modeling revealed four distinct growth mindset trajectories: High Stable (64%), Low Stable (14%), High Decreasing (12%), and Low Increasing (10%). Gender and socioeconomic status (SES) predicted trajectory membership, with girls and higher SES students more likely to belong to the High Stable trajectory. In contrast, neither guided inquiry instruction nor school belonging significantly predicted trajectory membership. Students in the High Stable trajectory showed higher academic achievement by the end of middle school than those in the Low Stable and Low Increasing trajectories, even after accounting for differences in initial achievement. These findings underscore the value of examining individual differences in mindset development. Early identification of and support for students at risk of stable fixed mindset beliefs or declining growth mindset beliefs may help promote adaptive mindsets and long-term academic success.

TI Shifting social and cultural narratives in pharmacy education: a
   summative content analysis
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Social determinants of health; Cultural competency; Content analysis;
   Terminology
ID HEALTH EQUITY TOURISM
AB Background: Pharmacy education has experienced substantial changes in educational guidance, professional priorities, and the broader policy environment surrounding social and cultural topics. However, little is known about how these changes have been reflected in pharmacy education scholarship over time. The purpose of this study was to examine trends in the presence, terminology, and contexts in which social and cultural topics were represented in U.S. pharmacy education, as reflected in titles presented at the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy annual meetings. Methods: A summative content analysis was conducted on titles from peer-reviewed research and education posters, school posters, and main conference programming at AACP Pharmacy Education meetings (2018-2025). Titles were analyzed to identify social and cultural content and characterize associated terminology and context codes, which were iteratively grouped into themes. Trend analyses included calculation of the proportion of relevant titles by year and format, as well as frequency analyses of terminology and context themes. Results: Of 4410 conference titles, the proportion addressing social and cultural topics ranged from a low of 5.41% in 2019 to a peak of 16.78% in 2022 before declining, while remaining above levels observed during the early years of the study period. Diversity-, equity-, inclusion-, and anti-racism-related terminology peaked in 2022 and declined thereafter, whereas references to culture, social determinants of health, and special or vulnerable populations remained consistently represented. Teaching or curricular interventions and campus climate were the most frequently identified context themes, although titles related to campus climate-related titles declined following their 2022 peak. Conclusion: These findings provide a longitudinal perspective on the evolution of social and cultural discourse within U.S. pharmacy education.

TI Artificial intelligence in psychiatric care and education: a qualitative
   study of factors influencing adoption in Singapore
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Continued education; psychiatry; thematic analysis; artificial
   intelligence integration
AB Objectives: This study aimed to understand how AI's perceived role interacts with emerging barriers and facilitators to identify factors influencing its adoption across clinical and educational professions in Singapore. Methods: This study followed a qualitative approach guided by a medical-pedagogical theoretical framework. Semi-structured interviews were conducted between May and July 2025 and followed an interview guide based on the medical-pedagogical framework. Twenty-four people participated, including eight nurses, six psychiatrists, and 10 allied health professionals. All were clinicians and educators. Data were analysed using thematic analysis, with attention to emergent patterns across patient care and educational contexts. Results: Participants recognised significant potential for AI in patient care and healthcare professions education, particularly for information access, retrieval, clinical documentation, AI-augmented training methods such as virtual patients and educational content creation. Barriers included fears of professional skill degradation, role confusion, lack of familiarity with capabilities and the need for personal evidence of benefit. Enablers encompassed integrated, context-specific training, clear governance frameworks, and peer networks facilitating experiential learning and responsible use. Participants emphasised maintaining human connection and reflective practice as essential to psychiatric care and education. Conclusions: Effective AI adoption in psychiatric care and education can be facilitated by clearly delineating tasks, embedding digital literacy into training, communicating robust governance structures, and introducing peer-led communities of practice. Relevant stakeholders should be engaged to align AI deployment with real clinical workflows, optimising both patient care and educational outcomes.

TI Psychoeducational Challenges of Dyslexic Children During the COVID-19
   Pandemic: A Systematic Review
SO DYSLEXIA
LA English
DT Article
DE COVID-19; dyslexic children; psychoeducational challenges; systematic
   review
AB Dyslexic students faced psychological and educational challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic and online learning, including increased anxiety, low self-esteem, reduced reading interest, limited access to educational technologies, insufficient teacher support, and difficulties with reading fluency and concentration. Examining these challenges is crucial for implementing effective measures and enhancing post-pandemic learning. This study investigates the psycho-educational challenges of dyslexic children during the pandemic, highlighting the need for targeted interventions to support them in current and future contexts. This systematic review identified relevant articles through electronic searches of PubMed, Wiley, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect, supplemented by the snowballing technique, which involved examining the bibliographies of retrieved references. The study identified two main categories of challenges for dyslexic children: psychological (mental health, emotional well-being, behavioural issues, parental stress) and educational (socioeconomic status, technology access, special educational needs, teacher support, remote learning difficulties) affecting children with learning disabilities. The research results show that dyslexic children faced various psychological and educational difficulties identified in this review during the COVID-19 pandemic. Therefore, targeted, evidence-based strategies-such as teacher training, family-school collaboration, adaptive learning technologies, and psychological support-are needed to mitigate these challenges in the post-pandemic period.

SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Fractions; Noticing; Online laboratory school; Prospective mathematics
   teachers
ID FRAMEWORK; STUDENTS
AB The purpose of this study was to examine changes and growth in prospective mathematics teachers' (PMTs) noticing skills of fractions in terms of attending, interpretation, and decision-making. Twenty PMTs at a foundation university participated in an 8-week online laboratory school (OLS). In the context of the OLS, we provided PMTs with opportunities for online fieldwork. This included collaborative lesson planning on fractions with peers under mentor supervision, teaching experiences with Grade 4-5 students, and receiving feedback on their instruction. We discuss implications of those results to advance PMTs' noticing of fractions in the OLS.

TI A closer look at the impact of gender on test performance through a
   multivariate G-theory approach
SO LANGUAGE TESTING IN ASIA
LA English
DT Article
DE Generalizability theory; Decision studies; Generalizability studies;
   Dependability; Iranian university entrance examination
ID GENERALIZABILITY THEORY; SCORES
AB Psychometricians have voiced their concern over the psychometric quality of a test in the realms of educational measurement and language assessment. Validity and reliability are interdependent, and sources of construct-irrelevant variance may jeopardize the validity of test score interpretations and use, leading to inconsistencies in test scores. Thus, the investigation of such irrelevant sources of variance is of utmost importance for test users. The current study used multivariate Generalizability Theory to examine whether gender was associated with differences in the dependability of scores from a university entrance examination. The outcomes revealed uneven relative contributions of the sources of variance across gender groups, alongside moderate divergences in dependability indices. Decision studies further indicated that, under an equal-items-per-subtest design, the two groups would need different numbers of items to reach a composite G-coefficient of 0.90.

TI Diagnostic assessment of L2 academic writing needs among doctoral
   scholars in Tamil Nadu universities
SO LANGUAGE TESTING IN ASIA
LA English
DT Article
DE L2 academic writing; Doctoral scholars; Diagnostic assessment; Academic
   writing needs; Multilingual higher education; Writing support; Tamil
   Nadu universities
AB Academic writing in English is a central requirement of doctoral education in multilingual higher education contexts, yet many doctoral scholars receive limited systematic support in identifying and addressing their writing needs. This study presents a diagnostic assessment of second language academic writing needs among doctoral scholars in Tamil Nadu universities. Using a quantitative cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 230 doctoral scholars across Sciences, Engineering, Arts and Humanities, and Social Sciences. The final questionnaire, revised after a separate pilot study, included demographic and academic background items and 26 three-point Likert-type items covering grammar and syntax, vocabulary, academic style and structure, cultural-linguistic factors, and technological/resource-related conditions. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, non-parametric group comparisons, and Spearman correlation. The results showed perceived difficulty across all five domains, with vocabulary recording the highest mean score, followed by academic style and structure. Group comparisons indicated that perceived writing difficulty varied across selected background variables, especially self-rated English proficiency and first language. Support-practice indicators, including grammar-guide use, vocabulary-resource use, style/feedback support, help-seeking, and technology-training attendance, were positively associated with related difficulty domains, suggesting that scholars experiencing greater difficulty may be more likely to seek support. The findings support diagnostic, development-oriented writing support that addresses academic vocabulary, genre awareness, multilingual writing practices, and access to writing-related resources, rather than focusing only on grammar. Although grounded in Tamil Nadu universities, the domain-based diagnostic framework may be analytically useful for comparable multilingual higher education contexts where doctoral scholars write in English as an additional academic language.

TI Authorial voice and textual ownership in AI-assisted EFL academic
   writing
SO COMPUTERS AND COMPOSITION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; Authorial voice; Textual ownership; EFL academic writing;
   Source-based writing; Writer agency
ID STRENGTH
AB As generative artificial intelligence becomes normalized in L2 writing, questions of authorial voice and textual ownership require analysis beyond broad claims of benefit or risk. This study reanalyzes the focal-case subcorpus of a semester-long EFL writing dataset drawn from Englishmajor undergraduates at a public university in Jordan. The analysis is limited to 24 focal participants because only these cases contained the linked evidence needed to trace authorship across process and text: interviews, reflections, AI-use logs, prompt-output examples, Essay 2 draft histories, focal profile indicators, and paired first and final drafts. Using a qualitativedominant mixed-methods multiple-case design, the study combines codebook thematic analysis of the process corpus with a structured paired-draft voice-comparison layer applied to the sourcebased Essay 2 drafts. The bounded quantitative strand suggested stronger final-draft voice where agency and verification were higher and direct text uptake lower. AI did not itself diminish voice; risk arose when fluent output displaced writer judgment and evaluative control.

TI Agency in Academic Career Development Within Neoliberalism: Chinese as
   an Additional Language Teachers' Trajectories
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic career; career agency; Chinese as an additional language (CAL)
   teachers; neoliberalism
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION
AB The pursuit of academic careers within neoliberal higher education is increasingly characterised as uncertain, insecure and fragmented. Previous studies have predominantly depicted the challenges and tensions experienced by language teachers in sustaining their career development. However, there remains a lack of research on how career agency (i.e., agentic actions and choices) is negotiated and exercised by individuals at the micro level. This multiple case study traces the career trajectories of a group of Chinese as an additional language (CAL) teachers, focusing on how they make decisions and enact actions to navigate their academic careers. The findings reveal diverse manifestations of career agency among the participants. Their career accounts indicate how different elements, such as neoliberal norms, personal values, professional status and career goals, intersect in their choices and actions as they navigate individual academic careers. Practical implications are discussed to support language teachers in developing their career paths within neoliberalism.

TI Teacher professionalisation at the intersection of open, moral and
   critical Global Citizenship Education: Reflections from an international
   comparative study
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE global citizenship education (GCE); teacher education; global
   sensitivity; internationalisation of universities
ID COMPETENCES
AB New social contracts for education, such as those promoted by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and the Dublin Declaration on Global Education to 2050, outline the need to prepare student teachers to be change agents who can help address growing global challenges, using innovative Global Citizenship Education (GCE) approaches. To create and offer their students experimental learning opportunities on how to deal with these challenges, student teachers need to develop global sensitivity and position themselves to think globally, act locally and reflect "glocally". While various models have been developed to describe these competencies in teacher education, research about their effectiveness is still emerging. The study presented in this article outlines the formal evaluation of an Erasmus+ project on developing global sensitivity in 301 student teachers (187 female, 114 male) from five partner universities. The project developed an interculturally sensitive teacher training concept designed to facilitate an international virtual exchange between the student teachers. It included four key elements: content introduction, lesson planning, international virtual dialogues and reflection. The findings illustrate how the student teachers transferred GCE perspectives into their own teaching practice and outline associated qualification affordances. They also show how didactical arrangements such as international dialogues about "hot topics" influenced the student teachers' global knowledge, values and dispositions to (at least potentially) better address the pedagogic challenges of teaching global citizenship. Conceptual ideas and empirical results on didactic challenges in the university context are thus reported to stimulate further debate on future GCE implementation in higher education.

TI Why Do Victimized Youth Feel Lonely? Cognitive Flexibility as a Mediator
   and Social Support as a Contextual Moderator
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE adolescent; cognitive flexibility; loneliness; peer victimization;

ID PEER VICTIMIZATION; SUICIDAL IDEATION; LONELINESS; SCHOOL; ADOLESCENTS;
   BIAS
AB Background Guided by the cognitive-behavioral model of loneliness and the healthy context paradox, we tested whether cognitive flexibility mediates the link between peer victimization and loneliness in adolescents and whether social support moderates this pathway.Methods Using a two-wave, short-term prospective design, we followed 833 Chinese first-year junior middle school students (Mage = 12.22, SD = 0.43; 49.1% male). Findings caution against assuming uniform benefits of global support. Schools should combine anti-bullying efforts with skills for flexible thinking and tailor supports to avoid inadvertent harm, ensuring equitable access.Conclusions Cognitive flexibility partially mediated victimization's effect on loneliness. Unexpectedly, high social support amplified adverse effects, underscoring nuanced, context-sensitive school strategies.

TI Intergenerational Reading in Increasingly Mediatised Contexts: An
   Inquiry With Chilean Tweens and Parents
SO LITERACY
LA English
DT Article
DE digital media; intensive parenting; intergenerational reading; literary
   reading; tweens
ID LITERACY
AB Reading is increasingly situated within mediatised assemblages: dynamic configurations of people, devices, platforms, texts and domestic spaces that together shape what reading means in everyday family life. In this article, we propose the concept of intergenerational reading to capture how reading functions as a relational practice across generations, moving beyond both the book/digital binary and deficit frameworks that have long dominated family literacy research. Drawing on interviews with tweens (aged 8-12) and caregivers from the Chilean #EstoTbn project, we analyse how parents and children negotiate reading and cultural consumption in contexts of rapid mediatisation. Our analysis identifies two dynamics. First, the physical book retains a near-inescapable normative centrality, anchoring dominant ideals of the 'good reader' and the 'good parent' within an assemblage that includes furniture, home libraries and reading routines as much as texts themselves. Second, what we call 'family taste'-a collectively negotiated aesthetic disposition-operates across media formats as a site of intergenerational connection and contestation, shaped by peer culture, algorithmic environments and parental curation alike. We argue that intergenerational reading, understood as a more-than-human relational practice, opens an analytical space where the value of shared cultural engagement lies not in measurable learning outcomes but in the affective, reciprocal and present-oriented bonds that reading, in its broadest sense, makes possible. These bonds become especially visible in moments when tweens invite adults into their own media worlds, reversing conventional flows of cultural authority and generating a different kind of intergenerational space.

TI Between expertise and engagement: a qualitative study of Namibian
   geoscientists' views, attitudes, motivations, and objectives regarding
   public engagement with science
SO GEOSCIENCE COMMUNICATION
LA English
DT Article
ID COMMUNICATION TRAINERS; SCIENTISTS
AB Geoscientists are increasingly expected to engage with society on issues such as mining, groundwater management, energy transitions, and environmental sustainability, yet public engagement in the geosciences remains limited. This is largely due to reliance on one-way communication models and the tendency for geoscientists to communicate primarily within their own discipline. Drawing on qualitative interviews with Namibian geoscientists from government, industry, and academia, this study examines how geoscientists understand public engagement, how they perceive public audiences, and what motivates or constrains their participation. The findings reveal a strong reliance on deficit-model assumptions, including the belief that public resistance to geoscientific issues stems mainly from a lack of knowledge and that education plays a central role in fostering public trust and support. While participants expressed positive attitudes toward public engagement and confidence in their communication abilities, engagement was largely framed as informing and educating rather than listening, collaboration, or shared knowledge production. Structural barriers, including limited institutional support, lack of training, time constraints, and minimal incentives, further restrict meaningful engagement. At the same time, the study identifies emerging recognition of the importance of trust-building, mutual learning, and community involvement, particularly in contexts affected by resource extraction. The study argues that strengthening the role of geoscience in Namibian society requires moving beyond deficit-based communication toward dialogic, context-sensitive, and participatory engagement approaches.

TI Citizen science as a long-term environmental baseline: assessing impacts
   of a small dam removal in Montana, USA
SO GEOSCIENCE COMMUNICATION
LA English
DT Article
ID PEBBLE COUNTS; DATA QUALITY
AB As dam removals increase in frequency across Europe and North America, most research has focused on the impact of larger dam removals, despite the removal of small dams being much more common. There are hundreds of small dams in Montana, USA, and this research investigates impacts on stream ecology and morphology using citizen science data collected over eight years spanning before and after a 2020 small dam removal in Rattlesnake Creek. We analyzed pebble count grain size distributions and aquatic macroinvertebrate biotic indices from 2017 to 2024 to assess changes in sediment transport and macroinvertebrate population as well as evaluate the efficacy of citizen science for long-term stream monitoring. Our analysis includes comparisons of pre- and post-dam removal data collected from above and below the dam site. Our findings revealed no significant changes in grain size or macroinvertebrate index values between upstream and downstream reaches post-dam removal, suggesting that the removal of this small dam had minimal detectable impact on sediment transport and macroinvertebrate communities within the study period. Our study also demonstrates the capacity for citizen science programs to effectively collect robust and valuable datasets. This study underscores the importance of meticulous data management along with the potential for, and challenges of, citizen science for environmental research. We provide recommendations for "best practices" to improve future citizen science monitoring and informing decision-making for future dam removals, particularly for the nine dams further upstream within the Rattlesnake Creek watershed.

TI What students ask matters: LLM interaction depth, task quality, and
   immediate recall in higher education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Large language models; Learning analytics; Higher education; Knowledge
   recall; Explanation-seeking prompts; Process-outcome modelling
ID KNOWLEDGE
AB Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming higher education, yet evidence on how interaction patterns affect learning remains limited. This study examines whether explanation-seeking dialogue with an LLM is associated with task quality and immediate recall in a controlled learning session. Twenty-two postgraduate students completed a pre-test, an LLM-assisted neuroeconomics case task, and an immediate post-test. Fine-grained interaction logs captured per-turn telemetry, enabling extraction of Depth (proportion of "why/how/explain" prompts), Volume, and Pacing features. Results showed large immediate pre-post score gains (Cohen's d(z) = 2.12, p < .001). In the task-quality regression model, Depth was positively associated with task quality beyond baseline and Volume (beta = 6.27, p = .006), indicating that a one-standard-deviation increase in explanation-seeking prompts was associated with approximately six additional marks on a 0-100 scale. Depth was not associated with immediate recall (beta = - 0.014, p = .728); instead, gain scores were strongly associated with baseline knowledge, consistent with reduced headroom for improvement among students starting from a higher pre-test score (beta = - 0.161, p < .001). The findings indicate a dissociation between performance quality and short-term recall in LLM-supported study. This aligns with cognitive-psychology evidence that elaboration improves comprehension while retrieval practice consolidates retention. Pedagogically, the dissociation suggests that depth-oriented dialogue may need to be paired with deliberate memory-strengthening activities such as self-testing or spaced retrieval if comprehension gains are to translate into recall, although the present design does not test such activities directly. Methodologically, it contributes a replicable, privacy-preserving instrumentation pipeline linking conversational telemetry to learning outcomes. Limitations include single-group design, small sample (n = 22), immediate testing only, and keyword-based depth proxies. Future work should randomise assistance styles, incorporate delayed retention tests, and refine depth measurement through semantic coding.

TI Navigating neoliberalism: women leaders in Pakistani' higher education
   and the intersection of personal values and institutional demands
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF LEADERSHIP IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID FAMILY; MANAGEMENT; CONFLICT
AB The study investigates the complex interplay between women's personal values and neoliberal institutional demands in higher education leadership within Pakistan. Despite an increase in female participation in higher education, women remain underrepresented in senior leadership roles, constrained by both patriarchal norms and the market-driven, competitive frameworks of neoliberalism. TI Play, regulate, retain: The mediating role of self-regulation in
   playfulness and motor learning among kindergarteners
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Playfulness; Motor learning; Self-regulation; Invented letter task;
   Preschool children
ID DEVELOPMENTAL COORDINATION DISORDER; CHILDREN; SKILL; ACQUISITION;
   ATTENTION; SCHOOL
AB Background: Playfulness has been identified as a key factor in early childhood development, fostering creativity and cognitive skills. However, the specific role of playfulness in motor and graphomotor learning, and its underlying mechanisms, remains underexplored. Aims: This study aims to investigate the relationship between playfulness and motor learning in preschool children, with a particular focus on the mediating role of self-regulation. Sample: The study was conducted with a group of 120 Arab Israeli children in kindergarten, comprising an equal number of boys and girls (60 each), all between the ages of five and six. Conclusions: These findings underscore the importance of incorporating playful activities in early childhood education and therapeutic interventions to enhance motor skill acquisition and retention.

TI Starting Strong: Windows on Pre-Service Teachers' Wellbeing as They
   Transition to Higher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE initial teacher education; professional education; wellbeing;
   resilience; transition to higher education
AB This study explores pre-service teacher (PST) wellbeing and resilience as they transition into their first year in a university-based initial teacher education (ITE) programme, with a focus on how institutional, pedagogical, and relational supports facilitate this transition. Using a mixed-methods approach, data were collected from the 2024 cohort of PSTs through the Hua Oranga and Cantril wellbeing scales, the Professional Quality of Life Scale (ProQOL-5), Ego-resiliency Scale (ER89), and focus group interviews. TI AR-GenSTEAM: Generation of STEAM-Based Serious Games with Augmented
   Reality
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE augmented reality; interactivity; serious games; STEAM
ID EDUCATION; TEACHERS; DESIGN
AB STEAM education integrates science, technology, engineering, arts, and mathematics to foster interdisciplinary learning and support the development of 21st-century skills. However, implementing this approach requires the development of educational resources that meaningfully connect these disciplines. Augmented Reality (AR) can contribute to this effort by enabling interactive and immersive learning experiences. This paper presents AR-GenSTEAM, a generator for creating STEAM-based serious games with AR for web and mobile platforms. The generator follows a three-stage development process comprising analysis, configuration, and generation. Through this process, users select STEAM areas, target skills, game templates, AR resources, and an export platform to generate a serious game. A case study of Enkrypto, a serious game focused on encryption and decryption, is presented to illustrate the use of AR-GenSTEAM. A hybrid evaluation was conducted to evaluate the performance of AR-GenSTEAM and students' experiences with the AR component of the Enkrypto game. The generator successfully generated web applications in 90% of attempts and mobile applications in 80%, while students rated the AR component positively in terms of pragmatic quality, hedonic quality, and overall user experience.

TI AI Literacy and Self-Perceived Cognitive Learning Outcomes Among
   University Students in AI-Integrated Courses: Associations with
   Instructor Feedback and AI Use Indicators
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE AI literacy; self-perceived cognitive learning outcomes; AI-integrated
   education; instructor feedback; higher education; cognitive offloading
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly being integrated into university curricula, yet quantitative indicators of AI use reveal little about how learners use AI as a learning resource or what educational outcomes follow. This cross-sectional survey study of 212 university students enrolled in AI-integrated courses examined the associations of AI literacy, instructor feedback, and two single-item AI use indicators-the proportion of in-class AI use and total weekly AI use time-with self-perceived cognitive learning outcomes, measured across the six cognitive processes of the revised Bloom's taxonomy. Confirmatory factor analyses supported multidimensional and higher-order structures, but the cognitive domains overlapped substantially (interfactor correlations up to 0.943; HTMT up to 0.946), so domain-level distinctions should be interpreted with caution. When all predictors were considered simultaneously, only AI literacy showed a significant positive association (B = 0.615, beta = 0.593, 95% CI [0.475, 0.754], p < 0.001); the data did not provide evidence for independent associations of instructor feedback or the two AI use indicators, whose weaker associations may partly reflect their single-item measurement. AI literacy remained significantly associated with all six cognitive domains after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. These findings suggest-within the limits of a cross-sectional, self-report design-that the quantity of AI use and learners' competency to understand, evaluate, and self-regulate AI use are empirically distinct indicators that universities should measure separately.

TI Learning Analytics of Students' Interaction with ChatGPT in Programming
   Education: A Process-Oriented Analysis
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE ChatGPT; learning analytics; self-regulated learning; programming
   education; lag sequential analysis
AB Generative AI tools are now widely used in undergraduate programming, yet most evidence about how students use them comes from self-report rather than from observed behaviour. This study examined the sequential structure of students' ChatGPT (GPT- 4o, OpenAI)-supported programming work and the cognitive complexity of their queries. Screen recordings of 363 second-year students completing an individual Python 3.12 data-visualisation assignment were coded into 3985 activity episodes and analysed using descriptive statistics, lag-1 sequential analysis, and cognitive network analysis; because recordings capture actions rather than cognition, the coded categories are treated as behavioural indicators interpreted within, rather than as measurements of, the Self-Regulated Learning framework. Programming activities accounted for 63% of coded actions and ChatGPT interactions for 20%. Behaviour was organised around a troubleshooting cycle, the strongest association being between submitting error messages and reviewing ChatGPT responses (PCM -> RF, Yule's Q = 0.84, a descriptive association measure, rather than a transition probability, whose stability across students was not tested). ChatGPT use was concentrated in activities indicative of monitoring and control and was largely absent from planning and reflection. High-achieving students produced a higher proportion of deep-level submissions (32.2% vs. 19.2%) and a lower proportion of surface-level submissions (23.2% vs. 38.4%) than low-achieving students; because submissions are nested within students, this difference is reported as a property of the observed distribution rather than as an inferential finding. Comparisons computed at the level of the student were tested inferentially and reached significance with small effect sizes; comparisons computed at the level of coded actions or query submissions are reported throughout as observed properties of the aggregate distributions rather than as inferentially established differences. These episode-level findings support instructional scaffolding that structures query formulation and reflection.

TI Music Is the Space Between the Notes (Claude Debussy)-The Power of
   Connection: Exploring Motivations, Barriers and Relational Pedagogy in
   Adult Music Learning
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE adult music learner; creative facilitation; Self-Determination Theory;
   relational pedagogy; music; connection; motivation; barriers; coaching
AB This research endeavoured to capture the lived experiences and perspectives of adult music learners. A qualitative collective case study using creative facilitation approaches was adopted, as part of an established Community of Practice: Adult Learner Meet Up event, to capture the voice of the adult music learner in relation to their experience of learning music within SETU Music School. Following inductive, thematic data analysis, emergent findings provided an insight into the motivations of adult music learners, barriers to their learning and strategies that they felt support their learning. Through the lens of Self-Determination Theory, this paper provides evidence that adult music learners are intrinsically motivated. The research identified that a connection with the wider Music Community through Adult Learner Meet Ups provided peer support and helped to sustain motivation for adult learners. This research identified barriers that are specific to adult music learners, including time pressure, emotional vulnerability and comparisons to younger players. This paper posits that adopting a relational pedagogy including a coaching ethos can foster relationships and help to mitigate such barriers. Drawing on Debussy's metaphor of the "space between notes", this paper argues that while the development of musical knowledge and skills is important to adult music learners, their relationships with their peers and lecturers are equally significant. The adult music learner Community of Practice provided a space to foster these relationships and contributed to learners' motivation, engagement, and commitment to continued music learning. This paper will conclude by discussing how these findings could be applied to adult learners generally and highlight the importance of fostering connection in supporting adult learner retention and lifelong learning.

TI Are Prisoners Getting the Right Education? Exploring Teaching and
   Learning of Functional Skills Mathematics and English in England and
   Wales
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE prison; prison education; curriculum; mathematics; English
ID CRIME
AB This paper addresses education in adult prisons for learners age 18 and over. Global concerns exist about the quality of education in prisons. Studies highlight a range of issues including weak curricula, lack of access to technology-enabled learning, lack of learner engagement and an over-emphasis on the role of education in serving employment-related goals. The result of this across a range of jurisdictions is a curriculum that is dominated by English and mathematics and a lack of focus on vocational skills and training. These principles are subsequently synthesised to produce a potential pathway to reduce reoffending.

TI Understanding the role of perceived drivers and barriers in shaping
   entrepreneurial intentions: the mediating effect of perceived value
   among higher education students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE entrepreneurial intention; higher education; India; perceived
   complexity; perceived cost; perceived enjoyment; perceived immersion;
   perceived usefulness
ID INTRINSIC MOTIVATION; MODEL; PERCEPTIONS; ACCEPTANCE; VARIANCE; GENDER;
   EASE
AB Background and aim Despite the growth of entrepreneurship education and government support for start-up initiatives, Entrepreneurial Intention (EI) among higher education students is still very low in developing countries, such as India. Most of the existing models have studied the motivation and perceived barriers separately, and have not explored the integrative value-formation mechanism that links these factors together to influence the intention. In this study, Value Based Adoption Model (VAM) is extended to the domain of career decision to understand how students develop their entrepreneurial intentions by cognitively integrating perceived drivers (Benefits) with perceived barriers (Sacrifices) with the mediating variable of Perceived Value (PV) in selected districts of Tamil Nadu. Methods A structured questionnaire was administered to 310 undergraduate and postgraduate students across five districts of Tamil Nadu. The model incorporates three benefit dimensions Perceived Usefulness (PU), Perceived Enjoyment (PE), and Perceived Immersion (PI) and three sacrifice dimensions Perceived Cost (PC), Perceived Complexity (PX), and Technicality (PT) with PV mediating the path to EI. PLS-SEM via SmartPLS 4 was used for data analysis, including PLSpredict out-of-sample assessment. Results The measurement model demonstrated acceptable reliability (rho c >= 0.808) and convergent validity (AVE >= 0.584). PU (beta = 0.124, p = 0.004) and PI (beta = 0.136, p = 0.002) positively influenced PV (H1a, H1c supported); PE was not significant (H1b not supported). PC negatively influenced PV (beta = -0.165, p = 0.005; H2a supported). PX (beta = 0.528) and PT (beta = 0.334) showed significant but positive effects on PV, contrary to H2b and H2c, attributed to suppressor dynamics among correlated barrier constructs. PV strongly predicts EI (beta = 0.670, p < 0.001; R-2 = 0.449; H3 supported) and mediates key antecedent paths (H4a, H4c, H4d supported; H4b not supported). PLSpredict confirms positive Q(2)predict values for all EI indicators. Conclusion This study is among the first PLS-SEM-based investigations to apply VAM's benefit-sacrifice-value architecture to the entrepreneurship intention domain. Nine of thirteen directional hypotheses were supported as predicted. Findings offer actionable guidance for educators, policymakers, and incubation managers in Tamil Nadu and comparable developing-economy contexts.

TI From K-12 experience to MATATAG preparation: perceived pedagogical
   preparedness of Bachelor of Physical Education students

LA English
DT Article
DE Bachelor of Physical Education; K-12 curriculum; MATATAG curriculum;
   perceived pedagogical preparedness; physical education pedagogy;
   pre-service teachers
AB The Philippine basic education system is undergoing curriculum reform through the phased implementation of the MATATAG Curriculum, creating new demands for teacher education programs that prepare future teachers for Kindergarten to Grade 10. This study explored the experiences and perceived pedagogical preparedness of Bachelor of Physical Education (BPED) students who completed Senior High School under the K-12 Curriculum and are preparing for future teaching roles within the emerging MATATAG context. The study employed a qualitative descriptive design involving 24 purposively selected BPED students from a state university in Laguna, Philippines. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis. Findings indicated that participants viewed the additional two years of K-12 education as strengthening their academic preparation, confidence, critical thinking, and transition to higher education. However, inadequate facilities and instructional resources, uneven implementation, limited specialization opportunities, and variable experiential-learning opportunities constrained their perceived preparation. Participants emphasized stronger alignment between Senior High School and teacher education, practice-based preparation, continuous faculty development, and closer collaboration between teacher education institutions and basic education schools. The study demonstrates that BPED programs can serve as an important bridge between basic education reform and teacher preparation, particularly by integrating physical education-specific pedagogies, contextualized learning, safety, assessment, and resource-sensitive instructional strategies. Because participants were early-stage pre-service teachers and the study relied on self-reported perceptions from one state university, the findings represent perceived preparedness rather than observed teaching competence.

However, despite the crucial role of coordinating technical work in engineering practice, formal education often provides limited structured development of team coordination skills. In light of this, our research endeavors to understand team experiences and identify areas where coordination improvements can be made using the following research questions. (1) What are the teams' coordination commitments as team members reflected upon completing three computational modeling assignments across the different projects? (2) How are the commitments changing across the three projects? (3) What are some common patterns in teams' coordination commitments?Methods The study included 110 undergraduate students organized into 24 teams who engaged in three computational modeling and simulation projects as part of their thermodynamics course. Time Management was mentioned at similar rates across the three projects.Discussion These findings indicate that teams emphasized different coordination concerns across the projects. However, the observed differences were primarily descriptive; after adjustment for multiple comparisons, only the decrease in Scheduling and Meeting Coordination from Project 2 to Project 3 was statistically significant.

TI School principals' job satisfaction: individual, structural, and
   macroeconomic factors: a multilevel analysis using TALIS 2018 data
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE job satisfaction; school principals; individual factors; structural
   factors; macroeconomic factors
ID EXTERNAL ACCOUNTABILITY; DISADVANTAGED SCHOOLS; LATE CAREER; LEADERSHIP;

AB In a global context marked by increasing demands and challenges in attracting and retaining school leaders, understanding principals' job satisfaction is key to the sustainability of educational leadership. This study examines the factors associated with school principals' job satisfaction using international TALIS 2018 data and multilevel models that distinguish between the school and country levels.    lexical-semantic intervention
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION

AB This study examined the effectiveness of a linguistically and culturally adapted Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) intervention targeting lexical-semantic language development in preschool children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) in Kazakhstan. Given the non-randomized design and the link between group assignment and institutional site, the findings should be interpreted as preliminary quasi-experimental evidence of intervention-associated lexical-semantic gains rather than as definitive causal evidence.

AB Introduction The aim of the study was to assess the association between the integration of digital technologies and the learning outcomes, motivation, and cognitive development of students in the Faculty of Education.Methods The study employed a quasi-experimental pedagogical design using standardised testing before and after the implementation of IT tools, participant surveys, and comparative analysis between the experimental and control groups. AB Introduction Principal job satisfaction is an indicator of occupational wellbeing and leadership sustainability, yet international evidence on temporal change and organizational correlates remains limited.Methods Harmonized TALIS 2013, 2018, and 2024 principal records (n = 16,257) were used to obtain design-based estimates for 54-81 education-system-by-cycle cells. TI Adapting and measuring mathematical problem-solving ability among
   secondary school students: a Rasch model analysis
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE instrument; mathematical problem-solving; Rasch model; secondary school;
   validity
AB Problem-solving ability are essential competencies that students need to develop from elementary education to higher education. However, in developing countries such as Indonesia, the assessment of process-based problem-solving skills remains limited. Educational practices in Indonesia still focus more on outcome-based assessment rather than evaluating the problem-solving process itself. Therefore, this study aimed to develop and validate an instrument for assessing process-based problem-solving abilities among lower and upper secondary school students. This study employed an instrument development and validation research design using a quantitative approach. The instrument was adapted from textbooks aligned with the Merdeka Curriculum, Indonesia's current national curriculum. After the validation stage, the instrument was tested on 322 secondary school students from three schools located in a city on the island of Java. The collected data were analyzed using the Rasch model. The results showed that all adapted items fit the Rasch model and demonstrated good validity and reliability. Item reliability was high, while person reliability was sufficiently consistent in capturing differences in student responses. Item difficulty levels were classified into easy (28.7%), moderate (28.7%) and difficult (42.86%) categories. Lower secondary students generally succeeded in answering moderate items, whereas upper secondary students were more capable of solving difficult items. Student abilities were grouped into low (4.66%), moderate (87.26%) and high (8.07%) levels. The instrument showed no gender bias, although most items displayed bias across grade levels, likely due to differences in students' learning experiences. Overall, the Rasch model explained 44.7% of the variance, indicating that the instrument is unidimensional, valid and reliable for measuring process-based problem-solving ability that the instrument is suitable for research and assessment in mathematics education.

SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE citizenship; Kazakhstan; qualitative research; social responsibility;

AB This study explores Kazakhstani teachers' views on value-oriented education, citizenship, and social responsibility in the context of social, cultural, and technological change. TI 'It's here and we can't fight it': engineering faculty perceptions of
   generative AI, student use, and the future of engineering education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE engineering education; faculty; focus groups; generative artificial
   intelligence; higher education; student AI use
AB Engineering education faces a distinctive challenge from generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). Tools such as ChatGPT can now generate working code, solve multi-step quantitative problems, and produce technical reports, thereby performing tasks that coursework is intended to develop. However, faculty perceptions and responses to this shift remain understudied from a qualitative perspective. This study examined engineering faculty perceptions of GenAI and its influence on teaching and learning through three semi-structured focus groups with n = 16 faculty at a research-intensive university in the United States. Thematic analysis identified three overarching themes: faculty perceptions of AI as a technology, AI's impact on student learning and pedagogical practice, and faculty visions for the future of engineering education. Findings indicate that faculty engage with GenAI through a posture of reluctant engagement, accommodating AI not from conviction but from perceived inevitability, while expressing sustained concern about cognitive offloading, the erosion of productive struggle, and the disruption of established feedback and assessment systems. Faculty also described GenAI as a source of intragroup conflict in student teams and reported bearing the emotional and pedagogical costs of institutional policy gaps largely without coordinated support. Participants anticipated inevitable curricular redesign and reasserted the irreplaceable value of experiential, in-person, and mentorship-based learning. These findings provide a discipline-specific portrait of engineering faculty navigating a rapidly shifting educational landscape and underscore the need for institutional governance, professional development, and assessment redesign to transform individual adaptation into sustainable, equity-conscious pedagogy.

TI Student well-being: an integral definition and conceptual framework
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE definition; framework; intervention; student; university; well-being;
   student well-being; higher education
ID QUALITY-OF-LIFE; SOCIAL SUPPORT; UNIVERSITY-STUDENTS; COLLEGE-STUDENTS;
   MENTAL-ILLNESS; HIGH-SCHOOL; SATISFACTION; SENSE; INSTAGRAM; ADULTHOOD
AB Well-being is a widely used concept to characterize differences in how well students are feeling and doing. Yet, numerous conceptualizations of well-being exist, which hampers conceptual and empirical research on student well-being, and the development of measurement instruments of and interventions on students' well-being. To advance research and practice, we propose a definition and conceptual framework of student well-being that may serve as a basis for measuring, understanding, and promoting students' well-being. We formulated four guiding postulates based on philosophical underpinnings of established perspectives on well-being that guided the development of our definition and framework, which was further shaped by existing literature and the input from meetings with experts. We define student well-being as a multi-facetted concept that reflects a student's degree of positive or negative cognitive appraisal about and affective experience with the self. Student well-being comprises seven interrelated facets (i.e., meaning in life, self-esteem, autonomy, relatedness, sense of belonging, subjective health, body acceptance) grouped into three domains: psychological, social, and physical. The conceptual framework outlines predictors and outcomes of student well-being. We discuss implications of our definition and framework for science and practice, as well as outline several key avenues for future research on student well-being.

TI Addressing educational inequities through DI: a cross-national study of
   teachers' perspectives

DT Article
DE comparison; cross-country; DI; educational inequities; inclusive

ID DIFFERENTIATED INSTRUCTION; INCLUSIVE EDUCATION; STUDENTS; ABILITY;
   GENDER; EQUITY
AB Cross-national comparisons of differentiated instruction (DI) are often challenging because educational contexts vary across countries. Even so, DI consists of concrete pedagogical practices that teachers can use to tailor learning for all students, especially those at risk of educational disadvantage, which provides a strong basis for comparative inquiry. This study examines how teachers in Austria and Mexico enacted DI during the transition back to in person schooling after the COVID 19 pandemic. We used a qualitative design and conducted twenty semi-structured interviews with primary and secondary school teachers selected to capture variation in school level, subject area, and local context. At the same time, notable cross-national differences emerged in how these strategies were chosen and implemented, reflecting distinct institutional conditions and classroom constraints. The study contributes to comparative research on DI by identifying shared practices and context specific adaptations during a period of educational recovery. We discuss implications for policy and teacher professional development, including sustained coaching, time for collaborative planning, and targeted resources for students who experienced learning loss, and outline directions for future research.

TI The validity of school socio-economic status measures: how do indicators
   from TIMSS and PISA compare to national administrative data sources?
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Programme for International Study Assessment (PISA); Trends in
   International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS); Socio-economic
   status; Administrative data; Validation; Ireland; Disadvantage
ID ACHIEVEMENT; CONVERGENT
AB Background Policymakers and researchers collect data on student and school socio-economic background for various purposes, such as prioritising students from socio-economically disadvantaged backgrounds for additional resources, understanding the background characteristics associated with educational achievement, or monitoring the progress of policy reforms and initiatives. International large-scale assessments gather detailed information from participating students and school principals and use this to calculate composite measures of socio-economic status. At the same time, policymakers usually have access to national socio-economic indicators based on administrative data. Given the impact of socio-economic indicators on monitoring and shaping education policy, key issues related to the convergent and criterion-related validity of the international and national socio-economic measures are of concern to both policymakers and researchers.Methods In this paper, we compare socio-economic indicators from the 2019 Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study and the 2022 Programme for International Student Assessment with two key indicators used in policy-making in Ireland (the Pobal HP Deprivation Index and school participation in the Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools programme) and examine their associations. Analyses include correlations, linear and logistic regression, and multilevel modelling.Results Findings show strong associations between the socio-economic indicators examined, with stronger associations among indicators derived from aggregated student-level data (r approximate to 0.7) than among inherently school-level indicators (r approximate to 0.6). Principals' judgements about the proportion of disadvantaged students in their schools, collected via TIMSS and PISA, are found to be quite accurate insofar as these estimates align well with both national indicators and other ILSA-derived aggregated indicators. International indicators were more strongly predictive of achievement in mathematics than the national indicators, with the national indicators explaining little additional variance in TIMSS and PISA mathematics outcomes beyond the ILSA-derived SES indicators.Conclusions This paper provides valuable empirical validity evidence for both international, and Ireland's national, socio-economic indicators. The methodological approach presented here may also be valuable as a model for other countries participating in international large-scale assessments, particularly those that use their own administrative socio-economic data for policy-related decision-making.

TI Teaching problem solving in undergraduate physics courses: An
   endorsement for deliberate practice
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID EXPERT; KNOWLEDGE; STUDENTS; DESIGN; THINK
AB Developing expertlike problem-solving skills is a central goal of undergraduate physics education. In this study, we investigate the impact of teaching explicit problem-solving frameworks, combined with deliberate practice, on students' problem-solving approaches. Using multidimensional scaling to analyze students' decision-making patterns, we compare the similarity of students taught with these methods to physics experts and to students taught with traditional repeated practice. TI Ethnographic investigations of the emerging culture on departmental
   teams: Evidence of transforming physics faculty's practices and values
   around departmental change
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID DRIVEN DECISION-MAKING; ORGANIZATIONAL-CHANGE; PARTNERSHIPS; STRATEGIES;
   STAFF
AB Many organizations and researchers within the physics community have highlighted the need to improve undergraduate programs in areas such as pedagogy and the representation of marginalized students. Although many physics programs have actively attempted to address these challenges, the impact of these efforts has yet to be reflected broadly in the physics community. Our previous work highlighted standard cultural practices around the approach of physics faculty to educational change. We found that physics faculty often initiate educational change in an individualistic way that is rushed and ad hoc, while ignoring the use of formal evidence. To address this shortcoming, disciplinary organizations have developed initiatives like the Departmental Action Leadership Institute (DALI). In particular, DALI was developed to support physics faculty in becoming better change agents and learning effective leadership and collaboration practices to pursue educational change in their local programs. In our investigations of this institute, we developed case studies of five DALI physics programs. Each case study program followed the DALI recommendations and built teams following the Departmental Action Team (DAT) model to pursue local change. In this project, we studied and documented the emerging idioculture within these five DATs. We used a multiple case study methodology and collected data from multiple sources. We found that the emerging idioculture was different from the departments' dominant cultures in ways that support collaborative approaches to educational change. We also found that these DATs take a deliberate and strategic approach to the change effort by taking time to consider the context and feasibility of the change effort. Finally, we found that these DATs center formal evidence and students' voices in their decisionmaking processes. We present the results and discuss how the emerging idioculture in these DATs is situated within dominant departmental cultures of educational change.

TI Understanding Barriers to EPA Microassessment Completion Among
   Low-Assessment-Completion Surgical Faculty and Residents: A Two-Cohort
   Qualitative Study
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE entrustable professional activities; compe-tency-based medical
   education; qualitative research; sur-gical education; assessment;
   faculty engagement; resident education
ID PROFESSIONAL ACTIVITIES
AB OBJECTIVE: To identify barriers to entrustable professional activity (EPA) microassessment completion among surgical faculty and residents and to examine whether those barriers converge across roles and institutional contexts. DESIGN: Two-cohort qualitative study using semistructured interviews and focus groups. Faculty participants were identified through purposeful sampling of low-assessment-completion (LAC) attendings from a national EPA database (Firefly). Resident participants were recruited from 2 institutions using different EPA delivery platforms (Firefly and Society for Improving Medical Professional Learning [SIMPL]). Transcripts were analyzed using a constructivist-informed hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis framework with a structured code-book held open to emergent codes. Data saturation was confirmed using cumulative code analysis. Reporting follows the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ). SETTING: Faculty were identified through a national EPA database and practiced across 5 surgical subspecialties at a single academic medical center and its affiliated Veterans Affairs hospital; residents were drawn from 2 academic general surgery residency programs using different EPA delivery platforms. PARTICIPANTS: Five general surgery faculty and 10 PGY4 to 5 general surgery residents, including 2 maximum variation interviews with self-described high-and LAC EPA users. RESULTS: Across both cohorts, faculty and residents described EPA microassessment completion as an administrative act disconnected from the educational interaction it is intended to represent. Four faculty themes were identified: structural workflow limitations, misaligned perceived value, cultural and motivational gaps, and training and conceptual ambiguity. Five resident themes were identified: lack of perceived value, institutional priorities and accountability, feedback modality dissatisfaction, lack of training standardization, and selective initiation. The conceptual core uniting both cohorts was the conflation of formative feedback with formal entrustment assessment: both groups treated EPAs as duplicative of feedback conversations that had already occurred. Residents reported being more likely to request assessments after strong performances and less likely after challenging ones, while faculty described reluctance to document poor performance in a permanent record, producing bidirectional pressure toward a positively skewed entrustment signal. Platform architecture shaped engagement culture, with resident-initiated patterns predominating on SIMPL and attending-initiated patterns on Firefly. CONCLUSIONS: Low EPA microassessment completion rates among surgical faculty and residents reflect modifiable failures in workflow design, conceptual framing, and assessment culture rather than fundamental limitations of the EPA framework. The widespread conflation of formative feedback with formal entrustment assessment represents a conceptual gap that undermines the construct validity of EPA-generated data and must be addressed through targeted education before structural interventions can be fully effective. Electronic health record (EHR)-integrated assessment workflows, platform-agnostic sampling standards, and faculty and resident development focused on the distinct longitudinal function of EPA microassessments are needed to realize the construct validity and educational utility the framework is designed to provide. TI The healthy eating challenge: An experiential project for learning and
   applying behavior change theory
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
AB Introduction: Chronic diseases are largely driven by modifiable behavioral risk factors yet training in behavior change strategies remains limited. This study evaluated the Healthy Eating Challenge (HEC) as an experiential, nutrition-based intervention designed to develop behavior-change competencies in pharmacy students. Methods: The HEC was integrated into a psychiatric pharmacotherapy elective for third-year pharmacy students and implemented over nine weeks. The program included educational materials, breakfast recipes, self-monitoring tools, and individualized SMART objectives. Pre-and post-surveys assessed readiness to change, perceived facilitators and barriers, and engagement with behavior change techniques. Debriefing sessions were used to reinforce learning. Descriptive statistics were used for analysis. Results: Of 20 enrolled students, 16 completed the intervention and evaluation. After participation in the HEC, readiness for dietary behavior change increased from an average score of 59.4 to 64.9, with 68.8% of students indicating readiness to make a dietary change. Students demonstrated engagement with behavior change strategies, including self-monitoring, journaling, reflection, and goal setting. Nearly all participants (93.8%) developed individualized SMART objectives, with 86.6% reporting achievement or ongoing progress toward their goals. Nutrition knowledge, selfawareness, and structured planning emerged as key facilitators of behavior change, while time constraints remained the primary barrier. Conclusion: The HEC supported the development of foundational behavior change competencies among student pharmacists. By experiencing lifestyle modification challenges firsthand, students gain insight into patient barriers and develop skills applicable to patient-centered counseling. Experiential behavior change training may strengthen pharmacy curricula and better prepare future pharmacists to support lifestyle modification in accordance with treatment guidelines.

   community-based interviews and sequential active learning on student
   pharmacist actual and perceived knowledge, skills, and attitudes

DT Article
DE Pharmacy; Active learning; Simulation; Social determinants of health;

ID TEACHING SOCIAL DETERMINANTS; SIMULATION
AB Background: It is essential that student pharmacists are equipped with the knowledge and skills to identify and address social/structural determinants of health (S/SDH) in practice. This study assessed the impact of a S/SDH module on student pharmacists' academic performance and perceived knowledge/skills/attitudes in navigating S/SDH. Methods: A six-week simulation/problem-based learning module was developed as part of a spiraled S/SDH curriculum and immersed within second-professional year courses at two universities. In week 1, students viewed recorded interviews of community members with complex S/ SDH followed by structured debriefing. In weeks 2-6, students completed four virtual-simulations and four practicums inclusive of S/SDH. Impact was assessed through practicum performance and a 51-item pre/post-survey utilizing a 5-point Likert scale. Results: Nearly 99% of practicum attempts met the pre-defined competence threshold and more than 50% met the threshold for mastery. Pre- and post-survey response rates were 79% and 71%, respectively. Students agreed that the module enhanced their understanding and skills in navigating S/SDH and prepared them for practice (mean Likert scores exceeded 4/5). Mean (SD) scores for the perceived value of recorded interviews, virtual-simulations, and practicums were 3.9 (0.9), 3.7 (1.0), and 3.8 (0.8), respectively. Five of eight knowledge items and 10 of 12 skill items improved, while S/SDH-related attitude items remained unchanged. TI Analysis ofSafety Competency: A New Assessment ofStudent Learning
   Behavior
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE safety education; online learning; learningbehavior; MOOC
ID LABORATORY SAFETY; STUDENTS
AB Chemical laboratory safety is paramount for conducting effective experiments and safeguarding the health of researchers. Traditional teaching methods have often provided a limited perspective on students' laboratory safety competency assessment. In this work, we presented the data of our course, entitled "Laboratory Safety in Chemistry" from the MOOC platform, which contained six years of discussion forum. By analyzing these data, we explored a new approach to better understand students' safety competencies. Because discussion forums alone are hard to quantify, we integrated a data-driven approach to analyze learning behaviors. By effectively examining these learning behaviors, we were able to outline their cognitive safety competencies. Based on these findings, course modifications were implemented and received favorable feedback. These results indicated that targeted changes in course content may facilitate a progression from superficial awareness to a deeper comprehension of laboratory safety principles. It reflected the rationality of using the data-driven approach to help understanding students' learning behaviors, thereby optimizing the course and enhancing students' safety competencies. It further highlighted the potential of interactive and discussion-based approaches in addressing the evolving challenges of safety education. Representative examples of consistently engaging discussion questions are provided in the Supporting Information.

TI When Flory Meetsthe Nano-World: An Experiment Validatingthe
   Flory-Huggins Parameter via Block Copolymer Self-Assembly
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Polymer Chemistry;
   Collaborative/Cooperative Learning; Instrumental Methods; Micelles;
   Thermodynamics; Flory-HugginsParameter (chi)
ID POLYMER SCIENCE; SOLVENT; DEPENDENCE; LENGTH
AB Ask any student of polymer physics to define the Flory-Huggins parameter (chi), and they will likely recite a cornerstone concept in polymer physics courses for understanding the thermodynamics and phase behavior of polymer solutions and that a high chi value means immiscibility. Yet, few can connect this abstract number to the tangible nanoscale structures it governs. Herein, we describe a laboratory module that makes this connection unmistakable. Using a "phenomenon-driven" approach, students verify the theoretical implications of chi by observing changes in the length of cylindrical micelles (CMs) assembled from a block copolymer in mixed solvents. This teaching practice transforms the abstract chi parameter into observable and measurable experimental results, challenges students to think like scientists by moving "from phenomenon to essence", and trains them to use classical theory to guide and interpret experiments in complex systems. Consequently, student learning moves beyond rote memorization toward genuine research literacy.
