TI Efficient Fabricationof WLEDs for Undergraduate Laboratory:From
   Phosphors Synthesis to Device Assembly
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE White Light Emitting Diodes; Experimental Teaching Design; Coordination
   Compounds; Crystal Field Theory; Fluorescence Spectroscopy
ID CHEMISTRY
AB White light-emitting diodes (WLEDs), as the fourth-generation lighting source, possess remarkable advantages in terms of energy efficiency, environmental friendliness, and prolonged lifespan. Currently, commercial WLEDs mainly achieve warm white light with a low color temperature and high color rendering index by using blue LED chips coated with green and red phosphors. Incorporating the preparation of phosphors and the fabrication of WLEDs into undergraduate experiments is highly meaningful, as it allows students to comprehend the application and development trends of LEDs in modern lighting while experiencing the practical utilization of professional knowledge in both manufacturing and daily life. The experiment comprises three modules: synthesis of copper complexes, characterization and analysis of products, and assembly of light-emitting devices. The solution for synthesizing copper complexes can enable students to become more proficient in basic experimental operations, such as dissolving substances, decantation, centrifugation, and the principle of like-dissolves-like. By observing molecular structures and analyzing the fluorescence of the complexes, students can gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between the structural characteristics and the luminescent properties of copper complexes. In addition, the assembly process of WLEDs not only connects theory with practice but also enhances students' interest in learning by providing an engaging hands-on experience. The experiment encompasses innovative content, streamlined synthesis, observable phenomena, and a captivating assembly. Besides cultivating students' practical experimental skills, this experiment also fosters their professional identities. Therefore, this is a very attractive experimental teaching design that is particularly suitable for first-year students.

TI Creating Podcasts with Generative AI Using Google's NotebookLM to
   Supplement Prelab Activities in Undergraduate General Chemistry
   Laboratories
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE First-Year Undergraduate; Second-Year Undergraduate; Laboratory
   Instruction; Multimedia-Based Learning; Generative Artificial
   Intelligence
ID FRAMEWORK
AB Preparation for laboratory in STEM courses is essential to ensure that student learning outcomes are achieved and that the students can participate in the lab in a safe and meaningful way. Often lab preparation comes in the form of prelab assignments, which can range from reading introductory material to completion of an assessment related to tasks the student will be performing in lab. Podcasts are a popular tool for enhancing student learning experiences due to their accessibility for both educators and students. However, the creation of a podcast is often time-consuming, requiring significant effort by the instructor to write, record, and edit the audio file. The work herein discusses how the free version of Google's NotebookLM can be used to create podcasts using generative AI for a general chemistry laboratory. The podcasts were provided to students to supplement their prelaboratory background reading and preparation. Student survey questions focused on feedback about the AI podcasts, including their design and how helpful students felt they were for the course. Student survey responses are used to highlight the usefulness of traditional course material alongside the podcasts, potentially carving a path for their joint use rather than replacement of traditional resources. The feedback suggests that the use of AI-generated podcasts may be a helpful tool to improve lab preparation and enhance the student learning experience.

TI A Systematic Needs Assessment of Rotation-Specific Onboarding Practices
   in General Surgery Residency Training
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital app curriculum; surgery residency; surgical critical care
   fellows education; resident rotation onboarding; surgical education
ID BOOT CAMP; ACCREDITATION COUNCIL; INFORMATION-TRANSFER; TEACH ONE; SEE
   ONE; COMMUNICATION; CURRICULUM; COMPETENCE; TRANSITION; SIMULATION
AB Objective Systems-based practice is an Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education competency that requires understanding healthcare delivery systems and rotation-specific workflows. Yet surgical residents frequently transition across surgical subspecialties without adequate orientation, creating gaps that compromise educational quality, delay clinical integration, and threaten patient safety. No systematic assessment has characterized rotation-specific onboarding practices or quantified unmet trainee needs. We conducted a needs assessments hypothesizing that general surgery residents would report limited formalized, rotation-specific onboarding, frequent reliance on peer-led onboarding, and preference for easily accessible digital resources. Design This was a cross-sectional survey study. Setting The study was conducted across two academic level 1 trauma centers with general surgery residencies and surgical critical care fellowships. Participants General surgery trainees were enrolled at 2 institutions. The survey assessed onboarding exposure, delivery format, timing and consistency, role clarity, feedback mechanisms, and access to essential clinical resources. Statistical analysis employed 1-sample t-test for Likert-scale accessibility ratings and McNemar's test to compare current vs. preferred modalities with significance set at p < 0.05. Results Among 86 respondents (61.4% response rate, median age 30 years), most were junior residents (postgraduate year 1/2: 58.3%), categorical residents (73.3%), and male (57.0%). Over half (n = 45, 50.6%) of residents received zero rotation-specific onboarding. For those who received onboarding, the most common delivery formats were survival guides (36%), handbooks (19.8%), and in-person lectures (14.0%), typically provided by residents (58.5%) or faculty (41.5%). Material accessibility averaged 3.67 +/- 0.98 on a 5-point scale (p < 0.001), but only 32.6% reported materials were up-to-date and 20.9% reported consistent delivery across services. Trainees preferred smartphone app-based onboarding compared to the current receipt (p = 0.035). Less than half (41.9%) of respondents understood their roles and responsibilities at rotation start; of these, only 50% received explicit expectations before the rotation began. There was a significantly higher preference for formal one-on-one feedback than the proportion who received it (27 [31.4%] vs. 12 [14%], Delta = +17.4 pp, p < 0.001). Conclusions Substantial gaps exist between current onboarding practices and resident needs in general surgery training. Most residents lack formal, rotation-specific orientation, and existing materials are inconsistently delivered, infrequently updated, and primarily peer-led. These findings establish an urgent imperative for standardized, faculty-supervised, digitally-delivered curricula supporting Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education competencies.

TI From Quantity to Quality: A New Framework for Evaluating the Research
   Productivity of Residency Applicants
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE research; research productivity; plastic surgery; residency application;
   cumulative research con-tribution; geometric adaptive counting
ID DUPLICATE PUBLICATION; BIOMEDICAL-RESEARCH; RESEARCH ARTICLES;
   AUTHORSHIP; FULFILLMENT; CRITERIA
AB OBJECTIVE: With USMLE Step 1 becoming pass/fail, publication count has become an increasingly important metric that medical students strive to maximize for residency applications. This has resulted in the pursuit of less meaningful research and engagement in unethical research practices (e.g., gift authorship) by students. We present a new metric designed for use by residency program directors to better evaluate a student's cumulative research contribution (CRC). DESIGN: We conducted a cross-sectional study of all 2024 PGY-1 integrated United States plastic surgery residents' publication profiles. We utilized Elsevier's Scopus to identify each applicant's total number of publications and variables related to each publication including authorship rank, publication study design, and SCImago Journal Rank indicator. Two independent reviewers agreed upon study design classifications for each publication. We then developed a general CRC formula, which was used to create 48 CRC models that were used to calculate a CRC score for each applicant and compared the distribution of students' ranks using their CRC scores within each model versus total publication counts. We calculated the mean, median, standard deviation, and quartile coefficient of dispersion for the total publication count and for each CRC score distribution. We then performed Kendall's Tau-B rank correlation tests to assess the strength of association between total publication count and each CRC model, and to determine whether student rank order differed significantly across these ranking methods. PARTICIPANTS: We analyzed 194 PGY-1 integrated plastic-surgery residents and 1467 publications in total. RESULTS: The most frequently published study designs were retrospective cohort studies (n = 417). Mean publication count was 7.56 +/- 6.77. Applicants with larger authorship teams produced more publications, but their individual contribution to the publications declined. Ranking applicants with any of the 48 CRC models significantly reshuffled student ranking relative to total publication count (tau = 0.69-0.87; all p < 0.001) and widened the spread of the cohort distribution (quartile coefficient of dispersion 0.58-0.68 for CRC models vs 0.54 for total publication count). CRC per publication showed no association with total publication count (tau <= 0.06, p >= 0.18 for all CRC models), indicating that simply publishing more does not equate to higher scholarly value. Students working in small teams (<= 5 authors) achieved an average CRC score of 16.1, which was comparable to the CRC score of those in medium sized teams (5.01-10 authors) (p = 0.18). Students working in small teams (<= 5 authors) achieved an average CRC score per publication of 2.52, which was significantly greater than the CRC score per publication of those in medium sized teams (5.01-10 authors) (p = 0.013). Medium sized teams (5.01-10 authors) achieved an average CRC score per publication of 2.09, which was significantly greater than the CRC score per publication of 2.18 of those in large teams (>= 10 authors) (p = 0.013). CONCLUSIONS: Ranking residents by publication count versus a CRC score that takes into account the of the contribution of a researcher's publications yields a significant difference when ranking the profiles of students who have successfully matched into integrated plastic surgery residency.
   Given that no metric has been publicly created for use to rank medical student research profiles, we recommend that residency programs adopt ours or a similar CRC metric when evaluating applicants. Rather than relying solely on total publication count, this approach may help encourage students to engage in higher quality research and promote ethical research practices.

TI From theory to practice: A quasi-experimental study on the effects of a
   training program on the (de)motivating teaching styles of pre-service
   physical education teachers
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-determination theory; Circumplex model; Physical education teacher
   education; Mixed-methods study; Motivation
ID INTERVENTION; SATISFACTION; BELIEFS; SUPPORT; NEEDS
AB Background: During the Physical Education Teacher Education Master's program, pre-service teachers begin to shape their (de)motivating teaching styles. Although research with in-service teachers shows that improving these styles enhances students' motivation and learning, little is known about how they are developed during initial teacher education. Aims: Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and the circumplex model, this study examined the effects of a training program designed to improve motivating teaching styles while reducing demotivating ones. Samples: Two natural cohorts of pre-service Physical Education teachers. An experimental group (n = 28; Mage = 22.96; SD =1.45; 21.4% female) that received the training and a control group (n = 25; Mage = 23.80; SD = 2.25; 36.0% female) that followed the standard education. Method: A quasi-experimental mixed-method design was implemented. The experimental group was assessed at three time points (T1/T2/T3), and the control group at two (T1/T3). Results: Between-group differences emerged only for clarifying, which showed a more favorable evolution in the experimental group. Within-group analyses indicated partial and non-uniform changes. Prior to the practicum, the participative approach increased, while demanding and domineering decreased. After the practicum, these changes were not sustained, returning to baseline. Additionally, clarifying and guiding approaches improved across the program, and awaiting declined after the practicum, while attuning and abandoning remained stable. Qualitative findings corroborated these trends, revealing the potential and challenges of applying autonomysupportive strategies in authentic contexts. Conclusions: The results highlight the need for sustained support during practicum, stronger school-university collaboration, and practicum mentor involvement to consolidate lasting motivating teaching approaches.

TI Processing (Our)Differences: Characterizing NeurodivergentStudents'
   Experiences Learning Chemistry and Reasoning withRepresentations
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE General Public; Second-Year Undergraduate; Chemical Education Research;
   Organic Chemistry; Problem Solving/Decision Making;
   Alkanes/Cycloalkanes; Minorities in Chemistry
ID DISABILITY; STUDENTS; MODEL; DISORDER; ADHD
AB Neurodiversity refers to natural differences in how individuals process and respond to information. It includes established cognitive differences like attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorder, and specific learning disorders. These differences can become barriers in courses that are not set up to support neurodivergent (ND) students. To design more-inclusive learning environments, it is important to understand how ND students approach chemistry learning and problem-solving. This exploratory study investigated how ND and non-ND students reason through molecular representation tasks in organic chemistry. Eighty-six students completed 40 computer-based tasks requiring translation between wedge-dash diagrams and chair conformations. Each participant then completed a follow-up interview explaining their reasoning for 8 of the 40 tasks. Of the participants, 26 (similar to 30%) self-identified as ND, allowing for comparisons between groups for accuracy, confidence, time-on-task, and reasoning strategies. Our findings showed that while time-on-task and confidence did not differ substantially, ND students demonstrated lower accuracy and less productive reasoning strategies, including frequent answer switching and reliance on oversimplified rules. We also explored ND students' reflections on their chemistry learning experiences. Three major themes emerged: (1) ND students perceive meaningful differences in how they learn compared to peers; (2) multiple factors, such as attention span, visuo-spatial ability, and cognitive load, shape their learning; and (3) ND students develop personalized self-accommodation strategies to manage learning challenges. We discuss implications of these findings for instructors and administrators.

TI Reframing SecondaryChemistry Laboratory Instruction:A Critical Review of
   Pedagogical Aims, Affordances, and Trade-Offsin JCE and CERP Studies,
   2016-2025
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE chemistry education; secondary school; highschool chemistry; laboratory
   teaching; inquiry-basedlearning; microscale chemistry; green chemistry;
   virtual laboratories; remote experiments; STEMeducation
ID HIGH-SCHOOL-STUDENTS; FOOD DYE; CHEMISTRY; DESIGN; INQUIRY; SCIENCE;
   MIDDLE; IMPLEMENTATION; PERCEPTIONS; CATALYSIS
AB Laboratory instruction remains a central feature of secondary chemistry education because it links abstract chemical ideas to observable phenomena, supports practical skill development, and provides opportunities for scientific inquiry. In recent years, research on school chemistry laboratories has expanded across inquiry-oriented practical work, technology-supported and virtual laboratories, and green or microscale approaches. However, this literature is often organized by innovation type rather than by a shared pedagogical logic, making it difficult to compare what different laboratory designs are intended to accomplish, what they enable, and what constraints accompany their use. This paper presents a journal-bounded critical review of secondary chemistry laboratory instruction studies published in Journal of Chemical Education and Chemistry Education Research and Practice between 2016 and 2025. The review was guided by the analytical lenses of pedagogical aims, affordances, and trade-offs and informed by a transparent process of studies identification, selection, and coding. A total of 79 studies were included in the review. Rather than cataloging laboratory innovations by type alone, the review examines how different laboratory designs align with different educational purposes and how their pedagogical promise is shaped by classroom realities. Across the 79 studies, conceptual understanding remained a dominant aim, but many studies also emphasized inquiry, evidence use, scientific reasoning, student engagement, and, in some cases, equity and sustainability. Inquiry-oriented designs, digital and sensor-based approaches, and green or microscale formats each offered distinctive pedagogical affordances. At the same time, these benefits were frequently accompanied by trade-offs involving time, curriculum pressure, teacher facilitation demands, resource availability, technology access, and uneven implementation conditions. This review shifts attention from laboratory formats alone to the pedagogical decisions that shape laboratory teaching within a bounded but influential subset of chemistry education research. It argues that the value of a laboratory design lies less in novelty than in its alignment with intended learning goals under real instructional conditions. The findings have implications for classroom practice, curriculum design, teacher education, and future research on secondary chemistry laboratory instruction.

TI MISSION: EPA Possible-Gamifying EPAs to Increase Engagement
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE entrustable professional activities; resident education; entrustment;
   competition
ID ENTRUSTABLE PROFESSIONAL ACTIVITIES; GAMIFICATION; COMPETITION;
   PARTICIPATION
AB OBJECTIVE: General surgery residency programs have implemented entrustable professional activities (EPAs) into daily feedback, however, consistent engagement remains a challenge. This study aims to increase resident engagement EPAs with entrustable through a year-long, team competition designed to promote meaningful participation and sustained EPA use. DESIGN: "MISSION: EPA Possible" is a point-based team competition rewarding residents for EPA completion, with extra points awarded for obtaining EPAs in areas historically lacking in engagement. An AI chatbot (Copilot) evaluates EPAs within the ABS app and calculates team scores using a predefined rubric. Residents are evenly divided into teams of four, each led by a resident EPA champion. Quarterly, the top team earns a $150 dinner while the top individual resident receives a half-day off clinical duty. All statistical analyses were conducted in SAS Version 9.4.1. SETTING: One general surgery residency program during the 2025 to 2026 academic year. PARTICIPANTS: Clinical general surgery residents (n = 19 eligible, divided evenly into five study teams). RESULTS: Total EPAs completed increased 12.3% in the first 9 blocks of AY25-26 compared to AY24-25. The average amount of EPAs collected per resident was 42.7, a 24% increase from 34.4 EPAs per resident preintervention. Residents rather than faculty initiated the majority of EPAs postintervention at 77% compared to 41% during AY24-25. Team success strongly correlated with EPA champion participation, with leaders of the top 5 teams completing 44, 31, 14, 24, and 3, respectively, during the first quarter. Net gain of 12 new attendings increased their number of EPAs completed, with 3 new attendings involved who had never collected an EPA preintervention. CONCLUSIONS: Gamifying EPAs through a team-based competition is an effective, low-cost method tailorable to any program looking to improve or maintain EPA engagement. MISSION: EPA Possible highlights that leveraging competition, peer leadership, and targeted incentives can effectively promote resident ownership. ( J Surg Ed 83:104109. TI Faculty leadership and psychological safety: a qualitative evaluation of
   a graduate gross anatomy course redesign
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Anatomy education; Graduate education; Learning environment;
   Psychological safety; Qualitative research
ID LEARNING-ENVIRONMENT
AB Psychological safety, the shared belief that an environment supports interpersonal risk-taking, is fundamental to engagement and learning in graduate education. This study examined student perceptions of psychological safety and faculty engagement following a redesign of a graduate-level gross anatomy course. A free-response descriptive analysis was conducted using open-ended comments from 88 students enrolled in a 13-week course in the Master of Biomedical Sciences program at Rutgers University. Evaluation responses were thematically analyzed using Moos' framework of learning environments, emphasizing institutional support, faculty-student relationships, and peer interactions. Coding was completed by a human reviewer and verified with AI-assisted text analysis. Students consistently emphasized that faculty accessibility, mentorship, and humour contributed to a psychologically safe learning environment. Themes aligned with Moos' framework, with faculty presence identified as the central factor linking the pillars of institutional support, relationships, and peer community. Students valued structured communication, consistency, and active learning strategies, particularly team-based learning that fostered belonging and collaborative accountability. Findings indicate that intentional faculty engagement and communication play essential roles in shaping psychologically safe environments in graduate education. Leadership characterized by approachability, structured support, and relational responsiveness enhances confidence, belonging, and meaningful learning outcomes for graduate students.

TI Equity-sensitive evaluation of networked improvement communities: A
   multilevel, replicable framework linking participation intensity to
   reading growth
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Networked Improvement Communities; Equity-Sensitive Evaluation;
   Difference-in-Differences; Educational Improvement; Reading Achievement
ID BILINGUAL EDUCATION; SCHOOL IMPROVEMENT; LANGUAGE; INSTRUCTION; SCIENCE;
   ACCOUNTABILITY; STRATEGY; PROGRAMS; STUDENTS; QUALITY
AB Networked Improvement Communities (NICs) are widely adopted to support instructional improvement at scale, yet rigorous and equity-sensitive evaluations of their student-level impacts remain limited. This study presents a replicable framework for estimating the association between NIC participation and changes in school-level reading performance. Using a multi-year panel of publicly available assessment and demographic data (2017-2024), we combine coarsened exact matching with difference-in-differences models incorporating school and year fixed effects. AB Mathematics in Industry Study Groups have operated worldwide for more than five decades, yet their educational impact has rarely been evaluated systematically. This study evaluates the stakeholders' perceptions of Mathematics in Industry Study Group - South Africa (MISG-SA) as a research-based learning intervention through parallel surveys of postgraduate students and early-career researchers (n = 40), academic mentors (n = 11), and industry representatives (n = 6) across two editions (2025-2026). TI Engaging future scientists: the effect of science museum visits on high
   school students' science identity development
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF STEM EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Science identity; Informal science learning; Science museums;
   Extracurricular learning
ID DOUBLY ROBUST ESTIMATION; EXPERIENCES; PARTICIPATION; EDUCATION
AB Background Expanding participation in STEM fields has been a longstanding national priority, with growing attention to informal learning environments as contexts for fostering students' science identity. Science museums offer hands-on, inquiry-based experiences that complement formal classroom learning, yet large-scale quantitative evidence on whether museum visits contribute to science identity development remains limited. This study addresses this gap by examining whether visiting science museums or planetariums during high school is associated with stronger science identity at the end of eleventh grade. Grounded in science identity theory and situated expectancy-value theory, the study applies a quasi-experimental design combining inverse probability of treatment weighting with doubly robust estimation to nationally representative longitudinal data from the High School Longitudinal Study of 2009 (HSLS:09), with an analytic sample of 7,290 students across 935 high schools.Results Students who visited science museums or planetariums between ninth and eleventh grade reported significantly higher science identity at the end of eleventh grade than comparable peers who did not visit, even after adjusting for baseline science identity, demographic characteristics, and a comprehensive set of school- and student-level covariates. Propensity score analyses revealed a steep socioeconomic gradient in museum visitation, with students from the highest SES quintile more than twice as likely to visit as those from the lowest. Women and Latino students were more likely to visit science museums, yet they reported significantly lower science identity than male students and the broader student population. Sensitivity analyses confirmed that the estimated treatment effect was robust to plausible levels of unobserved confounding.Conclusions and implications These findings suggest that visiting science museums during high school can meaningfully support students' science identity development. However, these benefits are embedded in a stratified opportunity structure that distributes access unevenly across socioeconomic, gender, and racial lines. Implications for equitable informal science education and directions for future research are discussed.

TI Assessing knowledge, use, quality, and effectiveness of self-regulated
   learning strategies - introducing the KUQE-SRL
SO METACOGNITION AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-regulated learning; Strategy knowledge; Strategy use; Strategy
   quality; Strategy effectiveness; Upper secondary school
ID MOTIVATIONAL REGULATION; METACOGNITIVE KNOWLEDGE; STUDENTS; ACHIEVEMENT;
   ALPHA
AB Self-regulated learning (SRL) is a process in which learners plan, monitor, and reflect on their learning while adaptively using cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational strategies. It involves strategy knowledge, that is, understanding what strategies are available and when and how to apply them effectively. However, even students who possess substantial strategy knowledge do not always translate it into consistent, effective strategy use. The present study developed a new test instrument to efficiently assess upper secondary school students' strategy knowledge, strategy use, strategy quality, and strategy effectiveness in the domain of SRL (KUQE-SRL, "cookie-SRL"). After an expert validation study (N = 16), the data of N = 1650 upper secondary school students were used to assess the reliability and validity of the KUQE-SRL. Supporting convergent validity, all the KUQE-SRL subscales were significantly positively interrelated. Furthermore, supporting criterion validity, they all showed comparable and predicted associations with external variables such as mindset, stress, gender, and academic achievement. While all the KUQE-SRL subscales were positively associated with both SRL growth and SRL relevance mindset, they were all negatively associated with academic stress. Girls outperformed boys, and the KUQE-SRL was positively associated with academic achievement, largely confirming prior studies' findings. By introducing the KUQE-SRL, the present work aims to help close the gap between strategic knowledge and effective strategy use.

TI What Promotes and Enables EFL Classroom Engagement? Evidence From
   PLS-SEM and Necessary Condition Analysis
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE autonomy support; classroom engagement; EFL learning; foreign language
   classroom anxiety; necessary condition analysis; PLS-SEM; teacher
   clarity
ID ANXIETY; STUDENTS; ENJOYMENT; CLARITY; CHINESE
AB Classroom engagement is central to English as a foreign language (EFL) learning because many learners rely heavily on classroom instruction for language input, interaction, feedback and communicative practice. This study examined how teacher autonomy support, teacher clarity and foreign language classroom anxiety (FLCA) are associated with EFL students' classroom engagement. A total of 487 undergraduate EFL learners in China completed a questionnaire measuring perceived autonomy support, teacher clarity, FLCA and classroom engagement. Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to test the direct and indirect relationships among the variables, and necessary condition analysis (NCA) was conducted to identify whether autonomy support, teacher clarity and low FLCA were necessary conditions for achieving high classroom engagement. The PLS-SEM results showed that autonomy support and teacher clarity were positively associated with classroom engagement and negatively associated with FLCA. FLCA was negatively associated with classroom engagement and mediated the relationships between both teaching-related factors and engagement. Teacher clarity showed a relatively stronger direct and indirect role than autonomy support. The NCA results further indicated that autonomy support, teacher clarity and low FLCA were all necessary conditions for high classroom engagement. The bottleneck analysis showed that the required levels of these conditions generally increased as the target level of engagement became higher, with low FLCA becoming especially important at the highest engagement level. These findings highlight that EFL classroom engagement can be promoted through English teaching practices that combine autonomy-supportive task design, explicit instructional guidance and anxiety-sensitive support for classroom communication.

TI EFL Learners' Well-Being Affected by Their Self-Efficacy and Resilience
   in AI-Integrated Learning Environment
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence-based context; EFL learners; resilience;
   self-determination theory; self-efficacy; well-being
AB With the advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the academic context, the traditional learning settings have been changed to advanced instruments that boost the learners' achievement. A critical factor of learners' achievement in AI-based settings is Psychological Well-being (PWB). Nevertheless, detecting the effect of mental factors such as resilience and self-efficacy on PWB in these settings is a recent issue in teaching because enhancing these constructs is critical for both educational success and PWB in digital EFL settings. Through Self-determination theory (SDT), this study seeks to examine the interplay among PWB, self-efficacy and resilience. Both self-efficacy and resilience were identified as significant predictors of PWB. Self-efficacy emerged as the stronger predictor, uniquely accounting for 21.81% of the variance in PWB scores, while resilience explained 14.52% of the variance independently. Based on the results, the two mental concepts have a crucial and statistically significant effect on how meaningfully and actively learners take part in AI-based settings. The findings contribute to the broader view of SDT's utilization in AI-based settings, paving the way for subsequent studies on motivational aspects in such settings.

TI Pre-Service English Teachers' Reported Roles and Practices in Promoting
   Self-Regulated Learning During the K-12 Practicum
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE K-12 education; pre-service teachers; professional development;
   self-regulated learning; SRL strategies
ID PERCEPTIONS; STRATEGIES; MOTIVATION
AB This study examines pre-service English teachers' reported roles and practices in promoting self-regulated learning (SRL) in K-12 classroom contexts during their practicum, as well as the challenges they encounter. Adopting a multidimensional view of SRL encompassing cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, and behavioural strategies, the study involved three pre-service English teachers undertaking their practicum in K-12 settings with prior teaching experience in either state or private schools. TI Governing generative AI in higher education: emerging policy approaches
   and support ecosystems at innovative US Universities
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL FOR EDUCATIONAL INTEGRITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Generative AI; ChatGPT; AI policy; Academic
   integrity; Higher education; Institutional guidance; Educational
   technology
AB This study examines how the 50 U.S. universities ranked as most innovative by U.S. News & World Report articulate policy, guidance, and support for generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in teaching and learning. Using qualitative document analysis and inductive thematic analysis of official institutional websites, the study identifies five convergent patterns: instructor-led, syllabus-level governance; disclosure and attribution expectations; privacy-oriented data guardrails and vetted tools; caution toward AI-detection systems; and expanding investment in AI literacy. It also identifies important divergences in default permission stances, the maturity of enterprise governance, and tooling strategies, including campus-hosted platforms and consumer tools governed by risk controls. Across institutions, GenAI support is distributed through teaching centers, libraries, IT/security units, and academic integrity offices. The findings suggest that academic integrity in the GenAI era is shifting from a primarily punitive model toward a pedagogy-first ecosystem that combines clear expectations, assessment redesign, equitable access to vetted tools, and iterative governance. The study offers an early comparative baseline for longitudinal tracking and evidence-informed institutional policy design.

TI From learning analytics to educational interventions: enhancing
   decision-making and learning design
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning analytics; Trustworthiness; Educational intervention; Enablers;
   Learning design; Decision-making; Artificial intelligence
AB Since the early development of learning analytics (LA), the cyclical nature of the process that starts with learning data and ends with educational interventions has been widely acknowledged. However, while LA research abounds, and LA practices are becoming more widespread, the final step of the cycle - introducing educational interventions - remains a challenge. The recently revised definition of LA puts a stronger focus on actionable insights to enhance learning and teaching. Recognizing that only trustworthy LA presents a basis for meaningful educational interventions, we conducted a study relying on group decision-making to explore and determine the key enablers of LA-based educational interventions. Our findings revealed seven enablers: institutional strategic orientation, pedagogical & other research foundations, available resources, pedagogical support, ethics & data governance, stakeholder engagement, and quality assurance. These enablers provide a foundation for the development and use of trustworthy LA systems to support data-informed decision-making, learning design, and educational change.

TI Moral disengagement and fear of retaliation: why adolescents choose to
   be passive bystanders to school bullying
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE School bullying; Bystander behavior; Moral disengagement; Fear of
   retaliation
ID VICTIMIZATION; BEHAVIOR; MECHANISMS; CHILDHOOD; RESPONSES; EMOTIONS;
   EXERCISE; JUDGMENT
AB This study examined the potential functional overlap between fear of retaliation and moral disengagement as justifications for peer bystander inaction in school bullying. Although often treated as distinct barriers to intervention, the study investigated whether fear of retaliation could function as a self-exonerating justification to reconcile inconsistencies between one's moral standards and passive behavior, similar to moral disengagement, and whether the two constructs empirically overlap. 163 students (aged 15-16) justified their decisions about defending victims in hypothetical school bullying scenarios. Justifications included fear of retaliation, moral disengagement, downplaying of risk, and moral engagement. Results from linear mixed-effects models showed convergence between fear- and disengagement-based justifications across phases, with endorsements of disengagement increasing under conditions involving cues suggestive of social support. Gender-stratified analyses further indicated that this convergence occurred more consistently among female participants. The findings refine theoretical models of bystander behavior and suggest that fear-based justifications can sometimes serve self-exculpatory functions in situations involving cognitive dissonance. Therefore, interventions may benefit from addressing both fear- and disengagement-based justifications for inaction to promote peer intervention in schools.

TI In Redefining the Capital(s): Fanon and Monopolised Eurocentric
   Mathematics Versus the Collective Power of Mathematics in the Margins
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE power; capital; knowledge colonization; Eurocentric mathematics;
   indigenous mathematics knowledge
ID EDUCATION
AB This paper judges Eurocentric mathematics and its role in sustaining colonial inequalities. Drawing on Fanon's work and a redefined concept of capital, we highlight the taken-away power (and knowledge) within margins, such as Indigenous communities, which influences the maintenance or diminution of the capital of taken-for-granted social structures. We present two examples. The first highlights an initiative that is reclaiming Indigenous mathematical knowledge by actively resisting colonization. The second illustrates the dangers of seemingly well-intentioned initiatives that inadvertently reinforce knowledge colonization, despite translating workbooks into Indigenous languages. We conclude by emphasizing the need to move beyond simply including knowledge from the margins in the existing Eurocentric framework, and to instead recognize and build on the transformative power of those margins to reshape and redefine the very nature of capital, power and knowledge.

TI Comparing Parent-Child Shared Reading and Children's Understanding of
   Non-Rhyming, Rhyming, and Magazine Information Texts: An Exploratory
   Study
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE genre; magazines; inference; rhyme; preschoolers; early literacy
ID PICTURE BOOKS; COMPREHENSION; STORYBOOK; ALOUDS; SKILLS; TALK
AB The home and preschool settings serve as important contexts for children's early language and literacy development. There is limited research on parent-preschooler shared reading and children's comprehension of information texts that vary in their format, structure, or mode of presentation. Comparing different types of information texts can help identify which features are associated with particular forms of parental scaffolding and children's understanding, be used to guide parents, and perhaps find ways to promote children's comprehension of these important text types. As such, this exploratory quantitative study examined shared reading of non-rhyming, rhyming, and magazine information texts and children's listening comprehension, taking into consideration parental education, children's age and gender, frequency of reading information texts at home, and total parents' words in the interaction. The participants were 63 children (28 boys and 35 girls) and one of their parents (55 mothers and 8 fathers). On average, the children were 5 years, 11 months old (SD = 10.18 months). Data were collected in January-February of 2021 during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Parent-child dyads participated in three recorded online meetings, sharing two texts during each meeting and six texts in total: two non-rhyming information texts, two rhyming information texts, and two information magazine texts. Following each text, children answered two literal and two inferential comprehension questions. Negative binomial regression with generalized estimating equations revealed that overall, parents tended to ask more open questions and included significantly more elaborations and references to illustrations when reading the non-rhyming information texts. Children answered significantly more literal than inferential questions for both the non-rhyming and magazine texts compared with the rhyming texts. Various parent and child characteristics predicted parent talk and children's comprehension. Results highlight how adult, child, and text characteristics can relate to the shared-reading discourse and children's understanding. Future studies should be conducted to replicate and extend these findings.

TI A Problem-Level Cognitive Framework for Analyzing Learning Performance:
   An Empirical Application in AI-Supported and Teacher-Mediated Statistics
   Instruction
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE cognitive framework; problem-level analysis; cognitive difficulty;
   statistical reasoning; AI-supported instruction; learning performance
ID INTELLIGENT TUTORING SYSTEMS
AB Students with similar overall test scores may nevertheless succeed or struggle with very different kinds of problems. Aggregate performance measures can conceal these differences when assessment problems require different forms of reasoning or different levels of structural complexity. Existing cognitive theories and educational taxonomies describe important aspects of knowledge, reasoning, and complexity, but were not designed to classify individual problems simultaneously according to these two characteristics. This study therefore develops a purpose-built Problem-Level Cognitive Framework that represents assessment problems along two analytically independent dimensions: the dominant reasoning required for a conceptually adequate solution-Formal, Procedural, Theoretical, or Critical-and the structural complexity of the minimal valid solution path, expressed through seven ordinal difficulty levels (D1-D7). The framework was empirically examined using semester-long data from 121 undergraduates enrolled in one of two instructional conditions: AI-supported or teacher-mediated introductory statistics instruction. Binary outcomes for each student-problem pair were analyzed using generalized linear mixed-effects models with crossed random effects for students and problems. Successful problem solving varied substantially across reasoning dimensions, difficulty levels, and assessment timings. In contrast, instructional condition made little explanatory contribution, and neither the condition-by-reasoning nor the condition-by-difficulty interaction was significant. The framework thus revealed a stable cognitive organization of performance across two substantially different instructional environments, while also identifying pronounced variation among cognitively differentiated problems. By separating the form of reasoning governing a valid solution from the structural complexity of the required solution process, the framework transforms heterogeneous assessment problems into cognitively comparable analytical units. It provides an operational basis for investigating problem-level performance structures and for examining their stability across learners, assessments, instructional environments, and educational domains.

TI Mapping Teacher Preparation Priorities for Inclusive Education: A Group
   Concept Mapping Study
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE inclusive education; methodology; teacher training; training needs
ID PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; UNIVERSAL DESIGN; SELF-EFFICACY; CLASSROOMS;
   METHODOLOGY
AB The need to strengthen teacher preparation for inclusive education has become an international priority. Despite the growing body of research on inclusive education, few studies have empirically identified and prioritised teacher preparation needs from the perspective of key stakeholders. This study employed Group Concept Mapping (GCM) to explore the teacher preparation priorities identified by primary school teachers and teacher educators specialising in inclusive education. Through collaborative idea generation, sorting, and rating processes, participants identified and prioritised key areas for teacher preparation. The findings revealed both shared priorities and differences between groups. While primary school teachers tended to associate diversity more closely with learning difficulties and support needs, teacher educators adopted a broader understanding linked to learner variability and participation. Across both groups, practical and experiential preparation emerged as the most highly valued dimension of inclusive teacher education. Participants also emphasised the importance of inclusive pedagogies, Universal Design for Learning, inclusive assessment, collaborative practices, and knowledge of learning difficulties and support needs. Overall, four shared training domains were identified: practical preparation, theoretical preparation, teachers' professional skills, and personal and interpersonal competences. The findings provide a stakeholder-informed map of teacher preparation priorities that may support the revision of initial teacher education and continuing professional development programmes for inclusive education.

TI Drawing Sustainability: Students See Dimensions but Miss Systems
   Thinking-Exploring Learning Progressions in Education for Sustainable
   Development
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE systems thinking; ESD; multidimensionality; Conceptual Metaphor Theory
   (CMT); students' conceptions; Model of Educational Reconstruction (MER)
AB This study examines how students aged 10-20 conceptualize Education for Sustainable Development (ESD), focusing on their ability to think multiperspectively and justify decisions multidimensionally. In a classroom-based teaching experiment, 131 high school students from Lower Saxony completed a drawing task visualizing sustainable village transformations, followed by interviews with twelve participants. Their negotiation processes, verbal responses, and drawings were analyzed using qualitative content analysis. The visualization of village transformations functions as a biology-didactic ESD activity, where students apply decision-making and problem-solving strategies to address biological system levels (e.g., individuals, populations, ecosystems) and their interconnections (trophic levels, food webs, biodiversity). Results indicate age-related differences: students in grades 5-7 primarily emphasized social and ecological aspects, designing idealized living spaces for themselves. Upper-secondary students (grades 11-13) incorporated societal, political, and economic considerations, prioritizing economic development. However, no consistent relationship between multiperspectivity and multidimensional reasoning was identified. Based on these findings and related research, the study advocates integrating systems thinking with a comprehension-oriented approach, combining the Conceptual Metaphor Theory (CMT) and the Model of Educational Reconstruction (MER). This aims to address the complexity of ESD more effectively, avoiding oversimplified, monocausal narratives that undermine the multidimensional nature of sustainable development.

TI Competently Mastering Practising Phases in Inclusive Physical Education:
   Development of a Draft Sub-Competency Profile for Physical Education
   Teachers
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE PE teacher training; diversity; student-centered teaching
AB Research on the specific competencies teachers need to design and guide practising phases in inclusive physical education (PE) is limited. This study aimed to develop a draft of a PE teachers' sub-competency profile for planning and supporting during practising phases in inclusive PE classes, based on an integrative understanding of competency as a continuum. A corpus of 104 lessons (at 45 min each) of videographed PE classes was created to analyze real daily teaching situations. Using an interpretive analytical approach, performances, situation-specific skills, and dispositions were examined within and across 10 different cases of practising phases and reflexively evaluated at the case level. This led to two key partial requirements: (1) identifying the need for intervention and evaluating the effectiveness of measures, and (2) developing and implementing supportive measures. Moving beyond a technological view of as mere drilling, teachers' actions in inclusive PE need to reflect a paradigmatic shift from focusing on the aim of practising to the practising individuals themselves.

TI Building Cultural Competence: Bridging 'Āina and STEM in an Elementary
   Classroom
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE cultural competence; Hawai'i culture-based education; STEAM (science;
   technology; engineering; arts; mathematics); critical making; mo'olelo
   (storytelling); place-based learning; productive struggle
ID EDUCATION
AB This qualitative case study explores how two elementary classrooms of predominantly Pacific Islander students (the majority of whom identified as Native Hawaiian) worked toward developing their cultural competence through participation in an interdisciplinary classroom-based learning experience focused on Hawaiian culture-based STEAM and maker learning. Over a four-unit series focused on wildfire prevention, watersheds, and traditional mo'olelo (storytelling), students engaged in collaborative, place-based learning. Findings reveal that cultural and academic competence were fostered through three primary mechanisms: integrating ancestral storytelling as a pedagogical tool; grounding academic content in hyper-localized ecological contexts; and navigating the "productive struggle" caused by the lack of any Pacific Island cultural representation in standard digital tools like Scratch and Canva. By adapting technologies to reflect their own identities, students simultaneously advanced their digital literacies and academic skills in science and language arts while honouring their heritage. This study underscores the importance of viewing cultural and STEAM learning as concurrent, mutually reinforcing processes. Our bounded case in particular highlights the possibility of how, when educators centre culture-based learning, classrooms can become spaces of cultural reclamation while supporting necessary academic competencies, helping to bridge the gap between student identity and the compulsory educational system.

TI Beyond Strategy Use: Examining Strategy Stability in Complex Problem
   Solving Through Logfile Data
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE complex problem solving; logfile data; VOTAT strategy; strategy
   stability; transition probability analysis
ID ACQUISITION
AB Complex problem solving (CPS) is a key educational outcome in technology-rich environments. Previous logfile studies have demonstrated that effective exploration strategies are associated with higher CPS performance. However, little is known about whether students can sustain effective strategy use across successive problem-solving tasks. This issue is important because strategy stability may represent a distinct dimension of CPS skill that is not captured by static indicators of strategy use alone. This study examined students' Vary-One-Thing-At-A-Time (VOTAT) strategy use across eight computer-based MicroDYN scenarios. A sample of 197 secondary school students from a through-train school in Macao completed the assessment. Exploration behaviours were coded as no VOTAT, partial VOTAT, or full VOTAT. Latent class analysis identified strategy classes, while transition-probability analysis examined the stability and change in strategy use across adjacent tasks. Three strategy classes emerged: proficient strategy users (65.5%), low strategy users (20.3%), and intermediate strategy users (14.2%). Proficient strategy users achieved the highest CPS performance and showed high stability in full VOTAT use across tasks. Low strategy users rarely transitioned to full VOTAT, whereas intermediate strategy users had difficulty sustaining full VOTAT once they adopted it. Educational-stage differences in class membership were not significant, although senior students outperformed junior students in knowledge application. The findings indicate that students differ in both their use of effective strategies and their ability to sustain effective strategy use across problem-solving situations. They also highlight the value of logfile-based transition analyses for understanding students' problem-solving processes.

TI Why Become a General Practitioner? Career Intentions Among Medical
   Students at an Italian University: A Cross-Sectional Study
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE General Practice; Primary Health Care; medical students; career choice;
   undergraduate medical education
ID SPECIALTY CHOICE; HEALTH; SYSTEMS
AB Background: General Practice is facing workforce shortages across Europe. In Italy, the estimated shortage was 5575 General Practitioners in 2024, with high retirement rates and persistent difficulties in attracting new physicians to the profession. This study investigated postgraduate career intentions among medical students and factors associated with interest in General Practice. Methods: A cross-sectional survey using an anonymous 39-item questionnaire was conducted among fifth- and sixth-year medical students at the University of Milan. Associations were assessed using ordinal and multinomial logistic regression. Results: Among 359 respondents (response rate: 46.8%), only 2.2% identified General Practice as their preferred postgraduate career. Students considering General Practice attributed greater importance to community-based work (OR = 18.49, 95% CI 3.35-102.02) and professional autonomy (OR = 4.47, 95% CI 1.03-19.44). Previous community-based primary care experience was associated with choosing General Practice (OR = 32.43, 95% CI 3.85-273.50). Most students perceived theoretical and practical General Practice training as less adequate than that of other specialties, and only 25.1% considered their preparation sufficient to support career decision-making. Conclusions: Strengthening the academic integration of General Practice and meaningful community-based learning opportunities may contribute to more informed career choices while better preparing future physicians for healthcare systems increasingly centred on Primary Health Care.

TI Reinterpreting multimedia learning principles for extended reality: a
   perspective on XR learning design
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE augmented reality; design; extended reality; instructional design;
   multimedia learning principles; virtual reality
AB Extended reality (XR) enables users to interact with and control simulated 3D elements, creating opportunities to support meaningful learning experiences, but it also introduces cognitive load due to its novel interactions. Researchers and designers have attempted to address these challenges by manipulating the user experience through the design of the virtual environment or by varying the level of interaction complexity. While traditional media benefit from established instructional frameworks, immersive media such as XR lack similarly refined design guidelines. In this perspective article, we argue that Mayer's multimedia learning principles cannot be directly transferred to XR learning environments without reinterpretation, as XR introduces distinctive cognitive and interaction demands, including embodiment, spatial interaction, presence, agency, and environmental complexity. From this perspective, we organize XR design considerations around cognitive load processes and discuss how these choices may either support or hinder learning. We then propose key considerations for designing effective XR-based learning experiences, including content representation (e.g., 2D and 3D elements, color, positioning), virtual environment settings (e.g., background elements, haptic feedback, sound, voice interactions), and the structure of learning materials (e.g., pre-training materials, interactions and tasks, assessment).

TI Interactive digital mnemonics accelerate lexical retrieval and enhance
   long-term vocabulary retention in adolescent EFL learners
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adaptive learning environment; associative memory; cognitive load;
   digital mnemonics; EFL vocabulary acquisition; long-term retention;
   reaction time; spaced repetition
ID 2ND-LANGUAGE; AUTOMATIZATION; AUTOMATICITY
AB This study examines how interactive digital mnemonics reshape the temporal dynamics of associative retrieval during foreign-language vocabulary acquisition among adolescent learners. A quasi-experimental design compared an adaptive digital learning environment with conventional paper-based methods in a sample of 102 middle-school students (aged 12-14), assigned at the intact-class level to an experimental group (n = 51) and a control group (n = 51). Participants studied 45 health-and sport-related English lexical items. A computerized lexical decision task programmed in PsychoPy measured reaction time (RT) in milliseconds and response accuracy across three phases: baseline pre-test (T0), immediate post-test (T1), and four-week delayed post-test (T2). The experimental group exhibited a statistically significant reduction in RT latencies at T1 [M = 942 ms vs. 1,520 ms; F(2, 200) = 84.30, p < 0.001, eta & sup2;p = 0.46] and maintained faster retrieval at T2 (1,055 ms vs. 1,710 ms). Accuracy at T2 remained substantially higher in the experimental cohort (81.5% vs. 54.1%), indicating greater retention resilience. These findings provide behavioral evidence that the integrated digital mnemonic package was associated with faster associative retrieval and more durable L2 vocabulary retention. Because cognitive load was not measured directly, the results are interpreted as evidence of improved retrieval efficiency rather than as direct confirmation of reduced extraneous load.

TI Deficiency of value-navigation in AI-augmented English instruction and
   resolution to practice
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE deficicency; value-navigation; AI-augmented English instruction;
   resolution; practice
AB This paper discusses a rarely-explored issue-deficiency of value-navigation in AI-augmented English instruction practice in China and proposes resolution. While AI is increasingly employed in English classrooms, students are more likely to be exposed to an environment with social ethnic risk concomitant in content generation process. Through classroom observation with further investigation into three cases, interview and follow-up data analysis, the research reveals precarious deficiency of value navigation manifested in AI-augmented practice and teachers' and students' cognition in Chinese elementary school, secondary school, and university. Based on data analysis and grounded in the distinctive sociocultural milieu of English education in China, a three-phase AI-augmented framework resolution is proposed for practice: articulating Chinese indigenous value propositions, implementing a practical value-navigation scaffold, and establishing a value-based feedback mechanism, for making good use of AI, and to provide a reference for English education practitioners all over the world.

TI A framework for integrating large language models in secondary physics
   education: practical design, opportunities, risks, and pedagogical
   principles
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI in education; cognitive load theory; instructional design; large
   language models; physics education; secondary science
ID STUDENTS; KNOWLEDGE
AB The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) offers transformative potential for secondary physics education. However, theoretical and practical frameworks for responsible, pedagogically sound LLM integration remain underdeveloped. This paper proposes a structured, theory-grounded framework for embedding LLMs into secondary physics instruction, informed by constructivism, cognitive load theory, and the TPACK model. We identify three core application modalities: teacher-facing instructional design tools, guarded student-facing inquiry tools, and assessment-augmentation tools. We analyze domain-specific opportunities (targeting misconceptions in mechanics and electromagnetism) and risks (cognitive offloading, epistemic opacity, algorithmic bias). Drawing on empirical evidence from a small-scale single-class pilot feasibility study rather than systematic full empirical verification, we formalize six pedagogical principles: progressive autonomy, epistemic transparency, cognitive load optimization, disciplinary fidelity, ethical scaffolding, and human-AI complementarity. A one-group pretest-posttest pilot exploration was implemented with 36 secondary school students (ages 14-16) learning Newton's Third Law solely to examine the preliminary practicability of the proposed framework instead of validating its universal effectiveness. Data analyses included paired-samples t-tests, effect size calculation, compliance coding, and descriptive survey statistics. Results showed significantly improved conceptual understanding within this limited pilot sample (p < 0.001, d = 1.32, large effect), high in-class observed adherence to AI use guardrails (91.7%), and generally positive learner perceptions among the participating cohort. This pilot-tested operable framework clarifies the evolving role of physics teachers as orchestrators of human-AI collaboration and offers actionable preliminary guidance for educators, instructional designers, and policymakers.

TI Differential relations of mathematics vocabulary and academic skill
   performance in middle school

AB One barrier to students' success in mathematics is misunderstanding mathematics vocabulary (MV), which may be particularly pronounced in middle school when students encounter hundreds of terms. We administered a MV measure to 305 students in Grades 6 (n = 145) and 8 (n = 160) to examine their accuracy in identifying MV terms and performance patterns. Findings from this exploratory study are discussed in relation to prior research and middle-school MV instruction.

TI Exploring the impact of multimodal generative artificial intelligence on
   CT dispositions in inquiry-based academic writing: a quasi-experimental
   analysis in higher education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic writing quality; cognitive theory of multimedia learning; CT
   dispositions; genAI; higher education; inquiry-based writing; multimodal
   learning; quasi-experimental design
ID CRITICAL THINKING; CHINESE
AB Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new possibilities for scaffolding inquiry-based writing (IBW). However, its impact on critical thinking (CT) dispositions remains empirically underexplored, particularly regarding how the modality of GenAI interaction shapes this impact. Grounded in the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning, this study examines whether multimodal GenAI, which simultaneously processes and generates text, images, and visual representations, cultivates CT dispositions and improves academic writing quality more effectively than text-based GenAI or no GenAI support.Methods A quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design with three conditions (multimodal GenAI, text-based GenAI, and no GenAI control) was implemented with 165 undergraduate students over an eight-week IBW intervention. One-way ANCOVAs were conducted to compare condition effects on posttest outcomes, controlling for pretest scores.Results Analyses revealed significant main effects of condition on both CT dispositions and academic writing quality. The multimodal GenAI group showed the greatest improvement on both outcomes, followed by the text-based GenAI group, with the no GenAI control group showing the smallest gains. Subdimensional analyses indicated that the multimodal advantage was concentrated in openness and analytical thinking within CT dispositions, and in evidence use and analytical depth within writing quality.Discussion These findings extend the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning into GenAI-assisted learning contexts and demonstrate that the modality of GenAI interaction is a consequential design variable for cultivating CT dispositions through IBW. Practical implications for educators and instructional designers are discussed.

TI The perception of heutagogy among members of an educational community: a
   case study of an Arab authority in Israel
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Arab education; Arab local authority; heutagogy; pedagogical innovation;
   self-determined learning (SDL); traditional society
AB Background Education systems around the world face a profound challenge-preparing learners to cope with rapidly changing economic, technological, and cultural realities, while at the same time correcting gaps that limit access to meaningful education. Globalization, digitization, and the consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic have revealed long-term structural gaps in education and increased calls for innovative pedagogies that promote lifelong learning. Accordingly, independent learner skills have become more essential, and recognition of the need for change in the perception of education, learning, and teaching has expanded. Heutagogy or "self-directed learning" offers a response to these challenges by placing the learner at the center of the process. Heutagogy, coined by Hayes and Kenyon, is described as a practice and theory of learning that is directed and guided by the learner himself. The current study seeks to examine perceptions of Heutagogy among members of an educational community in an Arab local authority in Israel as an alternative approach to traditional elementary school teaching. It is interested in the possible tension between the principles of Heutagogy, and in particular the transfer of agency, responsibility, and power to learners, and cultural norms that emphasize hierarchy, authority, and respect for adults. The study aims to provide important insights into the acceptance and perception of Heutagogy in a traditional society, and also into the integration of the Heutagogical approach in the junior division of an elementary school.Methodology The study was conducted using a case study approach, as part of a project to establish a school based on innovative teaching and learning. The project focused on developing a pedagogical program for an elementary school, according to the Heutagogical approach and took place in cooperation with an Arab authority in the north of the country. During a process of training and exposing the Heutagogical concept among the education community, 11 meetings were held with the education communities and interested parties. The meetings included structured lectures and in-depth discussions about the principles of the approach and its implementation in a school. This process made it possible to examine perceptions of Heutagogy within the complex socio-cultural context in which it existed, and led to a deep understanding of the conditions, limitations, and opportunities involved in implementing Heutagogy in the Arab society. The study was based on the qualitative approach, drawing on thirteen semi-structured interviews that dealt with participants' attitudes toward Heutagogy.Findings The findings indicate a complex picture of the perception of Heutagogy among members of an educational community in an Arab authority in Israel. On the one hand, there has been clear enthusiasm for the possibility of designing an innovative school that places the child at the center, expands spaces of choice, fosters self-management, and develops awareness and responsibility. On the other hand, enthusiasm was accompanied by significant caution. Heutagogy was not seen as a model that could be immediately and directly transferred from theory to the field, but rather as a process that required conditions: Students are gradually mature or accompanied, recognition of differences between students, a home infrastructure of independence and decision-making, teachers who are able to move from authoritarian teaching to flexible guidance, and parents who share in understanding and trusting the path.
   In addition, concerns and objections were raised relating to both the cultural context and the practical aspects of implementation. The interviewees asked whether broad student freedom is appropriate for local culture, how social and cultural values can be maintained within a modern model, will parents accept a change that does not focus on grades, and will the system be able to provide the necessary conditions?. Therefore, the overall interpretation of the findings is that Heutagogy is perceived by the interviewees as an important educational opportunity, but one that is conditioned by sensitive and local translation. Its success depends on the ability to combine innovation with cultural context, freedom with framework, student responsibility with adult guidance, and pedagogical vision with actual implementation conditions. In this sense, it is not just a new structure or use of technology, but an attempt to rebuild relationships between students, teachers, parents, and the community around the idea of independent, conscious, and responsible learning.Discussion The research findings highlight the tension between the principles of Heutagogy and the unique social and cultural contexts of the Arab education system in Israel. The variety of positions that have emerged in research on Heutagogy, as offering an innovative but also challenging model for application in conservative contexts that rely on educational hierarchies. A finding that is consistent with the results of the study by Harduf and others, who found that the attitude towards the idea of Heutagogy among lecturer communities was multifaceted and complex. On the one hand, there were voices criticizing the traditional approach and sympathetic to the Heutagogical idea, and on the other hand, there were also concerns and criticism. The findings add to and point to recommendations needed to promote Heutagogy, including the importance of developing partnerships with all interested parties, focusing teacher training, and building supportive systemic conditions. These recommendations are particularly important in a context where tradition shapes the boundaries of pedagogical innovation.

TI "Not giving up when I can't express myself": toward an entrepreneurial
   mindset framework in English language learning
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adaptive learning strategy; confident expression; entrepreneurial
   mindset; foreign language learning; strategic persistence
AB This study examined students' entrepreneurial mindset in English language learning (EM-ELL) by investigating its overall level and pattern, underlying factor structure, and variation across gender, year level, and self-reported English proficiency. A total of 1,990 students participated in the study. Descriptive statistics indicated that students generally reported a moderately high level of EM-ELL, as all item means were above the midpoint of the 4-point scale. Overall, the findings indicate that EM-ELL may be represented as a multidimensional construct and that its scores were more closely associated with year level and self-reported proficiency than with gender in this sample.

AB Stress has detrimental impacts on K-12 teachers' occupational health, yet there is no consensus on how best to define and measure it. TI Network analysis of smartphone addiction, attentional control, and
   learning adaptation among nursing undergraduates
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing undergraduates; Smartphone addiction; Attentional control;
   Learning adaptation; Network analysis
ID PHYSICAL-ACTIVITY; COLLEGE-STUDENTS; MEDIATING ROLE; MOBILE PHONE;
   ANXIETY; BIASES
AB Background In the digital learning environment, learning adaptation and attentional control have been shown to be important factors associated with academic success among nursing undergraduates. Smartphone addiction has been associated with impaired attentional control and poorer learning outcomes; however, although previous studies have investigated smartphone addiction and learning-related outcomes, the multidimensional relationships among smartphone addiction, attentional control, and learning adaptation remain unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to examine the network structure among these constructs and identify candidate targets for future intervention research.Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 452 nursing undergraduates from two universities in China from February to May 2025. Participants completed the Mobile Phone Addiction Index Scale, the Attentional Control Scale, and the Learning Adaptation Scale. An EBICglasso Gaussian graphical model was estimated using R. Node strength and bridge strength were calculated, and bootstrap procedures were performed to assess network accuracy and stability. To examine sex-specific mechanisms, we applied NCT to compare network structure, global strength, and node strength across sexes.Results Network analysis shows that the strongest associations were observed between attentional focusing (A1) and attentional shifting (A2) (edge weight = 0.38), feeling anxious and lost (M2) and withdrawal or escape (M3) (edge weight = 0.27), and teaching methodology (L2) and learning attitude (L4) (edge weight = 0.23). Attentional focusing (A1), learning capability (L3), and learning motivation (L1) showed the highest strength centrality values and emerged as the most central nodes in the network. Bridge strength identified attentional focusing (A1), learning motivation (L1), and productivity loss (M4) as key bridge nodes linking the three domains.Conclusion Smartphone addiction, attentional control, and learning adaptation were found to be closely interconnected among nursing undergraduates. The identified central and bridge nodes may serve as candidate targets for future intervention research aimed at reducing smartphone addiction and improving learning adaptation in this population. However, given the cross-sectional design, these findings should be interpreted as preliminary and require validation through longitudinal and experimental studies.

TI Between Complicity and Resistance: Higher Education Reform and Academic
   Community Responses in Georgia amid Authoritarian Resurgence
SO EUROPEAN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
AB This paper examines how Georgian universities respond to higher education reform amid democratic erosion and authoritarian consolidation. Drawing on ethnographic engagement with the reform space and Actor-Network Theory, we conceptualize the reform process as a politico-academic assemblage, tracing associations between academic and governmental actors in which the political agenda rather than academic logic shapes reform design. Within these assemblages, identity, power, and agency are contested, generating divergent institutional responses and outcomes. To analyze how universities navigate differentiated and targeted interventions, we employ Gramsci's military metaphors-the war of maneuver, the war of position-and additionally introduce a third-the war of tricks-as the most consequential institutional strategy. The cases reveal that what appears to be consolidated authoritarian power is, in practice, self-contradictory and fragmented-yet progressively reshapes the institutional terrain, narrowing the conditions under which universities can meaningfully sustain their academic autonomy and substance.
