TI Teachers' acceptance and understanding of a reduced Dirac formalism and
   the Bloch sphere
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID PHYSICS; QUBIT; KEY
AB Mathematical descriptions are the focus of quantum physics education research, as quantum physics is inherently described by its mathematical structures. However, there is a lack of research regarding the role of mathematical descriptions for understanding fundamental principles of quantum physics in teacher preparation and training. In order to investigate how preservice teachers and in-service teachers assess and understand the mathematical formalism in quantum physics, an explorative interview study was conducted. Therefore, we developed a teaching-learning sequence employing a reduced Dirac formalism in the context of single-photon polarization serving as an exemplary two-state system. In that respect, the focus was on two mathematical representations. The ket notation was used as an algebraic representation in connection with the Bloch sphere as a graphical representation of quantum states. On that basis, semistructured and material-based interviews with N = 15 preservice teachers and N = 15 in-service teachers were conducted. The data suggest that the reduced Dirac formalism is well understood and accepted by both preservice teachers and in-service teachers. However, some in-service teachers raise critical concerns about the abstract nature of the mathematical formalism, pointing to a perceived lack of experimental or phenomenological connection. The ket notation is valued not only for its communicative clarity and its role as a language but also for its structural role. By comparison, the Bloch sphere is met with more cautious acceptance-yet its use in visualizing experiments and measurement processes is positively assessed.

TI Work-related motivational and self-regulatory characteristics and

ID PERFORMANCE; SYSTEMS
AB This study primarily examined the associations between students' self-regulation-related characteristics and mean overall academic transcript grade within a Project-Based Learning (PBL) environment in Human Nutrition and Dietetics education. Secondary analyses examined satisfaction with PBL, while exploratory analyses assessed sex-related differences and student profiles. An observational study was conducted with 160 undergraduate students from two consecutive academic cohorts (2024-2025 and 2025-2026). Students' mean overall academic transcript grade, work-related motivational and self-regulatory characteristics, and satisfaction with PBL were assessed using academic records and questionnaire measures. Exploratory analyses identified sex-related differences in several motivational and self-regulatory variables and two differentiated student profiles according to academic achievement and motivational/self-regulatory characteristics. These findings identify statistical associations between students' motivational and self-regulatory characteristics and academic achievement within the PBL-based learning environment examined. The findings should not be interpreted as evidence of a causal effect of PBL, but rather as evidence of patterns of association observed among students participating in a common PBL learning experience.

TI Structured Visualization for Laparoscopic Skill Acquisition: A
   Randomized Controlled Study
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE laparoscopy; hand-eye coordination; training; simulation training;
   visualization
ID SURGICAL SIMULATION; EDUCATION
AB OBJECTIVE To evaluate whether structured visualization can support acquisition of basic laparoscopic skills during simulation training and whether this approach can achieve outcomes comparable to repeated physical practice. DESIGN Prospective randomized comparative study. SETTING Simulation-based laparoscopic skills training at a university-affiliated teaching center. PARTICIPANTS Fifty laparoscopy-naive medical students were randomly assigned to a laparoscopic practice group or a visualization group. The laparoscopic practice group performed a validated Gynecological Endoscopic Surgical Education and Assessment (GESEA) Laparoscopic Skills Training and Testing (LASTT) hand-eye coordination task 7 consecutive times. The visualization group performed the same task physically on attempts 1, 4, and 7, while attempts 2, 3, 5, and 6 consisted of guided visualization. Each attempt lasted up to 2 minutes, and performance was scored as the number of correctly placed rings (range 0-12). RESULTS Baseline performance was comparable between groups (2.92 +/- 2.14 vs 2.88 +/- 1.72; p = 0.94). Both groups improved significantly over time (p < 0.001). No statistically significant between-group differences were found on the 4th attempt (6.52 +/- 3.25 vs 5.76 +/- 2.57; p = 0.48) or 7th attempt (8.24 +/- 2.86 vs 7.44 +/- 2.99; p = 0.39). The final physical performance of the visualization group was significantly better than the 3rd physical attempt of the laparoscopic practice group (p = 0.025). CONCLUSIONS Structured visualization may support early laparoscopic skill acquisition and achieve short-term outcomes comparable to repeated hands-on simulator training. Visualization should be considered an adjunct, rather than a replacement, for physical practice in simulation-based laparoscopic education. (c) 2026 The Authors. TI Effectiveness of adaptive versus non-adaptive intelligent tutoring
   systems in early primary mathematics
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Adaptive learning; Intelligent tutoring system; Mathematics; Primary
   school
ID DIFFERENTIATED INSTRUCTION; COGNITIVE-LOAD; HELP-SEEKING; SCHOOLS;
   INEQUALITY; ACHIEVEMENT
AB Adaptive intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) are considered promising tools to address increasing heterogeneity in classrooms by tailoring instruction to individual learners. However, prior research often bundles multiple adaptive features, relies on non-equivalent instructional conditions, and predominantly focuses on older learners, limiting conclusions about specific adaptive mechanisms and younger students. To address these limitations, this field experiment investigated the isolated effect of task difficulty adaptation by comparing an adaptive and a non-adaptive ITS in early primary mathematics education among second-grade students (N = 132). Both systems were identical in content, interface, feedback, and hints, differing only in the dynamic adaptation of task difficulty. We hypothesized that the adaptive system would outperform the non-adaptive system regarding students' outcomes. Students engaged in a 30-minute training session, and pre-post assessments measured learning outcomes, cognitive load, and enjoyment. Additionally, an exploratory latent profile analysis based on motivational and cognitive learner characteristics examined differential effects. Results revealed no significant differences between conditions for learning outcomes, cognitive load, or enjoyment. Exploratory analyses indicated moderation by conscientiousness for subjective difficulty and enjoyment and differences in students' progression through the ITS. Learner profiles did not moderate the effects. These findings suggest that isolated task difficulty adaptation did not yield clear advantages over a non-adaptive system and highlight students' progression through the ITS and individual learner characteristics as promising targets for future research.

TI Improving care for patients exposed to intimate partner violence: An
   interprofessional simulation case study
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Intimate partner violence; Health professions; Interdisciplinary
   professional education; PREMIS
ID EDUCATION; STUDENTS; TOOL
AB Background: Intimate partner violence (IPV) is a prevalent public health issue. Healthcare professionals play an important role in identifying and supporting individuals experiencing IPV, yet opportunities for interprofessional IPV training remain limited, particularly for student pharmacists. Case description: An interprofessional simulation-based educational activity was implemented for students in pharmacy, medicine, nursing, dentistry, and dental hygiene programs. The simulation utilized an adaptation of the "Staying Game," in which participants role-played individuals experiencing IPV and navigated resource constraints, safety decisions, and escalating violence scenarios. A facilitated debrief followed the simulation. Participants completed a post-assessment to evaluate perceived knowledge, perceived preparedness, actual knowledge, and satisfaction with the activity. Case findings: A total of 287 students completed the survey. Perceived knowledge and preparedness were strongly correlated, whereas actual knowledge was not associated with either domain. Pharmacy students reported the lowest levels of perceived knowledge and perceived preparedness, but the highest levels of actual knowledge. Participants reported high satisfaction and indicated that the activity increased their understanding of IPV, empathy for victims, appreciation of interprofessional collaboration, and confidence in their professional role. Conclusion: Interprofessional simulation is a valuable educational strategy and may impact perceived preparedness, empathy, and collaborative awareness related to IPV among health professions students.

TI The non-performance-based benefits of attendance: a qualitative study of
   third year doctor of pharmacy students
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Attendance; Engagement; Student pharmacist education; Professional
   identity formation; Qualitative research
AB Introduction: Previous studies have analyzed the relationship between student attendance and academic performance, but few evaluate the less tangible benefits of attendance, such as forming a professional identity, practicing professionalism, and building camaraderie with peers and faculty. This study sought to gather and qualitatively evaluate the experiences of student pharmacists regarding course attendance, to understand possible benefits of course attendance beyond academic performance, and to identify opportunities for faculty to modify course design and teaching style to enhance student attendance and engagement. Methods: Semi-structured qualitative key informant interviews were conducted with student pharmacists from the class of 2025. An interview script was developed to collect student perspectives about course attendance and benefits of participation beyond academic performance. Interviews were conducted via Zoom and were transcribed and evaluated using deductive coding procures and Piaget's Cognitive Constructivism learning theory as a framework. Results: Thirty-minute interviews were conducted with 11 student pharmacists during spring 2024. Student pharmacists found in-class attendance helpful for building professional relationships between student peers and faculty, practicing problem-solving skills, and creating opportunities for professional identity formation. Faculty can encourage student attendance by showing authenticity, bringing personal experiences into the classroom, and demonstrating enthusiasm. Conclusion: With increasing absenteeism among student pharmacists, faculty play an important role in ensuring an engaging classroom environment to influence student desire to attend class. Students believe having faculty experts providing authentic interactions is important. Students are motivated to attend class when they understand the benefits extend beyond course performance and towards their identity formation as a pharmacist.

TI What works and at what cost to improve foundational learning for
   school-aged children in conflict and protracted crisis? A meta-analysis
   and cost-effectiveness analysis of education interventions for
   school-aged children
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Meta-analysis; Foundational learning; Literacy; Numeracy; Education in
   conflict and crisis; School-aged children
ID DEVELOPING-COUNTRIES; IMPACT
AB This study synthesizes evidence on education interventions that improve foundational learning outcomes for school-aged children in conflict and crisis-affected settings. Drawing on a comprehensive evidence review and meta-analysis of 36 experimental and quasi-experimental studies conducted between 2000 and 2024, we examine the impacts and cost-effectiveness across multiple categories of education interventions. Guided by the Education Research in Conflict and Crisis (ERICC) framework, we organize findings across four drivers of learning: access, quality, continuity, and system coherence. Across studies, the average effect size for foundational literacy is 0.27 standard deviations and 0.21 SD for numeracy, both exceeding the median effect size of 0.10 SD reported across low- and middle-income countries more broadly. Software with academic games exhibits strong and consistent positive impacts across literacy and numeracy outcomes, while structured pedagogy shows similar effects for literacy and phone-based tutoring for numeracy. Other interventions such as targeted instruction show emerging evidence of high impact for literacy but have not demonstrated impact on numeracy, despite being well established in more stable settings. Results indicate that interventions associated with larger gains tend to operate through common mechanisms, including reducing access and participation constraints, aligning instruction with learners' skills through personalization, strengthening instructional capacity, and sustaining learning during periods of disruption. However, many interventions with evidence of impact lack costing data in conflict settings. Analysis of cost-effectiveness reveals substantial heterogeneity, with phonebased tutoring yielding strong evidence of higher cost-effectiveness, while evidence for several other intervention categories remains limited or uneven. The findings highlight the potential for meaningful learning gains in crisis settings and the importance of cautious interpretation given data constraints, contextual variability, and gaps in cost reporting.

TI Self-regulated learning strategy transitions and academic performance in
   blended learning: Insights from learning analytics
SO INTERNET AND HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-regulated learning; Strategy transition; Tactics and strategies;
   Cognitive regulation; Higher education; Blended learning; Learning
   analytics
ID BIG DATA; ONLINE; DESIGN
AB Blended learning plays an important role in the digital transformation of higher education and requires students to regulate their learning with greater independence. Although learning analytics studies have increasingly used clickstream data to identify self-regulated learning (SRL) tactics and strategies, many rely on platform-specific behavioral categories whose theoretical meaning is not always explicit. Moreover, less is known about how SRL strategies change across the structured phases of compulsory courses. This study examined the online behaviors of first-year undergraduates in an institution-initiated blended general education course at a Chinese university. Drawing on Pintrich's SRL framework, five learning tactics were identified and consolidated into four strategies, by using sequence analysis and clustering. The findings indicate that students frequently relied on strategies characterized by limited regulation and oriented toward rapid task completion. Strategy use also followed distinct phase-specific trajectories, that is many students began with cognitively demanding approaches, shifted mid-course to lower-order strategies, and then returned to deeper forms of engagement during exam preparation. Although a considerable proportion of students shifted toward strategies characterized by lower levels of regulation, upward shifts toward elaboration-oriented regulation were associated with better academic performance. These findings suggest that SRL dynamics in blended learning are shaped by both learners' regulatory choices and the temporal structure of course design, highlighting the need for instructional scaffolding that supports the sustained use of higher-order strategies.

TI Are Urology Residents Losing Autonomy? A National Analysis of ACGME Case
   Log Data from 2013 to 2023
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE case log data; clinical competence; surgical autonomy; urology residency
ID GENERAL-SURGERY RESIDENTS; OPERATIVE EXPERIENCE
AB OBJECTIVE: To examine national trends in urology resident surgical autonomy using Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) case log data. DESIGN: A retrospective cohort analysis of ACGME case logs for all graduating urology residents from 2013 to 2023. Resident-defined operative role ("assistant," "surgeon," or "teaching assistant") was used as a proxy for surgical autonomy, and an autonomy score was calculated for each resident. Trends over time were evaluated using mixed-effects regression, and differences by procedure subtype, ERAS geographic region, and sex were assessed using analysis of variance. SETTING: A novel national database encompassing all urology residency programs across the United States. PARTICIPANTS: Graduating urology residents who completed ACGME-accredited urology residency programs between 2013 and 2023. A total of 3391 residents across 145 programs met inclusion criteria. RESULTS: Mean case number per resident increased from 1243 in 2013 to 1404.6 in 2023 (p < 0.001). Autonomy varied significantly by ERAS geographic region (p <0.001) and sex, with males reporting higher autonomy scores than females (p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: This national cohort analysis demonstrates a significant and sustained decline in urology resident self-reported surgical autonomy, with variation according to procedure subtype, geographic region, and sex. These findings are concerning and highlight the importance of re-evaluating and prioritizing autonomy within urology residencies. (c) 2026 Association of Program Directors in Surgery. TI Unique Performance Problems in Surgical Residency as Novel Predictors of
   Negative Postresidency Outcomes
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE resident performance; educational outcomes; predictors of poor
   performance
ID IDENTIFICATION; REMEDIATION; ATTRITION
AB OBJECTIVE: Surgical educators have an interest in ensuring graduates of residency programs are able to pass board examinations and build a surgical practice. We sought to learn if there are indicators in residency that can be used to predict propensity for difficulty in passing boards or in later practice. DESIGN: We reviewed the residency and postresidency (board results) files of 104 residents in our general surgery program, cataloging performance problems using a checklist we had developed for a previous study. We then used online resources including state licensing boards to assess nonboard postresidency outcomes. We used binary logistic regression to assess which predictors pointed to negative outcomes, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis to determine if there were cutoff scores for American Board of Surgery In-Training Examination (ABSITE) exams, seriousness of problems, and number of unique problems identified in the file. They were also at statistically significantly higher risk than residents who had 1 to 4 unique performance problems documented in their files. Residents who had 1 to 4 documented performance problems were at statistically significantly higher risk than residents who had zero documented performance problems only for negative online mentions. CONCLUSIONS: Capturing unique performance problems during residency is a novel method to assess risk for negative postresidency outcomes, both in passing board exams and mounting a successful practice. TI Large language models and social-emotional learning: Promise, limits,
   and conditions for responsible use
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Large language models; Social-emotional learning; AI in education;
   Commentary; Cross-cultural assessment
AB The educational artificial intelligence literature has developed rapidly around cognitive uses of large language models (LLMs), with comparatively little systematic attention to their role in social-emotional learning (SEL). In this paper, we synthesize two strands of recent research to argue that contemporary LLMs warrant serious consideration as infrastructure for SEL. The first strand documents that contemporary LLMs can generate responses on social-emotional tasks that approach or exceed average human performance. The second strand reports growing empirical evidence that LLM-based interventions can support social-emotional skills development. We also provide further evidence with our own cross-linguistic evaluation of five LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, DeepSeek-R1, Ernie, and Qwen) using the OECD Survey of Social and Emotional Skills framework. Our results suggest that current models can display broad SEL-relevant response patterns, especially in English, and that these patterns are highly responsive to simple prompting. We close by outlining application scenarios and safeguards for responsible deployment, including privacy protection, cultural validation, transparent AI labelling, crisis escalation, and human oversight.

DT Article
DE Multimodal assessment literacy; Knowledge; Competence; Value; GenAI

TI Connection, control, and competence: A career-stage perspective on
   teacher wellbeing
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher wellbeing; Career stage; School-based support;
   Self-determination theory
ID RESILIENCE; EDUCATION; STRESS
AB Teacher wellbeing is increasingly recognised as essential for sustaining an effective and resilient education workforce. However, most school-based initiatives adopt a universal approach that overlooks how wellbeing needs may differ across career stages. This qualitative study aimed to identify which activities in-service teachers believe contribute to their wellbeing and compare these perceptions across early-, mid-, and late-career stages. Drawing on self-determination theory, which emphasises the psychological needs of autonomy, relatedness, and competence, the study analysed open-ended survey responses from 138 Australian primary and secondary teachers. Thematic analysis identified both shared and stage-specific wellbeing needs. While collegial support and workload management were important across all stages, early-career teachers prioritised social connection; mid-career teachers emphasised recognition and leadership support, while late-career teachers valued structured collaboration and professional contribution. These findings suggest that a one-size-fits-all approach may be inadequate and that career-stage-sensitive strategies are needed to support teacher wellbeing throughout the professional lifespan.

TI Integrating generative AI into physiotherapy education: students' use,
   perceptions, and generative AI literacy following curricular
   adaptations: a repeated cross-sectional programme evaluation
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative Artificial Intelligence; Medical Education; Physical Therapy
   Modalities; Students; Health Occupations; Clinical Competence
AB Background Structured generative artificial intelligence (GAI) training has been proposed as an effective approach to strengthen healthcare students' confidence in navigating AI-related challenges and ethical considerations. However, few studies have evaluated the impact of implemented GAI-related curricular adaptations and learning activities, particularly within physiotherapy education. This study aimed to evaluate: 1) physiotherapy students' use and perceptions of GAI in their studies during implementation of GAI-related curricular adaptations; and 2) GAI literacy in semester 1 before participation and in semester 3 after completion of structured GAI learning activities. Methods A two-part repeated cross-sectional programme evaluation with non-equivalent, unlinked samples was conducted among physiotherapy students at Link & ouml;ping University, Sweden. Students' use and perceptions of GAI were assessed after implementation of GAI-related curricular adaptations in 2024 and again in a separate survey wave in 2025. GAI literacy was evaluated using the 10-item Generative Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale (GAILS-10) before and after the GAI learning activities delivered during semesters 1-3. Results Reported GAI use differed significantly between 2024 and 2025 surveys, chi(2)(3) = 62.40, p < 0.001, with daily use reported by 57% of respondents in the 2025 survey compared with 13% in the 2024 survey. Respondents in the 2025 survey reported more diverse use of GAI, including brainstorming, question generation, and text refinement (p < 0.001). Perceptions of GAI as contributing to learning were also more positive in the 2025 survey, chi(2)(4) = 24.94, p < 0.001, whereas perceptions of information about permissible and impermissible use were similar in both surveys. Semester 3 students assessed after completing the GAI learning activities reported higher GAILS-10 scores across all dimensions than semester 1 students assessed before participation, with a large between-group effect size for the total score (d = 1.0). Conclusion Physiotherapy students reported more frequent and diverse GAI use and more positive learning perceptions in the 2025 survey than in the 2024 survey. Semester 3 students, assessed after completing the GAI learning activities, reported higher GAI literacy than semester 1 students assessed before participation in these activities. These findings suggest a need for curricular adaptations and educational support to promote appropriate GAI use, reduce misuse, and strengthen student GAI literacy.

TI From clinical and typical separation to autism spectrum disorder and
   global developmental delay differentiation: Interpretable
   eye-tracking-based machine learning
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism; Machine learning; Eye tracking; Global developmental delay;
   Hide-and-seek
ID CHILDREN; ATTENTION; INDIVIDUALS; PATTERNS; SCENES
AB In clinical practice, objectively distinguishing children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from those with typical development (TD) and other neurodevelopmental conditions with overlapping symptoms, such as global developmental delay (GDD), is critical for improving developmental outcomes. This study aimed to investigate the feasibility of eye-tracking-based machine learning (ML) models in distinguishing children with developmental concerns (ASD + GDD) from TD children, and in further differentiating ASD from GDD. A total of 168 toddlers (45 ASD, 56 GDD, and 67 TD; aged 18-48 months) viewed a socially dynamic "hide-and-seek" video. Both conventional area-of-interest (AOI)-based features and combined features derived from AOI combinations were used to train five ML classifiers. A two-stage classification framework was adopted, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was used to interpret feature contributions. Combined features consistently outperformed isolated AOI features. For TD versus clinical classification, the random forest model achieved the highest accuracy of 80.36% (sensitivity = 84.16%, specificity = 74.63%). In differentiating ASD from GDD, the k-Nearest Neighbors model achieved the highest accuracy of 79.21% (sensitivity = 71.11%, specificity = 85.71%). SHAP analysis indicated that cross-regional attention features contributed substantially to model performance. These findings suggest that eye-tracking-based ML models may provide a promising approach for early screening of developmental conditions and ASD-GDD differentiation. Combined features reflecting cross-regional attention distribution demonstrated higher discriminative value than conventional AOI measures. Future studies should validate these findings in larger, multicenter, and more balanced samples with richer dynamic eye-tracking representations.

TI Are science subjects consistent? Evidence from Chinese students and
   schools using multivariate multilevel modeling
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Science education; Consistency across science subjects; Multivariate
   multilevel modeling; Chinese students and schools
ID STABILITY
AB Cross-subject consistency in science achievement among students and schools, and its stability across contexts and over time, remains insufficiently examined in science education. A multivariate multilevel model was applied to secondary data from two waves of a large-scale regional science assessment in China to examine crosssubject consistency in science achievement among Chinese students and schools. TI Understanding Auditory Temporal Processing in Chinese Children With
   Dyslexia: The Mediating Effect of Phonological Awareness and Rapid
   Automatised Naming
SO DYSLEXIA
LA English
DT Article
DE auditory temporal processing; Chinese; developmental dyslexia; mediating
   effect; phonological awareness; rapid automatised naming
ID READING DEVELOPMENT; PERCEPTION; SKILLS
AB This study investigated the temporal processing deficit hypothesis in Chinese children with developmental dyslexia. Thirty-two children with dyslexia and 34 typically developing children (grades 2 and 3) completed nonverbal and verbal auditory temporal order judgement (ATOJ) tasks. Structural equation modelling was used to examine whether phonological awareness and rapid automatised naming (RAN) mediated the relationship between auditory temporal processing and reading abilities. The results have implications for early identification and intervention of reading difficulties in Chinese children.

TI Learners' Attitudes Towards Generative Artificial Intelligence,
   Technology Comfort and Intentions to Adopt AI Tools in Education
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-assisted music creation; AI-generated music; learner attitudes; music
   education; technology adoption; technology comfort
ID INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; USER ACCEPTANCE
AB The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in music education and creative production has introduced new opportunities for music learners to compose, arrange and refine musical works through AI-assisted technologies. However, music learners differ considerably in their acceptance and intended use of these tools. This study examined the relationships among music learners' attitudes towards AI-generated music, technology comfort level, technical expertise in music, frequency of AI tool usage and intention to adopt AI tools for future music creation. A quantitative survey was conducted with 543 Chinese music learners enrolled in universities, music conservatories and private training institutions. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis and multiple regression analyses. The findings revealed that positive attitudes towards AI-generated music significantly predicted both the frequency of AI tool usage and learners' intention to adopt AI technologies in future music production. Technology comfort level also showed a significant positive association with adoption intention, indicating that greater confidence in using digital technologies facilitates acceptance of AI-assisted music tools. In contrast, technical expertise in music demonstrated only a modest relationship with AI tool usage and had little influence on attitudes or future adoption intentions. Furthermore, age and formal music education did not significantly predict intention to adopt AI tools. Overall, the findings suggest that psychological factors and digital readiness play a more influential role than demographic or educational characteristics in shaping music learners' engagement with AI-assisted music creation. The study contributes to the growing literature on AI in music education by identifying key factors associated with the acceptance and adoption of AI technologies among music learners and offers practical implications for music educators, curriculum developers and designers of AI-supported music production systems.

AB Background To date, little research has explored children with intellectual disabilities' own experience of the Covid-19 pandemic. Despite looking forward to seeing family/friends, children reported worries and hesitancy about returning to 'normal', indicating potential lasting effects of the lockdown.

TI Pruned Exact Linear Time Method for Multiple Change-Point Detection in
   Aberrant Responses
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL MEASUREMENT
LA English
DT Article
ID MODEL; IDENTIFICATION; BEHAVIOR
AB In educational measurement, examinees' response patterns often undergo abrupt transitions due to factors such as cheating, random guessing, or test fatigue. These transition points are defined as change points. Accurate identification of aberrant responses is crucial for ensuring test reliability and validity. However, most existing research on aberrant response detection focuses solely on single change-point scenarios. Such methods may be inadequate when examinees exhibit multiple behavioral transitions during a test. This study developed a multiple change-point detection method for response behavior based on the Pruned Exact Linear Time (PELT) algorithm. To address the limitations of fixed penalty criteria in balancing detection power and Type I error control, this study employed an adaptive penalty calibration method based on the false-positive rate. Simulation results showed that the proposed method controlled the Type I error rate at approximately 5% while achieving overall, single-change-point, and multiple-change-point detection rates of 75%, 78%, and 70%, respectively. Empirical analysis of the PISA 2015 financial literacy data revealed that approximately 21% of test-takers exhibited detectable response pattern shifts, with 29% of these test-takers exhibiting multiple change points, demonstrating the method's applicability in real-world low-stakes testing contexts.

TI What University signs might tell us about contemporary pedagogic
   practices
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Signage; Signs; Teaching and learning; Pedagogy
ID EDUCATION LEARNING SPACES
AB University teaching and learning spaces are saturated with signage that signals how we understand academic classroom activity, yet these artefacts remain unexamined within learning environments research. This paper positions such signage not as neutral directives but as artefacts that work to actively shape and narrate how teaching, learning, and bodies are governed in contemporary higher education. Drawing on photomapping, categorisation, and critical semiotic analysis of signage across teaching and learning spaces in an English and a Swedish university, the study demonstrates how these messages can construct classrooms as depersonalised, tightly controlled environments in which technological systems are privileged and embodied presence is framed as a potential disruption. Suggestively, we need to reimagine campus environments that narrate and discursively support more relational, humane, and innovative forms of teaching and learning.

TI Beyond DEI and the culture war: Liberal technocracy, MAGA
   authoritarianism, and the rentier order in U.S. schooling
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION PEDAGOGY AND CULTURAL STUDIES
LA English
DT Article
DE DEI; MAGA; rentier capitalism; digital educational privatization;
   educational inequality
AB This article argues that the dominant conflict over schooling in the United States, often framed as a struggle between liberal inclusion and MAGA exclusion, conceals a deeper convergence. Liberal technocracy and MAGA authoritarianism appear opposed, yet both depoliticize education by displacing democratic struggle over power, property, and social reproduction. The article contends that liberal defenses of public schooling, DEI, expertise, and the Department of Education are inadequate when they preserve a technocratic order that has translated structural inequality into metrics, bias training, and administrative process. Situating these developments within rentier capitalism, the article argues that schooling has increasingly been reorganized as an extractive infrastructure tied to property regimes, privatized platforms, and digital enclosure. Digital educational privatization, including platform-based instruction, data extraction, and AI-driven schooling, intensifies this transformation by converting students and teachers into immediate sources of value while insulating educational governance from democratic oversight. Against both liberal technocracy and MAGA hierarchy, the article calls for a democratic alternative that links redistribution to reconstruction through the decommodification of educational infrastructure, the reclamation of data and platforms as public goods, and the severing of school finance from racialized property markets.

TI Unpacking English Language Teachers' Professional Learning Needs in the

SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence (AI); descriptive qualitative; EFL teachers;

ID GENERATIVE AI
AB Professional learning, a significant factor in teacher education, has received increasing attention across contexts and fields. However, there is a wide gap in the literature of how Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies have affected English language teachers' professional needs and their associated expectations and practices to fulfil such needs. In order to provide a fresh insight into the ecology of AI-mediated professional needs, this study takes a descriptive qualitative approach to examine English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers' perceptions, expectations, and supporting practices. Moreover, the participants suggested workshops, collaborative discussions, and local meetups to support and fulfil professional needs in the age of AI. The study highlights actionable and belief-oriented professional learning practices for teachers and teacher educators.

TI Final-year dental students' self-perceived knowledge and self-reported
   clinical approaches to vital pulp therapy: a single-institution
   cross-sectional survey
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Dental students; Vital pulp therapy; Undergraduate dental education;
   Pulp capping; Pulpotomy; Cross-sectional survey
ID MINERAL TRIOXIDE AGGREGATE; PULPOTOMY
AB Background Undergraduate dental education should prepare students to understand and apply contemporary vital pulp therapy (VPT) procedures in permanent teeth. However, students' self-perceived knowledge, stated treatment preferences, and self-reported clinical approaches regarding VPT may vary according to their theoretical and clinical training. This study aimed to describe final-year dental students' self-perceived knowledge, recognition of VPT procedures, stated treatment preferences, and self-reported clinical approaches regarding VPT.Methods This single-institution cross-sectional survey was conducted among final-year dental students at a dental faculty in T & uuml;rkiye in June 2025. Of 100 eligible students, 88 completed a 17-item questionnaire (response rate, 88.0%) addressing self-perceived knowledge, sources of information, treatment preferences, reported clinical approaches, rubber dam isolation, hemostatic agents, and material selection in VPT. Data were summarized descriptively using frequencies and percentages.Results Most students rated their self-perceived knowledge of VPT as moderate (60.2%), while theoretical courses (42.0%) and clinical practice (36.4%) were the main reported sources of VPT information. Direct pulp capping (94.3%), partial pulpotomy (Cvek; 89.8%), and indirect pulp capping (86.4%) were most frequently identified as vital pulp therapy procedures, whereas total pulpotomy was identified as a vital pulp therapy procedure by 53.4% of students. In mature teeth, direct pulp capping was reported more frequently than partial or total pulpotomy. Treatment preferences varied according to pulp exposure size, with a shift from direct pulp capping for 0-1 mm exposures to partial pulpotomy for 1-2 mm exposures and total pulpotomy or root canal treatment for exposures larger than 2 mm. Only 15.9% of students reported applying rubber dam isolation at the beginning of the treatment, and the combined response option "ferric sulfate or aluminum chloride" was selected most frequently for hemostasis (46.6%).Conclusions Final-year dental students reported moderate self-perceived knowledge of VPT and recognized several commonly used VPT procedures, but their self-reported approaches varied, particularly regarding pulpotomy procedures, rubber dam timing, hemostatic-agent selection, and simplified pulp-exposure scenarios. These findings should be interpreted as self-reported educational indicators rather than objective evidence of clinical competence or broad curricular inadequacy. Multicenter studies using case-based and performance-based assessments are needed to guide undergraduate VPT teaching.

TI Identifying morphological errors in the English of Deaf learners in
   Lesotho
SO READING & WRITING-JOURNAL OF THE READING ASSOCIATION OF SOUTH AFRICA
LA English
DT Article
DE morphological awareness; error analysis; second-language acquisition;
   interlingual errors; intralingual errors; Deaf literacy; literacy;
   Lesotho Sign Language
ID HARD-OF-HEARING; PHONOLOGICAL AWARENESS; READING-COMPREHENSION;
   SIGN-LANGUAGE; KNOWLEDGE; LITERACY; STUDENTS; FRENCH; SKILLS; ROLES
AB Background: Morphological awareness (MA) is widely recognised as contributing to successful reading and reading comprehension. Despite this, research examining the nature of morphological errors among second-language (L2) English learners remains limited, particularly among Deaf learners. Objectives: This study identified and classified English MA errors made by Deaf learners in Lesotho and determined the most prevalent error types and their possible underlying sources. Method: Data were collected from 26 Deaf learners in Grade 3 to Grade 7 at a school for Deaf learners in Lesotho. Learners completed five MA tasks assessing inflectional and derivational morphology. Some errors appeared to be interlingual and may have resulted from transfer from Lesotho Sign Language (LSL) and Sesotho. These included the use of a zero morpheme, which may reflect transfer from LSL, and the addition of a word-final vowel, which may reflect the influence of Sesotho. Conclusion: Learners experienced substantial difficulties in applying English inflectional and derivational morphology. The identified error patterns reflect an incomplete understanding of English morphological processes, task-related factors, cross-linguistic transfer, limited explicit instruction in morphology, and the possible influence of learners' multilingual repertoires. Contribution: These findings provide insight into the morphological challenges faced by Deaf learners in developing English MA and highlight areas for targeted educational support.

TI Reforming the preschool application system to reduce enrollment gaps
   evidence from a default enrollment policy
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Preschool enrollment; Foreign background; Default enrollment
ID CHILD-CARE; EDUCATION; TECHNOLOGY
AB While all children in Sweden are entitled to free, universal preschool from age 3, enrollment rates for children with an immigrant background-and especially for those in newly-arrived families-remain well below the 95 percent national average. At the same time, studies suggest that these children have particularly high returns from preschool attendance. Thus, policies that increase preschool enrollment among children with an immigrant background have potential to improve long-term educational and labor market outcomes and narrow gaps relative to native-born children. We evaluate a reform in 2023 that required municipalities to offer reserved preschool slots to 3-5-year-olds in newly-arrived immigrant families without the parents needing to apply-socalled automatic offers. Using a difference-in-differences specification, we compare next-year enrollment rates for currently non-enrolled children in newly-arrived families and other families and find that the policy substantially increased preschool enrollment. Our results suggest that administrative hurdles prevent some immigrant families from enrolling their children and that simplifying the application process is an effective policy tool for increasing preschool enrollment in this group.

TI Renewed policy interest in extended mother tongue instruction: From
   mother tongue-based bilingual education as transition to mother
   tongue-based bilingual education as transformation
SO SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF CHILDHOOD EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE mother tongue instruction; translanguaging; languages of learning and
   teaching; bilingualism; epistemic access
ID 1ST
AB Background: Despite the rhetoric of additive bilingualism, post-apartheid South African education is characterised by hierarchical colonial arrangements in which early-exit mother tongue-based bilingual education (MTBBE) models undermine literacy at the Grade 4 transition, reproducing linguistic and epistemic injustices. Aim: The article critiques, maps out and deconstructs the power assumptions, dynamics and knowledges embedded in MTBBE to elevate the model from a temporary scaffolding strategy to an epistemic strategy. Setting: The study analysis draws attention to the multilingual South African school system in the wake of the Basic Education Laws Amendment (BELA) Act. Methods: Rather than a traditional empirical, participant-led method for data gathering, the study engages in a conceptual analysis based on the critical interpretivist paradigm, and relies on three interrelated conceptual lenses: Postcolonial language theory, decolonial epistemic justice and translanguaging theory. Results: The study reveals how the current resurgence of MTBBE is plagued by policy amnesia of cosmetic and cyclical revivals and a profound conflict between performative symbolism and real decolonisation. The analysis unpacks five MTBBE prevailing myths (transitional, monolingual, reactive, utilitarian and magical). In opposition to these myths, the article offers an alternative theoretical framework based on five essential principles, along with a corresponding three-phased implementation approach (R-3, 4-7 and 8+). Conclusion: Educational transformation entails an epistemological reorientation as well as infrastructural investments, which will ensure the permanence of African languages as part of epistemic success. Contribution: This article fills an important theoretical void through offering a decolonial praxis-based framework of MTBBE.

TI Case-based CDIO learning and decision-making performance in
   undergraduate health sciences education
SO EDUCACION MEDICA
LA English
DT Article
DE Health sciences education; Case-based learning; CDIO; Decision-making;
   Self-confidence; Safety awareness
ID ACHIEVEMENT EMOTIONS; MEDICAL-EDUCATION; INSTRUCTION
AB Introduction: Innovative teaching approaches are increasingly adopted in health sciences education to support the development of students'decision-making skills. However, evidence regarding the effectiveness of case-based CDIO learning and the role of learner-related factors associated with performance remains limited. This study examined changes in students' decision-making performance following the implementation of case-based CDIO learning and explored the associations of safety awareness and self-confidence with post-intervention performance. Materials and methods: A quasi-experimental pre-post study was conducted with 89 undergraduate students enrolled in a health-related course. Decision-making performance was assessed before and after the intervention using a rubric-based evaluation. Safety awareness and self-confidence were measured using self-report questionnaires. A paired t-test was used to examine changes in performance, and multiple linear regression analysis was conducted to assess the associations of safety awareness and self-confidence with post-intervention decision-making performance while controlling for baseline performance. Results: Decision-making scores increased significantly following the intervention (t(88) = 8.31, p < 0.001). The regression model was statistically significant (F(3, 85) = 15.04, p < 0.001), explaining 34.7% of the variance in post-intervention decision-making performance (R-2 = 0.347). Baseline performance (beta = 0.41, p < 0.001) and self-confidence (beta = 0.29, p = 0.004) were significant positive predictors, whereas safety awareness was not significantly associated with performance (p = 0.840). Conclusion: Case-based CDIO learning appears to be a promising instructional approach for supporting the development of students' decision-making performance. Self-confidence was identified as a significant factor associated with performance after controlling for baseline performance, suggesting that learner perceptions may influence how effectively students apply knowledge in practice-oriented contexts. TI Are dental congresses fulfilling their educational mission?
   Transparency, scientific integrity, and commercial influence in
   continuing professional development
SO EDUCACION MEDICA
LA English
DT Article
DE Education dental; Education dental continuing; Congresses as topic;
   Conflict of interest; Disclosure; Education professional
ID CONFERENCES; OUTCOMES
AB Dental congresses support continuing professional development, research dissemination, networking, and technology transfer, but their educational value depends on design and tion in some specialties, concerns about commercial influence, and unequal access. Direct dental evidence is insufficient to establish that social media popularity drives speaker selection, that prestige-driven visibility shapes programs, or that award favoritism occurs; these remain governance concerns requiring study. Drawing on evidence from adult and experiential learning and continuing professional development, this commentary proposes transparent speaker selection, separation of sponsored and scientific content, structured abstract and award review, complication-focused learning, active and hybrid formats, and outcome assessment beyond satisfaction. Implementation should be locally adapted, and comparative research should determine which congress features improve learning, professional development, clinical practice, and patient care. TI Subjective and HRV-based Data Assessing Supervising Surgeon
   Intraoperative Stress with Perceived Trainee Breast Surgery Skill
   Proficiency
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE surgical education; intraoperative stress; supervising surgeon; heart
   rate variability; breast surgery
ID HEART-RATE-VARIABILITY; STATE
AB OBJECTIVE: To examine the association between perceived trainee technical skill proficiency and supervising surgeons' intraoperative stress using both subjective assessments and heart rate variability (HRV)-based physiological indicators and to explore whether this association differs according to the supervisor's operative role. DESIGN: Prospective observational study. After each procedure, supervisors completed structured questionnaires assessing subjective intraoperative stress and mood states. Trainee technical proficiency was evaluated by supervisors using a 10-item scale developed for breast surgery training. HRV was continuously recorded, and 2 indices were calculated: LF/HF up arrow% (percentage of operative time with LF/HF ratios exceeding the intraoperative mean) and RR down arrow% (percentage of RR intervals shorter than the preoperative baseline). Correlations were analyzed separately for each group. SETTING: Single academic institution. PARTICIPANTS: Supervising surgeons served either as primary surgeon (Group 1) or 1st assistant (Group 2) during breast surgeries involving trainees. RESULTS: A total of 123 procedures were analyzed (Group 1: n = 52, Group 2: n = 71). Trainee technical skill scores showed significant negative correlations with supervising surgeons' subjective stress scores in both groups (Group 1: r =--0.592, p < 0.001; Group 2: r =--0.706, p < 0.001). In contrast, no significant associations in either group were observed between trainee skill scores and HRV-derived indices. CONCLUSIONS: Supervising surgeons' perceptions of trainee technical proficiency were associated with self-perceived intraoperative stress in both primary and assistant roles, while HRV-based physiological markers showed no such associations. Subjective stress ratings may capture supervisory cognitive load and educational burden more sensitively than HRV metrics alone. ( J Surg Ed 83:104120. TI Peer instruction in chemistry stratified exercises: Cognitive and
   metacognitive effects
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Peer instruction; Chemistry stratified exercises; Structured discussion;
   Cognitive load; State metacognition
ID COLLABORATION; PERFORMANCE; SKILLS; STRATEGIES; FRAMEWORK; STUDENTS;
   IMPROVES
AB Background: Chemistry post-lesson exercises often include tasks that differ in cognitive demand, but it remains unclear how peer instruction can be embedded in such exercises to support students' task performance and learning-related cognitive processes. Aims: This study examined PI in teacher-organized chemistry stratified exercises differing in task cognitive demand, comparing PI with individual practice and investigating how grouping method and discussion format were associated with delayed post-test performance, cognitive load, and state metacognition. Sample: Participants were 389 Grade 10 students aged 15-16 from two public high schools in southwestern China. Methods: Three quasi-experiments were conducted in the Ionic Reactions unit. Experiment 1 compared PI with individual practice on delayed post-test performance and descriptively tracked changes in immediate exercise accuracy before and after peer discussion. Experiments 2 and 3 examined how grouping method and discussion format shaped PI implementation in lower- and higher-order exercises, respectively. Additional outcomes included cognitive load and state metacognition. Results: Within the PI conditions, immediate exercise accuracy increased after peer discussion, and PI groups showed higher delayed post-test performance than individual-practice groups across both exercise levels. In lower-order exercises, structured discussion provided the more consistent support across outcomes. In higherorder exercises, heterogeneous pairing combined with structured discussion showed the clearest advantage for delayed performance and a favorable pattern in extraneous and germane cognitive load and state metacognition. Conclusions: The findings clarify how peer instruction may be implemented in chemistry stratified exercises and suggest that discussion structure and grouping decisions should be aligned with task cognitive demand.

TI Art therapy for autistic adults against depression: A multi-perspective
   study
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism; Depression; Psychological Well-being; Art Therapy
ID UK QUALITATIVE FINDINGS; CHILDREN
AB Purpose: Building on the socio-ecological model of health, this study investigates the barriers to delivering and accessing art therapy for autistic adults with depression, drawing on insights from both art therapists and autistic adults. Methods: Through a mixed-methods online questionnaire, participants responded to closed-ended questions that asked about their experiences and/or perceptions of art therapy, attitudes towards art therapy, and the extent to which they identified with barriers reported in past literature. Open-ended questions followed to uncover lived experiences that might speak to barriers specific to art therapy not captured by past literature. Results: Overall, both groups believed art therapy to be an effective treatment. Barriers identified by both groups primarily reflected systemic challenges, while other barriers highlighted stakeholders' unique experiences and perspectives about treatment. Thematic analysis revealed similar and additional multidimensional barriers to delivering and accessing art therapy. Participants highlighted barriers associated with 1) accessibility (i.e. affordability, availability, and simplicity); 2) professional practice (i.e. autism knowledge, concurrent diagnoses, familial support, integrated care, and relationship building); and 3) making the experience individualised (i.e. with the right approach, environment, and emotional support). Conclusion: This is one of the first studies to systematically report and analyse art therapy experiences on autism and depression. Lived experiences highlight that barriers across different levels of the socio-ecological model interact dynamically and influence the interactions between different stakeholders. Future interventions should leverage on influencing these interactions to support overall accessibility and effectiveness of art therapy.

TI The relationship between teacher characteristics and standardised
   mathematics achievement in fourth through eighth grade: A systematic
   review and meta-analysis
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Mathematics Achievement; Meta-Analysis; Systematic Review; Teacher
   Characteristics; Teacher Education; Teacher Effectiveness
ID NATIONAL BOARD CERTIFICATION; STUDENT-ACHIEVEMENT; SCHOOL RESOURCES;
   QUALITY; GENDER; ELEMENTARY; IMPACT; SIGNAL; GAINS; RACE
AB Evidence on which teacher characteristics are most strongly associated with student achievement remains mixed, particularly across subjects and grade levels. Drawing on human capital theory, this systematic review and metaanalysis (employing Robust Variance Estimation to account for dependent effect sizes) synthesises findings from 40 peer-reviewed studies published between 1966 and 2019 to clarify the relationship between five teacher characteristics - same-gender match, certification type, teacher test scores, graduate degrees, and teaching experience - and standardised mathematics achievement in grades four through eight. Teaching experience shows the strongest positive association with mathematics achievement, with effects peaking beyond the early career years. General teacher certification demonstrates a small but significant positive association with student achievement, while the evidence for mathematics-specific certification remains uncertain due to limited studies. Teacher test scores demonstrate small but consistent positive relationships. Same-gender match does not demonstrate a statistically significant association with mathematics achievement, though individual studies suggest a modest positive trend for female students. Graduate degrees show no meaningful association with student mathematics achievement. Substantial variation in outcomes remains unexplained by the characteristics examined. Findings carry policy implications for teacher recruitment, certification pathways, and professional development investment at key career stages.

TI Teacher leadership in classroom technology integration: A case study of
   corpus-based language pedagogy
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher leadership; Classroom technology integration; Corpus-based
   language pedagogy; Professional development
ID PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; KNOWLEDGE; ROLES
AB Classroom technology integration offers significant promise for language learning, but its implementation remains constrained by limited pedagogical adaptation and insufficient institutional support. Teacher leadership has become a crucial yet understudied driver of colleagues' technology integration, especially in complex settings such as corpus-based language pedagogy (CBLP), where technological and pedagogical demands intersect. This qualitative case study explored how teacher leadership facilitated technology integration during a semester-long CBLP implementation in a Chinese high school. Data were collected from one teacher leader and two teachers through semi-structured interviews, group discussions, and artifact collection. The study identified stage-specific leadership behaviors and their corresponding impacts. During the technology training stage, teacher leadership fostered colleagues' technological readiness and skill acquisition by connecting external resources, conducting practice-oriented training, clarifying task goals, and allocating tasks. During the implementation stage, it enhanced teachers' motivation and expanded their pedagogical competencies by leading technology-facilitated teaching, monitoring progress, building collaborative relationships, and offering emotional support. During the diffusion stage, it enabled pedagogical transformation by organizing pedagogy-based research and empowering teachers to diffuse technology. These findings unpack the dynamic and developmental nature of teacher leadership in classroom technology integration and offer practical insights for language education and technology adoption in schools.

TI An English language teacher educator's feedback literacy journey: Who
   educates the teacher educator in Indonesia?
SO LEARNING CULTURE AND SOCIAL INTERACTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher educator feedback literacy; Dialogic feedback; Indonesian
   teacher educator; Dialogic professional learning; Collaborative
   reflection; Narrative
ID DIALOGIC FEEDBACK
AB Dialogic feedback practices are widely recognised as crucial in initial teacher education, yet the knowledge required to implement them - what the authors term 'teacher educator feedback literacy' - remains underconceptualised. Collaborative dimensions of this feedback literacy and the influence of context on its development are particularly understudied, a gap especially significant for South-East Asia, where dialogic feedback discourse is only recently emerging. This qualitative case study employs narrative-based inquiry and reflexive thematic analysis, and draws on transcript data from three extended interviews with 'Khadijah', an experienced Indonesian English language teacher educator. The study design featured six dialogic professional learning workshops exploring theoretical and practical approaches to feedback, in which Khadijah was a participant. The authors present contextualised narrative findings of her developmental journey, and propose seven generic elements of teacher educator feedback literacy - elements with potential applicability across diverse educational contexts. The study demonstrates how each element manifested within Khadijah's situated learning experience, underscoring the value of dialogic professional learning and community-supported reflection in developing her feedback literacy. While grounded in the Indonesian context, the findings carry broader implications for teacher educators' professional learning about feedback internationally, offering a transferable framework for understanding and cultivating this underexplored dimension of educator expertise.

TI Taking Aristotle seriously in liberal democracy
SO JOURNAL OF MORAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Aristotelian character education; liberal democracy; legitimacy;
   flourishing
AB This paper replies to Randall Curren's review of my book, Against Aristotelian Character Education. I argue that Curren's response leaves the book's central dilemma untouched. First, I argue that liberal freedom and equality place demands on compulsory public education that extend beyond avoiding indoctrination and preserving students' capacities for independent judgment. Liberal legitimacy also requires that the state exercise its coercive educational authority in ways that leave citizens holding different reasonable comprehensive doctrines equally free to pursue their own ways of life. Either public education remains sufficiently liberal that it cannot reliably cultivate Aristotelian virtue, or it succeeds in cultivating those virtues by relying on a conception of flourishing that liberal legitimacy forbids the state to privilege. Second, I argue that attempts to reconcile Aristotelian character education with liberalism continue to depend upon separating the Aristotelian virtues from the distinctively Aristotelian evaluative outlook from which they derive. I examine two strategies suggested by Curren's review and argue that neither succeeds. Either the educational ideal retains its distinctively Aristotelian character and fails to satisfy the demands of liberal freedom and equality, or it satisfies those demands only by ceasing to preserve what is distinctively Aristotelian about the theory itself.

TI School digital conditions and student computer and information literacy
   across 12 education systems: system-specific multilevel evidence from
   ICILS 2023
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ICILS 2023; Computer and information literacy; Digital inequality;
   Generative AI; School digital conditions; Multilevel modeling; Plausible
   values
AB This study examined associations between school digital conditions and students' computer and information literacy (CIL) in 12 ICILS 2023 education systems that administered the optional ChatGPT questionnaire. The analysis used student achievement and questionnaire data linked with principal and ICT coordinator reports for 24,273 students in 1,049 schools. System-specific weighted two-level models were estimated for five CIL plausible values, adjusting for student sex, home internet access, computer experience, within-school socioeconomic background, and school socioeconomic composition. Five school-level conditions were examined jointly: positive ChatGPT expectations, negative ChatGPT expectations, pedagogical ICT hindrances, instructional ICT-use expectations, and ICT collaboration expectations. False-discovery-rate control was applied to the 60 primary focal tests, and a secondary equal-system-weight common-slope model and prespecified sensitivity analyses were used to assess the stability of the findings. None of the five school conditions produced an FDR-retained association with CIL. Three system-specific coefficients had raw p values below 0.05: ICT collaboration expectations were negative in Korea and positive in the Slovak Republic, and pedagogical ICT hindrances were negative in Korea; all had q = 0.730. The secondary common-slope model yielded confidence intervals including zero for all five focal predictors, and sensitivity analyses did not materially alter the primary conclusion. In contrast, student socioeconomic background and computer experience showed more consistent positive adjusted associations with CIL. Overall, the findings support cautious interpretation of pooled summaries alongside system-specific estimates and indicate no single common direct association between the measured school digital conditions and student CIL across the participating systems.

TI Mode effects in the transition to digital testing: evidence from TIMSS
   in Ireland, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, and Flanders
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE TIMSS; Mode effects; Computer-based assessment; Digital assessment;
   Devices; Replication; Content; Cognitive
AB Background About half of the countries participating in TIMSS 2019 transitioned from paper-based to digital assessment in that cycle, with most remaining countries completing the transition in TIMSS 2023. All countries transitioning in 2019 completed a paper-based 'bridge' study to examine mode effects (differences in achievement related to the mode of administration) and ensure the comparability of scores from previous cycles. However, only four countries opted to administer a national comparison (bridge) study in 2023: Ireland, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, and Flanders (Belgium). This Brief Report documents findings from these four national comparison studies. The aim is to verify the extent to which the transition to digital testing may have affected student performance in these countries, noting that ten countries in TIMSS 2019 were previously found to have displayed country-level mode effects in at least one subject or grade.Findings We find no evidence of significant differences in overall performance by mode of administration, in either mathematics or science, in any of the four included countries. We also find no evidence of significant mode effects among boys or girls in Ireland, Flanders, or Bahrain. In Azerbaijan, boys achieved a significantly higher science score on the digital version of TIMSS compared to the paper version. Some differences in achievement by mode are observed at the level of the mathematics and science content and cognitive domains. These are limited and present no distinctive pattern in three of the countries studied although, again, more consistent differences are noted in Azerbaijan. Finally, some preliminary evidence is presented of differences in student performance on the digital assessment related to students' access to a computer at home in Flanders, Bahrain, and Azerbaijan.Conclusions The findings provided here confirm that achievement estimates in TIMSS 2023 in these four countries were substantively unaffected at a high level by the change in the mode of administration. This should strengthen confidence in the use of these data for policymaking, educational practice, and further research. In particular, trend data from 2019 to 2023 in these countries can be more confidently interpreted as reflecting substantive trends or changes in achievement, giving researchers greater confidence that trends have not been significantly confounded by the procedural change of assessment mode. Evidence of some specific differences in each country could be considered further by national experts in curriculum and assessment. In particular, several differences have been observed that merit further consideration by researchers and policymakers in Azerbaijan.

   European countries
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Affective factors; Mathematics achievement; Machine learning; Latent
   profile analysis; Multilevel modeling
ID MATH ANXIETY; ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; AFFECTIVE VARIABLES; DIMENSIONS;
   ATTITUDE
AB Background Mathematics achievement is associated with interacting individual and contextual factors, but these associations are often examined separately. As a result, existing research may overlook how affective characteristics combine within students and how these configurations are distributed across school settings.Objectives This study aimed to investigate the multilevel predictors of mathematics achievement by integrating machine learning and latent variable approaches using PISA 2022 data from nine European countries.Methods The analysis was conducted in a sequence of stages, summarised in Fig. . First, predictive models were used to identify the most important predictors of mathematics achievement. Second, Latent Profile Analysis was performed to classify students based on key socioeconomic and affective indicators. These findings suggest that mathematics achievement is associated with synergistic combinations of individual and contextual factors, highlighting the importance of personalised interventions and equity-oriented policies that account for school-level selectivity.

   cognitive load perspective
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Problem solving; Cognitive load; Mental effort; Task complexity;
   Pre-training
ID EVIDENCE-BASED PRINCIPLES; TERM RETENTION; DESIGN; MEMORY; ACQUISITION;
   PERFORMANCE; EXAMPLE; STORAGE; TOWER; MODEL
AB Effectively managing cognitive demands during problem solving is crucial for academic success. While instructional design research offers strategies to support learners, the effects of task complexity and pre-training on cognitive processes and performance require further investigation. This study reports on four experiments to examine their individual and combined effects on problem-solving performance, cognitive load, and mental effort. Participants completed three task rounds with either high or increasing complexity. Cognitive load and mental effort were assessed using self-report questionnaires, and performance was measured in the final round. Across three experiments, pre-training was provided and compared with a condition without pre-training. However, the effects of task complexity on performance were not consistent across experiments. Pre-training was associated with fewer moves needed to solve the task, whereas effects on completion time, cognitive load, and mental effort varied across experiments. No significant interaction effects between task complexity and pre-training were observed.

   Set-ESEM and Latent Profile Analysis
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic buoyancy; behavioural engagement; growth language mindset;
   latent profile analysis; Set-ESEM
ID ACADEMIC BUOYANCY; CONSERVATION; ENGAGEMENT
AB While the positive influence of growth language mindset (GLM) on academic outcomes is well-documented, its multidimensional mechanisms and learner heterogeneity remain under-explored. To bridge this gap, this study examined how a multifaceted GLM, comprising general language intelligence beliefs, second language aptitude beliefs, and age sensitivity beliefs, relates to academic buoyancy and behavioural engagement. SO LINGUISTICS AND EDUCATION

DT Article
DE Disciplinary literacy; Project-based learning; STEM education; Identity;
   Multilingual university
ID ENGLISH-MEDIUM INSTRUCTION; HIGHER-EDUCATION; LECTURERS; DISCOURSE
AB Disciplinary literacy has gained more recognition in STEM education as understanding subject is inextricably linked to mastering specialised ways of communicating science to different audiences. In projectbased learning (PBL), STEM students must apply such literacies across multiple communicative contexts. However, current pedagogies often prioritise high-stakes academic communication while overlooking the everyday interactional processes through which student disciplinary literacy and identities are developed. This study explores the communicative practices of a group of engineering students during a PBL course in Sweden. The study highlights disciplinary literacy as an interactional, identity-mediated practice and emphasizes the need for STEM education to move beyond text-centric approach to support students' identity work and communicative competence across contexts. AB Neoliberal reforms increasingly frame early childhood education and care (ECEC) as an investment in human capital, with science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) education prioritised from the earliest years of learning. This policy orientation draws attention to teachers' content knowledge, as scientific concepts require explicit guidance beyond experiential exploration. TI Teaching videos in initial teacher education: a qualitative study of
   pre-service teachers' reflections
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE DigCompEdu; pre-service teachers; reflective practice; reflexive
   thematic analysis; scholarship of teaching and learning; teacher

AB Introduction Teaching videos, defined here as recordings of authentic classroom practice in schools, have become an important resource in initial teacher education. This study examines how pre-service teachers of English as a foreign language (EFL) reflect on the use of teaching videos during a university seminar in EFL pedagogy and linguistics.Methods The sample comprised 28 pre-service teachers. They also have implications for learning through reflection on other teachers' practice and for the design of video-based learning environments in initial teacher education.

TI An extended End-User Computing Satisfaction model for learning systems
   in higher education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational technology; end-user computing satisfaction; exploratory
   scale development; higher education; learner experience; learning
   systems; pilot study; student satisfaction
ID STUDENT ENGAGEMENT; PREDICTIVE-VALIDITY; ONLINE EDUCATION; ACCEPTANCE;
   REGRESSION; VARIANCE; SUCCESS; ITEM; HETEROSCEDASTICITY; TECHNOLOGY
AB Background This study reports an exploratory, single-institution scale-development pilot of a learner-centered extension to the End-User Computing Satisfaction (EUCS) framework, hereafter EUCS-LS, that adds three candidate dimensions, user participation, technical support, and multimodal accessibility, to the five classic EUCS dimensions for use with higher-education learning systems. Methods A cross-sectional pilot survey was administered to undergraduate students at one private university using stratified sampling with a proportional allocation target across ten faculties; after deduplicating by student ID, the analytic sample was N=394. Each of the eight constructs was operationalized as a single-item indicator. Joint covariation with overall satisfaction was assessed using hierarchical OLS regression with an intercept, principal component analysis, single-factor maximum-likelihood exploratory factor analysis, partial least squares regression with Variable Importance in Projection (VIP) scores, and post-stratification weighted least squares as a sensitivity check. Variance inflation factors, the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure, Bartlett's test of sphericity, and scale-level Cronbach's alpha were used as diagnostics, and the OLS assumptions (linearity, normality, homoscedasticity, and independence of residuals across faculties) were tested formally, with heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC3) and faculty-clustered standard errors estimated as robustness checks. Results The eight items jointly accounted for 62.1% of the variance in overall satisfaction (adjusted R-2; F(8,385)=81.50, p<.001), and adding the three candidate learner-centered items to the classic block produced a small block-level gain (Delta R-2=0.041, F-change(3,385)=14.24, p<.001). Seven of the eight items reached the p<.05 threshold; timeliness did not (p=.093). Collinearity diagnostics were unproblematic (all VIF between 1.75 and 2.24), yet the predictors shared a single dominant covariance pattern: one principal component captured 59.0% of their joint variance, PLS VIP scores fell within a narrow band (0.928-1.091, spread 0.16), and treating the eight constructs as items of one general scale yielded Cronbach's alpha=0.900. Formal assumption tests supported linearity and independence, detected mild non-normality and heteroscedasticity, and the substantive conclusions were preserved under robust standard errors. Together, these diagnostics indicate that the predictor set behaves as a single general perceived-quality factor with several correlated facets and that the rank order of individual coefficients is not statistically identifiable at this sample size.
